title: COP31: 197 states face challenge of delivering climate pledges - The New Arab
description:
Its location in the Mediterranean basin makes it particularly relevant to discussions about climate change, given the region's exposure to drought, wildfires and other climate-related risks.
Industry accounts for around 25 percent of global emissions, while sectors where emissions are difficult to reduce face complex decarbonisation pathways.
It is held under the UN Framework Convention on Climate Change, adopted in 1992, and serves as the main platform for negotiations, international cooperation, assessing global progress and coordinating responses to climate change.
The 1992 convention was the first comprehensive global agreement aimed at combating climate change.
The United States will not participate in the official negotiations after President Donald Trump withdrew from the Paris climate agreement for a second time following his return to the White House.
text:
The Turkish city of Antalya is hosting the 31st United Nations Climate Change Conference (COP31), with 197 countries expected to negotiate ways to accelerate the implementation of the 2015 Paris Agreement and expand funding to address the consequences of climate change.

The conference will run from 9 to 20 November under the slogan "Together for a Cleaner Future", bringing together world leaders and government delegations to discuss the implementation of existing climate commitments and the development of new environmental policies.

Since 1995, annual UN climate conferences have helped shape the future of the planet through environmental legislation and commitments. They have produced significant decisions, including the agreement reached at the Paris conference to limit global warming. COP31 is expected to help steer international environmental policies in a new direction.

Antalya's selection as host was not accidental. Its location in the Mediterranean basin makes it particularly relevant to discussions about climate change, given the region's exposure to drought, wildfires and other climate-related risks.

Australia is leading the negotiations under an unusual arrangement that resolved a dispute over which country would host the conference during COP30, held in the Brazilian Amazon city of Belém in November 2025.

Around 100,000 people are expected to visit the UN-managed Blue Zone, alongside official country delegations, while the Green Zone, managed by the host country, is expected to receive 1.5 million visitors.

According to organisers, participants will include 91 heads of state, more than 300 ministers, as well as officials from the European Union and the United Nations Development Programme. More than 45,000 volunteer applications have been received from 154 countries, while around 2,000 non-governmental organisations have announced their participation.

Organisers have also approved 160 applications for exhibition pavilions and 90 for offices. The leaders' summit will take place on 11 or 12 November, unlike previous COP conferences, where world leaders generally attended only the opening sessions. The new arrangement is intended to involve them directly in technical negotiations.

The 12-day conference will focus on the "Zero Waste" and "Resilient Cities" initiatives, alongside discussions on binding carbon emissions commitments, the green transition in energy policies, climate financing and its distribution, and sustainable development models.

The agenda will prioritise implementing previous pledges before introducing new rules, particularly in food and agriculture, health, green manufacturing and clean energy.

COP30 concluded in Brazil with an agreement calling for a threefold increase in funding for developing countries to protect their populations from the worsening effects of the climate crisis and strengthen support for communities transitioning to clean energy.

COP31 is expected to advance previous commitments through three main priorities: implementing emissions reduction targets under the Paris Agreement; financing responses to climate change through the achievement of the collective quantified climate finance goal set for developing countries at COP29; and adaptation, by increasing the resilience of countries and communities most exposed to climate risks.

The conference will also promote the deployment of low-carbon and climate-resilient technologies, strengthen international cooperation and knowledge-sharing, and support policies that improve the ability of vulnerable communities, ecosystems and economies to withstand climate threats.

Another priority is accelerating climate solutions and investment through structured cooperation between governments and private-sector institutions, and supporting scalable climate solutions with tangible results.

Clean energy, waste and resilient cities

Sustainable cooling, electricity supply and the production of clean, safe and accessible energy will feature prominently in discussions. The agenda includes transforming energy sector infrastructure and supporting access to biotechnology.

According to UN figures, approximately 730 million people worldwide lack access to electricity, while two billion still rely on polluting cooking methods, contributing to 3.7 million premature deaths annually.

COP31 aims to increase electricity's share of final energy consumption to 35 percent by 2035.

Waste management is another major focus, with delegates expected to explore how climate action can unlock the potential of scalable circular economy solutions.

The waste sector is the third-largest source of human-caused methane emissions and has been responsible for 30 percent of global warming since the beginning of the Industrial Revolution. Global waste production is also expected to increase by 50 percent by 2050, according to the UN.

The Antalya conference aims to expand circular economy initiatives that prevent emissions at source, including measures to reduce food waste and incorporate methane emissions into countries' nationally determined contributions (NDCs).

Discussions will also address the development of cities capable of withstanding climate change. Cities account for approximately 70 percent of global greenhouse gas emissions and face some of the most severe consequences of climate change. Meanwhile, 15 percent of major cities worldwide are exposed to the risk of severe flooding or drought.

COP31 aims to reduce energy intensity in the construction sector by 25 percent by 2035.

Green manufacturing will also feature prominently. Industry accounts for around 25 percent of global emissions, while sectors where emissions are difficult to reduce face complex decarbonisation pathways. Many developing countries also need support to establish the foundations of green industry from scratch.

Youth participation, implementation challenges

COP31 has also dedicated space to young people, recognising that they are not merely the generation inheriting climate risks but also potential builders of solutions.

People aged between 10 and 24 account for 1.8 billion of the global population and will experience the consequences of climate change over a longer period. Despite this, their participation in decision-making remains limited.

The conference will seek to raise climate awareness and encourage knowledge-sharing between generations.

A further priority will be identifying ways to implement existing climate protection commitments and bridge the gap between priorities, investment and action. The UN has emphasised the need to accelerate the translation of climate pledges into tangible results.

Although many countries have established ambitious climate targets through their NDCs, adaptation action plans and long-term strategies, implementation continues to face obstacles. These include limited institutional capacity, fragmented investment opportunities and insufficient alignment between policy priorities and financing solutions.

The annual Conference of the Parties is the most important international forum for climate negotiations. It is held under the UN Framework Convention on Climate Change, adopted in 1992, and serves as the main platform for negotiations, international cooperation, assessing global progress and coordinating responses to climate change.

Among its key functions is reviewing national communications on greenhouse gas emissions and assessing the impact of measures adopted by individual countries.

The 1992 convention was the first comprehensive global agreement aimed at combating climate change. Subsequent conferences helped shape international climate policy, including the Kyoto Protocol, adopted in 1997 and entering into force in 2005, and the Paris Agreement of 2015.

Meanwhile, a US congressional delegation is heading to Turkey to attend COP31 following the Democratic Party's sweeping victory in the midterm elections.

The United States will not participate in the official negotiations after President Donald Trump withdrew from the Paris climate agreement for a second time following his return to the White House.

text:
North Carolina's coast is more than a popular getaway. It's home to fishing, aquaculture, and research that could grow into what's known as a blue economy.

RTI (Research Triangle Institute) International, based in Research Triangle Park, recently produced a study with NC EcoTech that looks at ways to create new opportunities for coastal businesses. It recommends adopting new technologies, developing a statewide plan, and removing regulatory hurdles that will allow businesses to test new ideas.

WUNC News' Bradley George spoke with two researchers who worked on the report: Jessica Wilkinson, a economic development researcher at RTI, and Adams Bailey, a research economist.

This conversation has been lightly edited for clarity and brevity.

What is a blue economy?

Jessica Wilkinson: The blue economy is all types of economic activity that's tied to oceans, coasts, marine ecosystems. So you can think about fish and shellfish farming, anything from boat building, commercial fishing, shipping, coastal resilience at all falls under the blue economy.

There's already a lot of economic activity on North Carolina's coast. Of course, it's a popular tourist destination. Lots of people are moving there. Where does this idea of a blue economy fit into the economic activity that's already happening along the coast?

JW: One thing we talk about in this report in particular is that North Carolina's got a lot of heritage in the blue economy and a lot of diverse assets. But one of the things that we realized when we were working in this area is that a lot of it's disconnected. So we, of course, we have tourism. We didn't talk about that too much, and sometimes that can be kind of at heads with aquaculture, so I think that's something you know that people probably have heard of before. But we have a long history of fishing and aquaculture and fish farming and fin fish farming across the state from the west to the coast.

Adams Bailey: At one point, I would add is North Carolina is really unique in just how many miles of coastline we have, protecting those from erosion is maintaining habitats. If you're building in resilient coastline, you're building in cleaner habitats and are just overall good for sustainability in the environment of our state.

Jessica, you mentioned seafood. Most of what we eat in the U.S. is imported. What are some of the recommendations you came up with to encourage more seafood production in North Carolina?

JW: One thing we talk about is just the big importance of introducing these new technologies that are coming online every day, and helping to make sure that current farmers and future farmers and fishermen are aware and able to access these technologies. So, of course, AI is a huge one. Remote sensing is a huge one. Another one are some of these recirculating aquaculture systems we talk about, making sure that they're accessible.

Adams, are there examples of other states in the U.S. or even other places around the world that have adopted these blue economy strategies and have seen benefits from them?

AB: Absolutely. So, one of the companies we're really excited about is Hima Seafood in Norway. Has been adopting RAS (recirculating aquaculture systems) to farm fish in Norway. They've been considering a North Carolina investment. They still haven't made an announcement on where that investment could be, but if they did come here, it would be a major economic win for our state, both in terms of jobs created and value created, but also in you know adopting advanced systems here that are producing fish in a clean and sustainable way, and create a lot of jobs and allow us to eat seafood that was grown locally.

You've produced this report, so what are the next steps?

JW: This project, the NC EcoTech project, ended about a year ago. And some of this work was catalyzed by these federal investments I mentioned through the National Science Foundation. A lot of the federal funding landscape has changed, and some of these efforts that were time limited have ended. And so, part of this report was like a call to action as well for who could step in with some of this federal support. And then other calls to action were about the regulatory environment. We had spoken to many people who said that the regulatory environment is perceived as acting in kind of a case by case basis, and there were some bottlenecks, and it could kind of slow down the implementation of new technologies that come online.

UN Climate Change News, Antalya, Türkiye, 9 November 2026 – As world leaders gather for COP31, the Yearbook of Global Climate Action 2026 shows climate solutions scaling across sectors – from energy and transport to nature and food – while highlighting where implementation must go further and faster.

Produced by the Climate High-Level Champions and UN Climate Change, this tenth edition tracks progress, gaps and practical approaches to implementing the Paris Agreement.

“Behind every number in this Yearbook is a family, a farmer or a city. Even as floods, heatwaves and droughts intensify, climate action is building resilience and driving innovative, tangible solutions. Now we must scale these solutions, so the benefits reach every community, everywhere,” said Samed Ağırbaş, COP31 Climate High-Level Champion.

Where progress is being made

Among the strongest climate action success stories:

Clean power is scaling: Renewable capacity grew 17 per cent to 5,149 GW in 2025, a record 108 GW of battery storage was added, and renewables overtook coal in electricity generation (33.8 compared to 33.0 per cent).

Transport is electrifying: Electric vehicles made up a quarter of light-duty sales in 2025, public charging points passed seven million, and zero-emission trucks rose from 1.8 to nine per cent of heavy goods vehicle sales.

Explicit Fossil fuel subsidies are falling: These subsidies fell from USD 1.4 trillion in 2022 to USD 725 billion in 2024.

Forest and ocean protection are gaining ground: Deforestation fell by nearly 14 per cent in 2025, 11.8 million hectares are under active restoration (up from 10.6 million in 2024), and marine protected areas more than doubled in a decade, from 4.1 to 10 per cent of the ocean.

Food security is improving: Undernourishment fell from 9.1 to 7.8 per cent (2023–2025), and the share of people unable to afford a healthy diet fell from 37.4 to 32.7 per cent (2021–2025).

Cities and resilience planning are advancing: National climate plans with strong urban content doubled from 52 to 104 (2024–2026), countries with multi-hazard early warning systems rose from 108 to 119, and developing countries with updated National Adaptation Plans rose from 59 to 81.

Finance and jobs are growing: Climate finance passed USD 2 trillion in 2024, and renewable energy jobs reached 16.6 million.

text:
Environmental advocates are focused on efforts to reduce greenhouse gas emissions, and are pointing their efforts on industrial agriculture's impact.

That was the focus of a recent webinar led by the Minnesota Center for Environmental Advocacy in late October.

The conversation was led by MCEA’s Chief Impact Officer Leigh Currie. It centered around “industrial agriculture’s role in Minnesota’s accelerating climate crisis and what it will take to create change.”

She made the point that the topic of a climate crisis cannot be discussed without also talking about industrial ag.

“In Minnesota today, agriculture is the second biggest climate-polluting sector of our economy,” Currie said. “It trails just slightly behind transportation, and it is historically and notoriously hard to regulate.”

She added that agriculture has become very polarized and thus has been difficult to make change from a political standpoint.

Currie shared that sustainable agriculture practices are out there, but that state lawmakers need to make sure large-scale agricultural operators are using those practices.

Talking on the subject were Matthew Sheets, a policy organizer for Land Stewardship Project, Jay Eidness, supervising attorney at MCEA, and Laura Fox, a clinical lecturer and research scholar at Yale Law School.

Prompted by Currie, Sheets spoke about Minnesota’s shift toward industrial agriculture, specifically from his view from Morris, Minnesota, where he has helped organize against the permitting of the largest feedlot in the state, the recently approved Riverview LLP West River Dairy expansion, which is set to become the state’s largest dairy with around 19,000 head permitted.

Environmental groups continue to challenge that project's future.

Sheets used that dairy as an example, saying that when he first got started with Land Stewardship Project, they were using dairy data from 2018, when there were around 5,000 dairies in the state. He said that number fell off a cliff and now includes about 1,600 dairies.

“So we’re losing farms at an incredibly fast rate,” Sheets said.

At the same time, the number of dairy cows in the state is nearly unchanged. Sheets explained that what he sees happening is the majority of the economic power is going to fewer hands, and the livestock are more concentrated than ever.

“It's a really important topic for us to be talking about like this, because it is having massive impacts on the land, the people and just the economy of our area,” Sheets said.

Eidness touched on how he saw industrial agriculture contributing to the climate crisis.

“Agriculture emits about a quarter of our state's greenhouse gases,” he said. That means agriculture emits more than it takes to generate all the electricity needed to power every home and business in Minnesota.

This is more than just cow gas. Eidness broke it down further, explaining how livestock emit gases through the digestive process, but there are also greenhouse gas emissions associated with raising the crops to feed the livestock. Another area of concern is when land is cleared for farming or peat grounds are drained for farming to occur.

“When we drain land, we expose a lot of the carbon sequestering ability of the landscape to oxygen, which then releases the greenhouse gas emissions,” Eidness said. “When we cut down trees to make way for arable land that too will lose the tree's ability to sequester the carbon and will create more greenhouse gases in that way,” Eidness said.

While Eidness sees the agriculture industry failing to lower emissions, he said sectors like transportation have made significant drops.

“And I don’t find that to be surprising because we really don’t have any measures in place to intentionally focus efforts to bring those greenhouse gas emissions down,” Eidness said.

Fox said the big concern is that without change, the world is headed toward warming by 3 degrees Celsius this century. She warned that now is not a time to surrender to the warming.

“The higher temperatures climb even by a fraction of a degree, the greater risk of extreme heat, flooding, drought, ecosystem collapse,” Fox said.

Fox pointed at animal agriculture’s methane production as a major contributor of greenhouse gases, and reducing that methane is one of the most effective opportunities to reduce warming in the near term.

While she considered methane reduction similar to “pulling the emergency brake on the climate crisis,” she explained that pulling that brake faces stiff opposition from a political standpoint.

“One of the recurring findings is that industrial animal agriculture has largely escaped from climate accountability, even environmental accountability more broadly,” she said.

While her research has shown increased scrutiny on fossil fuels, power plants, and transportation systems, the same scrutiny has not yet been applied to large industrial agriculture.

Eidness said change needs to start from legislatively mandated greenhouse gas emission reduction goals. Fox said methods to control greenhouse gas emissions are already in place for other sectors and those same measures should be placed on animal agriculture, too.

“We can't effectively regulate pollution that we're not adequately measuring,” Fox said. “And you know, large industrial livestock operations should be required to quantify and report their greenhouse gas emissions. And we need to account for their full climate footprint. Not just emissions, right, from the animals and manure but also emissions associated with growing feed, energy use, you know, other activities throughout the supply chain and lost carbon sequestration opportunities from land use changes, right?”

Fox mentioned that this must be an approach taken by states. She gave California as an example of a state that has set a goal of reducing methane emissions by 40% by 2030. She said, in that case, incentives are in place to help producers achieve the goal.

Fox gave another example of giving farmers pathways to help them transition.

“We shouldn't be simply demanding farmers change practices, right, without creating viable economic pathways for them to do so,” she said. “And states can be helpful in providing those resources and incentivizing through the procurement it undertakes itself.”

The entire conversation is available at youtube.com/watch?v=DyFlsxgWZh0.

text:
BMW is expanding its global electric vehicle battery supply network by adding Samsung SDI in Europe and LG Energy Solution in the United States as new suppliers of next-generation battery cells. The move is part of the German automaker’s strategy to strengthen regional production, diversify its supply chain and secure a reliable supply of batteries for its upcoming electric vehicles.

The two battery manufacturers will supply BMW with cells for its sixth-generation (Gen6) high-voltage batteries from their existing regional production facilities starting in the late 2020s. The partnerships further strengthen BMW’s commitment to its “local for local” approach, which prioritizes sourcing components close to vehicle production sites.

Battery cells are among the most important components of an electric vehicle, directly influencing driving range, charging performance and overall efficiency. Securing a reliable supply of advanced battery technology is therefore essential as BMW prepares to expand its next generation of electric vehicles.

Under its latest supplier agreements, BMW will source battery cells produced in Europe from CATL, EVE Energy and Samsung SDI. In the United States, LG Energy Solution will become another key supplier.

By working with several leading battery manufacturers across different regions, BMW aims to reduce its dependence on individual suppliers while improving the flexibility and resilience of its global production network.

The company says this diversified approach will also help strengthen industrial value creation in Europe and North America, supporting local manufacturing and shortening transportation distances between battery suppliers and vehicle assembly plants.

Nicolai Martin, BMW AG’s Board Member responsible for Purchasing and Supplier Network, said the company is committed to developing regional supply chains while taking advantage of global procurement opportunities.

The strategy is intended to keep BMW competitive across international markets while building stronger partnerships with battery manufacturers in key production regions.

Five New Battery Assembly Facilities Support BMW’s Gen6 Strategy

BMW’s local-for-local approach extends beyond battery cell sourcing. The automaker is also establishing battery assembly operations close to its vehicle production facilities around the world.

For its sixth-generation high-voltage batteries, BMW has built five new battery assembly facilities in strategically important locations:

– Irlbach-Straßkirchen, Germany: Supporting BMW’s battery production network in Europe.

– Debrecen, Hungary: Serving the company’s expanding European manufacturing operations.

– Shenyang, China: Strengthening BMW’s production presence in the Chinese market.

– Woodruff, United States: Supporting regional battery manufacturing in North America.

– San Luis Potosí, Mexico: Expanding the company’s battery production capabilities in Mexico.

Locating battery assembly facilities close to vehicle factories helps reduce logistics costs, shorten delivery times and improve production flexibility.

It also supports regional industrial infrastructure and employment while reducing the risks associated with long-distance transportation and disruptions to international supply chains.

Building Local Battery Supply Chains Is a Long-Term Challenge

Establishing competitive battery production in different regions is not a straightforward process. Battery cell manufacturing requires substantial investment, advanced technology, specialized infrastructure and reliable partnerships with experienced suppliers.

BMW believes that developing comprehensive regional battery ecosystems will be essential to the long-term competitiveness of the electric vehicle industry.

However, attracting battery manufacturers and establishing local production capacity also depends on favorable economic conditions, suitable industrial infrastructure and predictable government regulations.

The company is therefore pursuing a long-term strategy that combines established global battery suppliers with localized manufacturing operations.

Rather than relying on a single geographical production hub, BMW is spreading its battery supply network across major automotive markets to improve its ability to respond to changing market conditions.

BMW Expands In-House Battery Technology and Recycling Expertise

Alongside its partnerships with external battery manufacturers, BMW continues to invest in its own battery research, development and recycling capabilities.

The company operates several specialized competence centers in Bavaria, Germany, focusing on different stages of battery technology development.

The Battery Cell Competence Center (BCCC) in Munich focuses on researching and developing new battery cell technologies for future electric vehicles.

Meanwhile, the Cell Manufacturing Competence Center (CMCC) in Parsdorf investigates how these cells can be manufactured at industrial scale while maintaining high quality and resource efficiency. The facility also produces and tests near-series battery cells.

BMW is also expanding its work on battery recycling through the Cell Recycling Competence Center (CRCC) in Salching.

The facility focuses on recovering valuable raw materials from used battery cells through an innovative direct recycling process developed by BMW. The recovered materials can then be reintegrated into the battery production process.

Although Encory GmbH will build and operate the recycling competence center, BMW retains ownership of the intellectual property behind the recycling technology.

This approach reflects the company’s broader ambition to develop a more sustainable battery ecosystem, covering everything from cell development and manufacturing to material recovery and reuse.

text:
UN Climate Change Executive Secretary, Simon Stiell

COP31 Opening Statement

Excellencies, colleagues, friends,

In this new era of implementation, at COP31, we’re doing things differently.

Not discarding what went before. But building on it. Honing it. To deliver progress faster.

COPs have traditionally sent signals:

Setting global targets. Deciding the direction of travel. Building momentum and resolve.

Since forging the Paris Agreement together, we’ve sent signal after signal to political systems and global markets.

That changed our world.

90% of large renewable projects are now cheaper than fossil fuel alternatives.

And adaptation is moving from the margins to the mainstream.

But progress is nowhere near far enough or fair enough.

So, as well as sending signals, COP31 must supercharge solutions. Breaking-down existing global targets and national plans into component steps.

And landing practical solutions:

Solutions to deliver on the tripling of finance for adaptation – as agreed last year.

Solutions to tackle the immense frustration countries face in accessing committed, available finance.

Solutions to triple global renewables capacity by 2030...

To transport energy across grids and borders, to power the electric age…

And to slash super-polluting methane emissions, particularly in the oil and gas, and waste sectors – including learning from leading energy producers.

Together, action on methane and electrification are the planetary icepack – able to cut half a degree from projected global heating.

Excellencies,

This is the best way we can tackle overshoot right now: lassoing it back with solution after solution.

And from now on, there’ll be more space at COPs for countries to coordinate their delivery.

Doing things differently includes this year’s unique partnership between Türkiye and Australia:

Driving solutions across both the negotiations and the Action Agenda.

I sincerely thank our gracious hosts, and commend the COP31 President Minister Murat Kurum, for your clear Action Agenda calls.

At UN Climate Change we want to support countries to engage with all that the Action Agenda has to offer.

We’re working on a moment on the final day of the COP, bringing together progress made over these two weeks.

We’re interested in exploring – with you – ways we can support government counterparts to boost collaboration with non-party stakeholders, and mobilize action towards shared priorities.

Many developing countries have not been able to engage fully with the Action Agenda. That means they’re missing out. Missing out on the chance to harness its benefits to build resilience and transition to clean energy.

We must help them to do so. So, I invite all countries – on a voluntary basis – to communicate focal points to me, who the Secretariat can keep up to date on Action Agenda progress and opportunities.

We also want to rally more doers across economies. This includes coordinating with other climate weeks around the world to convene around the six axes of the Action Agenda.

The Action Agenda is not about giving countries a way out of delivering on their commitments. It is about boosting their implementation.

As we adapt our approach, the negotiations remain central.

Consensus remains at the heart of this process, guided by COP31 President of Negotiations Minister Chris Bowen.

Strong outcomes on the mandated negotiation items are absolutely essential.

The stronger the outcomes, the more they will help Parties convert their targets into real-world outcomes, spreading more benefits to more people.

Agreement on the Just Transition Mechanism will make it easier for countries to bring whole societies through the transition together.

Agreements on adaptation will give us a board to disburse funds to countries, and help indicators drive forward progress at the national level.

Agreements on mitigation that help countries accelerate implementation across sectors and economies and send stronger signals to markets and societies on cutting planet-heating pollution.

Agreements on finance will give us clarity on how to achieve the 300 billion and 1.3 trillion commitments, without reopening previous agreements.

That will require the whole financial system to step-up.

Excellencies,

The urgency of this moment must drive us forward.

Global heating is already costing the Earth:

Appalling tragedy has hit the Himalayas, adding to the ever-expanding catalogue hitting communities across every region.

A monster El Niño is piling fuel on the climate fire that’s already burning through communities and economies everywhere.

The vulnerable everywhere pay the highest price – underscored by the Pre-COP in Fiji, in partnership with Australia and Pacific islands.

Profound injustice threatens our solidarity and collective progress.

Frustration is palpable.

Fairness must be at the heart of a truly global shift to clean energy and resilience. Because it is right.

And because it serves every countries’ interests: to limit global heating, and protect every community and every economy.

Meanwhile, this year's fossil fuel cost chaos has delivered a global shockwave, hitting households hard and spreading inflation like a cancer.

The fall-out has been severe, both economically and politically, as we've just seen.

But the solutions are clear:

Global renewables saved around half a trillion dollars last year. And another $265 billion in the first half of this year alone.

Adaptation delivers proven returns on investment.

Practical solutions are how we roll-out these remedies to more people, in more places, much faster...

Amid these pressures bearing down around the world.

And in doing so, build a solid foundation for the second global stocktake in two years from now.

UN Climate Change stands with you over these two weeks and beyond.

But we too face our challenges.

Mandates are growing. Funds are shrinking.

We’ve delivered extensive efficiencies. And will continue doing so. But serious work is needed with Parties on our budget consultations over the next six months. We can't keep doing more with less.

Excellencies,

No COP is a silver bullet.

No single conference can bridge the chasm between the science and reality.

We must deal with the world as it is, not as we might wish it to be.

Every recent COP has delivered strides forward. This one must too.

A climate solutions step-up creates a real chance for faster progress.

We have a responsibility to take it.

Friends, this is what the era of implementation looks like.

So let’s get to work.

I thank you.

COP31 President Murat Kurum

COP31 Opening Statement

English version & Turkish version below

My dear colleagues André and Chris, Executive Secretary Simon, Distinguished delegates, Ladies and gentlemen,

I extend a warm welcome to you all, here in Antalya, Türkiye.

Dear friends,

As we meet today, let us begin by looking at the world around us. It is changing fast, under pressure from many challenges at once.

War and geopolitical tension persist. Trade routes, energy networks and supply chains are being redrawn.

For millions, economic uncertainty, heavy debt and the high cost of living shape daily life. Hundreds of millions struggle to put food on the table.

Technology and artificial intelligence are moving ahead at extraordinary speed. Yet access to capital, knowledge and technology remains deeply unequal. All of this is unfolding in a world that is hotter, more fragile and more exposed to disasters. Across continents, we now live by the same climate calendar. A drought in one part of the world is felt at the dinner table in another.

When a river bursts its banks in one region, production schedules change in factories thousands of kilometres away. When water runs short in one country, the consequences reach other societies, affecting their economies, migration patterns and security.

Extreme heat is straining cities, agriculture and human health all at once.

The world’s message is unmistakable: each crisis makes the others worse.

Climate shapes our food supply. Food influences migration. Energy shapes the economy. Economic fragility affects the ability of societies to withstand shocks.

That is why climate policy today is also development policy. It is food policy. Energy policy. Urban policy. Health policy.

Above all, it is how we protect humanity’s future.

That is what has brought us to Antalya. As crises feed off one another, we must make sure our solutions strengthen one another too.

We may come from different places. Our circumstances, resources and priorities may differ. Yet we increasingly share the same climate calendar.

Sharing that calendar means sharing responsibility.

This is Antalya’s call: let dialogue grow as divisions deepen. Restore trust where it is under strain. Put resources to work as needs grow. Close the gap between our promises and people’s lives.

We want COP31 to deliver on that call as an Implementation COP.

Dear friends,

For centuries, this land has been a crossroads of trade and culture, a place where routes converge and ideas meet.

We now draw on that experience for a new purpose: connecting humanity’s needs with the means to meet them.

Some of the distances that divide our world cannot be seen. They separate those able to secure finance from those unable to do so.

They separate those with technology from those who need it. They separate countries able to withstand shocks from societies that remain vulnerable.

Narrowing those distances is one of climate diplomacy’s greatest responsibilities.

Türkiye has long served as a bridge. We are ready to take on that responsibility again. Our aim is to find common ground that reflects the expectations of North and South, of developed and developing countries.

Together with Australia, we are ready to ensure the Pacific is heard and to help find solutions to the challenges facing vulnerable countries.

We know that delay carries one of the heaviest costs in climate action.

Postpone an investment in resilience today, and tomorrow we may face the cost of a disaster. Fail to deliver adaptation finance today, and tomorrow’s humanitarian crisis may be worse. The costs we will face in the future must therefore inform the decisions we take now. The 1.5°C goal remains our guide. We will be frank about what the science tells us. And we will bring the voices of the most vulnerable countries and communities to the centre of our agenda.

The decisions we take in Antalya will only truly come to life when they leave these halls.

From here, I appeal to countries, peoples and young people everywhere:

Let us make Antalya the starting point of a historic partnership.

Let our promises deliver results. Let our decisions unlock investment. Let our knowledge be put to work.

Our decisions must take shape in a city’s infrastructure, on a farmer’s land and along a factory’s production line. Families must feel their impact in lower energy bills.

A decision proves its worth when it makes a difference to someone’s life.

Dear friends,

Three principles guide our COP31 Presidency:

Dialogue. Consensus. Action.

We begin by listening to each other. We then build on what we share. And we turn that shared resolve into action on the ground. The world already has knowledge, technology, capital, science and human talent. Our task is to bring them to the people and places that need them, at the moment they are needed.

The last mile of climate action may lead to a field where a farmer watches the soil dry out. To the shores of a small island state facing rising seas. Or to a city street struggling with extreme heat.

Success begins when our decisions reach that last mile.

This is why Zero Waste matters to us. Led by First Lady Emine Erdoğan, the Zero Waste Movement makes conserving resources, cutting waste, improving efficiency and taking responsibility part of everyday life. We see children and young people as the strongest force driving this change. The habits we form today become tomorrow’s culture. We bring the same thinking to the energy transition.

Under our 35-by-35 Global Electrification Pledge, we aim to raise electricity’s share of final energy consumption to 35 per cent by 2035.

This transition brings together renewable energy, strong grids, storage capacity, energy efficiency, clean transport and green industry. Each supports the others. We want people to feel the results of climate talks in daily life: in buildings that use less energy, in clean public transport, in energy they can afford and in new jobs.

All this calls for a strong financial architecture. Alongside finance, we need another kind of infrastructure: trust.

Trust, too, is infrastructure for climate action.

For a country, trust means seeing its commitments bear fruit. Being able to access the resources it needs. Receiving promised finance on time. And having confidence that decisions will be put into practice.

That is the unseen foundation on which global cooperation rests.

In Baku, countries agreed on a climate finance target for developing countries: at least 300 billion dollars a year by 2035. They also called for public and private finance to increase to at least 1.3 trillion dollars a year.

Now our promises must be backed by capital. That capital must fund investment. And that investment must deliver results. A map of the world’s needs today shows us one picture.

A map of its capital, technology, knowledge and expertise shows us another.

We want those maps to align. We will connect investors with projects that need funding. We will connect countries that need technology with those able to provide solutions. And we will match local needs with global capacity.

That is what the Climate Implementation Bridge is designed to do. We will put resources where they are needed, and responsibility where the capacity to act exists.

Ladies and gentlemen,

We want the legacy of Antalya to be a culture of working together, not a list of decisions.

Countries listening to each other. Institutions trusting one another. Scientists sharing what they know. Entrepreneurs creating solutions. Businesses accepting responsibility. Financial institutions putting their resources to work.

In Belém, Brazil shared the spirit of mutirão with us. A powerful expression of that same spirit has been part of our culture for centuries:

İmece. It means everyone doing their part when the task is too great for one person alone. It means sharing hope as well as sharing the burden.

That is the spirit our world needs now.

Every country has knowledge to contribute. Every society has experience. Every generation has energy. Every institution has capacity. We need them all.

Years from now, we want Antalya to be remembered above all for the work that began here, more than for the words spoken here.

Let them remember the investments that got under way. The technologies that crossed borders. The cities that became more resilient. The farmer who was able to keep farming. The child who could face the future with greater confidence.

Let Antalya leave a legacy greater than our words.

Let Antalya narrow the distances we cannot see.

Let it connect needs with the means to meet them.

Let it replace delay with action.

Let it bring climate action into people’s lives.

Guided by the spirit of imece,

let us open the way together:

from dialogue to consensus,

from consensus to action,

from action to implementation,

and from implementation to people’s lives.

This is the strongest message we can send from here today:

If we are to share a future, we must share the responsibility for it.

I am deeply grateful to our President, His Excellency Recep Tayyip Erdoğan, and to First Lady Emine Erdoğan for their strong support for this process. I also extend my sincere thanks to UN Secretary-General António Guterres, Executive Secretary Simon Stiell and the Climate Change Secretariat. My thanks also go to Prime Minister Anthony Albanese and the Government of Australia; my dear friend Chris Bowen; our teams; the people of Antalya; and our volunteers. You all have my sincere thanks and respect.

Hepinizi saygıyla selamlıyor, Antalya’ya, Türkiye’ye hoş geldiniz diyorum.

Ve her şeyden önce, insanın geleceğini koruma politikasıdır.

Tam da bu nedenle Antalya’dayız. Krizlerin birbirini büyüttüğü bir çağda, çözümleri birbirini güçlendirecek şekilde kurmak için buradayız.

Coğrafyalarımız farklı olabilir. Şartlarımız, imkânlarımız ve önceliklerimiz farklı olabilir. Fakat dünyanın iklim takvimi ortaklaşıyor.

Bu topraklar yüzyıllar boyunca yolların kesiştiği, fikirlerin karşılaştığı, ticaretin ve kültürlerin birbirine dokunduğu bir coğrafya oldu.

Gelin, tarihi bir iş birliğini Antalya’da birlikte kuralım.

Başarı, kararın bu son kilometreye ulaştığı yerde başlar.

Sıfır Atık anlayışını bu nedenle önemsiyoruz. Sayın Emine Erdoğan Hanımefendi’nin öncülüğündeki Sıfır Atık Hareketi; kaynaklara sahip çıkmayı, israfı azaltmayı, verimliliği artırmayı ve sorumluluğu günlük hayatın parçası hâline getiriyor. İklim görüşmelerinin sonucunu insanların günlük hayatında; daha verimli binalarda, temiz toplu taşımada, uygun maliyetli enerjide, yeni iş imkânlarında görmek istiyoruz.

Tabii bütün bunlar güçlü bir finansman mimarisi gerektiriyor. Fakat finansmanın yanında başka bir altyapıya daha ihtiyacımız var: Güven.

Bir ülkenin verdiği sözün karşılığını görmesi, ihtiyaç duyduğu kaynağa erişmesi, taahhüt edilen finansmanın zamanında ulaşması ve alınan kararların hayata geçeceğine inanması…

Şimdi sözün sermayeye, sermayenin yatırıma, yatırımın sonuca dönüşme zamanıdır. Bugün dünyanın ihtiyaç haritasına baktığımızda bir tablo görüyoruz.

Sermaye, teknoloji, bilgi ve uzmanlık haritasına baktığımızda başka bir tablo görüyoruz.

Biz bu iki haritayı üst üste getirmek istiyoruz. Finansman arayan projeyle yatırımcıyı… Teknolojiye ihtiyaç duyan ülkeyle çözüm sahibini… Yerel ihtiyaçla küresel kapasiteyi buluşturacağız.

İklim Uygulama Köprüsü’nün amacı budur. İhtiyacın olduğu yere imkânı, imkânın olduğu yere sorumluluğu taşıyacağız.

Hanımefendiler, Beyefendiler,

İmece. İmece, bir insanın gücünün yetmediği yerde herkesin elini taşın altına koymasıdır. İmece, yükü paylaşmak kadar umudu da paylaşmaktır.

Antalya’nın mirası sözlerimizden büyük olsun.

Görünmeyen mesafeleri azaltan bir Antalya…

İhtiyaçla imkânı buluşturan bir Antalya…

Gecikmenin yerine harekete geçmeyi koyan bir Antalya…

İklim eylemini insanın hayatına ulaştıran bir Antalya.

COP31 Opening Statement

Excellencies, delegates and friends.

Australia and Türkiye have founded a special and constructive partnership for the delivery of COP31.

I acknowledge my dear friend, Murat Kurum the COP31 President. I think I speak for all of us when I say the Government and people of Türkiye and Antalya have excelled themselves when it comes to preparing for COP31.

The eyes of the world are on us and Türkiye has given us the very best platform.

As we have done all year, we repeat our request to all parties to come to COP31 in the same spirit of cooperation, respect, determination.

And focus on the real issues that matter the most.

I acknowledge the COP30 President, Andre Corea Do Lago of Brazil, the UNFCCC Secretariat, and Executive Secretary, Simon Stiell.

I also want to acknowledge all Indigenous Peoples joining us here in Antalya from around the world, for their leadership in climate action.

Drawing on their unique relationship with lands, skies and waters they have had stewardship of over the millennia.

I also acknowledge our Pacific family as close partners and hosts of the recent Pre-COP in Fiji and Tuvalu – representing in a very real way those who have done the least to cause climate change, but have the most at stake.

Friends, it has been a long road to reach this place and be here with you all today.

This year, we have witnessed again the devastating consequences of climate change – and welcomed the inspiring solutions and responses.

The latest science tells us that we will overshoot 1.5 degrees.

But we can still return if we work together and act with urgency, solidarity and resolve.

That is our challenge here in the next fortnight.

To come together to meet the challenges and seize the opportunities ahead of us.

We saw the spirit of Talanoa, of dialogue and cooperation, at the Pacific Pre-COP.

We welcomed delegates from right across the globe.

From India, Nepal, Brazil and the EU.

From Saudi Arabia, Ethiopia, and the island nations of the Caribbean.

The message from the world that came out of Fiji and Tuvalu was clear:

Keep 1.5 degrees within reach.

Speed up climate action.

Make finance easier to access and deliver on our commitments.

Strengthen the resilience of our communities.

Our economies and our ocean.

And ensure no country faces the impacts of climate change alone.

I know that the same spirit of determination is present here with us in Antalya.

We meet at a moment of consequence.

Whether it be glacial collapse in Nepal, heat deaths in Europe, or an intensifying El Niño.

Climate change is here.

It is not a forecast. It is not a prediction.

It is the lived reality for billions of people.

Its’ impacts are growing more frequent and intense.

Every fraction of a degree, and every delay, increases the risks to lives, communities, economic growth and the environment.

Raising the cost of adaptation, deepening future losses and making the task ahead harder.

While the challenge is growing, so is our response.

Before Paris, the world was heading for warming approaching 4 degrees.

Today, projections are closer to 2.6 degrees.

Since 2015, global renewable electricity generation has almost doubled.

Around US$2.2 trillion was invested in clean energy last year.

Nearly twice the amount flowing to fossil fuels.

More than 160 countries have submitted updated NDCs.

More than 130 have now submitted their first BTRs.

This should give us confidence.

We are seeing our efforts turn into action on the ground.

The clean energy transition is not only reducing emissions.

It is reshaping investment, industry and employment across the global economy.

But we must move faster.

We have the tools.

The technologies we need are proven, commercial and scalable.

What we need is to speed up deployment.

This year, I have talked to Parties from around the world on their priorities and key ambitions for COP31.

And for those that I haven’t yet met personally – my door is open.

One of the strongest messages I’ve heard is this:

There is enormous momentum on electrification.

Electricity supplies only around one-fifth of global final energy consumption.

Much of the remainder still comes from burning fossil fuels in transport, buildings and industry.

Accelerating electrification, powered by clean and resilient energy systems, is key to setting this right.

We need to shift electricity from a fifth to a third of global energy consumption.

Not only is this good for our planet. It strengthens nations’ energy security.

It reduces emissions and helps us better shield households from volatile bills and price shocks.

This is why the Action Agenda goal of a global effort to increase electricity's share of final energy consumption to 35 per cent by 2035 is so important

Delivering on that ambition requires investment in renewable energy, modern grids, energy storage, efficiency and skills.

Of course, countries will always take pathways that best suit them.

And each country will pursue electrification in their own way.

Just as clearly, I’ve heard that we need to unlock finance.

This includes both scaling up climate finance, but also making it easier to access.

Too many countries with credible energy transition and adaptation plans can't access finance at the speed, scale or terms required to put those plans into action.

The countries that need climate finance the most, are getting it the least.

That’s why at the Pacific Pre-COP, Australia launched the Access to Finance Statement and Action Plan for SIDS and LDCs focused on a practical objective:

Making access to finance faster and simpler.

We must strengthen project pipelines.

Mobilise public and private investment together.

And ensure climate finance reaches countries and communities when they need it.

Finance must be disbursed faster.

More simply.

And more fairly.

We have made our commitments.

Now we must deliver on them.

Parties have demonstrated their ambition, and ensuring timely, accessible and scaled up climate finance is critical to climate action.

Delivering on the commitments we’ve made builds trust.

Trust in the process, trust from communities that we are collectively working for, and for the future

And trust between us as parties.

Through this process we have shown we can deliver new and innovative streams of finance.

Finance is part of the engine that drives our efforts and we will not let it falter here.

We must also address and strengthen adaptation and resilience.

Climate impacts are already disrupting lives, economies and development.

Countries need stronger infrastructure, stronger communities, stronger early-warning systems and stronger institutions.

We must help countries prepare for, withstand and recover from climate impacts.

And we must ensure that countries most exposed to climate risk have access to the partnerships, support and finance required to build resilience.

Both before and whenever disaster strikes.

More broadly, success in Antalya means making progress across every front.

This year, there are over 160 items and 60 substantive negotiations mandates on our agenda.

Each is an opportunity to make progress and advance climate action.

This includes:

Operationalising the Just Transition Mechanism to provide practical support for countries.

Strengthening the Mitigation Work Program, speeding up real world implementation, cooperation and investment.

Taking forward the Global Goal on Adaptation by establishing the technical taskforce.

Giving confidence to climate finance delivery and investment flows, including through improving access.

Taking forward our work in the Climate Finance Work Program.

Finalising the transition to the Adaptation Fund.

Following up on the tripling of adaptation finance, and enhancing action and cooperation under Article 2.1c.

And importantly, we need to keep science central to our work.

We must make progress across all these mandates, as well as a range of other important mandates due for decision this year.

Friends, after extensive consultations with Parties throughout this year, Minister Kurum and I have agreed to take forward a Presidency-initiated, Party-driven decision for COP31.

This decision will be led by the Presidencies, but it must be owned and driven by the Parties.

Ensuring it respects national circumstances and responds to the global moment.

We will build it together, from the ground up.

We have spoken clearly about our intentions at the Pacific Pre-COP and in virtual consultations since.

Because transparency, consultation and inclusion remain central to our approach.

There will be no surprises.

This is not about duplicating negotiations.

It will not be a lengthy political declaration.

But a focused, practical and concrete response to the challenges and opportunities before us.

A decision that reflects the urgency of the climate challenge and the enormous opportunities created by the global transition.

One that gives confidence to governments, investors, businesses and communities that the world is moving faster and working together.

Such an outcome could:

Recognise the progress we have made together.

Reflect on the real world challenges that we face, and opportunities before us as well.

Accelerate the high-impact, concrete solutions that can help keep 1.5 degrees within reach, and strengthen resilience, means of implementation and international cooperation.

We can send a message to the world:

That despite our challenges, the world is committed to implementing our Paris goals and moving faster.

We know there will be a difference of views - on the value of the decision, on its elements, on how far we go.

But our job is to work to close those differences and provide the most ambitious, most outcome-orientated decision that consensus will allow.

Australia is proud to serve in the role of President of Negotiations in our partnership with Türkiye.

This partnership has been built on trust, solidarity and a shared resolve to go further and faster.

Throughout the year, we have asked Parties to come to Antalya with the same spirit of cooperation.

To build confidence for governments to act.

For businesses to invest.

For communities to plan for a safer and more prosperous future.

No country can achieve this alone.

But together we can and must.

Friends, let’s show the world that multilateralism works.

Let’s show the world that we are equal to the challenge.

Let’s join in a spirit of cooperation and respect.

Let’s show future generations that this generation was equal to the moment, equal to the challenge.

Let’s rise to this moment together.

Thank you.

title: U.N. climate talks begin today. Here are 3 things to know
description:
For the next two weeks, country leaders will be in Antalya, Turkey, for the annual United Nations climate conference, called COP31.

text:
For the next two weeks, country leaders will be in Antalya, Turkey, for the annual United Nations climate conference, called COP31. This year, the ongoing U.S.-Israeli war with Iran will loom over the negotiations. Now in its ninth month, the war has sparked a global energy crisis. The unprecedented closure of the Strait of Hormuz and spiking oil and natural gas prices have laid bare the fragility of relying on fossil fuels.

But this energy crisis – unlike the energy crisis in the 1970s and the one following Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022 – is different, says Kingsmill Bond, an analyst at the energy think tank Ember.

"This is the first time you've really had a global energy shock where you've got really cheap solutions to address it," Bond says.

Those solutions include solar panels, batteries and electric vehicles. In recent months, countries around the world have pivoted sharply towards these technologies. Many of them are produced in China and offer economic security, as well as reduced emissions.

The economic case for climate solution technologies will make it easier for countries to support them at the conference, Bond says. "There's much more opportunity, I think, for people to get behind change at COP."

Here are three things you need to know about this year's COP.

It's all about electrification

Climate technologies like solar, batteries and electric vehicles are also called electrification technologies. Bond says that's why some are calling this "the electrification COP."

"The big target that the COP is setting is for the world to increase the electrification rate from around 23% today to around 35% by 2035," Bond says. "So 35 by '35 is the mantra."

These electrification goals assume countries will grow their electricity mix with cleaner renewable energy. Energy experts say that is a reasonable assumption, because that's what has been happening in recent years. Large solar and wind projects provide more cost-competitive energy than natural gas and coal projects, according to financial services firm Lazard.

"Think about solar, wind," says Li Shuo, director of the China Climate Hub at the Asia Society Policy Institute. "More green energy will help you decarbonize better and faster."

Roadmap off fossil fuels

As the COP process enters its 31st year, many countries have argued that the U.N. process has not done enough to tackle the single biggest driver of climate change: burning fossil fuels.

Fossil fuel producers such as Saudi Arabia and Russia have consistently opposed having fossil fuel language in the text of final conference agreements.

In April, more than 50 countries came together to discuss ways to phase out oil, gas, and coal at the First International Conference to Transition Away from Fossil Fuels. Conference organizers told NPR the conference was a way to complement the U.N. process.

More than 25 of those nations are developing a legally binding treaty that would advance a phase-out of fossil fuels. Supporters of the Fossil Fuel Treaty Initiative hope more countries will join their cause at COP31.

The U.S. is not in the room

The U.S. State Department told NPR in an email that the U.S. will not be sending a delegation to COP31. They also did not send anyone to last year's COP in Brazil.

The Trump administration has reversed action on climate progress, phasing out subsidies for electric vehicles, solar and wind, reducing regulations for greenhouse gases, and halting renewable energy projects.

Last year, some countries told NPR they were happy that the Trump administration was not at the climate talks. "Generally, it's a good thing they're not here because we have less recalcitrants to deal with," Ralph Regenvanu, minister of climate change of Vanuatu, told NPR then.

But some democratic lawmakers will be at COP31, including Sen. Sheldon Whitehouse, a Democrat representing Rhode Island. Fresh off Democrats' midterm victory sweep, Whitehouse says he and the other lawmakers plan to keep the focus on fossil fuels and a potential carbon pricing mechanism.

" It cannot remain free for the fossil fuel industry to pollute if we want to have any chance of a pathway to climate safety," Whitehouse says.

In a letter to congressional leaders, the companies call on lawmakers to quickly send the bipartisan legislation to the President’s desk. The signatories note that solar and storage account for 70% of new electricity capacity added to the grid thus far in 2026, while $120 billion in clean energy investment remains caught in permitting delays.

“You can’t lower energy costs if you can’t build the energy projects, and these companies know that this bipartisan legislation will help get America building again,” said Tim Pawlenty, CEO of the Solar Energy Industries Association (SEIA).

BAAJA would modernize the federal permitting system by ensuring fair treatment for all technologies, protecting lawfully issued permits from politically motivated delays, establishing predictable timelines for federal reviews and judicial proceedings, modernizing transmission planning, and expanding distributed energy resources’ access to wholesale electricity markets.

New SEIA analysis shows that BAAJA could unlock 167 gigawatts of additional solar capacity between 2028 and 2035, bringing solar to over 18% of U.S. electricity generation by 2035. The analysis finds that the bill’s reforms could reduce cumulative power sector CO2 emissions by approximately 20% and avoid $54 billion in public health damages.

The message from more than 300 companies comes as voters made clear in the midterm elections that lowering energy costs is a top concern. Permitting reform is urgently needed to meet rising demand and get more reliable, affordable solar and storage projects built.

text:
TAIPEI, Nov. 9, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- Delta marks its 19th consecutive year of participation in the 31st United Nations Climate Change Conference (UNFCCC COP31), which opens today in Antalya, Türkiye. Delta will support the host country's "35×35" initiative, targeting a 35% electrification goal by 2035, by sharing how smart microgrids accelerate electrification at an official side event. Earlier, at the 17th Conference of the Parties to the Convention on Biological Diversity (CBD COP17) in late October, Delta partnered with the International Union for Conservation of Nature (IUCN) to showcase the world's first application of the Species Threat Abatement and Restoration (STAR) metric for coral restoration and conservation assessment. Through international collaboration, Delta addresses climate mitigation and adaptation challenges with technological innovation and ecosystem restoration.

Shan-Shan Guo, Vice Chairperson of the Delta Electronics Foundation, said, "As global electrification accelerates and AI drives growing electricity demand, Delta leverages its core technologies to improve energy efficiency and resilience through microgrids and smart energy management, support electrification, and help AI data centers increase their use of clean energy. As Delta celebrates its 55th anniversary, we are participating in international climate conferences under the theme 'Smarter is Greener.' At COP31, our EMEA leadership and Foundation colleagues will engage with international thought leaders at official side events and the France Pavilion. We also shared our coral restoration experience and achievements at CBD COP17. Through innovative technology, we hope to collaborate with climate partners and move forward toward a more sustainable future."

During COP31, Delta will host its 9th official side event in the Blue Zone, joining the Association for Renewable Energy and Clean Technology (REA) and the German Federal Environmental Foundation (DBU) to exchange insights on microgrid applications. Delta will also share its experience deploying microgrids in Indigenous communities to strengthen disaster resilience. In 2025, renewable electricity accounted for 91% of Delta's global electricity consumption, and Delta achieved its RE100 target in 32 countries.

Delta Presents World-Leading Coral Restoration Experience at CBD COP17

Wim Chang, CEO of the Delta Electronics Foundation, said, "Delta combines technology with coral restoration and conservation, aiming to preserve more than half of the coral species in the Pacific Ocean by 2030. This year, in partnership with IUCN, we became the first globally to apply the STAR metric to coral reef areas where Delta conducts restoration. By scientifically quantifying threats to species survival, we aim to make conservation outcomes more measurable and credible."

Nicholas Macfarlane, Head of Conservation Science and Technology at IUCN, said, "We are delighted to have partnered with Delta on the world's first application of the marine STAR metric. This collaboration demonstrates the potential of corporate and scientific partnerships, and we look forward to advancing marine biodiversity through innovative, measurable conservation strategies."

At CBD COP17 in late October, Delta presented its research at the Nature Pavilion, a flagship venue hosted by IUCN. This year, Delta applied the STAR methodology to coral reef areas in Kenting, Taiwan, and calibrated the results against IUCN's global database, aligning its restoration methodology with international standards.

Delta also invited Professor David Obura, lead author of the coral chapter of the IUCN Red List of Threatened Species, to a side event at the Ocean Pavilion. Together with international organizations including the UK's Plymouth Marine Laboratory (PML) and the International Coral Reef Society (ICRS), participants discussed ways to strengthen coral reef resilience.

From biodiversity conservation to electrification goals, leveraging scientific research and technological innovation to address global environmental challenges remains a core focus for the United Nations. To help the international community combat climate change and biodiversity loss, Delta has participated in two COP summits 22 times, and hosted or been invited to 43 side events to date.

ABOUT DELTA

Delta, founded in 1971, and listed on the Taiwan Stock Exchange (code:2308), is a global leader in switching power supplies and thermal management products with a thriving portfolio of IoT-based smart energy-saving systems and solutions in the fields of industrial automation, building automation, telecom power, data center infrastructure, EV charging, renewable energy, energy storage and display, to nurture the development of smart manufacturing and sustainable cities. As a world-class corporate citizen guided by its mission statement, "To provide innovative, clean and energy-efficient solutions for a better tomorrow," Delta leverages its core competence in high-efficiency power electronics and its ESG-embedded business model to address key environmental issues, such as climate change. Delta serves customers through its sales offices, R&D centers and manufacturing facilities spread over close to 200 locations across 5 continents.

Throughout its history, Delta has received various global awards and recognition for its business achievements, innovative technologies and dedication to ESG. Since 2011, Delta has been listed on the Dow Jones Best-in-Class World Index (formerly the DJSI World Index of Dow Jones Sustainability™ Indices) for 15 consecutive years. Delta has also won CDP with double A List for 4 times for its substantial contribution to climate change and water security issues and has been named Supplier Engagement Leader for its continuous development of a sustainable value chain for 8 consecutive years.

description:

text:
Input

2026-11-09 18:13:55

Updated

2026-11-09 18:13:55

[Financial News] Academics and the government agreed that the benchmark for assessing greenhouse gas emissions from cars should shift from tailpipe emissions to life-cycle assessment (LCA), which covers everything from production to disposal. But they differed over the carbon-reduction benefits of EVs as measured by LCA: some said EVs emit no less carbon than internal-combustion vehicles, while others said the gap is growing. The government plans to sharply increase next year its support for small and midsize parts suppliers, which face a heavy burden in calculating LCA figures.

Min Kyung-deok, a professor in the Department of Mechanical Engineering at Seoul National University, and Park Jun-hong, head of the Mobility and Environment Research Center at the National Institute of Environmental Research, each gave a presentation at the 2026 KAIDA Automotive Policy Seminar at FKI Tower in Yeongdeungpo District, Seoul, on the 9th. Their topics were “Proposals for Automotive Environmental Policy in an Era of Major Transformation in the Automotive Industry” and “The Current State of Environmental Regulations for Motor Vehicles Manufactured in Korea and Future Directions,” respectively.

■ “EVs also emit as much carbon as internal-combustion vehicles”

Current regulations on greenhouse gas emissions from cars count only the carbon dioxide (CO2) emitted from the tailpipe while a vehicle is being driven. EVs, which have no tailpipe, are calculated as having “zero” emissions. LCA, by contrast, adds up all the carbon emitted over a vehicle’s lifetime, from extracting raw materials and manufacturing parts and the vehicle to driving, scrapping and recycling it.

Professor Min pointed out, “All of our country’s current policies, regulations and incentives are determined by whether CO2 or exhaust gases come out of the tailpipe.”

He said, “Nitrogen oxides (NOx) and fine particulate matter (PM) have an immediate impact on city residents, but CO2 is a global problem,” adding, “It is somewhat more appropriate to view CO2 from an LCA perspective.” Air pollutants harm the areas where they are emitted, whereas CO2 contributes to global warming no matter where it is released.

As supporting evidence, he cited LCA data released by Hyundai Motor. Total carbon emissions across the life cycle, from production to disposal, were 39.9 tCO2eq (tonnes of CO2 equivalent) for the internal-combustion version of the Hyundai Kona and 33.2 tCO2eq for the Hyundai Kona Electric. The electric commercial vehicle Hyundai ST1 recorded 42.3 tCO2eq, while the second-generation Hyundai Nexo recorded 39.2 tCO2eq, including 3.6 tonnes from parts manufacturing. EVs emit less while being driven, but produce substantial carbon emissions during battery manufacturing.

Professor Min explained, “People think EV emissions are zero, but from an LCA perspective, EVs emit no less carbon than internal-combustion vehicles,” adding, “Much more CO2 is emitted when batteries are made.”

LCA is already being factored into subsidies overseas. France converts the carbon footprint of production and transport into an environmental score and provides subsidies only for EVs scoring 60 or higher. The United Kingdom sets subsidy levels according to the electricity carbon-emissions factors of the countries where vehicles are assembled and battery cells are produced. The system means that cars made in countries with a higher share of coal-fired power receive smaller subsidies.

In Korea, a draft notice on “Regulations on Methods for Life-Cycle Assessment of Greenhouse Gas Emissions from Motor Vehicles” was announced for public comment on the 7th of last month. However, manufacturers submit the information voluntarily if they choose, so it is not yet linked to regulations or subsidies. Professor Min proposed that subsidies and other systems should also shift to an LCA basis over the long term.

On hybrids, he said, “They can certainly play a role for the next 20 to 30 years,” adding, “To do that, their efficiency must also improve.” He also called for increased investment, noting that although the government’s overall R&D budget rose 19.5% this year, the Ministry of Trade, Industry and Energy’s automotive R&D budget fell 6.9%, from 499 billion won to 464.5 billion won.

■ “LCA is still an estimate ... support for small and midsize parts suppliers to increase”

Center Director Park urged caution in interpreting LCA results. “LCA is based on modeling and, in a sense, is closer to an estimate,” he said. “Most of the research results currently available are at Level 1 or 2, with a high degree of uncertainty.”

LCA is divided into Levels 1 through 4 according to precision. Levels 1 and 2 estimate a vehicle’s carbon emissions using average values from commercial databases. Starting at Level 3, measured data—including the energy used in the actual manufacturing process and the proportion of recycled materials—is incorporated for key components that account for a large share of carbon emissions. Greater precision increases reliability, but also places a heavier burden on parts suppliers, who must calculate the data themselves.

The United Nations World Forum for Harmonization of Vehicle Regulations (WP29) considers Level 3 the minimum required to use LCA for regulations or government reporting. The idea is that calculations need to be more precise when used for policymaking. France and the United Kingdom, however, set EV subsidies using less detailed calculations. Under the two countries’ systems, vehicles produced outside Europe are excluded from subsidy eligibility.

Center Director Park said, “They use simple Level 1 or 2 calculations for subsidies,” adding, “You can probably guess why.” He was pointing out that LCA is being used to favor vehicles produced domestically or within the region, rather than to assess carbon emissions precisely.

His view differed from Professor Min’s on EV assessments. LCA assumes a vehicle is used for 15 to 20 years and calculates emissions over that period as well. Center Director Park said, “If the expansion of renewable energy over that time is also factored in, the figure for EVs could be lower than the values currently known.” In other words, as electricity generation becomes cleaner, the carbon emissions associated with the electricity used to charge EVs also fall.

He said, “A few years ago, some results showed hybrids and EVs were comparable, but recent results seem to show that the gap is growing.”

On institutionalizing LCA, he said, “There is a very long way to go,” and stated that the government would take a phased approach. First it will establish a calculation method, then proceed to voluntary reporting by manufacturers, and then introduce standards. Incentives will also be considered as part of the process.

He also outlined plans to expand support for small and midsize parts suppliers. Center Director Park said that large manufacturers such as Hyundai Motor are building up their capabilities, while smaller suppliers further down the supply chain are facing considerable difficulties.

He said, “Under a 2025–2026 pilot program, we are spending around 1.2 billion won a year to support small businesses with their calculations,” adding, “We plan to sharply increase the level of support next year.” The plan is to broaden assistance beyond calculation and verification to include consulting on emissions-reduction technologies. He said the specific amount could be disclosed after the National Assembly’s budget review.

■ “Cars as a main source of fine-dust pollution is an outdated notion” ... Greenhouse gas standards pressure automakers to “switch power sources”

He assessed that efforts to control emissions from internal-combustion vehicles had delivered results. Compared with their peak levels in the 2000s, the share of total air pollutant emissions attributable to road vehicles (mobile sources on roads) had fallen by 2023 from 46% to 2% for PM10, from 42% to 28% for NOx, and from 17% to 3% for volatile organic compounds (VOCs).

Center Director Park stressed, “Vehicle exhaust emissions have fallen so much that I can say the claim that cars are a major source of fine-dust pollution is no longer valid.”

On greenhouse gas standards, he explained, “They may appear to regulate tailpipe CO2, but in practice they are a system that requires a shift in power sources.” As the standards become stricter, improving the efficiency of internal-combustion vehicles alone will no longer be enough to meet them, making a successive shift to hybrids, plug-in hybrids and EVs unavoidable.

According to Center Director Park, hybrids, too, have difficulty reducing CO2 emissions below 90 grams per kilometer because of the characteristics of their systems. Meeting the 2030 standard of 70 g/km with room to spare would require plug-in-hybrid-level performance. In July, the government announced for public comment a proposal to tighten the standard to 54 g/km. By August this year, the share of zero-emission vehicles (EVs and hydrogen vehicles) among new passenger cars had exceeded 24% for the first time.

Regulations are also being prepared for pollutants produced beyond the tailpipe. These are fine particles generated as brakes and tires wear down, and are considered a source of fine dust and microplastics. The European Union (EU) began applying standards for wear particles to newly introduced brake systems this month, and Korea is also considering adopting them.

For tires, discussions on international testing methods are being delayed because results from tests conducted on actual roads do not match those from indoor drum testing equipment. The government is pursuing domestic legislation, in consultation with industry and importers, for the Euro 7 heavy-duty vehicle standards that take effect in 2028.
