A modern and more connected electricity grid also comes with new grid forming capabilities, which adds system strength and builds greater resilience.
text:
It's almost 100 years since consumers were captured by the ‘Now you’re cooking with gas’ campaign.

Almost half a century later, the electricity industry in Australia had a go with its own ‘Switched on Living’ drive, while who could forget the natural gas ‘Living Flame’ ads on rotation across Australian TV screens throughout the 1980s.

Well, it’s now time for another energy focused campaign to capture our attention – The 35 by 35 pledge.

The 35 by 35 electrification pledge was announced recently by the United Nations’ COP 31 Presidency, alongside Australia’s Minister for Climate Change and Energy and COP31 President of Negotiations Chris Bowen.

The 35 by 35 mantra was also adopted by the Electrify Now campaign in Australia with the support of 30 industry bodies, consumer groups, and trade unions.

It was part of the global Electrify Now campaign, launched during London Climate Action Week.

35 by 35 is memorable in its phrasing, but also timely in helping to focus our attention on the productivity potential of electrification here in Australia.

The 35 by 35 pledge plans to increase electricity’s share of global final energy consumption from just over 20 per cent today to 35 per cent by 2035.

For Australia, it’s hoped that it will mobilise action to accelerate electrification across transport, industry – including the resources sector and data centres, as well as residential and commercial buildings.

Australia’s mining sector consumes about 10 percent of the country’s energy, yet it only sources about one third of that energy from electricity.

Demand for critical, strategic and rare earth minerals is expected to drive continued growth in the sector, meaning there are significant opportunities to increase electricity’s share of total energy use.

There are also large gains to be made in the electrification of transport in Australia. The sector accounts for about 22 percent of the country’s carbon emissions, but that has started to fall with the rapid uptake of electric vehicles.

The growth in energy use from data centres in Australia is expected to outpace every other sector by a long way. Data centres currently use about three percent of all electricity use across the National Electricity Market. That share is expected to increase seven fold by 2050.

There is a lot of upside in meeting the 35 by 35 electrification target.

Roughly 90 percent of all the oil and diesel used on our roads, farms and across industrial processes in Australia is imported. In a volatile world, this leaves us vulnerable to shortages, price spikes and the associated economy-wide impacts.

Increasing the use of electricity generated on shore across these sectors improves our energy security and independence.

It’s also cheaper. According to a report recently released by the International Energy Agency, greater electrification could cut the world’s energy import bills by more than USD 500 billion every year.

Lastly, as we replace carbon intensive sources of energy with electricity made from renewable sources, there is a comparable reduction in carbon emissions and pollution. That’s good for human health, and the health of the planet.

The environmental impacts of a warming planet are very real issues for Australia’s neighbours in the Pacific, and this forms a key part of its policy platform at COP 31.

This includes improving Pacific nations’ access to climate finance and putting more focus on resilience and oceans as a critical pillar of climate action.

According to the Green Building Council of Australia, on our existing trajectory, electricity will account for around 25% of final energy demand by 2035.

To reach 35%, we need to electrify around four times faster than we are today.

And to feed this growing demand we must step up the expansion of least cost renewable energy and storage. However, as we were reminded recently by the Australian Energy Market Operator, we won’t be successful without the support of a bigger and stronger electricity grid.

This grid expansion plays two equally essential roles. It connects new sources of renewable generation and storage with the cities and regions that need it.

Secondly, it strengthens our electricity system through more interconnection.

Australia’s renewable energy and storage credentials are well known.

According to the Clean Energy Council, Australia’s utility scale and home storage market is one the largest in the world, with only China and the United States higher up the list.

Rates of household solar installations in Australia are the highest in the world, and the commercial and industrial solar market is expected to hit new heights following new government programs and support.

Renewables are consistently supplying around 50 percent of our national energy demands, with states like Tasmania and South Australia increasingly supplied by 100 percent renewable generation.

Interestingly, new data released this month from Rystad Energy also showed that wholesale electricity prices in Australia were lower than almost every other major economy for the first three quarters of 2026.

However, to achieve greater electrification, keep a lid on prices, and reduce carbon emissions we need our grid to step up.

The National Electricity Market is one of the world’s longest interconnected power systems, stretching around 44,000 kilometres and connecting with a distribution network spanning 764,000 km.

However, it lacks connection between states and from new generation heavy regions.

It’s estimated that only 5-10% of total generation in the NEM is traded across state borders each year. This means network faults, demand spikes or generation shortfalls can leave states vulnerable to higher prices or reliability concerns.

AEMO has now forecast that more than 6,000 km of new electricity transmission lines will be required across the country by 2050 – a 14 percent expansion. It has highlighted 20 critical projects that are required – eight of those are currently underway.

About 40% of the additional length is needed to strengthen the connection between states, adding reliability and stability to electricity supply across the NEM.

The other 60% connects new capacity in state based Renewable Energy Zones to energy-intensive industries in regional hubs, or demand centres in big cities.

A more connected grid means less curtailment and more sharing of existing renewable generation. It means we won’t have to over-build local generation.

A modern and more connected electricity grid also comes with new grid forming capabilities, which adds system strength and builds greater resilience.

So this grid expansion in Australia is not just critical to meeting the COP31 35 by 35 electrification target, it’s also key to realising energy security, affordability and sustainability benefits for the country.

title: US ESS boom lifts Korean battery makers as China faces oversupply squeeze - Chosunbiz
description:
◇ Korean battery makers spread their wings on rising U.S. ESS demand Korean battery makers, by contrast, are beating market forecasts with improving results.
◇ U.S. midterms: Democrats win by a landslide; ESS demand seen rising, China curbs to continue Industry officials expect the U.S. ESS market to grow quickly, likely extending domestic makers' run of stronger results.
Some, however, see a chance for a rebound by Chinese battery makers.
China is also ramping up ESS investment, and once plants under construction in Europe start up, they could further encroach on Europe's EV battery market.
In response, Chinese battery makers including CATL and BYD are building plants in Hungary and Poland.
text:
Fortunes are diverging lately for Korean and Chinese companies competing in the global battery market. Expectations are rising that domestic manufacturers including LG Energy Solution and Samsung SDI will keep improving results on stronger demand in the U.S. energy storage system (ESS) market. Chinese companies, by contrast, face a red light as oversupply worries and U.S. restrictions on Chinese-made products cloud growth.

◇ China's CATL grows in size, but profitability flashes warning signs

According to the battery industry on the 9th, China's CATL, the world's largest battery maker, posted third-quarter revenue of 165.221 billion yuan (about 33.3 trillion won), up 58.9% from a year earlier. Net profit rose 14.5% to 21.246 billion yuan (about 4.3 trillion won).

Despite double-digit increases in both revenue and net profit from a year earlier, the results fell well short of market expectations. London Stock Exchange Group (LSEG) had projected CATL's third-quarter revenue growth rate at 60.2% and net profit growth rate at 41.2%, respectively.

The underwhelming results were immediately reflected in the share price. On the 20th of last month, when the third-quarter results were released, CATL's stock on the Hong Kong market fell 6.6% from the previous day. Global investment bank JPMorgan also cut its rating on CATL shares listed in Hong Kong to Neutral from Overweight.

Chinese battery makers including CATL continue to expand in scale. In particular, Chinese products have increased their share of the electric-vehicle market this year.

Market researcher SNE Research said that from January through September, Chinese companies—seven suppliers including CATL—accounted for a 73% share of batteries installed in electric vehicles (EVs), plug-in hybrids (PHEVs) and hybrids (HEVs) worldwide, up 3.5 percentage points from a year earlier. Korea's big three—LG Energy Solution, Samsung SDI and SK On—had a 12.6% share, down 4.1 percentage points.

The problem is profitability is slipping relative to topline growth. With domestic competition saturated, China has been pushing large volumes overseas at low prices. Automakers struggling amid cutthroat competition are also diversifying supply chains to smaller battery vendors that sell cheaply to cut costs, a trend seen as squeezing margins at major manufacturers including CATL.

According to the South China Morning Post (SCMP), Chinese EV makers Xiaomi and Li Auto said they will team up with battery manufacturers such as CALB and EVE Energy to reduce battery procurement costs. CALB and EVE Energy are classified one tier below giants like CATL and BYD in China.

◇ Korean battery makers spread their wings on rising U.S. ESS demand

Korean battery makers, by contrast, are beating market forecasts with improving results. They have struggled in EV batteries against a flood of cheap Chinese products, but demand for ESS batteries has surged in the United States, benefiting domestic suppliers.

Samsung SDI posted third-quarter revenue of 4.6856 trillion won and operating profit of 407.8 billion won. Revenue rose 52.6% from a year earlier, and operating profit swung to a surplus from a 591.3 billion won loss. Operating profit, in particular, was twice the previous quarter's 203.8 billion won and the highest in 12 quarters since the third quarter of 2023.

Samsung SDI's operating profit far beat the market consensus—an average forecast—of 235.4 billion won, an earnings surprise that stood in contrast to CATL.

LG Energy Solution also saw revenue jump 59% in the same period to 9.6434 trillion won, while operating profit rose 25.7% to 756 billion won. Both were record highs on a quarterly basis. Its third-quarter operating profit was more than double the 320 billion won market consensus.

Samsung SDI and LG Energy Solution said soaring demand for ESS used in U.S. artificial intelligence (AI) data centers drove the improvement. A gradual recovery in Europe's EV market, which lifted EV battery sales, was also a tailwind.

◇ U.S. midterms: Democrats win by a landslide; ESS demand seen rising, China curbs to continue

Industry officials expect the U.S. ESS market to grow quickly, likely extending domestic makers' run of stronger results. Many also see the Democrats' landslide in the U.S. midterms held on the 3rd—on a platform of expanding energy infrastructure including ESS—as a boon for Korean companies.

Voice of America (VOA) reported on the 9th that although counting was not yet complete, the Democrats had already secured 252 of the 435 House seats, far more than a majority and beating the Republicans' 161. They also won 52 Senate seats to the Republicans' 44. In gubernatorial races, Democrats won in 28 states, ahead of Republicans who won in 20.

The Democrats announced in May an energy agenda that included plans to expand investment in the national power grid and energy storage systems (ESS). While they take a dim view of regulating AI data center construction, they intend to keep growing the ESS market as part of grid expansion.

Hyundai Motor Securities said in a pre-midterm report, "If Democrats control both chambers, they will push to restore renewable energy tax credits and expand ESS investment," adding, "Both parties have previously toughened tariff policy on Chinese batteries, so the post-election direction will likely remain to block China's supply chain."

Some, however, see a chance for a rebound by Chinese battery makers. China is also ramping up ESS investment, and once plants under construction in Europe start up, they could further encroach on Europe's EV battery market.

The European Union (EU) is currently imposing high tariffs on Chinese EVs. It is also finalizing details of the Industrial Acceleration Act (IAA), pursued to counter China and protect domestic industry, ahead of its entry into force. In response, Chinese battery makers including CATL and BYD are building plants in Hungary and Poland.

A battery industry official said, "The U.S. administration of Donald Trump and Congress are tightening curbs on Chinese products, but China is also a powerhouse with over a 90% share in the global grid-scale ESS market," adding, "Korean companies should diversify supply chains beyond the United States to other countries."

title: Democratic Win Set to Reshuffle U.S. Energy Policy: Capacity Ambitions, Manufacturing ...
description:
Operational U.S. solar manufacturing includes capacity for ~65 GWdc modules, ~20 GWdc cells, limited wafers (~3 GWdc), and polysilicon.
In November 2024, a Chinese manufacturer (Deye/Sol-Ark related) remotely disabled some U.S. inverters amid a commercial dispute, demonstrating operational control capability.
Of the utilities surveyed (representing about 12% of installed U.S. capacity), 86% relied on at least one such supplier.
Strider identified at least 5.4 GW of solar capacity at sites in 22 states using equipment from companies it rated high-risk.
U.S. manufacturing has expanded meaningfully for modules and storage systems, yet China retains decisive control of upstream capacity and large shares of critical components.
text:
Blue states and Democratic-led policies continue to drive aggressive targets for wind, solar, and battery storage as part of broader clean-energy mandates. California aims for 100% carbon-free electricity by 2045, New York for a zero-emissions grid by 2040, and similar Renewable Portfolio Standards (RPS) or Clean Electricity Standards (CES) in other Democratic-leaning states push high shares of intermittent resources plus storage. These policies, layered on federal incentives from the Inflation Reduction Act (IRA) era and subsequent measures, seek major grid additions amid rising demand from data centers, electrification, and economic growth.

How Much More Will Be Added to the Grid?

Recent data show rapid growth. In Q2 2026, the U.S. added nearly 7.5 GW of utility-scale solar (up 21% year-over-year), a record 5.6 GW of battery storage, and 5.1 GW of wind, according to S&P Global analysis. Solar and storage accounted for a large share of new capacity in the first half of 2026. EIA data and industry reports indicate utility-scale solar capacity expanding significantly, with projections for tens of GW more in the near term; one analysis noted nearly 300 GW of solar and over 212 GW of storage targeted for 2026–2031.

BloombergNEF forecasts more than 1 TW of combined solar, wind, and storage additions from 2026 to 2036—more than double end-2025 levels—driven in part by data-center demand, even as some tax credits phase down. Storage is particularly strong: U.S. deployments hit records, with cumulative utility-scale capacity rising sharply (e.g., reports of ~165 GWh installed by early 2026 in some tallies) and further tens of GWh expected annually. Co-location of solar with storage is rising (to ~16% of solar projects recently, projected higher). Red states currently hold a larger overall planned capacity pipeline (including substantial gas), while blue states’ plans are more heavily weighted toward pure renewables. Actual additions face interconnection queues, transmission needs, and supply constraints.

Manufacturing: U.S. Progress vs. China Dominance

The U.S. has made measurable gains in domestic manufacturing, spurred by the IRA’s production tax credits and related policies. Rhodium Group’s Clean Investment Monitor (Q3 2026) tracks roughly doubled capacity for battery modules/cells and solar cells versus early 2025 levels, plus ~50% expansion in solar modules, wind blades, and nacelles. Operational U.S. solar manufacturing includes capacity for ~65 GWdc modules, ~20 GWdc cells, limited wafers (~3 GWdc), and polysilicon. SEIA and other reports note module capacity sufficient for much or all of near-term U.S. demand in some assessments (~60–70+ GW range cited), with battery pack/module capacity also ramping toward or meeting domestic storage needs in recent tallies (e.g., tens to hundreds of GWh operational or announced). Wind component capacity largely covers current deployment levels. Dozens of new or expanded facilities have come online, supporting jobs and reducing some import reliance (solar imports fell notably in 2025).

China remains dominant in the global supply chain. It accounts for roughly 80% of solar modules, 85–95%+ of wafers/cells/polysilicon in various segments, ~70%+ of lithium battery cells, major shares of cathode/anode materials, and substantial inverter and wind component production. Chinese firms hold large shares of global battery shipments for storage. Even as U.S. assembly and some midstream capacity grows, upstream materials, cells, and specialized components often trace back to Chinese production or Chinese-linked investment. Some U.S. factories involve Chinese technology, partnerships, or capital attracted by incentives. Tariffs, Foreign Entity of Concern rules, and domestic-content bonuses aim to shift this, but full independence is incomplete—especially for high-volume, low-cost upstream steps. The result is partial onshoring rather than decoupling: more final assembly in the U.S., persistent dependence on China for key inputs.

Cybersecurity Concerns: Inverters, Radios, and Remote Risks

Rapid deployment of inverter-based resources (solar and storage) introduces cybersecurity questions, particularly with Chinese-manufactured equipment. A May 2025 Reuters investigation reported that U.S. experts examining Chinese solar inverters and batteries found undocumented communication devices, including cellular radios, not listed in product documentation. These could potentially enable remote access bypassing standard firewalls. In November 2024, a Chinese manufacturer (Deye/Sol-Ark related) remotely disabled some U.S. inverters amid a commercial dispute, demonstrating operational control capability.

Reports from Strider Technologies and others note high reliance on PRC-linked suppliers among utilities, with companies like Huawei, Sungrow, and others holding significant market shares in utility/commercial segments (Chinese vendors ~half or more in recent years). Washington Post coverage and congressional letters have highlighted risks of remote manipulation that could contribute to grid instability or blackouts. Software vulnerabilities in various inverter brands have been documented and patched; broader concerns include China’s national security laws requiring cooperation with intelligence services and documented pre-positioning activity (e.g., Volt Typhoon) on U.S. critical infrastructure. No widespread proven “kill switch” has been publicly confirmed across the fleet, and many systems have layered protections. However, the combination of scale, remote connectivity, and foreign-origin hardware creates material openings that utilities, CISA, DOE, and lawmakers continue to assess. Domestic or allied inverter manufacturing and stricter supply-chain rules are part of mitigation efforts.

Manufacturing of Wind, Solar, and Storage Components: Progress and Persistent Gaps

U.S. manufacturing of renewable components has expanded substantially since the Inflation Reduction Act, but the gains are uneven and concentrated in downstream assembly rather than a fully independent supply chain. As of Q3 2026, Rhodium Group’s Clean Investment Monitor tracks 131 operational solar manufacturing projects (up from 110 earlier in 2025). These facilities offer roughly 10 GWdc of polysilicon capacity, 3 GWdc of wafers, 20 GWdc of cells, and 65 GWdc of modules (including thin-film). SEIA data from around the same period puts operational module capacity higher in some tallies (approaching or exceeding 70–75 GWdc in later 2026 updates), enough on paper to meet or exceed near-term U.S. demand in certain scenarios. Cell capacity has grown sharply from near-zero post-2019 levels, and the first new ingot/wafer lines in years came online in late 2025. Battery progress is stronger still: operational cell and module capacity has roughly doubled since early 2025 in Rhodium tracking, with some industry figures citing tens of GWh of cell capacity and over 100 GWh of module/pack capacity operational or ramping—sufficient in reports to cover a large share of domestic storage demand. Wind component capacity (blades, nacelles, towers) largely matches current annual deployment levels of several GW.

These numbers represent real onshoring. Solar module capacity rose several-fold from pre-IRA levels of around 7–8 GW, and dozens of new factories support tens of thousands of jobs. Battery assembly has scaled particularly quickly as automakers and others pivot capacity toward stationary storage. Imports of finished modules and some storage systems have declined as a result.

The gaps remain large, however. Upstream production lags: polysilicon capacity covers only a fraction of deployment needs (around 20% in some 2025 comparisons), and wafer capacity is even thinner (single-digit percentages relative to demand). Much of the module capacity still relies on imported cells, wafers, or materials. China retains overwhelming global shares—typically 80%+ of modules, 85–95%+ of wafers and cells, and the large majority of polysilicon—while also dominating battery cell production (~70%+ globally, with Chinese firms capturing the bulk of storage shipments). Critical minerals processing and anode/cathode materials are similarly concentrated. Even U.S.-assembled products frequently incorporate Chinese or Chinese-linked inputs. Some Chinese firms or technology partners have invested in U.S. facilities to access IRA credits, further blurring the line between “domestic” and foreign-controlled capacity. Wind is less extreme but still sees substantial Chinese influence in global nacelle and blade production.

The net effect is partial success: the U.S. can assemble more finished modules and storage systems at home, reducing some finished-goods import dependence, but it has not closed the upstream bottlenecks that keep it reliant on Chinese capacity for the highest-volume, lowest-cost steps. Full vertical integration remains limited, and announced capacity often exceeds what is operational or under firm construction. Tariffs, Foreign Entity of Concern restrictions, and domestic-content bonuses are pushing further shifts, yet scale and cost advantages still favor Chinese supply chains for many components.

Cybersecurity Risks: Inverters, Radios, and Remote Access Vectors

The rapid addition of inverter-based resources creates concentrated points of potential vulnerability, especially where equipment originates from Chinese manufacturers with ties to the Chinese state. Inverters convert DC power from solar panels or batteries to grid-compatible AC and are increasingly networked for monitoring, control, and firmware updates. They sit at the interface between generation/storage and the bulk power system.

A May 2025 Reuters investigation reported that U.S. experts examining Chinese-made solar inverters and batteries found undocumented communication devices, including cellular radios, that were not listed in product documentation. These could enable remote communication channels outside normal utility firewalls and controls. Separately, in November 2024, the Chinese firm Deye (associated with some Sol-Ark branded units) remotely disabled inverters in the U.S. and elsewhere during a commercial dispute with a distributor—demonstrating retained manufacturer-level operational control over installed hardware. Software vulnerabilities are better documented: analyses such as Forescout’s have identified dozens of issues across brands (including Chinese ones), many later patched.

Strider Technologies’ late-2025 report “In Broad Daylight” quantified exposure using utility data and import records. Nearly half of inverter and battery energy storage system imports into the U.S. from 2015–2024 came from high-risk PRC manufacturers. Of the utilities surveyed (representing about 12% of installed U.S. capacity), 86% relied on at least one such supplier. Specific high-risk names cited include Huawei (Entity List, banned from U.S. 5G networks for espionage concerns, though no blanket federal ban on its solar inverters), Sungrow, and CATL (labeled a Chinese military company by the U.S. Department of War in 2025). Strider identified at least 5.4 GW of solar capacity at sites in 22 states using equipment from companies it rated high-risk. Wood Mackenzie data indicate Chinese-headquartered makers held roughly half the U.S. commercial/utility inverter market in 2024–2025 (higher shares in some utility segments), with more than 90% of U.S. inverters over the prior decade imported. Globally, Huawei and Sungrow alone have accounted for roughly half of utility-scale shipments in recent years.

Chinese law requires companies to cooperate with intelligence services, creating a structural pathway for potential state access. Broader context includes documented Chinese pre-positioning activity (Volt Typhoon and related groups) on U.S. critical infrastructure networks. Congressional letters (including from dozens of lawmakers) and Washington Post reporting have highlighted the risk that compromised or remotely controllable inverters could contribute to grid instability or cascading outages. No public evidence has confirmed a widespread, intentional “kill switch” deployed across the U.S. fleet, and many systems incorporate layered protections, vendor monitoring restrictions, and air-gapping practices. Nonetheless, the combination of scale (tens of GW of Chinese-linked equipment already installed), remote connectivity features, undocumented components, demonstrated remote disable capability, and state-linked suppliers constitutes a material national-security concern that utilities, CISA, DOE, and lawmakers continue to evaluate. Mitigation steps under discussion or underway include stricter import rules, domestic or allied inverter production incentives, supply-chain transparency requirements, and enhanced testing of connected equipment.

These manufacturing and cybersecurity realities mean that accelerated renewable additions under blue-state and Democratic priorities will, in the near term, continue to rely heavily on Chinese upstream capacity and components that carry documented security risks, even as U.S. assembly capacity grows.

Political Landscape and Consumer Willingness

State policies remain the primary driver in blue states, with Democratic priorities emphasizing rapid renewable and storage buildout alongside federal tax incentives. Recent national politics have introduced more protectionist and all-of-the-above elements (tariffs, selective credit adjustments), but blue-state mandates continue. Electricity prices are higher on average in many blue states with aggressive RPS/CES (California rates roughly double the national average; New York elevated), though causation is debated. Factors include wildfire mitigation and distribution costs in California, rate design, transmission needs, and historical baselines—not solely the renewable share. Some analyses find utility-scale renewables correlated with lower or neutral prices, while rooftop solar and certain mandates can shift costs. Wind-heavy red states often have lower prices.

Consumers show broad support for more renewables in principle (polls often in the 70% range favoring expanded clean energy), but cost sensitivity is high. Large majorities report rising bills and prioritize affordability and reliability over pure emissions reductions. Willingness to pay premiums appears limited; many prefer efficiency, all-of-the-above mixes, or lower bills. Data-center and load growth is amplifying pressure everywhere. Whether voters in high-mandate states accept sustained higher rates for faster renewable penetration remains an open political question as deployment scales.

In short, Democratic-leaning policies are set to accelerate wind, solar, and storage additions measured in tens to hundreds of GW over coming years. U.S. manufacturing has expanded meaningfully for modules and storage systems, yet China retains decisive control of upstream capacity and large shares of critical components. Cyber risks in connected Chinese-origin equipment are documented enough to warrant ongoing scrutiny and diversification. Consumers broadly like the idea of renewables but show clear limits on paying significantly more.

title: Opinion - Educators and families, read past the talking points on tax credits - Yahoo
description:
For more than 20 years, I was a public school teacher and a proud member of the National Education Association.
First, taxpayer-funded nonprofits and parents, alongside teachers, can decide how to use the tax credit, putting resources where families know their children need them.
The NEA calls the new tax credit a "private school voucher" that diverts money from public education.
The tax credit program is built around what a student needs, whether that's tutoring, special needs services, or other learning expenses.
Governors are now deciding whether their states will participate in the federal Education Freedom Tax Credit program.
text:
For more than 20 years, I was a public school teacher and a proud member of the National Education Association. I still believe in the work public schools do, which is why I'm excited about the opportunities the federal Education Freedom Tax Credit provides and why I'm urging my fellow educators to give it a serious look.

Two important things are happening, and both will benefit students across the country. First, taxpayer-funded nonprofits and parents, alongside teachers, can decide how to use the tax credit, putting resources where families know their children need them. As teachers, we don't need a long policy paper to know that when parents are engaged, students benefit.

Right now, most of what teachers hear about the program comes from organizations they've trusted for years, including their unions. The NEA calls the new tax credit a "private school voucher" that diverts money from public education. That description leaves out how the program actually works.

The tax credit program is built around what a student needs, whether that's tutoring, special needs services, or other learning expenses. Some estimates show 90 percent of students nationwide could qualify, including those in their existing public schools.

Beginning Jan. 1, people who donate to approved nonprofit scholarship granting organizations can claim a federal tax credit of up to $1,700, or up to $3,400 for a married couple. Those organizations then provide funding for eligible students to cover qualified education expenses.

Picture a student who loves his school but is struggling in math. His teacher knows that a few hours of one-on-one tutoring each week would make an enormous difference. But with 25 other students to teach, the teacher simply doesn't have the extra hours that the boy needs.

Traditionally, that extra time is paid for out of pocket by a family hiring a tutor. But not every family can afford this option. A family without those additional resources hopes the school's supports will be enough. That gap has always bothered me. Educational customization already exists. The real question is who can afford it.

Teachers feel that gap acutely. We're asked to differentiate instruction, manage classrooms, meet special education requirements, support students emotionally and personalize it all for every learner. Great teachers try, but right now, they're in desperate need of additional support.

Recent polling found that only one in three educators feels that they matter a great deal at their school, with those who feel undervalued reporting higher rates of burnout and a greater likelihood of leaving the profession.

Educators know there are only so many hours in a school day and only so much expertise one person can hold. Saying so isn't an indictment of public education. It's an acknowledgment that teachers are human, and resources are limited.

The new tax credit will ease that burden and provide students access to scholarship funds to cover tutoring, learning materials or specialized services. Parents will have financial support to meet the needs that too often land on a teacher's desk, and teachers will get back time for what we came to do: teach.

Too often, education debates cast parents and teachers as opponents when they're frustrated by the same problem. A parent sees a child struggling and asks for more. The teacher agrees but lacks the staff, time or expertise to deliver it. Both want the same thing: for that child to thrive.

Governors are now deciding whether their states will participate in the federal Education Freedom Tax Credit program. Taxpayers nationwide can claim the credit by donating to scholarship granting organizations in participating states, regardless of where they live. However, students in states that choose not to participate will miss out on the educational opportunities these scholarships will provide.

That's why teachers and parents need to read beyond the talking points. The NEA has made its position clear. Treasury and the IRS describe the program as a tax credit for contributions to organizations that fund K-12 scholarships. Read both. Look at the statute and the regulations. Find out whether your state is participating and what that means for kids in your community. Then reach your own conclusion.

Supporting public schools and recognizing that a student sometimes needs something more are not contradictory ideas. Just ask, could this be one more tool that helps a child get what they need to thrive?

If the answer might be yes, teachers and families deserve the chance to invest in our students' futures.

Tracie Canestrari is the senior manager of Implementation at yes. every kid. foundation. She taught in public schools for more than 20 years and was a longtime member of the National Education Association.

text:
An electric vehicle can do more than get its driver from one place to another. For U.S. homeowners, EVs can keep appliances, and even entire homes, running, even when the power goes out.

One resident with a Hyundai Ioniq 5 shared their experience using their EV to power their home on Reddit's r/AnkerSOLIXCommunity.

Here's what to know

In a Reddit post, the original poster described connecting an S5000 to their home's electrical panel, with the Ioniq 5 serving as an additional battery source during outages. After the homeowner purchased the power station, they reported spending about two hours installing the setup.

Once the homeowner disconnected the panel from grid power, the S5000 supplied electricity to the house through its 240-volt output. The installation included a panel interlock and a generator inlet connected to a 30-amp breaker.

Meanwhile, the Ioniq 5 supplied power through a vehicle-to-load adapter, with the S5000 reporting approximately 1,700 watts of charging input.

The OP added, "With all this in place, the S5000 was happily charging at about 1,700W while handling whatever loads the house needed. I was totally pleased with how easy this install went and how well the system works in practice. I was surprised at how little power my house draws at steady state. My house has a natural gas furnace, hot water heater, and stove. I should be able to run for multiple days during an outage with this setup."

With ordinary household appliances running, demand settled around 1,000 watts. Switching on both the gas-fired furnace and the electric dryer brought that figure only slightly above 2,000 watts, according to the OP.

Commenters streamed into the thread to compliment the setup and ask clarifying questions. One wrote, "Nifty, for some reason I had never thought of using an EV as a house battery too, that's pretty cool."

Another commenter added, "I'm doing the same with my Ioniq 5 and an EcoFlow Delta 3 Pro, works very well. I've had the setup for two years." A third user simply wrote, "Using the Ioniq as a bigger battery bank is a clever setup."

Where can I learn more?

Making an EV part of a home backup setup means figuring out what needs power during an outage.

• In California, researchers are testing EVs that power homes during outages and reduce peak-hour bills.

• A homeowner used a 5-kWh battery backup system to keep four circuits running through storms.

• A homeowner powered two-thirds of the house with a Guardian 6000, revealing two weak spots.

title: Strategies for supply chain risks in energy transition - The Korea Times
description:

It has become virtually impossible to rely solely on price competition to address supply chain risks in energy transition technologies.
However, supply chain risks associated with energy transition technologies are global in nature, and there are limits to addressing these risks through fragmented, domestically-focused policies alone.

Discussions primarily focused on which demand-side measures to adopt and how to collaborate to reduce supply chain risks.
text:
Having painfully experienced the vulnerability of fossil fuel dependence through the war in Ukraine and conflicts in the Middle East, the world is accelerating the transition to clean energy.

Paradoxically, however, in an effort to escape the risks of fossil fuel supply chains, countries are now facing a new risk: dependence on specific nations for energy transition technologies. Korea is highly dependent on China for its energy transition technology supply chains.

In the solar power sector, the share of Chinese-made modules rose sharply from 29 percent in 2023 to 58 percent in 2024 and reached 69 percent last year. In just two years, dominance has shifted from domestically produced products to ones from a single foreign country.

Furthermore, the share of Korean-made cells — the core components of solar modules — plummeted from 35 percent in 2021 to just 4 percent last year. This is attributed to the fact that more than 80 percent of domestic solar power plants are small-scale facilities under 100 kW, making them price-sensitive for smaller investors. Moreover, the cells produced domestically are primarily exported to the United States.

The situation is not much better for batteries used in electric vehicles (EVs) or energy storage systems (ESS). In August alone, domestically produced EVs equipped with Chinese-made batteries accounted for over 40 percent of sales, a 16 percentage point increase from a year earlier.

Dependence on the supply chain is even more severe. As of last year, Korea relied on China for approximately 98 percent of its graphite, a key material for anodes, and 94 percent of its precursor materials critical for cathodes. This means that any restrictions on upstream materials could impact the entire industry. The same applies not only to batteries used in electric vehicles but also to ESS batteries, which are experiencing explosive growth due to the proliferation of artificial intelligence (AI) data centers and the need to stabilize power grids.

It has become virtually impossible to rely solely on price competition to address supply chain risks in energy transition technologies.

Consequently, the Korean government has recently been formulating various non-price policies encompassing subsidies, tax incentives and public procurement systems. Notable examples include the Korea Energy Agency’s competitive bidding process for meeting renewable energy supply obligations, which awards differential points based on whether carbon emission-verified modules are used, and the Ministry of Climate, Energy and Environment’s introduction of bonus points for low-carbon certification in its carbon-neutral facility support program.

Furthermore, through amendments to the Act on Restriction on Special Cases Concerning Taxation, low-carbon modules with carbon emissions of 655 kg·CO₂/kW or less have been included in the scope of the integrated investment tax credit.

In addition, the government plans to grant tax credits starting next year for products in the solar power, wind power and secondary battery sectors if they are produced domestically. Linking tax benefits not only to simple technological investment but also to the installation of power generation facilities and the production of specific items represents a significant step forward across various clean energy sources.

However, supply chain risks associated with energy transition technologies are global in nature, and there are limits to addressing these risks through fragmented, domestically-focused policies alone.

This is not unique to Korea. I led a delegation of Korean companies to attend the Europe-Asia Clean Policy Workshop held in Paris from Oct. 26 to 27. Now in its fourth year, this event organized by the Institut Montaigne, a leading European think tank, served as a forum for Europe, Korea and Japan to discuss how they can collaborate on energy transition. The key topic at the event, which included government officials, corporate representatives and experts from each country, was focused strongly on supply chain risks for energy transition technologies.

Discussions primarily focused on which demand-side measures to adopt and how to collaborate to reduce supply chain risks. In particular, participants shared their countries’ experiences and proposed cooperation strategies regarding environmental, social and governance (ESG) criteria in public procurement, local content requirements, long-term offtake arrangements, carbon contracts, industrial partnerships for advanced technologies, and joint ventures aimed at strengthening supply chain security.

One notable proposal was “mutual recognition and market sharing” based on ESG and trust. The aim is to jointly reduce supply chain risks by linking and mutually recognizing the standards of each country’s relevant policies such as government support, public procurement and ESG regulations.This involves actions like mutually recognizing the verification of product-specific carbon emissions, which serves as the basis for imposing carbon border taxes or providing electric vehicle subsidies. If one country’s calculations of product-specific carbon emissions are recognized by another, the effectiveness of supply chain risk mitigation policies — which grant preferential treatment based on these emissions — will increase. This approach capitalizes on the fact that China’s carbon emissions from electricity used in manufacturing are relatively high.

The energy transition is not simply a matter of replacing or expanding power plants; it also requires the broader industrial ecosystem to evolve and demand for these technologies is expected to keep growing. Rather than becoming ever more dependent on a single country because of low prices and large volumes, countries should link their markets and standards and pursue cooperation on a principled basis. In my view, Korea already has the industrial base, ESG standards and international trust needed to make this happen.

Kim Sung-woo, head of Environment & Energy Research Institute at Kim & Chang, is a board member of Korea Institute of Energy Technology Evaluation and Planning.

title: COP31 starts Monday. As global temperatures continue to rise, do climate talks matter?
authors: Rachel Waldholz, Ayesha Rascoe, www.tpr.org, ayesha-rascoe
description:
AYESHA RASCOE, HOST: Tens of thousands of people are gathering in Antalya, Turkey, for U.N. negotiations on climate change - COP31.
NPR climate editor Rachel Waldholz joins us now.
This is a question I ask myself every year as I'm preparing to spend two weeks following the ins and outs of U.N. climate negotiations.
You know, the big idea behind COP is that climate change is a global problem, and it requires a global solution.
They need money to adapt to the impacts of climate change and to deal with the damage they're already experiencing.
text:
AYESHA RASCOE, HOST:

Tens of thousands of people are gathering in Antalya, Turkey, for U.N. negotiations on climate change - COP31. These annual talks have been going on for more than three decades. In that time, the planet has only gotten hotter. That raises the question, what's the point of all this talking? NPR climate editor Rachel Waldholz joins us now. Hi, Rachel.

RACHEL WALDHOLZ, BYLINE: Hi, Ayesha.

RASCOE: So another year, another U.N. climate conference. What is the point?

WALDHOLZ: Yeah. This is a question I ask myself every year as I'm preparing to spend two weeks following the ins and outs of U.N. climate negotiations. You know, the big idea behind COP is that climate change is a global problem, and it requires a global solution. No one country can manage it on their own.

So you have countries like the U.S. and in Europe and now China, as well, which are responsible for most of the past pollution that has caused global warming. You have countries like India and Indonesia whose emissions have been growing.

And then you have developing countries that have hardly contributed to climate change at all that are (ph) dealing with some of the worst impacts, you know, just like the massive flooding that we saw in Nepal this year. And those countries need money. They need money to adapt to the impacts of climate change and to deal with the damage they're already experiencing.

And so the goal of COP climate talks comes down to, like, those two things - finding the money and cutting greenhouse gas emissions, which mainly means transitioning away from fossil fuels - like coal, oil and gas - and is not easy.

RASCOE: President Trump calls climate change a hoax and a con job, a scam. Is the U.S. playing any role at all this year?

WALDHOLZ: The U.S. will not be taking part in the talks this year, and that's because the Trump administration announced last year that it would withdraw from the U.N. climate negotiations altogether. The State Department says the U.S. isn't sending anyone to Turkey.

And if you talk to negotiators for other countries, the attitude towards the U.S. is often sort of can't live with them, can't live without them. Historically, the U.S. has been at the negotiating table, and other countries often found it very frustrating because the U.S. blocked a lot of climate efforts over the years. But the U.S. was also instrumental in getting the Paris Climate Agreement, sort of the biggest success of these talks so far.

So ultimately, the U.S. is the second biggest climate polluter after China. It's the world's biggest economy. It's really hard to make progress when it's not in the room.

RASCOE: So are these negotiations having any impact?

WALDHOLZ: I mean, the world is making progress. You know, after years of growing steadily year over year, global greenhouse gas emissions this past year were basically flat, although U.S. emissions did tick up. And some countries have actually managed to cut their emissions, including countries in the European Union. It looks like China's emissions have plateaued or might be dropping. And renewable energy is growing way faster than anyone thought was possible a decade ago.

We now have the Iran war, which is prompting these major shifts in the global economy, and that's spurring some countries to invest in electric vehicles, more wind and solar power, battery storage - what are called electrification technologies. It's just that right now, none of these changes are happening fast enough to avoid, frankly, pretty disastrous levels of warming in the decades ahead.

RASCOE: So, Rachel, what are you going to be watching for this year?

WALDHOLZ: One key issue this year is, can countries agree to speed up that transition away from fossil fuels? Can they electrify more of their economies? And the other is, can they find more creative ways to provide climate finance to the countries that need it? And I'll also be watching to see if players like China or potentially the European Union can step into that gap left by the absence of the U.S.

RASCOE: That's NPR's Rachel Waldholz. Thank you so much.

WALDHOLZ: Thanks, Ayesha. Transcript provided by NPR, Copyright NPR.

text:
Mercedes-Benz Chairman Ola Källenius told reporters at a media roundtable in Pune on November 4 that the combustion engine isn't going anywhere soon. "The combustion engine, it will be around for minimum 10, probably 15 years more," he said, pushing back directly on the idea that automakers are racing toward an all-electric lineup by 2030 or 2035.

This wasn't a hedge or a vague talking point. Källenius backed it with real product news: Mercedes has updated its entire combustion lineup, including a new V8, to meet Euro 7 emissions standards, making it the first manufacturer to do so. Diesel stays in the mix too. If you're shopping a combustion or hybrid Mercedes right now, the company just told you it plans to keep building, selling, and supporting that powertrain well into the 2030s.

Why Mercedes Is Still Investing In A New V8

Building a Euro 7-compliant V8 from scratch isn't cheap, and it's not the move of a company quietly planning to kill combustion off. Källenius framed it as proof that Mercedes is serious about serving customers who aren't ready to go electric, or whose driving habits don't suit it yet.

Diesel gets the same treatment. "Our portfolio of diesel engines is ready for the future," Källenius said, pointing specifically at drivers who rack up 60,000 to 70,000 kilometers a year and light commercial vehicle operators. Those are buyers for whom an EV's range and charging downtime simply don't pencil out yet, and Mercedes isn't willing to lose them to a competitor still selling diesel wagons and vans.

The 20-25 Year Transition Nobody Wants To Say Out Loud

Källenius described the shift to electric mobility as a 20 to 25 year industrial transformation, not the decade-long flip that headlines about 2030 or 2035 EV mandates tend to imply. His reasoning: "If you're an incumbent, you don't cut off the leg that you stand on right now and you build a new one."

That's a notably blunt admission from the chairman of a company that announced in 2020 it would be ready to go fully electric by decade's end, market conditions permitting. The first wave of EVs undersold expectations, by his own account, and Mercedes is now only 12 to 18 months into what it calls its second generation of electric vehicles, including the newly launched electric GLC. Zero-emission mobility remains the eventual destination, he said, but a fully electric market is still a long way off.

What This Means If You're Buying A Combustion Mercedes Today

Mercedes says it will offer an electric alternative across every meaningful model position by the end of the decade, so EV shoppers won't be left without options. But the company is explicitly telling the other half of its customer base, the ones buying a gas or diesel C-Class , GLC, or Sprinter van this year, that parts, service, and engine development aren't going to dry up.

"As long as there's meaningful demand for... high-tech, in our case electrified ICE, we have that as well," Källenius said. For buyers weighing a combustion or hybrid Mercedes against an electric one, that's about as direct a reassurance as a luxury automaker is going to give.

title: Trump Admin Caught Illegally Canceling Billion-Dollar Solar Project That Would Have ... - Futurism
description:
Donald Trump and his Republican lackeys were decimated in this week’s midterm elections, in large part thanks to an ongoing cost of living crisis.
Much of that pain could have been avoided — or at least pre-empted — had the Trump administration allowed a billion-dollar solar panel development project go ahead as planned, Boston-area public radio station WBUR reported.
According to the broadcaster’s reporting, the Environmental Protection Agency under Trump appointee Lee Zeldin has refused to dish out billions of congressionally-approved funds meant to expand access to solar energy in low-income communities.
The Biden-era program, dubbed “Solar For All,” earmarked $7 billion for distribution to solar energy developments led by states and Tribal governments.
Though it might be one of the more ironic examples of Zeldin’s EPA shooting itself in the foot, it’s hardly the first.
text:
Donald Trump and his Republican lackeys were decimated in this week’s midterm elections, in large part thanks to an ongoing cost of living crisis. While there are many factors making life hard on Americans financially, one of the key stressors is the cost of energy, which has skyrocketed in the wake of the tech industry’s data center buildout.

Much of that pain could have been avoided — or at least pre-empted — had the Trump administration allowed a billion-dollar solar panel development project go ahead as planned, Boston-area public radio station WBUR reported.

According to the broadcaster’s reporting, the Environmental Protection Agency under Trump appointee Lee Zeldin has refused to dish out billions of congressionally-approved funds meant to expand access to solar energy in low-income communities.

The Biden-era program, dubbed “Solar For All,” earmarked $7 billion for distribution to solar energy developments led by states and Tribal governments. States like Massachusetts and Michigan were previously approved for $156 million, while others like Arkansas were set to receive over $93 million.

But when it came time for the federal government to pay the piper, Zeldin and the EPA refused, calling it a “boondoggle.” That decision set off an immediate legal battle, which was recently resolved in favor of the Solar For All recipients. Despite a federal court order that the government dish out the funds, the EPA has yet to loosen its purse strings, leaving questions as to whether the agency will appeal the decision — or even ignore it entirely.

“This is a program that has the potential to lower people’s energy bills, get inexpensive clean electricity on the grid, and help the communities that the Solar For All program was designed to help,” senior attorney at the Conservation Law Foundation James Crowley, who is representing plaintiffs in one of the court cases, told WBUR.

Though it might be one of the more ironic examples of Zeldin’s EPA shooting itself in the foot, it’s hardly the first. Zeldin, a former center-right Republican turned MAGA-die hard, has moved aggressively to dismantle dozens of environmental regulations since winning the job, many of which were explicitly designed to protect poor American communities.

So while Trump’s side may have lost handily in the midterms, it’s clear his administration’s war on poor and working class Americans is far from over — as the ongoing refusal to release cheap, green energy makes abundantly clear.

title: Democrats plan to push clean energy to lower bills and challenge Trump's fossil fuel agenda

text:
Some Democrats are promising to push for more clean energy to help tackle rising energy costs when they take control of Congress in January, though President Donald Trump says he will use his veto power aggressively.

With new majorities in the House and Senate after last week’s midterms, Democrats can set an agenda boosting clean energy and addressing climate change. While those are traditionally core priorities of the party, climate was not a central topic in this election cycle.

Democrats can begin investigations and hold hearings into climate policy rollbacks and elimination of green energy grants by the Republican administration, potentially trying to undo some changes and restore renewable energy incentives.

Sen. Sheldon Whitehouse of Rhode Island, the top Democrat on the Senate Committee on Environment and Public Works, said Trump’s clean energy attacks drove up prices for taxpayers. He said Democrats will “work every angle to lower consumers’ energy costs, and we will demand accountability for the massive corruption wrought by Trump’s fossil-fuel donors.”

American Clean Power Association CEO Jason Grumet said everybody who is trying to build clean energy “feels bolstered.”

Enacting major changes would require Republican support because Democrats will lack the numbers to override presidential vetoes. Even then, lower energy bills are not guaranteed because prices also depend on fuel costs, demand and the expense of maintaining the electric grid.

“The wins give Democrats more leverage over spending and more political power to advance a coherent agenda; the question is whether they’ll use that power effectively,” said Lisa Sachs, director of the Columbia Center on Sustainable Investment. “The vote was for affordability and opportunity. Democrats now need to be clear about which policies deliver them.”

Trump holds veto power but thinks he and Democrats can deal

Trump said after Tuesday’s election that Democrats will send over “things that are insane” and he will veto them, speaking generally about legislation. But in the comments to Fox News, he predicted that “after a couple of months of vetoes,” he and Democrats will find ways to work together.

The White House said in a statement Wednesday that Trump is “committed to unleashing reliable, affordable, and secure energy sources to lower prices, strengthen our grid, and protect our national security, and is willing to work with anyone to accomplish this.”

Trump promised to lower energy prices. Instead, his war with Iran and other policies increased the price of gasoline, diesel and electricity. At the same time, the administration canceled many clean energy projects and grants and slowed clean energy permitting.

Trump particularly dislikes offshore wind. Developer Orsted said Thursday that Revolution Wind, a large wind farm in federal waters off Rhode Island, has started operating commercially.

Will the president change his tune on green energy? That’s doubtful, said former Sen. Byron Dorgan, D-N.D., co-chair of the government relations practice at ArentFox Schiff.

“He is likely to keep pushing his energy issues, and I think he will be forced to give some room for a new Congress to recreate a different strategy that will add clean energy,” Dorgan said in an email.

Trump promotes expanding production of oil, natural gas and coal, which cause climate change, because he argues that would give the U.S. the lowest-cost electricity. Mike Sommers, CEO of the American Petroleum Institute, the oil and gas industry’s top lobbying group, said that as voters have changed the balance of political power in Washington, “the affordability message is unmistakable.”

Sommers said in a statement there is a real opportunity for bipartisan cooperation to reduce costs and strengthen the economy, starting with an energy permitting reform proposal announced in September. The Senate is expected to hold a procedural vote Monday on the legislation, which is aimed at shortening the timeline to get big energy projects started.

Ife Kilimanjaro, executive director of the U.S. Climate Action Network, said Democrats should reject that proposal and use their stronger position to pass legislation that actually builds out much-needed clean energy.

Reversing Trump’s anti-climate policies

The administration has reshaped the Environmental Protection Agency, reversing pollution limits as it promotes fossil fuels.

Clear Street energy transition analyst Tim Moore said he expects Democrats to investigate the climate and environmental rollbacks, in an effort to block some from taking effect. Democrats could also try amending the Clean Air Act to cut carbon pollution and push back against EPA budget cuts, he added.

Rep. Sean Casten, D-Ill., said he is cautiously optimistic some Republicans will now seek to differentiate themselves from Trump and back pro-environmental policies. But without Republican support, Democrats’ more ambitious bills will largely lay out their agenda for 2028, he added.

Climate is not necessarily at the top of Democrats’ list of priorities. They are targeting healthcare access, trade tariffs and the Iran war.

Rep. Frank Pallone, the New Jersey Democrat who is expected to become chair of the House Energy and Commerce Committee, said the party should focus on healthcare, affordability, consumer and environmental protections, clean energy and regulating Big Tech.

A potential stalemate seen on clean energy and climate policy

David Victor, a professor of innovation and public policy at the University of California, San Diego, largely expects a stalemate at the federal level on climate and energy policy because of the divided government. He said agreement could come on some bipartisan measures such as a permitting overhaul.

Victor thinks Democratic-led investigations and hearings will center on corruption and other topics that may only touch on energy and climate. Like Casten, Victor said many of the Democratic bills likely will not become law, but will outline what Democrats could accomplish if they win the White House in 2028.

“The Democrats are going to be drafting things that the administration’s not going to like. They don’t have the votes to override a veto, and on top of it, the administration is going to be in turmoil because of its own electoral failures and because of all the investigations,” Victor said. “This seems to me, at the federal level, largely a recipe for kind of intense chaos over the next two years.”

One of the biggest wild cards is the behavior of the administration, which could use executive power to double down on rollbacks of climate and environmental rules, he said.

States could advance clean energy without waiting for Congress

Democrats scored victories in races for governor in states long controlled by Republicans, including Texas and Georgia.

Leah Stokes, a political scientist at the UC Santa Barbara, said there could be a lot of state action on climate next year because of those wins. That is where climate leadership has traditionally come from, she noted. At the federal level, Stokes is optimistic about extending clean energy tax credits since some Republicans support that.

Jay Inslee, a former Democratic governor and congressman from Washington, also expects growing momentum for clean energy in states that elected Democratic governors, particularly in states where they also won legislative majorities.

“This is a really powerful instrument for the United States to join the rest of the world and get back in a leadership position, even if we still have a climate denier that might exercise a veto on some things that we want to do federally,” Inslee said. “So I hope people will pay attention to the big progress we’re going to make on a state-level basis.”

___

Associated Press writers Alexa St. John and Matthew Daly contributed to this report.

text:
AYESHA RASCOE, HOST:

Tens of thousands of people are gathering in Antalya, Turkey, for U.N. negotiations on climate change - COP31. These annual talks have been going on for more than three decades. In that time, the planet has only gotten hotter. That raises the question, what's the point of all this talking? NPR climate editor Rachel Waldholz joins us now. Hi, Rachel.

RACHEL WALDHOLZ, BYLINE: Hi, Ayesha.

RASCOE: So another year, another U.N. climate conference. What is the point?

WALDHOLZ: Yeah. This is a question I ask myself every year as I'm preparing to spend two weeks following the ins and outs of U.N. climate negotiations. You know, the big idea behind COP is that climate change is a global problem, and it requires a global solution. No one country can manage it on their own.

So you have countries like the U.S. and in Europe and now China, as well, which are responsible for most of the past pollution that has caused global warming. You have countries like India and Indonesia whose emissions have been growing.

And then you have developing countries that have hardly contributed to climate change at all that are (ph) dealing with some of the worst impacts, you know, just like the massive flooding that we saw in Nepal this year. And those countries need money. They need money to adapt to the impacts of climate change and to deal with the damage they're already experiencing.

And so the goal of COP climate talks comes down to, like, those two things - finding the money and cutting greenhouse gas emissions, which mainly means transitioning away from fossil fuels - like coal, oil and gas - and is not easy.

RASCOE: President Trump calls climate change a hoax and a con job, a scam. Is the U.S. playing any role at all this year?

WALDHOLZ: The U.S. will not be taking part in the talks this year, and that's because the Trump administration announced last year that it would withdraw from the U.N. climate negotiations altogether. The State Department says the U.S. isn't sending anyone to Turkey.

And if you talk to negotiators for other countries, the attitude towards the U.S. is often sort of can't live with them, can't live without them. Historically, the U.S. has been at the negotiating table, and other countries often found it very frustrating because the U.S. blocked a lot of climate efforts over the years. But the U.S. was also instrumental in getting the Paris Climate Agreement, sort of the biggest success of these talks so far.

So ultimately, the U.S. is the second biggest climate polluter after China. It's the world's biggest economy. It's really hard to make progress when it's not in the room.

RASCOE: So are these negotiations having any impact?

WALDHOLZ: I mean, the world is making progress. You know, after years of growing steadily year over year, global greenhouse gas emissions this past year were basically flat, although U.S. emissions did tick up. And some countries have actually managed to cut their emissions, including countries in the European Union. It looks like China's emissions have plateaued or might be dropping. And renewable energy is growing way faster than anyone thought was possible a decade ago.

We now have the Iran war, which is prompting these major shifts in the global economy, and that's spurring some countries to invest in electric vehicles, more wind and solar power, battery storage - what are called electrification technologies. It's just that right now, none of these changes are happening fast enough to avoid, frankly, pretty disastrous levels of warming in the decades ahead.

RASCOE: So, Rachel, what are you going to be watching for this year?

WALDHOLZ: One key issue this year is, can countries agree to speed up that transition away from fossil fuels? Can they electrify more of their economies? And the other is, can they find more creative ways to provide climate finance to the countries that need it? And I'll also be watching to see if players like China or potentially the European Union can step into that gap left by the absence of the U.S.

RASCOE: That's NPR's Rachel Waldholz. Thank you so much.

WALDHOLZ: Thanks, Ayesha. Transcript provided by NPR, Copyright NPR.

text:
WASHINGTON, D.C. — The National Wildlife Federation issued the following statement on the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act and the substitute amendment proposed by the bill’s sponsors:

“The National Wildlife Federation has great respect for the lead negotiators of the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act and is grateful for their willingness to consider input and improvements,” said Collin O’Mara, president and CEO of the National Wildlife Federation. “We share their urgency in the need to reduce climate pollution by modernizing our grid and deploying more clean energy. We particularly appreciate the efforts to maximize the capacity of the existing transmission system through grid-enhancing technologies, responsibly site infrastructure in existing degraded rights-of-way rather than disturbing intact greenfields and wildlife habitat, and improve interregional and offshore transmission planning, as well as fund abandoned hardrock mine cleanup and coastal resilience.

“However, first and foremost, the National Wildlife Federation is a conservation organization dedicated to ensuring wildlife and people thrive in our rapidly changing world. The greatest threats to wildlife include habitat loss, invasive species, disease, and pollution, all of which are exacerbated by climate change. While wildlife survival urgently requires accelerating emission reductions, those gains are not guaranteed under this bill. Meanwhile, adverse impacts to wildlife, waters, Tribal lands, public lands, and communities will result from the package's statutory concessions affecting the Clean Water Act, National Environmental Policy Act, Endangered Species Act, and National Historic Preservation Act, as well as from restrictions on judicial remedies and the ability to revisit ecologically harmful decisions. These certain impacts on nature and wildlife should not be traded away for uncertain climate benefits.

“After closely evaluating the full bill and the newly released substitute amendment alongside our state and territorial affiliates, Tribal partners, environmental justice partners, hunting, fishing, and outdoor recreation partners, water coalition partners, and other conservation partners, we have concluded we cannot support the legislation in its current form.

“We believe that the significance of the proposed revisions to our nation’s bedrock environmental laws and the numerous concerns raised about impacts on natural resources and communities warrant more deliberation than is possible during a truncated lame-duck session. It would be prudent for the incoming Congress to work collaboratively with states, Tribes, and the administration to deliver durable reforms that accelerate responsible energy development and reduce pollution, while conserving our waters, lands, and wildlife, upholding Tribal sovereignty and Treaty Rights, and ensuring meaningful community engagement.”

Restricting pipeline infrastructure also relies on higher-emission fuel oil, undermining the very environmental goals such policies are intended to advance. BAAJA seeks to lower energy costs and accelerate infrastructure development through permitting reform. Jeffries’ opposition raises a fundamental question: How will New Yorkers get more affordable, cleaner energy without the infrastructure to deliver it?

The Senator responded after Jeffries, who anticipates becoming the House Speaker after this week’s mid-term election wins by Democrats, contended through a spokesperson:

“We must once again support the clean energy economy and combat the climate crisis with the fierce urgency of now,” the spokesperson said. “However, the current Senate bill under consideration falls short in several areas, including the manner in which NEPA reform is undertaken and the failure to adequately protect tribal sovereignty.”

In his most recent blog posting, the Republican Senator charged that permitting delays for energy projects nationwide are costing American workers jobs and paychecks.

“An infrastructure announcement does not create a construction job. Breaking ground does.
