With a vote expected as soon as Monday on a far-reaching permitting reform bill in the US Senate, opponents to the legislation are raising the alarm over legislation they warn represents the worst kind of bipartisanship: the kind where corporate interests have twisted enough arms in each party to get what they want while the public and the common good get the short end of the stick.

The looming vote to advance S.5653, the so-called Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act, BAAJA for short, has largely been overshadowed by the midterm elections, but coming on the heels of the Democratic Party’s routing of Republicans last Tuesday, it is being pitched as one final chance for the current Congress to pass at least one piece of legislation before President Donald Trump becomes a truly lame duck president come January.

The Democratic co-sponsors in the Senate—Sens. Sheldon Whitehouse of Rhode Island and Martin Heinrich of New Mexico—have tried to thread the bipartisan needle by arguing that the benefits of their proposal outweigh what Republicans demanded in exchange.

“We need a fast, fair transition to clean energy, but not one built on the backs of communities that live next to mines and pipelines. These communities are the ones drinking the water and breathing the air and this bill gives them fewer protections.”

But the problem, according to critics, is that it’s a horrible and counterproductive bill that will empower utility conglomerates, mining companies, data center operators, and oil and gas behemoths to extract huge concessions on the future buildout of polluting projects while hiding behind the promise of a more efficient permitting process for clean energy infrastructure—a noble goal.

The crux, as summarized by The Verge, is that while the legislation, if passed, “could be a catalyst for lots of clean energy, it could also speed up polluting projects and limit oversight of new data centers.”

Green groups in the days leading up to Monday have intensified their opposition, even as lawmakers have introduced changes to make the bill more palatable. On Saturday, the Senate Democratic Caucus met in Washington, DC to discuss the bill and offer “manager’s amendments” in hopes of garnering enough votes for passage.

According to Elizabeth Bast, executive director of Oil Change International, however, “No amount of last-minute tinkering can disguise that this bill is a massive giveaway to fossil fuel companies and Big Tech at the expense of communities, the climate, and people’s energy bills.”

The bill, Bast added, “is exactly what the fossil fuel industry has been asking for years” and called on all lawmakers to vote against it.

Earthworks, one of the hundreds of advocacy groups lining up against BAAJA, warns that the legislation would give the public and Tribes less say in major energy projects, creating conditions that are a giveaway to the mining, data center, and fossil fuel industries.

“The bill would expand the 1872 Mining Law so companies could claim nearly unlimited public land for waste dumps, roads, pipelines and power lines,” Earthworks said in a statement. “The demand for minerals for the energy transition is real, but it is no excuse to let mining companies take more public land with fewer safeguards, under a law that already prioritizes mining ahead of other land use.”

The group’s policy director, Lauren Pagel, said, “We need a fast, fair transition to clean energy, but not one built on the backs of communities that live next to mines and pipelines. These communities are the ones drinking the water and breathing the air, and this bill gives them fewer protections.”

Veteran climate organizer Bill McKibben, writing about the legislation on Saturday, also pointed out the fundamental problem with legislation that treats permitting reform for clean energy projects and dirty energy projects as an equal endeavor.

While acknowledging that currently it remains “too hard to build stuff we badly need—housing, transit, energy,” when it comes to building energy infrastructure, “there’s a problem, and that problem (as so often) is climate change. Building more housing produces…more housing. But if you take climate change seriously, you have to build more clean energy and less dirty energy, or otherwise you don’t get anywhere.”

It’s a similar argument made by groups like Public Citizen, who said Friday that while some of the bill’s provisions—like those related to transmission lines and ratepayer protections from data centers—are “strong and sorely needed,” the problem remains that “the bill’s drawbacks are greater, more immediate, and more certain.”

Whatever benefits the legislation might secure, explained David Arkush, director of Public Citizen’s Climate Program, the downsides will be far worse, undercutting existing laws designed to protect public lands, endangered species, and the nation’s natural resources, including clean air and water.

BAAJA, said Arkush, “seriously weakens the Clean Water Act and Endangered Species Act and guts the National Environmental Policy Act and the National Historic Preservation Act. It fast-tracks the permitting of all manner of projects, then makes it virtually impossible to regulate or arguably even enforce existing rules against them, without an act of Congress.”

“Among other effects,” he continued, “the bill will open the door to a vast increase in exports of liquefied natural gas and facilitate a hasty and reckless buildout of data centers powered by fossil gas. And the bill would make it significantly more difficult to moderate, regulate, or alter these actions later, regardless of what public health, climate destruction, or public sentiment demand.”

As far as McKibben is concerned, “I think that if this deal had been made 30 years ago, it might have made sense—we’d be reaping the benefits now. But the fossil fuel industry made sure we didn’t. And this bill, which they’re backing with great enthusiasm, seems an awful lot like a hedge to make sure they can string their business model out for a few more decades—a way to lock in the fruits of their decades of political obstructionism.”

With Democrats soon returning to power, opponents of the permitting reform bill said it makes no sense to bend to Republicans now to pass a bill that falls short in such fundamental ways.

“In the November 3 elections, voters across the country resoundingly rejected data centers,” said Arkush. “This is not the time to pass a bill that enables Big Tech to charge forward with them, powered by fossil fuels, over the objection of local communities.”

Come January, he said, “the makeup of Congress will change substantially,” making it likely that a significantly “better deal can be reached then—one that enacts the laudable and important provisions in this bill, and more, without so many sacrifices.”

In October, veteran Democratic operator John Podesta warned that providing legislation like BAAJA to the Trump administration would be like giving the president and his party a “loaded howitzer” with which to attack environmental protections.

With Trump’s appointment on Friday of Stephen Miller to be his new White House chief of staff, McKibben connected that choice of the “single most vile character I’ve ever seen on our national scene” with Podesta’s comments and offered this guidance: “Handing Stephen Miller a loaded howitzer is not something any senator should even contemplate. Period.”

US datacenter demand spurs increased fossil fuel pipeline projects as rules are discarded

Datacenters are spurring a boom in fossil fuel pipeline projects at a time when the Trump administration is gutting rules that protect from disasters along the lines, a new review of federal records shows . The report, compiled by the Environmental Integrity Project, also found pipelines are being built to meet demand for natural gas exports fueled by wars in Ukraine and Iran. Federal records identified almost 200 pipeline projects that are proposed or in the works, and would collectively span 17,000 miles (27,000km).

Not only has the Trump administration targeted laws that protect the environment and human health from pipelines’ risks, it has also pledged not to enforce regulations around them, the report adds. Datacenters were on the ballot. US voters rejected them Read more The findings bring into focus a little-considered environmental threat in artificial intelligence and datacenter proliferation – the US already records about 1.7 pipeline accidents, spills, fires or explosions per day, and these projects would almost certainly lead to more.

The pipelines could help supply the at least 98 gas-fired power plants proposed to serve datacenters, and, if all the lines are completed, they would transport about 40% more natural gas daily than what the system carries today. “This is the largest boom in a couple decades … and it coincides with all this deregulation,” Alexandra Shaykevich, research manager with the Environmental Integrity Project, said. “That’s concerning because the pipelines do usually operate safely, but they can leak and explode, and so there are big risks for communities across the United States.”

Most of the pipelines would carry natural gas across 42 states, though many of them are concentrated in several fossil fuel-producing regions. About 42 are in or cross Texas, 27 are in Louisiana , and nine each are in Pennsylvania and Illinois. Advocates say they’re especially worried because of the wide-ranging attacks on foundational environmental protections, from the Clean Water Act to the Endangered Species Act, that until recently have been wielded to stop the riskiest projects, protect from accidents or hold polluters accountable.

View image in fullscreen Protesters demonstrate against building new natural gas pipelines in New York on 9 August 2025. Photograph: Bloomberg/Getty Images The report states that over 25% of the projects have requested an expedited environmental review, and the administration is largely using legally dubious mechanisms to push them through, like invoking the “energy emergency”. That has accelerated permit approvals, reduced the scope of environmental studies, and limited public and community input, the report alleges.

Meanwhile, the administration has used the Defense Production Act to push through projects over the objections of states. In March, it jump-started the Santa Ynez oil pipeline in Santa Barbara, California, despite the state shutting it down in 2015 following a major spill that harmed about 150 miles (240km) of coastline. The act is also being used to attempt to ram through controversial plans for the 125-mile (200km) Constitution pipeline that would run from Pennsylvania to upstate New York, which the latter has opposed.

The Trump administration in January issued a memo stating that it would “refrain from taking any enforcement action” against companies that violated Pipeline and Hazardous Materials Safety Administration regulations. By 2025, it had already cut the average number of enforcement actions initiated in half, recording only 117. skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Weekly Sign up to Down to Earth The planet's most important stories.

Get all the week's environment news - the good, the bad and the essential Enter your email Sign up after newsletter promotion The administration is also raising the risk of accidents and explosions by allowing companies to increase the pressure of pipelines in densely populated areas and letting them conduct fewer pressure tests, the report alleges. It has made changes like this despite the regularity of accidents, including some that are deadly.

The report points to a March 2023 disaster in which a crack in a gas pipeline in West Reading, Pennsylvania, caused an explosion in a chocolate factory that killed seven workers and injured 10 others. Last month, two workers were killed when a New Mexico pipeline exploded. The pipelines could also destroy thousands of acres of federally protected wetlands. At least 81 of the projects are expected to damage more than 19,000 acres (7,700 hectares) of federally protected wetlands, the report found.

This also comes as the Trump administration attempts to strip 94% of federal wetland protections. The dangers of this are felt in south-west Louisiana, which holds a large concentration of pipelines because of the high number of export terminals along the Mississippi River. These already cut through and harmed sensitive wetlands and fishing grounds, said James Hiatt, executive director of For a Better Bayou. “The people who live here carry the risks and bear the burden while the profits go elsewhere,” Hiatt said.

During The Edge’s first interview with Tan Sri Abang Johari Tun Openg at Wisma Bapa in March 2023, he explained why Sarawak’s state leader is called premier and not chief minister or menteri besar as in the peninsula.

The conversation then mostly revolved around the MA63 (the Malaysia Agreement 1963), the debate on rights to Sarawak’s rich hydrocarbon reserves and the state’s healthcare and education autonomy.

He told us that Sarawak recognises the Unified Examination Certificate (UEC), wanting graduates from Chinese schools to join the civil service in order to stop the brain drain. And he made it known that the state wanted to have a seaport, an international airport in Kuching (for connectivity) and an equity stake in a commercial bank (for investment capital), among others.

Three years on, Sarawak is the single largest shareholder of Affin Bank Bhd (KL:AFFIN), holding a 32% stake. It also has a 26.67% stake in Bintulu Port Holdings Bhd (KL:BIPORT), whose wholly owned subsidiary Bintulu Port Sdn Bhd was appointed the operator of the port by the Bintulu Port Authority Sarawak with all requisite approvals from the Sarawak cabinet. Hence, authority was transferred back to the state from the federal government. The state also took over MASwings and turned it into AirBorneo.

Sarawak’s gross domestic product rose to RM153.5 billion in 2025 — the fourth largest after Selangor (RM460.1 billion), Kuala Lumpur (RM265.1 billion) and Johor (RM170.9 billion), according to the Department of Statistics.

The state’s revenue grew from RM11.9 billion in 2022 to RM13.5 billion in 2025. Revenue is expected to reach RM13.6 billion this year and RM15.1 billion in 2027.

Now, the premier is looking beyond Malaysian shores and politics. He is mapping out strategies to make Sarawak an investment destination for technology-intensive industries.

The Petronas-Petros dispute is regarded as merely a technical puzzle now. “It is a question of understanding the law”, which an independent committee has been tasked to address, Abang Johari says. He is confident the issue will be resolved by year-end based on the joint declaration that he signed with Prime Minister Datuk Seri Anwar Ibrahim last year.

No longer dwelling on grievances, Abang Johari now talks about GPU (graphics processing units), gallium nitride chips and nano-satellites. He also mentions rare earth mining, insisting that Sarawak will not export the raw mineral.

“We want to export intelligence, rather than just energy,” he tells The Edge in an interview conducted a week after he tabled the 2027 budget at the state assembly.

Sarawak offers affordable green power and global players bring the latest technologies with them, he says. However, he acknowledges the need for the state to cultivate talents. “So I am giving free tertiary education to all Sarawakians. We are emphasising STEM subjects. The next one will be nano-satellite.”

He has stretched the horizon from 10 years to 25 years. The Post Covid-19 Development Strategy (PCDS 2030) is only the first leg, and his plan is “at least 25 years”.

His brainchild is a 2,000ha site at Tanjung Embang that will have a low-carbon gas hub, a seaport about 8km off shore, a Doha-style transit airport built on Sarawak’s own account and an artificial intelligence (AI) grid campus.

This isn’t just a grand plan on paper. Last month, Soft Bank Group Corp, Grab Holdings Ltd and Petroleum Sarawak Bhd (Petros) entered into a framework agreement to explore developing an AI and digital infrastructure platform in Sarawak. The three parties will develop a road map for the phased development of the platform.

In September, the 76-year-old leader dropped a bomb shell, saying that this could be his “final year”. When asked about the continuity of the state’s long-term grand plans, Abang Johari replies that no one can go against nature, so he needs to groom leaders.

The Sarawak state assembly was dissolved last Monday (Oct 26). Some say that may set the stage for his successor to step up.

The following are excerpts from the interview conducted by Isabelle Francis, Jose Barrock and Kathy Fong.

The Edge: Premier, under your leadership, Sarawak has achieved quite a lot. For instance, greater autonomy in education and healthcare, owning a substantial stake in Affin Bank, and you have an airline now. Are you happy with what you have gotten so far, and what’s the next plan under Post Covid-19 Development Strategy 2030 (PCDS 2030)?

Abang Johari: The basics are still based on what we have agreed under our PCDS policy, meaning we have to give emphasis to the future for Sarawak based on her strength. Sarawak’s strength is basically in energy. Energy is the key transformation agent, from the first revolution until today, which is the fifth revolution.

And from energy, then you have to formulate policies on how to get investments in. But it must be a high-end investment strategy. When you talk about, for instance, microelectronics, we cannot be just an assembler, we must be involved at the front end, in terms of producing the tool itself.

First, I introduced what I call the digital economy [as a means] to leapfrog. And after that, we talk about the hydrogen economy because hydrogen is clean energy. Hydrogen, you can extract it from water and natural gas. We have abundant water resources, hydropower dams, as well as natural gas.

And from then on, you have to assemble the strategic enablers to achieve the objective.

The acquisition of a bank is a commercial transaction. At the same time, we are on the island of Borneo. We must have connectivity. So I discussed with the federal government that perhaps we take over MasWing. So it has become Air Borneo now.

And developing ports is also important. I am very pleased that the government has agreed to give us back Bintulu Port.

Premier, you’re also going to build another seaport and a new airport?

Yes, yes. I have identified Tanjong Embang as another industrial hub. I call it both an aeropolis as well as a new gas hub — a low-carbon gas hub. And this area is more than 2,000ha.

Another one is our international airport. And then surrounding it, we will build what we call an AI grid campus. You see, AI now is basically connected to data centres. It requires a lot of energy and water, so we have to prepare for that.

In five to seven years, there will be the AI grid. We have to prepare for that because technology advances so fast. Now you have what we call a supercomputer. The computing will enable data to flow in real time. You don’t have to store data. The data will flow as long as you have very strong connectivity.

Is it fibre optic (connectivity)?

Not necessarily fibre (optic).

Cloud computing will be the key. When you have the flow of data at the speed of light, what you need is just the GPU (graphics processing unit). I went to Bristol in the UK. I saw a lab researching this. That’s why in IT, the next phase will be supercomputers. And then the result of that [is] what I call, AI grid. Actually, Europe has already started [on this].

When do you plan to start work on the AI grid campus?

Next year, January … the moment [the Sarawak state] budget is passed. Completion should be soon. It will fast track development by our state agencies. Of course, it is public-private partnership.

The Asian Development Bank in Manila asked us about this development because they are very interested.

So for the AI hubs, when will we see it happen?

I have a meeting on it after this. The developer [of the AI Grid campus] is Petros (Petroleum Sarawak Bhd). The whole area includes a deep seaport. The seaport will be about 8km [from shore]. It’ll be built with the carbon capture [facilities]. And it will be linked to our Bintulu Port.

When you say link with Bintulu Port, what does that mean?

The shipping industry is now shifting from hydrocarbon-based fossil fuels to low-carbon fuels.

And low-carbon fuel will be methanol or ammonia. Bintulu Port will be equipped with the production of [low-carbon fuel] because we already have our methanol there. Then you can provide bunkering facilities to the international shipping companies that come from the West, India, [through] Strait of Malacca, Japan, China …

And, of course, our advantage is that we still have the space. Singapore has also approached us. It’s Bintulu Port that will manage it.

What role will Singapore play?

They are just talking to us on how to collaborate with them. It’s very preliminary. What we are looking into is more on the services that they can provide to the shipping industry on that route to East Asia.

But one thing, we have our own strength, we have the gas. We are producing methanol after the [Strait of] Hormuz problem because some industries are depending on the Middle East supply. There are inquiries from the buyers whether we can increase the production of methanol because we’ve got one [production plant] in Bintulu and the other one in Labuan. What we’re going to do is we have to expand, include green methanol.

Is this low carbon hub a 10-year plan?

Oh no, no … it has to be a longer-term plan because we are now recognised by the World Economic Forum as a new emerging industrial cluster. You know, the only one in Malaysia, because of our low-carbon [fuel supply]. Out of 1,339 recognised in the world, [among] the new ones, one is in Malaysia — Samalaju.

So, for [the supply of] green energy, what are you looking at?

Gas is still green, [although] they call it blue; it’s still low carbon. And then we have hydro [power]. And hydro is being expanded into what we call [pumped] storage hydropower. And also cascading dams. And we have solar power. Floating solar panels as well as solar panels on the land. And then we got biomass. We got four [types of green energy]. So, we have a mixture of renewable energy, and that’s why we are able to participate in what we call Asean Power Grid. We are now supplying to Kalimantan, Indonesia. And we are supplying power to Sabah. Next will be Brunei. And then after that, Singapore, Peninsular Malaysia.

So the submarine cable is happening? And how about the funding?

Yes, it is. The only thing is that Singapore and us (Sarawak) have to work together with Indonesia because of the [sea] corridor for us to lay it. There is a corridor under Asean. I leave it to the federal government. It’s a government to government [matter].

I think the funding will be a collaboration between Malaysia and Singapore. In Malaysia, they’re talking about TNB (Tenaga Nasional Bhd) and PETRONAS. And Sembcorp is for Singapore. For us, Sarawak, it is just producing power.

Are you building the airport with Malaysia Airports Holdings Bhd (MAHB) or is it a state project?

It’s on our own. But now there has been discussion. Apparently, MAHB is interested in taking equity. We need a state-of-the-art airport.

I have seen how Doha Airport was built. The traffic to Africa, to Europe, as well to Asia … the design is such that passengers in transit won’t lose their direction. I don’t take 100% [of the design], but use that as a model.

Is there still a lot more gas to be discovered and developed in Sarawak?

Yes. There’s one gas field outside of Kuching, the western field, except that the gas is sour gas with high sulphur and carbon dioxide. But there is technology now to separate them, and then the sour gas will become sweet gas.

And based on the preliminary study, the gas reserve is quite substantial there. You must remember the [gas reserve] belt. The gas reserves and oil are from the northern part of Borneo; Kimanis, then it goes down to Brunei, to Baram, goes down to Mukah, and now it’s Balingian. It’s halfway [through Borneo]. And then after that, they go to Natuna. So the geology is there. Now is only the question of technology.

Premier, what we’re talking about now is old gas. But there’s a lot of new gas that has not contracted …

Yes, we have the Adong Kecil onshore, done by Petros. And that’s only one well, 800 barrels per day. It’s supposed to be about eight wells there, onshore. And now you’ve got a new technology on exploration of gas [onshore].

Balangian is onshore. Let’s see how it goes.

Premier, you shared with us in a previous interview the plan to install 10 gigawatts (GW) by 2020 and 15GW in 2035. Is that on track?

Yes, 2030 is on track [with] 10GW. Then 2035, we expect we can generate 15GW based on our development in solar, and you must also take into consideration the development of batteries [technology], because solar [power] depends on batteries. And then the new technology replaces lithium with sodium now.

Now they are saying, instead of four hours, the battery can supply 12 hours. At the moment, we are producing 50MW from Batang Ai (hydroelectric plant).

We are working with China. Number two is Masdar Abu Dhabi (Future Energy Company). And then there is one more [party] doing a study on our Murum Dam, Baleh Dam and Bakun Dam.

Premier, all these plans, but then you say you might step down.

Oh (laughs). Basically, I’m talking about age. You cannot go against nature. But we have the basics now, then we have to groom [the next] leadership to continue [with developments]. Because this one (AI grid campus) is not a 10-year plan. It could be 20 years. The direction is already there. What is also important is inclusivity and political stability. Now we are talking about the export of intelligence with energy [that we have].

Petros is now talking to SoftBank (Group Corp) and Grab Holdings Ltd.

That’s why I am preparing our human resources by giving free education. I am giving free tertiary education to all Sarawakians. So we are emphasising on STEM subjects.

The next one will be nano-satellite. I’m going into satellite also because the next trend is data intelligence — data and semiconductors going together. And Malaysia must be able to design semiconductors, design chips. And we are doing it now because we are supplying chips, even to China.

If you look at the semiconductor industry, Nvidia Corp is very strong in design. And then Taiwan’s TSMC is producing it. For us, we have our own foundry now, X-Fab; it’s been there more than 10 years. What we need now is a new semiconductor chip that can keep the volume of data. It has to be a new chip, a gallium nitride chip. At the moment, it’s silicon. But silicon chips cannot store a volume of data because when you store [a large volume of] data, it produces heat. If you are using silicon chips that cannot contain the heat, then habis lah.

I think Malaysia can do it. Sarawak can do it. We have tried. Our work is at a lab in Cardiff, the UK. Now we have produced it. They call it K-E-T-E-Q AI. Our chip is used by China for their electric meters. The chip is designed by Sarawakians.

Does that mean Sarawak already has a supply chain for the semiconductor industry?

More or less. That’s why we have to produce a new generation of chips, which will link to our nano-satellite. For a space economy, you must have your own satellite to keep your data, and at the same time, to detect new data.

And you must have a constellation of satellites. That’s why you go for a nano-satellite in low orbit. If you go for a higher one, it’s very costly. But what is important is that you can extract data from Earth.

Our university has a faculty now in space [science]. The Sarawak Space Agency now is chaired by former Chief of Defence Forces Tan Sri Affendi Buang. I studied the case of Measat. The ground station was not that well prepared. We have even studied RazakSat. What is important now is having a strong ground station capable of communicating with low-Earth-orbit satellites. If you want to go towards exporting intelligence, you must have all these ecosystems.

You’re looking at the satellite business as well?

Yes. [At the moment] I’m just studying what happened to Measat. And then we will analyse where the weaknesses are. Because our advantage is our location right on the equator.

So, you have an advantage with your satellites out there, low orbit. Then you must have a group of satellites. The communication must be consistent. For this, I have to work with the federal government. I told them, because your data is important, it’s sovereign data.

You mentioned political stability just now. How do you find the current situation in Malaysia?

I can’t talk about Peninsular. As far as Sarawak is concerned, we manage to have stability.

How’s your relationship with the federal government?

Cordial. We have worked with every prime minister. After (Datuk Seri) Najib Razak, then (Tun) Dr Mahathir Mohamad. After that (Tan Sri) Muhiyiddin Yassin and (Datuk Seri) Ismail Sabri Yaakob.

Has Umno approached you about the passing of the national budget?

Some people did ask for my view, but I said I’m concentrating on our state budget.

Under the Pakatan Harapan leadership, has it been better for Sarawak? If Umno comes back, do you think it would be different?

No, no, it’s up to them. But the ultimate is for Malaysia’s stability. You know, when I was called by the [previous] Agong (Sultan of Pahang, Al-Sultan Abdullah Ri’ayatuddin Al-Mustafa Billah Shah), the last time, His Majesty asked ‘Are you willing to join the unity government?’ Then I replied to the Agong, menjunjung titah demi untuk Malaysia (accepting the King’s order for the country).

Stability is very important. You know, we (Malaysia) were quite far ahead of Vietnam at one time. We were ahead of even South Korea. But now we are behind them. And all our neighbours are prospering. Malaysia has the strength. It is a question of how you manage it.

Sarawak’s potential to create plenty of energy, green power. Instead of exporting energy, the state wants to export intelligence. How is this concept different from the past?

This is the reason why I want to establish the AI grid campus, so all activities will be there, because all these — like storage of data, dissemination of data and transport of data intelligence — all require power. So, we establish the AI grid campus because we have energy to offer and then let the global players come here and that will create jobs for our people.

But we must have talents [to attract investments]. That’s why we have talent development through our universities. So that there will be high-pay jobs [available]. Our strength is having power, [while] investors’ strengths are knowledge and technologies. They come in with the ‘brains’; and then (we) export intelligence, backed by our graduates who will be under the top management. For all you know, our people can create something new.

That’s why I give free education. It cost me RM200 million for the first cohort. The second cohort will be another RM200 million. The third year, another RM200 million. At least, I have to allocate RM1 billion.

We then produce 10,000 [graduates] a year, graduates of high calibre in 64 disciplines, all science-based. Only a few in finance, banking, psychology and cybersecurity. Swinburne, Curtin, University of Technology Sarawak and also iCATS University College — they are the ones supplying [human capital]. Then, we sponsor them [the graduates] to do master’s programmes overseas.

The new area [of study] is the seven elements of rare earth.

I don’t want to export it. For instance, the chip gallium nitride is from rare earth. And your super magnet for your market chip is rare earth. We have deposits of rare earth that will produce gallium.

Have you discussed with the federal government regarding rare earth? Does Sarawak have autonomy over these rare earth resources?

You know very well the eastern states, Kedah, Terengganu, Kelantan have it. In Borneo, we have.

(For Sarawak, the autonomy) is similar to this CCUS (Carbon Capture, Utilisation and Storage) and carbon trading. I know the federal government is going to enforce a tax on carbon. But we have our own law (Land Code) on CCUS because the land is ours. So I told them (the federal government), separate law. They have agreed to it. In this [Sarawak] budget, I did mention the levy and it cannot be double taxation for the buyers.

Rare earth is our mineral, and when you add value to that mineral, it’s commercial value for the investor. But the federal government will gain because all the taxes go to them. Corporate tax goes to them, income tax goes to them, everything goes to them. Except what we (Sarawak) have is sales tax.

Is there any amount you’re investing in rare earth mining?

This sort of thing, you cannot rely on foreigners. So you must have the technology on your own. So what you do is you study, you send your student to do it and learn the technology. If you depend on other people, then teruk (bad) lah.

That’s why we are in the middle-income trap. Because you never go to the front end. But the value is up the chain; you must create [value]. That’s what Malaysia should do.

You know, what transformed South Korea are Samsung and these big, big companies; they create new things.

I’m not criticising, I’m thinking because we are just following people all the time. Penang, macro-electronics, these are assembly plants. The front end is still in the Silicon Valley [in the US]. That’s the front end; you must have the brains. That’s why I was talking the other day with Masayoshi Son (of Softbank Group) during his visit here. I said, it’s the artificial brain and the natural brain. It’s all basically neurons.

Artificial intelligence is actually algorithm plus neuron, kan? And I did mention, reverse ANN (artificial neural network) to detect fake data.

Where do you see Sarawak in 10 years’ time?

I think it has to be at least about 25 years. Now, this is my 10th year. Very short. My PCDS has not been completed. Succession is important. I’m grooming my colleagues. And then, you know, they must have that determination. And also to take risks. I mean, the leadership must take risks, calculated risks.

When I introduced hydrogen, [there were] a lot of sceptics. But now, because of the improvement in membrane technology, the cost of producing hydrogen is coming down now. And Germany is coming back to hydrogen. China is also coming back to hydrogen. And we got hydrogen. I mean, your gas is what? H is hydrogen, water is H2O. So what do you do? You retrieve that. And then in hydrogen also, there’s a molecule within hydrogen called deuterium. And deuterium is the basis for fusion energy, reaction of gas. And fusion energy is safer than nuclear [energy]. Malaysia should be going towards that. Then you have the transition from fossil fuels and hydrocarbons to fusion energy.

description:

text:
In this week’s Ask Nathan:

What’s Honda’s next steps?

Nissan blew our minds?

The first question comes from a fan who wants to know what Honda’s next steps will be.

Q (Via Facebook): RE: What will Honda’s next steps look like?

I’m trying to figure out what’s confirmed or what’s actually been reported about Honda’s next steps. What will it look like? Trying to iron out what I should expect versus what’s been canceled. I’m so confused right now about what they’re going to be doing for their future. I owned nothing but Hondas. Well, except for an old Ford F150 pickup truck that my father left me. I still don’t know what to do with that.

But I’ve had nine Hondas in the past 30 years that I’ve been driving. Some have gone to my kids, and others were swapped out only after accidents. Not a single one has left me by the side of the road.

So, as a Honda fan, I am wondering what’s going to happen next? Do you have any ideas?

Thanks.

– Anonymous

A: That’s a fair question, especially after Honda’s rocky stretch with its electric-vehicle plans.

The company canceled the Honda 0 SUV, Honda 0 Saloon, and Acura RSX EV, despite having already invited journalists to preview them. That’s a substantial change of direction, rather like organizing a wedding, mailing the invitations, and then deciding you’d prefer a boat. It was kind of sad to see.

However, Honda’s next move looks considerably more familiar: hybrids. The company already builds excellent hybrid powertrains, and the Prelude demonstrates that efficiency doesn’t have to eliminate personality. Whether you like its execution or not, I appreciate Honda trying to make something other than another anonymous family crossover.

Starting in 2027, its next-generation system will wear the straightforward “Honda Hybrid” name. Nifty, right? It builds on the existing two-motor e:HEV technology, rather than throwing everything into the dumpster. Honda’s updated plan calls for 15 next-generation hybrid models globally by March 2030, with North America a priority. The engineering targets include more than a 10-percent fuel-economy improvement through the combined new powertrain, platform, and electric AWD technology, plus a hybrid-system production-cost reduction exceeding 30-percent compared with its 2023 system. Those are targets, and cheaper manufacturing doesn’t automatically mean an equivalent discount at your dealership. Wouldn’t that be lovely?

The newly teased Avancier offers a glimpse of that direction. Honda Australia has published a “coming soon” page showing a sharper design and distinctive lighting. Reports point to a larger, three-row SUV positioned above the CR-V, but detailed specifications, pricing, and a firm Australian launch date remain unannounced. There’s no confirmed U.S. arrival, either, so don’t start rearranging the garage just yet.

About that bright green rendering I provided: it’s an unofficial design exercise combining the teaser-inspired shape with a Honda concept-style grille and slim headlights. It’s my little automotive science experiment, not a leaked production photo or confirmation that Honda has discovered radioactive guacamole.

For American buyers, another development deserves attention: Honda plans larger hybrids beginning in 2029, and Acura has confirmed a V6 hybrid powertrain in development for its larger models. Exact applications and output figures are still to come.

My take? Honda needs desirable vehicles with useful efficiency, competitive pricing, and some personality. A stronger hybrid lineup sounds like a sensible next step. Just keep the driving fun, Honda. I’d hate to see all that engineering result in a remarkably efficient sleeping pill.

— N

The last question comes from a fan who wants to know if we’re covering SEMA. Oh boy are we!

Q (Via Facebook): RE: Was Nissan at the SEMA show?

Is Nissan going to be at the (2026) SEMA show?

– EJSSE22

A: Heck ya! Nissan brought some nifty concepts.

Nissan showed up at the 2026 SEMA Show with a few slick concepts, including a badass Sentra, a Frontier with serious swagger, and a surprisingly interesting Pathfinder. Yes, a Pathfinder. Apparently, somebody remembered that the name should occasionally involve finding adventure.

We’ve already published videos covering some of these builds, but what caught my attention was the thinking behind them. Nissan gave us a reason to look at familiar vehicles differently. A Sentra with some swagger? I’m listening. A Frontier that makes you start mentally pricing accessories? That’s dangerous territory for my wallet.

The bigger question is whether any of this goodness will reach production. SEMA concepts are excellent at making promises that nobody technically made, so I wouldn’t assume these exact vehicles are heading to dealerships. Still, they give Nissan a chance to gauge interest in styling, accessories, and potential upgrades. I hope the enthusiastic response encourages somebody to approve more than another badge package.

Nissan brought some personality to the party. Now let’s see how much survives the trip from the show floor to the showroom.

— N

text:
Alaska could be transformed into a major data center hub following a new assessment of natural gas resources in the region which appear big enough to power huge advanced computing and AI sites.

The state is becoming a new frontier for data centers due to its cold climate, available land and access to energy resources, making it a cheaper alternative to hubs such as Northern Virginia and Texas. Alaska currently houses at least six operational data centers, while several additional projects have been announced or proposed.

One of the proposed sites, Project Aaka, is set to become the largest in Alaska. Developed by STAK Energy, the 3GW natural-gas powered data center is due to be built in an established industrial corridor on the North Slope and recently announced a 15-year deal with ExxonMobil Alaska Production Inc to supply its gas. Newsweek has reached out to ExxonMobil by email.

Read More on News

Why It Matters

In a first-of-its kind report covering the entire North Slope last month, the U.S. Geological Survey (USGS) estimated there could be as much as 96 trillion cubic feet (tcf) of technically recoverable, undiscovered natural gas resources on Alaska’s North Slope.

This is roughly three times the amount of known gas reserves on the North Slope, "or three years' supply for the U.S. at the 2025 rate of consumption," Alicia Lindauer, USGS Energy Resources Program coordinator told Newsweek.

STAK's chief development officer Kay Zinngrabe said the Project Aaka site will draw on fields that already produce but added: "The USGS estimate change adds further optimism for future expansion should demand for power generation continue to increase."

In addition to the data center usage, Alaska’s North Slope gas is already being eyed up for domestic and international markets as The Last Frontier’s $55 billion LNG pipeline to transport North Slope gas to Anchorage and beyond edges closer to overcoming its federal and financial hurdles.

Despite STAK Energy’s new data center drawing on the same North Slope supply as the pipeline, Zinngrabe brushed off any concerns.

"Nearly everyone on the STAK Energy team was born in Alaska or has lived here for many years. As Alaskans, we want to see both projects succeed as they both benefit the state’s economy.

"The latest USGS gas estimates reaffirm there’s enough North Slope gas to support both, and that’s a strong reason to move forward on each."

Midterm Election Could Reshape Industry

Abundant gas supplies alone may not determine whether Alaska becomes a major computing hub. One of the state’s biggest roadblocks to new data centers could be determined by the as yet unknown Alaskan Midterms results.

Although current Alaska Governor Mike Dunleavy supports data centers in the state, two of the four candidates to replace him are critics of AI. Democratic candidate Jonathan Kreiss-Tomkins said he would seek to temporarily ban new computing data centers in Alaska if elected.

One of his Republican rivals Bernadette Wilson, said: "I will never allow Alaska to be littered with hyperscale data centers that take our resources and spoil our lands."

In the wake of the USGS report, Secretary of the Interior Doug Burgum hailed the state’s abundant resources and what they could be used for.

"Alaska is one of America’s greatest energy frontiers, and President Trump is committed to unlocking its extraordinary potential.

"Alaska’s natural gas reserves can supply affordable, reliable, secure energy to Americans and our South Pacific allies for generations, and this assessment helps underscore the importance of understanding these vast resources beneath the North Slope and using world-class American science to turn that potential into opportunity.

"By advancing responsible energy development, we can strengthen American Energy Dominance, create jobs and deliver lasting economic benefits for Alaskans and the entire nation."

text:
After more than a decade of false starts, lawmakers in Washington are on the cusp of advancing a bill to reform the Byzantine system for approving projects needed to modernize power grids, build artificial intelligence data centers and revitalize clean energy development.

The Democrats’ sweeping victories in the midterm elections, however, has tossed a wrench into the effort.

Senators are now fighting to preserve a bipartisan permitting reform deal reached after months of painstaking negotiations, with a procedural vote on the bill set for Monday. Congress has two short months to pass the plan, which overhauls how projects including pipelines, power lines and solar and wind farms are approved.

House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries is opposing the bill in its current form, arguing it hasn’t received enough input from House Democrats. Other progressive Democrats say they should use their newfound control of Congress next year to negotiate for a better deal. The legislation is also facing mounting opposition from Native American tribes and environmental groups.

“The path to this has gotten more difficult,” said Chris Moyer, a Democratic strategist who has worked for former Senate Majority Leader Harry Reid and other lawmakers. “Every two years the party that takes power says let’s hold off for a better deal.”

Addressing the permitting system is a top priority for President Donald Trump’s administration. The energy industry has long complained about the regulatory hurdles in the US, which can add years of red tape delays and millions of dollars to renewable power and oil and gas projects alike. Reform has been floated for more than a decade, but there’s been little progress.

The latest effort aims to address government reviews that are slow and overlapping, but opponents say it does away with crucial environmental safeguards. The bill would impose deadlines on government reviews under the National Environmental Policy Act and changes other laws considered sacrosanct by environmentalists.

Senator Sheldon Whitehouse, a Rhode Island Democrat, led negotiations on the deal. He is the top Democrat on the Senate environment committee and his constituency is home to a major offshore wind project. He said input on the bill has already been solicited from House members and the bill’s authors on Saturday released an amendment designed to address concerns they raised.

“A good permitting bill comes together over years of complex negotiations,” Whitehouse said in a statement. “We don’t have more years to lose as clean energy projects sit on the sidelines.”

Jeffries said through a spokesman he is opposed to the plan as drafted and would “not rubber-stamp legislation that emerges from the Senate” without more involvement from the Democratic House caucus, according to Politico.

TD Cowen, in a note to clients the morning after election day, said they were reducing the likelihood of lame duck passage of the bill from 40% to 25%, on grounds it likely emboldens voices arguing that the bill gives too many concessions to the oil and gas industry.

Democratic Senators Whitehouse and Martin Heinrich of New Mexico, as well as Republican Senators Shelley Moore Capito of West Virginia and Mike Lee of Utah unveiled the 417-page draft before Congress took a monthlong break for the midterm elections.

Backers of the measure range from the American Petroleum Institute and the American Clean Power Association, which has lauded language in the bill that would make it easier to build high-voltage power lines.

But opponents fear it could undermine sovereignty of Native American tribes and cause lasting environmental damage.

“As currently drafted, this bill will hand more power to the executive branch, erode democratic norms, and cause environmental harm to our water, wildlife, and public health protections far beyond the scope of federal permitting,” Loren Blackford, executive director of the Sierra Club, said in a statement on Friday.

Flames from a burning battery storage system shoot into the sky in the AI-generated image that’s plastered across the front of the alarming mailer, which includes text that warns: “If the wind is blowing your way, the toxic plume of forever chemicals and carcinogens from the conflagration, which will be impossible to extinguish, will forever damage the habitability of the place you live.”

New Scotland Supervisor Douglas LaGrange called the mailer “horrendous” and an “embarrassment.”

It was apparently distributed by a group called “Not in our BESSt Interest Committee,” which was formed by residents who live near the proposed project. The group has an online petition with more than 900 signatures and has raised over $5,500.

Battery storage facilities, which store electricity from generation plants for times of high demand, are critical to both improving the reliability of New York’s aging grid and bringing online renewable energy sources like solar farms. Both California and Texas grid operators didn’t need to ask residents to dampen their energy use this summer as battery storage helped maintain reliability.

Advertisement

Article continues below this ad

New Scotland is a microcosm of the broader problems facing the battery storage and renewable energy industry as community pushback and misinformation has permeated siting decisions and frightened residents. More than 80% of the battery storage moratoriums in the country are in New York, according to the research firm, Carina Energy.

The mailer distributed in New Scotland had urged residents to argue for changes to the local battery storage law at a Town Board meeting in October. At the time that local law was approved two years ago, just one person offered comment at a public hearing.

“We’ll entertain tweaks to the law, no law is perfect,” LaGrange said. “But at the same time, you know, come to me with real stuff and don’t try to scare people.”

Advertisement

Article continues below this ad

Other communities have utilized similar tactics to push for action from elected leaders.

A GoFundMe page that’s raised about $3,400 to oppose a battery facility proposed in Saugerties includes an image claiming residents within 1 mile of the site face “direct danger” in the event of a fire. But the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency recommends an isolation zone of roughly 330 feet if there is an incident.

When a battery system caught fire in Warwick last year, air monitoring didn’t find elevated levels of pollutants in that Orange County community. This year, New York instituted more stringent safety regulations on battery energy systems to lower the likelihood of incidents and ensure they’re handled properly.

Alexandra Fasulo, a prominent anti-solar and land conservation activist with more than 600,000 Instagram followers, has been an influential force elevating local opposition to energy projects in New Scotland and across the state.

Advertisement

Article continues below this ad

Despite receiving state permits, a proposed solar farm in Montgomery County was canceled at least in part because of Fasulo’s advocacy, according to Marguerite Wells, executive director of the Alliance for Clean Energy New York.

“(She’s) caused enough of a furor locally that they still just can’t get the project over the finish line,” Wells said.

The developer cited difficulty obtaining the necessary materials and labor to build the project as well as the high cost of entering New York’s grid as factors for the cancelation.

Fasulo’s primary mission is disbanding the Office of Renewable Energy Siting and Electric Transmission, a state office that permits large-scale wind and solar farms.

Advertisement

Article continues below this ad

She’s attacked the office and renewable energy ecosystem both on social media and through the courts with her Schuylerville-based nonprofit, the American Land Rescue Fund, which she says is funded by donations from, “everyday people.”

“I don’t want anything less than the dissolution of (the Office of Renewable Energy Siting),” Fasulo said. “And I do think there’s this air of arrogance that comes out of Albany in the governor’s office with thinking that these you know everyday plebeians, these everyday peasants can’t make their own decisions.”

She wants renewable energy projects to be decided by local government officials rather than through a state process that can override home rule.

Fasulo also has targeted Dean Sommer, an area attorney who chairs the New Scotland Zoning Board of Appeals.

Advertisement

Article continues below this ad

Sommer and his law firm, Young/Sommer, are fomenting “the collapse of America,” she said in a social media post that got hundreds of likes. Fasulo has also called the firm “monopolistic,” for its representation of many wind, solar and battery storage developers.

She has also claimed that Sommer was placed on the Zoning Board to speedily approve battery projects.

“In order to ensure the zoning variances for the (battery storage) facilities in New Scotland are approved without any issues or slowdowns (renewable developers like to work speedily to cash in on subsidies/credits while market conditions are favorable), Mr. Sommer is strategically positioned, allegedly, to assure Young/Sommer’s clients he can deliver that kind of seamlessness to them,” Fasulo wrote.

No battery projects in New Scotland have gone before the Zoning Board of Appeals, so Sommer has had no involvement in their reviews. The Zoning Board meets only when it has agenda items and the members receive a stipend of a few thousand dollars a year.

Advertisement

Article continues below this ad

“Young/Sommer’s representation of multiple battery, wind and solar projects isn’t a ‘monopoly,’” said John McManus, an experienced energy attorney. “It’s not unusual for a law firm to represent a number of similar types of clients — here, battery, wind and solar developers — in a particular sector.”

In an interview, Fasulo said she stood by her online statements regarding Young/Sommer but didn’t want to discuss them further for fear of being sued.

The statements about Sommer are “blatantly ridiculous,” said LaGrange, the town supervisor. “Scrutiny is fine, and people should be scrutinized, but at the same time, don’t make up stuff.”

New Scotland officials are concerned incendiary online rhetoric could discourage residents from joining town commissions or boards and stifle civil and informed public debate.

Advertisement

Article continues below this ad

Social media “spreads a lot of misinformation and gets people riled up,” said Jeff Baker, chair of the New Scotland Planning Board.

“I have very thick skin,” said Baker, a longtime environmental attorney who retired from the Young/Sommer firm in 2019. “Lots of the people on my board are not like that. They’re normal people. They’re nice people, and they take offense when people yell at them.”

Sommer said he is rather befuddled by Fasulo’s accusation that he was appointed to the Zoning Board of Appeals to shepherd battery projects favorable to his law firm. He was previously on the board and left to care for his wife, who died of Parkinson’s in 2025.

“I don’t know why she is telling people they are in front of the Zoning Board. They are not,” Sommer said in a phone interview. “I’m just not involved. This is why people should get their news from newspapers and real news sources and not social media.”

Advertisement

Article continues below this ad

Sommer’s son, Jesse, who was also targeted by Fasulo, isn’t offended by the barbs. Jesse Sommer and Fasulo both benefit from an online ecosystem that rewards sharp broadsides.

“Social media has as its birthright the privilege and mission of completely destroying the fabric of our nation,” Jesse Sommer said. “It’s not my father who’s destroying America. It’s not even Alexandra who’s destroying America. … Social media itself is what is rewarding indictment, allegation, defamation.”

Jesse Sommer is an online provocateur under the moniker, “The Sheriff of Lark Street” and owns New Scotland Spirits.

He responded to the Fasulo post about his father by seemingly cheering on the sentiment.

Advertisement

Article continues below this ad

“It is absolutely VITAL that we protect the American farmland from which we distill our New Scotland Spirits,” Jesse wrote in response to the Fasulo post regarding him and his father.

“She knows I know what she’s doing,” Jesse Sommer said. “The masses that she’s whipping up, I might as well leverage it to see if I can sell a few bottles.”

Misinformation often represents a small component of people’s social media feeds, but the huge reach of individual posts make it consequential, said Joshua Tucker, who co-founded the NYU Center for Social Media, AI, and Politics.

Utilizing incendiary language isn’t the only way to build an influential and lucrative following, but it is a method, he added.

Advertisement

Article continues below this ad

“This kind of stuff that riles people up is one way to build a following online,” Tucker said. “And we do know, in this influencer world, there are economic incentives to building a following online.”

Jim Muscato, a partner at Young/Sommer, said the public paying greater attention to energy policy can benefit the renewable industry. He said he’s focused on fighting climate change, addressing reliability shortfalls and lowering costs by getting more clean power permitted rather than rebuking Fasulo’s statements.

“Energy issues are at the forefront of people’s minds, and that’s a good thing,” Muscato said. “I want people to be thinking about where we get our energy from because that’s when people will look at the potential impacts from the various sources and see that renewables are the answer.”

Advertisement

Article continues below this ad

Muscato doesn’t think that the renewable energy siting process has changed that much over the past 20 years, whether it is local towns having the authority to site projects or state offices taking the lead. He pointed out that the Office of Renewable Energy Siting has been operational for six years but with state siting authority for energy projects existing before that.

“Whether it’s a state process or whether it’s a local process, participation in that process can effectuate meaningful input,” Muscato said. “And that’s where I get concerned about mischaracterizing the process or making people feel as if their voice isn’t heard because that couldn’t be further from the truth.”

text:
Some Democrats are promising to push for more clean energy to help tackle rising energy costs when they take control of Congress in January, though President Donald Trump says he will use his veto power aggressively.

0:04

/

0:30

Keep Watching

With new majorities in the House and Senate after last week's midterms, Democrats can set an agenda boosting clean energy and addressing climate change. While those are traditionally core priorities of the party, climate was not a central topic in this election cycle.

Advertisement

Article continues below this ad

Democrats can begin investigations and hold hearings into climate policy rollbacks and elimination of green energy grants by the Republican administration, potentially trying to undo some changes and restore renewable energy incentives.

Sen. Sheldon Whitehouse of Rhode Island, the top Democrat on the Senate Committee on Environment and Public Works, said Trump’s clean energy attacks drove up prices for taxpayers. He said Democrats will "work every angle to lower consumers’ energy costs, and we will demand accountability for the massive corruption wrought by Trump’s fossil-fuel donors.”

American Clean Power Association CEO Jason Grumet said everybody who is trying to build clean energy “feels bolstered.”

Enacting major changes would require Republican support because Democrats will lack the numbers to override presidential vetoes. Even then, lower energy bills are not guaranteed because prices also depend on fuel costs, demand and the expense of maintaining the electric grid.

Advertisement

Article continues below this ad

“The wins give Democrats more leverage over spending and more political power to advance a coherent agenda; the question is whether they’ll use that power effectively,” said Lisa Sachs, director of the Columbia Center on Sustainable Investment. “The vote was for affordability and opportunity. Democrats now need to be clear about which policies deliver them.”

Trump holds veto power but thinks he and Democrats can deal

Trump said after Tuesday's election that Democrats will send over “things that are insane” and he will veto them, speaking generally about legislation. But in the comments to Fox News, he predicted that “after a couple of months of vetoes,” he and Democrats will find ways to work together.

The White House said in a statement Wednesday that Trump is "committed to unleashing reliable, affordable, and secure energy sources to lower prices, strengthen our grid, and protect our national security, and is willing to work with anyone to accomplish this.”

Advertisement

Article continues below this ad

Trump promised to lower energy prices. Instead, his war with Iran and other policies increased the price of gasoline, diesel and electricity. At the same time, the administration canceled many clean energy projects and grants and slowed clean energy permitting.

Trump particularly dislikes offshore wind. Developer Orsted said Thursday that Revolution Wind, a large wind farm in federal waters off Rhode Island, has started operating commercially.

Will the president change his tune on green energy? That's doubtful, said former Sen. Byron Dorgan, D-N.D., co-chair of the government relations practice at ArentFox Schiff.

“He is likely to keep pushing his energy issues, and I think he will be forced to give some room for a new Congress to recreate a different strategy that will add clean energy,” Dorgan said in an email.

Advertisement

Article continues below this ad

Trump promotes expanding production of oil, natural gas and coal, which cause climate change, because he argues that would give the U.S. the lowest-cost electricity. Mike Sommers, CEO of the American Petroleum Institute, the oil and gas industry’s top lobbying group, said that as voters have changed the balance of political power in Washington, “the affordability message is unmistakable.”

Sommers said in a statement there is a real opportunity for bipartisan cooperation to reduce costs and strengthen the economy, starting with an energy permitting reform proposal announced in September. The legislation is aimed at shortening the timeline to get big energy projects started.

Ife Kilimanjaro, executive director of the U.S. Climate Action Network, said Democrats should reject that proposal and use their stronger position to pass legislation that actually builds out much-needed clean energy.

Reversing Trump’s anti-climate policies

The administration has reshaped the Environmental Protection Agency, reversing pollution limits as it promotes fossil fuels.

Advertisement

Article continues below this ad

Clear Street energy transition analyst Tim Moore said he expects Democrats to investigate the climate and environmental rollbacks, in an effort to block some from taking effect. Democrats could also try amending the Clean Air Act to cut carbon pollution and push back against EPA budget cuts, he added.

Rep. Sean Casten, D-Ill., said he is cautiously optimistic some Republicans will now seek to differentiate themselves from Trump and back pro-environmental policies. But without Republican support, Democrats’ more ambitious bills will largely lay out their agenda for 2028, he added.

Climate is not necessarily at the top of Democrats' list of priorities. They are targeting healthcare access, trade tariffs and the Iran war.

Rep. Frank Pallone, the New Jersey Democrat who is expected to become chair of the House Energy and Commerce Committee, said the party should focus on healthcare, affordability, consumer and environmental protections, clean energy and regulating Big Tech.

Advertisement

Article continues below this ad

A potential stalemate seen on clean energy and climate policy

David Victor, a professor of innovation and public policy at the University of California, San Diego, largely expects a stalemate at the federal level on climate and energy policy because of the divided government. He said agreement could come on some bipartisan measures such as a permitting overhaul.

Victor thinks Democratic-led investigations and hearings will center on corruption and other topics that may only touch on energy and climate. Like Casten, Victor said many of the Democratic bills likely will not become law, but will outline what Democrats could accomplish if they win the White House in 2028.

“The Democrats are going to be drafting things that the administration’s not going to like. They don’t have the votes to override a veto, and on top of it, the administration is going to be in turmoil because of its own electoral failures and because of all the investigations,” Victor said. “This seems to me, at the federal level, largely a recipe for kind of intense chaos over the next two years.”

Advertisement

Article continues below this ad

One of the biggest wild cards is the behavior of the administration, which could use executive power to double down on rollbacks of climate and environmental rules, he said.

States could advance clean energy without waiting for Congress

Democrats scored victories in races for governor in states long controlled by Republicans, including Texas and Georgia.

Leah Stokes, a political scientist at the UC Santa Barbara, said there could be a lot of state action on climate next year because of those wins. That is where climate leadership has traditionally come from, she noted. At the federal level, Stokes is optimistic about extending clean energy tax credits since some Republicans support that.

Advertisement

Article continues below this ad

Jay Inslee, a former Democratic governor and congressman from Washington, also expects growing momentum for clean energy in states that elected Democratic governors, particularly in states where they also won legislative majorities.

“This is a really powerful instrument for the United States to join the rest of the world and get back in a leadership position, even if we still have a climate denier that might exercise a veto on some things that we want to do federally,” Inslee said. “So I hope people will pay attention to the big progress we’re going to make on a state-level basis.”

title: Bankers Prepare for AI 'in Every Conversation' at Climate Summit in Turkey
description:
The technology’s use of energy, water and land has galvanized a popular movement against data centers, while climate nonprofits have characterized AI’s carbon footprint as alarming.
“Data centers can be very, very efficient in their operations,” Drew said in an interview.
In April, the International Energy Agency said electricity consumed by AI-focused data centers is set to triple by the end of the decade.
By then, all data centers — including those that aren’t focused on AI — will account for about 3% of global electricity demand, according to the IEA.
Among them is JPMorgan Chase & Co., the largest US lender, which is sending a team of investment bankers and sustainability executives to the talks.
text:
As the AI trade shows signs of unraveling, senior bankers gathering on Turkey’s Mediterranean coast are hoping to lay the groundwork for deals that can change the technology’s long-term impact.

In the Turkish city of Antalya, where the 31st United Nations Conference of the Parties starts on Monday, government leaders, finance executives, business heads and nonprofits will spend the coming two weeks discussing how to convert the pledges of previous COPs into action. The host, Turkey, has identified electrifying more of the global economy as an essential plank in that agenda.

And that’s where AI comes in.

“It will be in every conversation,” said Daniel Hanna, head of sustainable and transition finance at Barclays Plc. AI can create the “long-term commercial demand that will help accelerate clean energy and scale certain climate technologies.”

Last week’s tech-stock selloff was fueled by anticipation that the results of the US midterms will lead to more AI regulations, including tougher energy and environmental standards for data centers in the world’s biggest AI market.

“What you’re seeing playing out in the US markets right now is that the reaction is that there will be much more regulation,” said Marisa Drew, Standard Chartered Plc’s chief sustainability officer and one of the bankers headed to Antalya.

From the perspective of capital allocators, AI infrastructure “is going to be trillions of dollars of investment requirement,” she said. Regulations that add transparency will help financiers make informed choices and support the companies “that are good environmental and social stewards.”

Treating AI as a potential solution to the climate crisis remains a controversial posture. The technology’s use of energy, water and land has galvanized a popular movement against data centers, while climate nonprofits have characterized AI’s carbon footprint as alarming.

Simon Stiell, executive secretary of the UN’s Framework Convention on Climate Change, has described AI as an “energy guzzling” technology that drives up emissions. “AI leaders are now on thin ice,” he said in September.

In a report published just before COP31, StanChart described data center growth as “neither environmentally benign nor inherently unsustainable.” Instead, the climate footprint depends on local choices, it said.

“Data centers can be very, very efficient in their operations,” Drew said in an interview. “But it’s about those design choices that you make, the technological choices that you make, and that also involves coalescence around what good looks like, which is where policy comes into play, which is critical for COP.”

For now, there’s no definitive estimate of the climate footprint of AI. The technology’s rapidly growing need for electricity, however, is uncontested. In April, the International Energy Agency said electricity consumed by AI-focused data centers is set to triple by the end of the decade. By then, all data centers — including those that aren’t focused on AI — will account for about 3% of global electricity demand, according to the IEA.

Hanna of Barclays says he has “conviction” that AI can lead to a “cleaner, more resilient” power system, though he also acknowledges it’s “not a given that it will.”

In its role as COP31 host, Turkey has pledged to work with the technology industry to figure out how to ensure AI is used in ways that help fight global warming rather than accelerate it.

Scaling AI will require huge investments in expanding and upgrading electric grids. Turkey has made it a COP31 goal to get nations to agree to have 35% of global final energy consumption come from electricity by 2035. That compares with about 23% today, according to a September IEA estimate.

Bankers heading to Antalya said in interviews with Bloomberg that they intend to use their time there engaged in talks about how to finance that goal.

Among them is JPMorgan Chase & Co., the largest US lender, which is sending a team of investment bankers and sustainability executives to the talks. It sees the COP31 agenda as one that fits neatly into its own $1.5 trillion security and resilience initiative, unveiled last year.

“The electrification ambition gives us more to latch on to and it is exactly where we are focused anyway,” said Luke Nelson, head of international sustainability at JPMorgan’s center for energy and the environment. “You can’t electrify without a functioning grid.”

Nelson said talks will include a focus on energy security, as war continues to fuel oil and gas price volatility. JPMorgan’s intention is to actively engage with clients on these topics while in Antalya, he said.

“Energy security can be delivered though scaling renewables,” he added. “And while the primary audience in Antalya will want the regular COP conversation,” JPMorgan’s expectation is that business leaders attending the summit will have more of a “pragmatic focus on security and resiliency, looking at the grid, nuclear and renewables.”

The COP31 electrification goal could become a new catalyst for investment, said Miranda Beacham, head of UK responsible investment at Aegon Asset Management. “It is good to see the presidency focusing on technologies and infrastructure the finance industry already understands and knows how to deploy capital at scale.”

Sudip Hazra, director at First Sentier MUFG Sustainable Investment Institute, said the electrification theme makes it more likely that bankers will leave COP31 having struck deals, or at least laid the groundwork for financing agreements.

“The investment opportunity extends beyond new electricity generation to the infrastructure required to support it, including grids, storage, substations, buildings, transport and industrial infrastructure,” he said.

Financial professionals attending the summit will be able to address a “mega-trend capturing a broad opportunity set for investors,” says Will Farrell, senior stewardship analyst at Federated Hermes’ EOS unit.

As for AI’s impact on the planet, “the book hasn’t been written yet,” Drew of StanChart said. “It’s all about the choices you make.”

title: Tata Raises Iveco Stake, Mahindra Accelerates Expansion, Bosch Eyes Chip Growth
