text:
India's automotive industry witnessed several major developments between November 2 and 8, with Tata Motors moving closer to full ownership of Iveco Group, Mahindra & Mahindra outlining an aggressive capacity expansion and product launch programme, and automakers reporting strong demand ahead of Diwali.

Tata Motors increased its provisional stake in Iveco to 96.29%, crossing the threshold required to initiate a squeeze-out of remaining shareholders. Mahindra announced plans to increase its monthly SUV manufacturing capacity by 27% to 82,000 units by March 2027 and introduce five new vehicles during the first half of calendar year 2027.

Festive demand remained a major theme. Maruti Suzuki, Tata Motors and Hyundai Motor India expected substantial deliveries during Dhanteras and Diwali.

Meanwhile, FADA's October retail data showed a year-on-year decline in passenger vehicle and two-wheeler registrations because of the shifting festive calendar, even as electric passenger vehicle sales rose sharply.

The week also saw developments in electrification, auto-component manufacturing, corporate investment and quarterly earnings, along with a dispute over ethanol blending levels in petrol.

Acquisitions, Investments and Expansion

Tata Motors Raises Iveco Stake to 96.29%, Plans Squeeze-Out

Tata Motors has increased its provisional shareholding in Iveco Group to 96.29% following the reopening period of its voluntary tender offer for the Italian commercial vehicle manufacturer.

An additional 18.31 million Iveco shares were tendered during the reopening period, taking the total holding to approximately 256.47 million shares. The additional shares carry an aggregate consideration of €263.65 million.

Having crossed the 95% ownership threshold, Tata Motors plans to initiate a Dutch legal squeeze-out process for the remaining shares, subject to confirmation of the provisional results. Final acceptance results are expected on November 12, while payment for the additional shares is scheduled for November 13.

The development follows the initial settlement completed in the previous week and moves Tata Motors closer to full ownership of the European commercial vehicle maker.

Mahindra to Increase SUV Capacity 27% by March 2027

Mahindra & Mahindra plans to increase monthly SUV manufacturing capacity by 27% to 82,000 units by March 2027 as strong demand continues to stretch its factories.

The automaker began FY27 with monthly capacity of 64,500 SUVs, which increased to 68,000 units by September. The planned expansion will add capacity for combustion-engine and electric SUVs.

Further additions at Chakan and a new factory in Nagpur are expected to take Mahindra's combined monthly SUV capacity to 1.32 lakh units by FY31, more than double its FY26-end level.

The company also plans five major vehicle launches by June 2027, including a model based on its NU_IQ architecture, an all-new electric SUV, the Scorpio Lifestyler pickup, a refreshed SUV and a new light commercial vehicle.

Mahindra Plans to Double Last-Mile Mobility Capacity by FY29

Mahindra's last-mile mobility business has lined up eight products and plans to double manufacturing capacity by FY29 as demand for its electric three- and four-wheelers exceeds available production.

Domestic sales increased 36.7% year-on-year to 52,869 units during Q2 FY27, with electric vehicles accounting for nearly 86% of volumes.

The company said strong demand for its Udo electric vehicle had put pressure on existing manufacturing capacity. Mahindra is targeting growth at twice the industry rate, supported by new products and higher production.

Mahindra Approves Up to Rs 1,450 Crore Investment in SML Mahindra

Mahindra & Mahindra has approved an investment of up to Rs 1,450 crore in SML Mahindra's proposed rights issue, strengthening its financial commitment to the commercial vehicle subsidiary.

The automaker will subscribe to its full rights entitlement of approximately Rs 855 crore and has approved an additional Rs 595 crore for further subscriptions, including any portion of the issue that remains unsubscribed.

The investment comes as Mahindra seeks to strengthen its presence in commercial vehicles alongside its expanding SUV and last-mile mobility businesses.

Castrol India Open Offer Valued at Over Rs 5,100 Crore

A Stonepeak-led consortium has announced an open offer worth up to Rs 5,129 crore for Castrol India, following the indirect acquisition of control in the lubricants company.

Motion JVCo Limited and persons acting in concert have offered to acquire up to 25.72 crore shares, representing 26% of Castrol India's equity, at Rs 199.45 per share.

The offer follows Stonepeak's acquisition of control through a 51% stake and represents a significant ownership development in India's automotive lubricants market.

Festive Demand and October Retail Trends

Maruti, Tata Motors and Hyundai Expect Strong Dhanteras-Diwali Deliveries

Leading passenger vehicle manufacturers reported strong festive demand ahead of Dhanteras and Diwali, with new model launches and continued consumer interest supporting deliveries.

Maruti Suzuki expected approximately 30,000 vehicle deliveries on Dhanteras, while Tata Motors Passenger Vehicles estimated more than 12,000 deliveries during the day. Hyundai Motor India expected around 16,000 deliveries across Dhanteras and Diwali, nearly 14% higher than last year.

Maruti's sales had increased 36% year-on-year through Dussehra, while Tata Motors reported more than 20% growth since Ganesh Chaturthi.

Separately, Maruti Suzuki disclosed that its Baleno facelift had sold 50,000 units within two months, while the Brezza's waiting period had exceeded three months. The automaker also reported approximately 1.2 lakh pending CNG bookings amid component supply constraints, with production expected to improve gradually from January 2027.

Passenger Vehicle Retail Sales Fall 14.23% in October

Passenger vehicle retail registrations declined 14.23% year-on-year to 5,07,768 units in October, according to the Federation of Automobile Dealers Associations (FADA). However, registrations increased 18.86% over September, making it the third-best October on record.

FADA attributed the annual decline largely to a high comparison base, as both Navratri and Diwali fell in October last year, alongside a demand boost following GST rationalisation. This year, Diwali fell in November, shifting a significant part of festive purchases into the current month.

Maruti Suzuki retained market leadership with a 41.75% share, followed by Tata Motors at 14.47% and Mahindra at 12.80%. Dealer inventory remained elevated at 43-45 days, with FADA expecting the Dhanteras-Diwali buying period to help reduce channel stock.

Two-Wheeler Retails Decline 28.35%; Honda Moves Ahead of Hero

Two-wheeler retail registrations fell 28.35% to 23.21 lakh units in October, compared with 32.40 lakh units a year earlier, according to FADA.

Despite the year-on-year decline, volumes increased nearly 30% sequentially from September. FADA attributed the annual contraction to the festive calendar shift and the high base of October 2025.

Honda Motorcycle and Scooter India emerged as the largest two-wheeler manufacturer by retail volumes during the month, with 6,37,630 registrations and a market share of 27.47%. Hero MotoCorp followed with 5,98,433 units and a 25.78% share.

Electric two-wheelers accounted for 9.65% of registrations, up from 4.66% a year earlier.

Electric Mobility and New Products

Electric Passenger Vehicle Retails Jump 76% in October

India's electric passenger vehicle retail sales increased 76.47% year-on-year to 37,049 units in October, according to FADA data. Electric vehicle penetration reached 7.3% of passenger vehicle registrations, compared with 3.5% a year earlier, although it declined from 8.5% in September.

Tata Motors retained its leadership in the electric passenger vehicle market with 14,669 registrations, followed by Mahindra at 8,538 units and JSW MG Motor India at 5,939 units.

VinFast recorded 2,571 registrations, while Maruti Suzuki reported 1,200 electric passenger vehicle registrations as competition continued to expand.

India Could Localise EV Battery Cells in Two to Three Years: Tata Motors

India could achieve substantial localisation of EV battery cells and their components within two to three years, according to Shailesh Chandra, Managing Director and CEO of Tata Motors Passenger Vehicles.

Speaking at Autocar Professional's India EV Conclave 2026, Chandra said domestic battery cell manufacturing was expected to begin within a year, followed by deeper localisation of battery materials and components.

He noted that several battery pack components, including cooling plates and busbars, were already manufactured domestically. However, battery cells and some electronic components continued to depend on imports, while critical minerals would remain an area of external dependence.

Agratas Develops Digital Battery Manufacturing Network Across India and UK

Tata Group's battery manufacturing arm Agratas is developing a common digital manufacturing architecture across its plants in Sanand and Somerset as it prepares to establish large-scale battery cell production.

The company plans to standardise manufacturing execution systems and information technology infrastructure across both facilities to enable consistent operations, data-driven monitoring and transfer of manufacturing processes.

Agratas is also working on battery chemistry development, battery management systems and greater control over production technology as it prepares to supply cells for Tata Motors and Jaguar Land Rover.

The strategy reflects the Tata Group's broader effort to establish battery manufacturing capabilities in India and the UK while reducing dependence on external technology suppliers.

Honda Names First Made-in-India Electric SUV ALPHA

Honda Cars India announced ALPHA as the name of its upcoming electric SUV, which is scheduled to make its global debut in India on December 2, 2026.

The model will be Honda's first electric SUV manufactured in India, with the country also expected to serve as its global production base.

Honda has not yet disclosed the model's battery specifications, driving range, pricing, or market launch timeline.

Mercedes-Benz Commits Additional Rs 200 Crore to India

Mercedes-Benz India announced an additional investment of Rs 200 crore in manufacturing operations, new products and factory digitisation, taking its cumulative investment in the country to Rs 3,200 crore.

The announcement coincided with the launch of the locally produced electric GLC 400 4MATIC at Rs 78.50 lakh, ex-showroom. The model is assembled at the company's Chakan facility on a flexible production line shared with combustion-engine vehicles.

In an exclusive interview with Autocar Professional, Mercedes-Benz Group Chairman Ola Källenius said the company's planned 40-model offensive over three years would expand electric vehicle choices and help accelerate EV adoption.

He also maintained that demand for combustion-engine vehicles would continue to be served alongside the company's expanding electric portfolio.

Renault's Duster Hybrid Strategy Comes Under Focus

Renault's efforts to strengthen its Indian business came under focus in Autocar Professional's Deep Drive discussion on the Duster Hybrid.

The discussion examined whether the hybrid SUV, priced below Rs 17 lakh, could help Renault improve its market position after a slow start and a phased launch that missed the festive season.

It also covered the vehicle's hybrid technology, pricing, product gaps, potential additional powertrain options and the importance of strengthening Renault's dealer network and retail execution in India.

Auto Components, Technology and Earnings

Bosch to Form Dedicated Semiconductor Division, Targets €5 Billion Sales by 2030

German technology supplier Bosch plans to establish a dedicated semiconductor division in 2028, targeting annual semiconductor sales of €5 billion by 2030.

The new unit will consolidate the company's global chip operations, currently part of its Mobility Electronics business, under a separate organisational structure.

Bosch plans to expand its semiconductor business beyond traditional automotive applications into areas such as robotics, consumer electronics and artificial intelligence infrastructure. Its existing Mobility Electronics division will continue to oversee automotive electronic control units and power electronics.

Schaeffler to Cut Nearly 3,500 Jobs, Close Five European Plants

German auto-component manufacturer Schaeffler plans to eliminate 3,460 jobs and close five European factories, according to a Reuters report.

The restructuring will affect 16 locations, including four plants in Germany and one in Belgium. Approximately 2,660 jobs are expected to be cut in Germany by 2028.

The company is responding to weaker demand for combustion-engine components, slower-than-expected electric vehicle adoption and rising competitive pressure.

Schaeffler expects the programme to generate annual savings of approximately €300 million by 2030, although implementation will involve one-time charges of around €480 million.

Minda Corporation Secures Over Rs 1,400 Crore in Display and EV Charger Orders

Minda Corporation has secured orders worth more than Rs 1,400 crore for automotive TFT displays and electric vehicle chargers, with production under both programmes expected to begin in FY28.

Of the total, orders exceeding Rs 1,000 crore are for displays ranging from five to 12 inches, covering two-wheelers, three-wheelers, passenger vehicles and commercial vehicles.

The company has also received an order exceeding Rs 400 crore for 3.5kW chargers from an electric three-wheeler manufacturer.

The orders reflect growing demand for connected vehicle features and electrification-related components. The values represent the cumulative revenue expected over the respective supply programmes.

Motherson Targets Over 1,000 Automation Projects by 2027

Samvardhana Motherson International is stepping up the use of robotics, artificial intelligence and digital technologies across its global manufacturing operations.

The auto-component maker has identified approximately 940 automation projects and aims to implement more than 1,000 projects by 2027.

The programme includes industrial robots, collaborative robots, automated guided vehicles, digital twins and AI-based production systems. The company is targeting a 15% improvement in efficiency as part of its Vision 2030 strategy.

Motherson reported a 27% increase in consolidated revenue to Rs 38,280 crore during Q2 FY27, while EBITDA increased 23% to Rs 3,353 crore.

Uno Minda Targets 18-20% Returns on Rs 5,300 Crore Project Pipeline

Uno Minda is executing manufacturing expansion projects involving approximately Rs 5,300 crore, with management targeting pre-tax returns on capital of 18-20% by the third full year of production.

The investments span alloy wheels, aluminium die-casting, sunroofs and other automotive components.

The company expects initial asset turnover of around 1.8-2 times across the investment pipeline, although returns will vary by business.

Uno Minda reported a 38% year-on-year increase in consolidated revenue to Rs 6,655 crore during Q2 FY27, while profit attributable to shareholders grew 38% to Rs 420 crore.

Bosch Approves Stock Split and Bonus Issue

Bosch Ltd's board approved a stock split and bonus issue, subject to shareholder approval. The company plans to subdivide each equity share with a face value of Rs 10 into five shares of Rs 2 each, followed by a bonus issue of three shares for every one share held after the split.

Together, the proposed corporate actions would result in 20 shares for every existing share. The announcement followed Bosch's Q2 FY27 results, in which consolidated net profit increased 19% to Rs 840 crore, while revenue rose 28% to Rs 7,655 crore.

Mahindra Cuts FY27 Tractor Industry Growth Outlook to Flat

Mahindra & Mahindra lowered its FY27 tractor industry growth forecast to broadly flat, from its earlier expectation of mid-single-digit growth. The company cited deficient rainfall, lower reservoir levels, pressure on farm incomes and rising agricultural input costs.

The slowdown has affected profitability. Mahindra's core tractor operating margin declined 300 basis points year-on-year to 17.6% during Q2 FY27, while tractor sales volumes, including exports, fell 6% to approximately 1.16 lakh units.

The revised outlook reflects growing concern about rural demand and farm-sector profitability during the remainder of the financial year.

Policy and Industry Developments

Karnataka and Oil Refiners Dispute E20 Petrol Testing Results

A dispute emerged over ethanol blending levels in petrol sold at retail outlets in Karnataka. Karnataka authorities alleged that some fuel samples contained ethanol concentrations of up to 31.2%, exceeding the prescribed E20 blend level of 20%.

Public sector oil marketing companies Indian Oil Corporation, Bharat Petroleum Corporation and Hindustan Petroleum Corporation disputed the findings, questioning the sampling procedures and testing methodology. The companies said their fuel complied with the applicable Bureau of Indian Standards specifications.

The disagreement has brought renewed attention to fuel quality monitoring and compliance with India's ethanol blending programme.

Entry, Exit, and Elevation

Toyota Redraws India MD and CEO Masakazu Yoshimura's Regional Responsibilities

Toyota Motor Corporation has restructured the responsibilities of Toyota Kirloskar Motor Managing Director and CEO Masakazu Yoshimura as part of a global management reshuffle.

Effective January 1, 2027, Yoshimura will oversee a newly defined India and Middle East region, while East Asia and Oceania will be separated into a different region under Takanori Azuma.

The restructuring is aimed at improving regional focus and enabling faster decision-making in markets with different growth opportunities and business requirements.

Apollo Tyres Appoints Ravi Kumar Shingari as CFO

Apollo Tyres has appointed Ravi Kumar Shingari as Chief Financial Officer, succeeding Gaurav Kumar, who stepped down in October 2026.

Shingari joined Apollo Tyres in 2018 as Group Head of Finance and has overseen budgeting, accounting, investor relations, and legal affairs.

Before joining the company, he spent more than 16 years with KPMG. He will report directly to Vice Chairman and Managing Director Neeraj Kanwar.

Tenneco Automotive India Names Arvind Gautam Managing Director

Tenneco Automotive India has appointed Arvind Gautam as Managing Director, replacing R.C. Subramaniam, who is moving to a new global leadership role within the Tenneco Group.

Gautam has more than 25 years of automotive manufacturing experience, including senior positions at SKH Group and Autoliv India. He will oversee business operations, profitability, workforce management, customer relationships and strategic growth.

Marelli Appoints Laurent Favre as CEO

Automotive technology supplier Marelli has appointed Laurent Favre as Chief Executive Officer with immediate effect, succeeding interim CEO Frederick Henderson.

Favre previously held senior positions at ThyssenKrupp, ZF, Benteler and Plastic Omnium, now known as OPmobility.

He will lead Marelli through its emergence from Chapter 11 restructuring and focus on improving financial performance and strengthening customer relationships.

Separately, the company's lenders plan to appoint former Audi CEO Bram Schot as Chairman following completion of the restructuring, subject to relevant conditions.

Minda Corporation Appoints Amit Srivastava as CEO of SSD and ASEAN Business

Minda Corporation has appointed Amit Srivastava as CEO of its SSD and ASEAN Business, effective November 6, 2026.

Srivastava brings more than three decades of experience across automotive and manufacturing businesses, having previously held senior roles at Remsons Industries, Bridgestone, Hindalco Industries and AMW Auto Component.

His responsibilities will cover the company's SSD and ASEAN operations, drawing on his experience in business strategy, operations and international market development.

Former Agratas Executive Deepak Khare Joins Exide Energy Solutions as COO

Deepak K Khare has joined Exide Energy Solutions as Chief Operations Officer. Khare was previously Vice President, Manufacturing Operations and Site Head at Agratas, the Tata Group's battery manufacturing business, where he was involved in developing the battery gigafactory at Sanand.

He brings nearly three decades of experience across automotive manufacturing, electric vehicle production and industrial operations, including roles at Lucid Motors, Ford, Airbus and Caterpillar. His appointment comes as Exide expands its lithium-ion battery manufacturing business.

text:
Some Democrats are promising to push for more clean energy to help tackle rising energy costs when they take control of Congress in January, though President Donald Trump says he will use his veto power aggressively.

With new majorities in the House and Senate after last week's midterms, Democrats can set an agenda boosting clean energy and addressing climate change. While those are traditionally core priorities of the party, climate was not a central topic in this election cycle.

Democrats can begin investigations and hold hearings into climate policy rollbacks and elimination of green energy grants by the Republican administration, potentially trying to undo some changes and restore renewable energy incentives.

Sen. Sheldon Whitehouse of Rhode Island, the top Democrat on the Senate Committee on Environment and Public Works, said Trump’s clean energy attacks drove up prices for taxpayers. He said Democrats will "work every angle to lower consumers’ energy costs, and we will demand accountability for the massive corruption wrought by Trump’s fossil-fuel donors.”

American Clean Power Association CEO Jason Grumet said everybody who is trying to build clean energy “feels bolstered.”

Enacting major changes would require Republican support because Democrats will lack the numbers to override presidential vetoes. Even then, lower energy bills are not guaranteed because prices also depend on fuel costs, demand and the expense of maintaining the electric grid.

“The wins give Democrats more leverage over spending and more political power to advance a coherent agenda; the question is whether they’ll use that power effectively,” said Lisa Sachs, director of the Columbia Center on Sustainable Investment. “The vote was for affordability and opportunity. Democrats now need to be clear about which policies deliver them.”

Trump holds veto power but thinks he and Democrats can deal

Trump said after Tuesday's election that Democrats will send over “things that are insane” and he will veto them, speaking generally about legislation. But in the comments to Fox News, he predicted that “after a couple of months of vetoes,” he and Democrats will find ways to work together.

The White House said in a statement Wednesday that Trump is "committed to unleashing reliable, affordable, and secure energy sources to lower prices, strengthen our grid, and protect our national security, and is willing to work with anyone to accomplish this.”

Trump promised to lower energy prices. Instead, his war with Iran and other policies increased the price of gasoline, diesel and electricity. At the same time, the administration canceled many clean energy projects and grants and slowed clean energy permitting.

Trump particularly dislikes offshore wind. Developer Orsted said Thursday that Revolution Wind, a large wind farm in federal waters off Rhode Island, has started operating commercially.

Will the president change his tune on green energy? That's doubtful, said former Sen. Byron Dorgan, D-N.D., co-chair of the government relations practice at ArentFox Schiff.

“He is likely to keep pushing his energy issues, and I think he will be forced to give some room for a new Congress to recreate a different strategy that will add clean energy,” Dorgan said in an email.

Trump promotes expanding production of oil, natural gas and coal, which cause climate change, because he argues that would give the U.S. the lowest-cost electricity. Mike Sommers, CEO of the American Petroleum Institute, the oil and gas industry’s top lobbying group, said that as voters have changed the balance of political power in Washington, “the affordability message is unmistakable.”

Sommers said in a statement there is a real opportunity for bipartisan cooperation to reduce costs and strengthen the economy, starting with an energy permitting reform proposal announced in September. The legislation is aimed at shortening the timeline to get big energy projects started.

Ife Kilimanjaro, executive director of the U.S. Climate Action Network, said Democrats should reject that proposal and use their stronger position to pass legislation that actually builds out much-needed clean energy.

Reversing Trump’s anti-climate policies

The administration has reshaped the Environmental Protection Agency, reversing pollution limits as it promotes fossil fuels.

Clear Street energy transition analyst Tim Moore said he expects Democrats to investigate the climate and environmental rollbacks, in an effort to block some from taking effect. Democrats could also try amending the Clean Air Act to cut carbon pollution and push back against EPA budget cuts, he added.

Rep. Sean Casten, D-Ill., said he is cautiously optimistic some Republicans will now seek to differentiate themselves from Trump and back pro-environmental policies. But without Republican support, Democrats’ more ambitious bills will largely lay out their agenda for 2028, he added.

Climate is not necessarily at the top of Democrats' list of priorities. They are targeting healthcare access, trade tariffs and the Iran war.

Rep. Frank Pallone, the New Jersey Democrat who is expected to become chair of the House Energy and Commerce Committee, said the party should focus on healthcare, affordability, consumer and environmental protections, clean energy and regulating Big Tech.

A potential stalemate seen on clean energy and climate policy

David Victor, a professor of innovation and public policy at the University of California, San Diego, largely expects a stalemate at the federal level on climate and energy policy because of the divided government. He said agreement could come on some bipartisan measures such as a permitting overhaul.

Victor thinks Democratic-led investigations and hearings will center on corruption and other topics that may only touch on energy and climate. Like Casten, Victor said many of the Democratic bills likely will not become law, but will outline what Democrats could accomplish if they win the White House in 2028.

“The Democrats are going to be drafting things that the administration’s not going to like. They don’t have the votes to override a veto, and on top of it, the administration is going to be in turmoil because of its own electoral failures and because of all the investigations,” Victor said. “This seems to me, at the federal level, largely a recipe for kind of intense chaos over the next two years.”

One of the biggest wild cards is the behavior of the administration, which could use executive power to double down on rollbacks of climate and environmental rules, he said.

States could advance clean energy without waiting for Congress

Democrats scored victories in races for governor in states long controlled by Republicans, including Texas and Georgia.

Leah Stokes, a political scientist at the UC Santa Barbara, said there could be a lot of state action on climate next year because of those wins. That is where climate leadership has traditionally come from, she noted. At the federal level, Stokes is optimistic about extending clean energy tax credits since some Republicans support that.

Jay Inslee, a former Democratic governor and congressman from Washington, also expects growing momentum for clean energy in states that elected Democratic governors, particularly in states where they also won legislative majorities.

“This is a really powerful instrument for the United States to join the rest of the world and get back in a leadership position, even if we still have a climate denier that might exercise a veto on some things that we want to do federally,” Inslee said. “So I hope people will pay attention to the big progress we’re going to make on a state-level basis.”

___

Associated Press writers Alexa St. John and Matthew Daly contributed to this report.

India Faces a Battery Recycling Capacity Utilization Challenge India’s battery recycling expansion faces a potential mismatch between announced capacity and available end-of-life batteries.
text:
The electric vehicle (EV) battery recycling industry is emerging as a major investment opportunity as demand for lithium, nickel, cobalt and other critical minerals increases. However, profitability depends on battery chemistry, recycling costs, metal recovery rates, plant utilization, capital expenditure (CAPEX) and revenue from recovered materials.

India’s battery circular economy, including reuse, repurposing and recycling, represents a potential ₹75,500 crore market, according to RMI’s Charting a Circular Battery Future in India report, published in November 2025.

Battery recycling companies are investing in mechanical processing, black-mass production, hydrometallurgical refining and lithium recovery technologies. The commercial challenge is converting announced recycling capacity into profitable operations supported by reliable battery supplies and long-term material sales contracts.

EV Battery Recycling Revenue and Cost Per Tonne

A 2026 study by The Energy and Resources Institute (TERI), prepared with support from NITI Aayog, highlights significant differences in recycling profitability across battery chemistries.

NMC batteries generate higher recovery revenue because they contain valuable nickel and cobalt alongside lithium. LCO batteries benefit from cobalt recovery, while lithium-iron-phosphate (LFP) batteries present more difficult economics because they contain neither nickel nor cobalt.

The study’s figures include material sales and extended producer responsibility (EPR) revenue. They are modelled estimates rather than audited commercial results.

As LFP adoption expands, recyclers will increasingly depend on lower processing costs, improved lithium recovery, EPR income and long-term feedstock contracts.

Economics of a 10,000-Tonne Battery Recycling Plant

The TERI model estimates total recycling costs of ₹294–350 per kilogram, compared with revenue of ₹368–408 per kilogram.

For a facility processing 10,000 tonnes annually, this translates into:

Annual revenue of ₹368–408 crore.

Annual costs of ₹294–350 crore.

Midpoint revenue of ₹388 crore.

Midpoint costs of ₹322 crore.

Modelled midpoint surplus of approximately ₹66 crore.

The estimated surplus equals ₹66,000 per tonne, but it is not equivalent to net profit or free cash flow. The cost model includes a capital allowance, while actual financing costs, taxes and working capital requirements may change returns.

Battery procurement represents the largest cost component at ₹130–151 per kilogram. Processing adds ₹95–122, logistics ₹12–15 and dismantling approximately ₹35 per kilogram.

Material sales contribute ₹256–283 per kilogram, while EPR income adds ₹112–125 per kilogram in the model.

These figures demonstrate why securing battery supplies at competitive prices can be as important as achieving high metal recovery rates.

Major EV Battery Recycling Projects and Investments in India

Gravita India – Mundra, Gujarat: Gravita announced an investment of approximately ₹14 crore in January 2026 for a lithium-ion battery recycling facility with 6,000 tonnes of annual capacity. The initial investment represents approximately ₹23,300 per annual tonne of nameplate capacity. The project began with black-mass processing, with downstream refining planned separately. This makes the investment unsuitable as a benchmark for fully integrated lithium refining.

Attero Recycling – India: Attero announced plans in 2026 to invest approximately ₹7,000 crore over five years in critical-mineral refining and processing facilities. Its broader expansion plans include increasing lithium-ion battery recycling capacity toward 300,000 tonnes annually. The proposed investment covers multiple critical minerals and cannot be attributed entirely to battery recycling.

Rubamin – Halol, Gujarat: Rubamin operates a lithium-ion battery recycling facility with 10,000 tonnes of annual shredding capacity and 7,500 tonnes of black-mass processing capacity. Commissioned in 2025, the facility uses hydrometallurgical processing to recover lithium, nickel, cobalt and manganese compounds. Rubamin reports recovery rates exceeding 90 percent for key metals.

LOHUM – Greater Noida: LOHUM combines lithium-ion battery recycling, critical-mineral recovery and battery repurposing. Its activities illustrate a business model that can generate revenue from recycling and second-life battery applications. However, recycling capacity and battery repurposing capacity must be evaluated separately.

RecycleKaro – Maharashtra: RecycleKaro has developed recycling and metal recovery operations targeting lithium-ion batteries, including nickel recovery. Its business model emphasizes recovering valuable metals rather than relying exclusively on black-mass sales.

LICO Materials – Karnataka: LICO Materials has pursued hydrometallurgical recycling and expansion of battery-processing infrastructure. The economics depend on achieving sufficient throughput, maintaining metal recovery efficiency and securing buyers for refined products.

These projects demonstrate different investment requirements. Mechanical recycling generally requires less initial capital, while integrated refining offers greater potential revenue per tonne but involves higher processing costs and technical risks.

Global Battery Recycling Projects: Redwood Materials, CATL and Primobius

Redwood Materials – United States: Redwood Materials operates a major battery recycling and refining campus in Nevada. The company reported producing 60,000 metric tonnes of critical minerals in 2025 and announced a $350 million Series E funding round. Its integrated operations demonstrate how recycling businesses can expand into battery-material manufacturing and other applications.

CATL – China: CATL reported recycling 210,000 tonnes of spent batteries in 2025 and regenerating approximately 24,000 tonnes of lithium salts. Its operations illustrate the scale achievable through integration with battery manufacturing and materials supply chains.

Primobius – Europe: Primobius’ engineering study estimated €274 million in CAPEX for a hydrometallurgical facility processing 12,000 tonnes of black mass annually, with annual operating expenditure of €56 million. A combined shredding and refining configuration was estimated at €377 million in CAPEX and €83 million in annual operating costs. These are engineering estimates rather than actual completed-project costs.

R3 Lithium – Georgia, United States: R3 Lithium acquired the former Ascend Elements recycling facility in Covington in July 2026 and announced the restart of operations in September. The company reported $15 million in Series A funding and approximately $1 billion in signed offtake agreements. Its experience highlights the importance of financing, customer contracts and continuous commercial production.

Lithium Recovery Efficiency and Black-Mass Revenue

Lithium recovery efficiency directly affects revenue from recycled batteries.

For example, one tonne of battery material containing 14 kilograms of elemental lithium could yield approximately 12.6 kilograms at a 90 percent extraction rate. This is equivalent to around 67 kilograms of lithium carbonate before further processing losses.

Actual revenue depends on lithium concentration, recovery efficiency, product purity, commodity prices and refining expenses.

Mechanical recyclers sell black mass containing lithium, nickel, cobalt, manganese and graphite. Integrated recyclers can generate additional value by converting these materials into higher-purity products.

However, refiners must finance chemical processing, purification equipment, environmental controls and additional working capital.

India Faces a Battery Recycling Capacity Utilization Challenge

India’s battery recycling expansion faces a potential mismatch between announced capacity and available end-of-life batteries.

A NITI Aayog assessment of battery recycling capacity estimates that available end-of-life lithium-ion battery feedstock could reach approximately 60,000 tonnes in 2030, compared with announced processing capacity of 115,000 tonnes.

This imbalance creates risks for plants that depend on high utilization to recover fixed operating costs and capital investment.

Battery manufacturing scrap, imports where permitted and long-term supply agreements may help improve utilization, but investors must verify actual feedstock availability.

EPR Revenue, Profitability and Investment Returns

India’s Battery Waste Management Rules, 2022 establish extended producer responsibility (EPR) requirements and a regulatory framework supporting battery recycling, material recovery and recycled-content obligations.

EPR certificate revenue is an important component of the TERI financial model, contributing ₹112–125 per kilogram. However, certificate prices, eligibility and payment timing can affect cash flow.

A 10 percent increase in battery procurement costs and a simultaneous 10 percent reduction in material sales revenue would reduce the illustrative midpoint surplus from ₹66,000 to approximately ₹25,000 per tonne, assuming other variables remain unchanged.

Investors should prioritize projects with contracted battery supplies, proven recovery technology, qualified material buyers and demonstrated plant utilization.

The economics of Gravita, Attero, Rubamin, LOHUM, Redwood Materials and CATL show that commercial success depends not simply on recycling capacity but on the cost of securing batteries, the value of recovered minerals and the ability to produce saleable materials consistently.

For the EV battery recycling industry, the most important investment indicators remain revenue per tonne, recovery cost per tonne, actual throughput, CAPEX, EPR cash receipts and risk-adjusted returns.

Among Railroad Commissioner Elect Joe Rosenthal’s priorities, including plugging orphan wells, banning flaring and increased groundwater monitoring, is a commitment to working with the industry where he built expertise. And oil and gas leaders seem to be welcoming that cooperation.

“Texans’ economic security and energy future depend on sound, science-based legislation, steady executive leadership, and a Railroad Commission that regulates with fairness and predictability,” [treasurer of the Texas Oil and Gas Association Good Government Committee Todd] Staples said. “Those taking office in January inherit this responsibility, and we intend to be a constructive partner in the legislative process and a committed advocate for the industry.”

Estimating the US Energy System Impacts of the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act | Rhodium Group

New analysis from the Rhodium Group models the effects of BAAJA on the country should it pass in current form. This comes as the bill’s future is uncertain following Democratic gains in the midterms.

We project that the combined impact of these provisions would reduce household electricity bills by $50-78 per year in 2040 compared to without BAAJA, both because easier permitting would allow lower-cost resources to connect to the grid and because the bill explicitly prohibits charging non-data center customers for data center costs. The transmission provisions of the bill enable accelerated average interregional transmission build rates nearly triple that of the last decade or more and drive an additional 17-249 GW of clean resources to be built through 2040… Taken together, these provisions uniformly reduce economywide greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions by 5-148 million metric tons annually in 2040 and as much as 1.5 gigatons cumulatively, compared to without BAAJA.

Grid Funding from Data Centers in the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act (BAAJA) | Grid Strategies

Grid Strategies also released estimates about what BAAJA might do, specifically what the ratepayer protection section would mean for data centers. The bill would have the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission allow so-called “and” pricing for transmission service, so data centers would pay both the embedded cost of the existing grid and the new transmission costs they trigger. ERCOT isn’t included in the estimate because FERC doesn’t regulate transmission service there.

“We estimate the ‘and’ pricing policy change in BAAJA will result in $55 billion in transmission service charges to data centers over ten years, or close to $6 billion per year.”

text:

FILE - President Donald Trump speaks in the Oval Office of the White House, Sept. 30, 2026, in Washington.

FILE - A person fuels up a vehicle at a gas station March 10, 2026, in New York.

FILE - Turbines are visible at Sunrise Wind offshore wind farm that is under construction off the coast of Montauk Point, New York, April 23, 2026.

FILE - American Electric Power's John Amos coal-fired power plant in Winfield, W.Va., stands across the Kanawha River, March 22, 2026.

Some Democrats are promising to push for more clean energy to help tackle rising energy costs when they take control of Congress in January , though President Donald Trump says he will use his veto power aggressively .

With new majorities in the House and Senate after last week's midterms, Democrats can set an agenda boosting clean energy and addressing climate change . While those are traditionally core priorities of the party, climate was not a central topic in this election cycle .

Democrats can begin investigations and hold hearings into climate policy rollbacks and elimination of green energy grants by the Republican administration, potentially trying to undo some changes and restore renewable energy incentives.

Sen. Sheldon Whitehouse of Rhode Island, the top Democrat on the Senate Committee on Environment and Public Works, said Trump’s clean energy attacks drove up prices for taxpayers. He said Democrats will "work every angle to lower consumers’ energy costs, and we will demand accountability for the massive corruption wrought by Trump’s fossil-fuel donors.”

American Clean Power Association CEO Jason Grumet said everybody who is trying to build clean energy “feels bolstered.”

Enacting major changes would require Republican support because Democrats will lack the numbers to override presidential vetoes. Even then, lower energy bills are not guaranteed because prices also depend on fuel costs, demand and the expense of maintaining the electric grid.

“The wins give Democrats more leverage over spending and more political power to advance a coherent agenda; the question is whether they’ll use that power effectively,” said Lisa Sachs, director of the Columbia Center on Sustainable Investment. “The vote was for affordability and opportunity. Democrats now need to be clear about which policies deliver them.”

Trump said after Tuesday's election that Democrats will send over “things that are insane” and he will veto them, speaking generally about legislation. But in the comments to Fox News, he predicted that “after a couple of months of vetoes,” he and Democrats will find ways to work together.

The White House said in a statement Wednesday that Trump is "committed to unleashing reliable, affordable, and secure energy sources to lower prices, strengthen our grid, and protect our national security, and is willing to work with anyone to accomplish this.”

Trump promised to lower energy prices. Instead, his war with Iran and other policies increased the price of gasoline, diesel and electricity. At the same time, the administration canceled many clean energy projects and grants and slowed clean energy permitting.

Trump particularly dislikes offshore wind . Developer Orsted said Thursday that Revolution Wind, a large wind farm in federal waters off Rhode Island, has started operating commercially.

Will the president change his tune on green energy? That's doubtful, said former Sen. Byron Dorgan, D-N.D., co-chair of the government relations practice at ArentFox Schiff.

“He is likely to keep pushing his energy issues, and I think he will be forced to give some room for a new Congress to recreate a different strategy that will add clean energy,” Dorgan said in an email.

Trump promotes expanding production of oil, natural gas and coal, which cause climate change, because he argues that would give the U.S. the lowest-cost electricity. Mike Sommers, CEO of the American Petroleum Institute, the oil and gas industry’s top lobbying group, said that as voters have changed the balance of political power in Washington, “the affordability message is unmistakable.”

Sommers said in a statement there is a real opportunity for bipartisan cooperation to reduce costs and strengthen the economy, starting with an energy permitting reform proposal announced in September . The legislation is aimed at shortening the timeline to get big energy projects started.

Ife Kilimanjaro, executive director of the U.S. Climate Action Network, said Democrats should reject that proposal and use their stronger position to pass legislation that actually builds out much-needed clean energy.

The administration has reshaped the Environmental Protection Agency , reversing pollution limits as it promotes fossil fuels.

Clear Street energy transition analyst Tim Moore said he expects Democrats to investigate the climate and environmental rollbacks, in an effort to block some from taking effect. Democrats could also try amending the Clean Air Act to cut carbon pollution and push back against EPA budget cuts, he added.

Rep. Sean Casten, D-Ill., said he is cautiously optimistic some Republicans will now seek to differentiate themselves from Trump and back pro-environmental policies. But without Republican support, Democrats’ more ambitious bills will largely lay out their agenda for 2028, he added.

Climate is not necessarily at the top of Democrats' list of priorities. They are targeting healthcare access, trade tariffs and the Iran war.

Rep. Frank Pallone, the New Jersey Democrat who is expected to become chair of the House Energy and Commerce Committee, said the party should focus on healthcare, affordability, consumer and environmental protections, clean energy and regulating Big Tech.

David Victor, a professor of innovation and public policy at the University of California, San Diego, largely expects a stalemate at the federal level on climate and energy policy because of the divided government. He said agreement could come on some bipartisan measures such as a permitting overhaul.

Victor thinks Democratic-led investigations and hearings will center on corruption and other topics that may only touch on energy and climate. Like Casten, Victor said many of the Democratic bills likely will not become law, but will outline what Democrats could accomplish if they win the White House in 2028.

“The Democrats are going to be drafting things that the administration’s not going to like. They don’t have the votes to override a veto, and on top of it, the administration is going to be in turmoil because of its own electoral failures and because of all the investigations,” Victor said. “This seems to me, at the federal level, largely a recipe for kind of intense chaos over the next two years.”

One of the biggest wild cards is the behavior of the administration, which could use executive power to double down on rollbacks of climate and environmental rules, he said.

Democrats scored victories in races for governor in states long controlled by Republicans, including Texas and Georgia.

Leah Stokes, a political scientist at the UC Santa Barbara, said there could be a lot of state action on climate next year because of those wins. That is where climate leadership has traditionally come from, she noted. At the federal level, Stokes is optimistic about extending clean energy tax credits since some Republicans support that.

Jay Inslee, a former Democratic governor and congressman from Washington, also expects growing momentum for clean energy in states that elected Democratic governors, particularly in states where they also won legislative majorities.

“This is a really powerful instrument for the United States to join the rest of the world and get back in a leadership position, even if we still have a climate denier that might exercise a veto on some things that we want to do federally,” Inslee said. “So I hope people will pay attention to the big progress we’re going to make on a state-level basis.”

___

Associated Press writers Alexa St. John and Matthew Daly contributed to this report.

Maine environmental regulators have fined a Bristol solar development almost $94,000 to resolve violations of Maine’s erosion control and water pollution laws.

The Maine Board of Environmental Protection approved a consent agreement between the state and Overlook Solar Partners last week.

According to the settlement, erosion control measures at Overlook’s 5 megawatt solar site failed in 2022 and sediment-laden water runoff polluted nearby wetlands.

The company later corrected the violations and stabilized the site, according to the settlement.

Overlook is an affiliate of Luminace Holdings, a solar development company that is itself a subsidiary of energy giant Brookfield. A Luminace spokesperson did not respond to a request for comment.

The Overlook case is the latest in a string of penalties imposed on solar developers for almost identical violations according to a review of Maine Department of Environmental Protection records.

Since 2022, the state has finalized settlements with at least six solar developers, nearly all for erosion control and stormwater runoff violations. Another settlement, with Fryeburg Solar, was proposed in October.

Another Luminace subsidiary, Tower Solar Partners was fined $236,000 by state regulators last year for violations in Emden that led to sediment pollution flowing into the Kennebec River.

To date, the state has recovered almost $660,000 in penalties, according to a review of the settlements.

The violations occurred in the last five years, during a boom in Maine solar construction as companies capitalized on generous rates year subsidized for community solar projects of 5 megawatts or less. Those incentives were electric rolled last back.

title: How China's clean-tech machine is reshaping the global climate fight - The Japan Times
authors: The Japan Times, No Author, int-no_author
description:
An investigation in 2024 found that most global climate finance comes in the form of loans — and sometimes at market interest rates that funnel billions of dollars back to rich countries.
But its huge clean tech exports mean it has also become among the biggest global forces in reducing climate-damaging emissions.
This year’s exports from China, meanwhile, are on track to avoid 337 MtCO2 in the Global South, the analysis shows.
The $132 billion figure for China’s global climate contribution also includes an estimated $40 billion of Chinese foreign direct investment into clean-technology projects in developing countries.
Export giant, diplomatic mouse Beijing has so far shown little interest in translating its commercial might into diplomatic leadership at global climate talks since President Donald Trump withdrew the United States from international climate cooperation in 2025.
text:
China sent $132 billion in clean technology and investment to the developing world last year, by far the largest contribution to carbon-dioxide reduction of any country.

In fact, the nation’s green-manufacturing juggernaut, built in part through heavy subsidies from Beijing, nearly matches the current total of grants, loans and private finance that all wealthy countries sent to poorer ones in 2024 to help fight climate change, according to analysis.

Those loans and grants stemmed from a climate-finance program the world’s wealthiest nations agreed to at a 2009 United Nations climate conference on the premise that industrialized nations made outsized contributions to the climate crisis — and had outsized means to help poorer countries pay to clean it up.

An investigation in 2024 found that most global climate finance comes in the form of loans — and sometimes at market interest rates that funnel billions of dollars back to rich countries.

China took a different approach, funneling billions in subsidies into its own green-energy industries, serving its own national interest to dominate next-generation manufacturing domestically and globally.

The result: massive and rapid market-share gains in solar panels, batteries and battery minerals, electric vehicles, wind turbines and other green products.

China remains by far the world’s biggest greenhouse-gas emitter because of its large population, concentration of heavy industry and reliance on coal power. But its huge clean tech exports mean it has also become among the biggest global forces in reducing climate-damaging emissions.

Analysis used customs data to calculate the value of Chinese exports of clean technologies to countries classified by the Organization for Economic Cooperation and Development as developing nations.

Those exports alone will help the Global South avoid 257 million metric tons of carbon dioxide emissions (MtCO2) per year once deployed — an amount equal to the annual carbon dioxide emissions of France, according to analysis by Lauri Myllyvirta, co-founder of the Helsinki-based Center for Research on Energy and Clean Air. This year’s exports from China, meanwhile, are on track to avoid 337 MtCO2 in the Global South, the analysis shows.

Reporters were unable to find a reliable single estimate of how much greenhouse gas emissions are avoided as a result of global climate finance from rich to poor countries.

The OECD estimates a fifth of all rich world climate giving in 2024 came from the private sector.

The United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change and the High Ambition Coalition — an informal coalition of nations that has advocated for substantial climate finance — did not immediately comment for this story.

The $132 billion figure for China’s global climate contribution also includes an estimated $40 billion of Chinese foreign direct investment into clean-technology projects in developing countries. The investment data was compiled by Mathias Larsen and Xiaokang Xue at the London School of Economics.

That brings China’s contribution to nearly equal to the $137 billion in climate finance that wealthy nations provided to poorer ones in 2024 under their U.N. climate pledges, according to the most recent figures provided by the OECD.

The figures are not directly comparable. China’s total largely reflects commercial transactions focused on clean energy development, while climate finance can also support other types of programs like developing climate-resilient agricultural techniques or cleaning up damage from major storms or floods.

But the comparison illustrates the extraordinary scale at which China’s manufacturing economy is now shaping the energy transition in poorer countries.

The findings point to a potential shift in the mechanics of the global energy transition, according to Li Shuo, a veteran observer of China at U.N. climate talks who heads the China Climate Hub at the Asia Society Policy Institute.

For years, climate talks focused on how much money and technology wealthy countries would provide to poorer ones to help them decarbonize. China’s manufacturing boom is creating another pathway: Driving down the price of clean technology through self-interested innovation and scale — until developing countries adopt it for economic reasons.

“You can align it to your economic agenda,” he said.

Export giant, diplomatic mouse

Beijing has so far shown little interest in translating its commercial might into diplomatic leadership at global climate talks since President Donald Trump withdrew the United States from international climate cooperation in 2025.

China’s diplomatic role likely will take center stage as nations gather this month for the U.N.’s COP31 climate conference in Antalya, Turkey.

Bilateral agreements between heavyweights Washington and Beijing have traditionally paved the way for international climate agreements, including the landmark 2015 Paris deal to limit global warming. But Beijing may be unwilling to go on alone without its geopolitical counterweight at the table, according to former climate negotiators.

Beijing may also be worried that taking a bold stance on global carbon reduction would bring unwanted pressure for China to give more climate aid or cut its own fossil-fuel emissions, observers say. China emits about a third of all carbon dioxide emissions and still burns coal for more than half its power.

“How China engages on different levels in the coming years is the most fundamental thing that is going to happen on climate because of both their role in clean-tech deployment … but also because of their emissions profile,” said Jennifer Morgan, Germany’s former climate minister.

China’s Ministry of Commerce said the country is an important contributor to the global green transformation, and that its wind and solar exports have cumulatively reduced global emissions by roughly 4.1 billion tons of CO2 over the past five years — the equivalent of around 80% of the total emissions of the United States in one year.

“Against the backdrop of a global climate governance ’action deficit,’ China will continue to uphold a responsible attitude, working with other countries to address challenges, overcome difficulties, and jointly promote global green and low-carbon transformation and sustainable development,” it said.

Forcing out fossil fuels

Meanwhile, China’s manufacturing boom has made renewable energy more affordable in the developing world.

When Ethiopia banned combustion engine car imports in 2024, for example, it was the first country to take such a dramatic step toward electric vehicles. The decision was less about emissions and more about cutting its fuel import bill, its deputy minister of transport at the time said.

“No one in Ethiopia is asking COP to pay for any of this; the economics have just switched. It is just the cheapest and best solution,” said Larsen, a senior policy fellow at the London School of Economics, who built the database of Chinese green investment used in this story.

China has been by far the world’s biggest supplier of electric vehicles over the past few years, as dozens of subsidized automakers have waged a fierce price war in China and dramatically increased exports.

The green transition has been similarly pragmatic in Pakistan, which imported 17GW worth of solar from China last year, according to data from Ember, roughly on par with Germany’s installations that year. Those panels will cut emissions and, more importantly, provide cheap, reliable power in a country that often has neither.

Nearly two thirds of China’s exports of solar panels, and the cells needed to make them, went to the developing world last year, according to analysis of customs data.

The picture is different in wealthy countries like the United States and parts of Europe, which in recent years have imposed tariffs and other restrictions on Chinese clean technology to protect their domestic manufacturers from the surge in shipments.

The United States, for example, imposes tariffs exceeding 100% on Chinese electric vehicles and has taken other measures to effectively block them from the market.

“What is striking is that policies originally designed to address climate change are now facing opposition not because of their climate impacts, but because of concerns about trade and competitiveness,” said André Corrêa do Lago, a veteran climate negotiator for Brazil, which hosted last year’s climate summit.

title: AI Is Queued Behind an Electrical Steel Transformer Shortage - Intelligent Living
description:
Around 95% of transformer cores in the United States use this steel, according to a Congressional Research Service analysis of distribution transformer supply.
Without qualified core steel, a transformer factory has a full order book and nothing to build.
A large transformer that took less than a year before the pandemic now takes two to four years.
DOE said in a 2024 notice that distribution transformer manufacturing uses either imported steel or steel from the sole domestic producer.
Why does the electrical steel transformer shortage delay AI data centers?
text:
The AI boom is queuing behind a steel almost nobody has heard of. Data-center projects that need power this year are being told their transformers will arrive in two to four years. The reason sits one step earlier in the supply chain, at the mills that roll the magnetic core inside every large transformer.

That core uses grain-oriented electrical steel. Grain-oriented steel means a specialty steel rolled and heat treated so its magnetic crystals line up in one direction. A transformer core means the stacked steel heart where voltage is stepped up or down. Lead time means the wait from order to delivery. Right now, that wait translates into years of delay for grid projects, power plants, and server campuses alike.

What This Obscure Steel Does Inside Every Transformer

Every transformer moves power by moving magnetism. Alternating current in copper windings creates a magnetic field. That field must pass through iron with as little waste heat as possible. Grain-oriented steel does this job better than ordinary steel because its crystals point the same way the field wants to go.

The process is exact. Mills control chemistry, rolling temperature, thickness reduction, and high temperature annealing. The result is thin sheets, each coated to insulate it from its neighbor, then stacked into a core. Windings of copper or aluminum wrap around that core. The assembly is dried under vacuum, placed in a tank, filled with insulating oil, and tested for weeks.

Around 95% of transformer cores in the United States use this steel, according to a Congressional Research Service analysis of distribution transformer supply. It is also the core material for large power transformers, the 100 megavolt ampere and larger units that step voltage between transmission lines. There is no drop in substitute that matches its loss performance at full load. Amorphous steel, the main alternative, works well at low loads but is larger, heavier, and less suited to dense urban substations.

This is why steel metallurgy now sets server schedules. Without qualified core steel, a transformer factory has a full order book and nothing to build. That dynamic echoes other single ingredient chokepoints, where a tiny specialty material can throttle jets, chips, and defense systems even when bulk raw materials are available.

How Many Years the Wait Has Become

The numbers are stark. A large transformer that took less than a year before the pandemic now takes two to four years. A distribution unit that took months took up to two years at the 2024 peak.

The table below keeps each figure with its publisher and date. Weeks convert at 52 weeks per year so rows share one unit. Compare averages to averages and estimates to estimates, not across different measures.

Some of these numbers are measured and some are projections, so it matters who published them. The 128 week and 144 week figures are confirmed survey averages from Wood Mackenzie’s Q2 2025 work, while the 30 percent power transformer supply deficit and 10 percent distribution deficit for 2025 are analyst estimates from Wood Mackenzie’s August 2025 outlook, not counted deliveries. Prices show the same split: the Bureau of Labor Statistics producer price index rose roughly 40 percent from 2020 to 2024 after inflation adjustment, a confirmed federal series, while the 77 percent rise for power transformers since 2019 is an industry survey estimate reported in trade coverage.

Before the pandemic, a large unit could be ordered with less than a year of lead time, according to DOE’s July 2024 resilience report. By 2024, DOE’s electricity chief was describing large units as growing from three to as much as four years. That shift turns the transformer from a late procurement detail into the first reservation on a project timeline.

One US Mill Gates Every Domestic Core

Only one mill in the United States makes grain-oriented electrical steel at scale. That mill is Cleveland-Cliffs Butler Works in Butler Township, Pennsylvania. DOE said in a 2024 notice that distribution transformer manufacturing uses either imported steel or steel from the sole domestic producer.

The dependence runs deep. Between half and three quarters of finished cores used in assembled domestic distribution transformers are imported, CRS found. Cores made domestically get 95 percent of their steel from that one supplier, CRS found in the same report. As of 2020, about 85 percent of imported grain-oriented steel came from South Korea, before tariff rules changed.

World supply is narrow. Qualified producers include Nippon Steel and JFE in Japan, POSCO in South Korea, ThyssenKrupp in Germany, Baosteel in China, Stalprodukt in Poland, NLMK in Russia, and Cleveland-Cliffs in the United States. Each line needs precise annealing and then an 18 month qualification with transformer makers before utilities will accept the steel. A new line is a multiyear capital project, not a shed with a rolling mill.

Butler is now expanding. Cleveland-Cliffs greenlit a 195 million dollar hot mill expansion that began production earlier this year and is expected to complete by 2028, a 25 percent capacity addition, with 75 million dollars from a DOE grant that survived the change from the Biden to the Trump administration, according to local reporting on the company’s August 2026 briefing. The company argues that stable demand for grain-oriented cores is needed to justify that investment.

Trade policy tightened around the same steel. Section 232 tariffs on steel reached 50 percent, with derivative products including cores and laminations added effective 15 August 2025. A separate 50 percent tariff on certain copper products took effect 1 August 2025. Copper matters because it forms the windings wrapped around the steel core. Tariffs do not create steel, but they change the math for domestic expansion.

Why Data-Center Growth Feels It First

Data centers do not wait like other loads. A campus needs a substation, one or more large transformers, and upstream reinforcement before servers can run. When those units quote at 128 to 144 weeks, the energization date moves by years, not months.

Demand hit at the same time from every direction. Wood Mackenzie’s August 2025 estimate put US power transformer demand up 116 percent since 2019, against 41 percent for distribution units. Generator step-up demand, the units that connect power plants to the grid, grew 274 percent in one industry tally. That surge is why federal efforts to count data-center power use site by site matter for planning, because averages hide local peaks that force transformer swaps.

Money alone cannot print a delivery slot. Framework agreements now reserve factory capacity years ahead, which favors large buyers who can promise volume. A municipal utility or a single campus pays more, waits for a cancellation, or buys through an intermediary. That structure explains why tech firms pledged to pay for new power supply and grid upgrades tied to their loads, yet still face physical queues for substations and transformers.

Two facts explain why servers wait on steel:

Each campus needs large units. Substation and step-up transformers are custom built for site voltage, impedance, and fault levels.

Each slot is shared. Wind, solar, replacement, and data-center orders all draw from the same test bays and annealing lines.

There is also a direct competition for slots and for steel. When offshore wind projects were canceled or delayed in 2023 and 2024, their transformer slots were reallocated. Data centers took some of them. That reallocation is useful, but it shows the queue is shared. One project’s exit becomes another project’s entry. Grain-oriented steel is also used in electric motors and EV chargers, so transformer makers compete with motor makers for the same mills.

Some data-center operators try to bypass the queue with on-site generation. That workaround has its own bottleneck, because gas turbines recently quoted at three to seven years with prices in 2027 expected near triple 2019 levels. The steel queue is not avoided. It is traded for a turbine queue.

Old Transformers Compete With New Data Centers

The grid must replace as well as expand. Between 60 million and 80 million distribution transformers serve the United States. Roughly half are over 33 years old and near end of life. Utilities add or replace 1.4 million to 2.4 million units per year. Large power units last 30 to 40 years, and many now in service were installed between the late 1950s and late 1970s.

A replacement order uses the same factory slot as a new data-center substation. A city substation with a failing 1968 unit cannot defer forever, because a summer peak with no spare is a blackout risk. Yet a replacement adds no new capacity, so it never shows up as progress toward connection targets. Utilities are therefore choosing between keeping old units alive and serving new load.

Condition monitoring buys time but not renewal. Dissolved gas analysis, thermal imaging, and partial discharge testing can extend safe life by years. They cannot restore aged cellulose insulation to new condition. The difference between replacing at year 35 and year 45 is a decade of avoided demand on a constrained supply chain. That decade is valuable when new capacity takes three to five years to arrive.

What Could Shorten the Queue

New plants are coming, on dated schedules. Siemens Energy announced its first US transformer plant in Charlotte, North Carolina in February 2024, first with early 2026 timing and later with production expected in early 2027. Prolec GE added a medium power line in Goldsboro, North Carolina in May 2025 with plans to double capacity by 2030. Hitachi Energy announced a large power facility in South Boston, Virginia in September 2025. Virginia Transformer is expanding in Rincon, Georgia with construction expected from January 2026. Each date is a company statement, while delivery dates still come only from a supplier quote.

Standardize designs. Ten design attributes can yield about 80,000 distribution configurations, an Oak Ridge National Laboratory speaker told a March 2026 DOE workshop. Fewer variants mean fewer changeovers. National Grid cut about 32 percent of its roughly 700 stock keeping units by March 2026.

Approve alternates early. Special arresters, breakers, fuses, and dual voltage switches still lagged in March 2026. Prolec GE estimates simpler connections and single voltage designs can cut cycle time 5 to 8 percent.

Settle the efficiency rule. The final efficiency standards published in April 2024 require compliance for units made on or after 23 April 2029. DOE says the final levels need far less amorphous steel than proposed and let about 75 percent of units stay on grain-oriented cores. A June 2026 request for information on grid security and material supply gathers data only. The 2029 date stands.

Pool spares and refurbish. Utilities are holding more spares and refurbishing units they once would have replaced. Spare large units need the same maintenance as working units, so storage records and oil history decide whether a bridge unit is safe.

None of these adds a transformer this quarter. New winding lines take one to two years to obtain. New plants take one to three years to build. Qualification adds months more. The realistic outlook is late decade relief for large units, with distribution improving first.

Frequently Asked Questions

What is grain-oriented electrical steel?

It is a specialty steel rolled and annealed so magnetic crystals align with the rolling direction. That alignment lets magnetic fields pass with low energy loss. It forms the laminated core inside most transformers.

What is a transformer core?

It is the stacked steel heart of a transformer. Thin insulated sheets are stacked into a shape that keeps magnetic flux inside the iron. Copper windings wrap around it to change voltage from high to low or low to high.

What is lead time in this context?

It is the wait from order or drawing approval to delivery. Published figures often leave the start point open. Always ask a supplier whether the date runs from order or from approved drawings, and when the factory test slot is booked.

Why does the electrical steel transformer shortage delay AI data centers?

Each campus needs substation and step-up transformers to connect. Those large units now average 128 to 144 weeks in confirmed 2025 survey results, or about 2.5 to 2.8 years. Without the transformer, the line and the servers wait.

How long do transformers take right now?

Distribution units eased to an estimated 30 weeks by Q2 2025 after a two year peak in 2024. Large power units still take years. DOE cites 36 months commonly and up to 60 months maximum. Wood Mackenzie’s 2024 range was 80 to 210 weeks, or 1.5 to 4.0 years.

Who makes this steel?

A handful of mills worldwide, including producers in Japan, South Korea, Germany, China, Poland, and Russia. In the United States, Cleveland-Cliffs Butler Works is the sole domestic source. Most US transformer steel beyond that mill is imported.

Will new factories fix it?

They help after 2027, not this year. Announced US plants add slots at the margin and must still qualify steel, hire welders and winders, and book test bays. Distribution should ease first. Very high voltage units ease last.

What Happens Next

The binding constraint is physical, not procedural. Queue reforms can shorten paperwork. They cannot add a transformer. The grid discovered all at once that it needs several hundred large units per year, plus millions of smaller ones, from a steel supply rolled in a handful of mills.

The constructive path is unglamorous. Order early. Standardize where protection settings allow. Qualify alternates. Track oil history on spares. Give mills like Butler a clear demand signal so annealing lines are worth building. The AI era will still arrive. It will arrive on the schedule of its steel.

authors: Graham Readfearn, Fiona Harvey, Oliver Milman, Adam Morton, www.theguardian.com, graham-readfearn, fiona-harvey, oliver-milman, adam-morton
