text:
The Cop31 summit must produce progress, “a tangible outcome ... that people can see is real”, its host has said as scores of world leaders and representatives of close to 190 countries gather in Turkey for the UN climate talks.

The high-stakes meeting begins on Monday, as countries around the world grapple with the strongest El Niño weather system on record, supercharged by fossil fuels, which is set to take hundreds of thousands of lives and cause damage costing trillions of dollars.

Friction is expected between the rich and poor worlds over who pays for the impacts of the climate crisis, and the slow pace of cutting greenhouse gas emissions. Temperatures have broken records this year, surpassing the limit of 1.5C above preindustrial levels aimed for in the 2015 Paris climate agreement.

Adão Soares Barbosa, the chair of the Least Developed Countries, a negotiating group of 44 nations, said: “Keeping 1.5C within reach by minimising the duration and magnitude of the overshoot, delivering accessible and predictable climate finance, strengthening adaptation, and addressing loss and damage [caused to poor countries by extreme weather] are not political choices but matters of survival. The credibility of the Paris agreement will be measured not by promises made, but by commitments fulfilled, and lives protected in vulnerable countries.”

Unusually, the talks will have dual hosts: they will take place in the Turkish city of Antalya but the formal negotiations will be presided over by Australia, following a compromise reached last year over their competing bids.

Chris Bowen, Australia’s climate and energy minister and president of negotiations for Cop31, told the Guardian in an interview: “We need a tangible outcome focused on implementation [of emissions cuts and finance] that people can see is real. We need progress, it needs to be a step forward on previous Cops.”

Australia also wants a “strong, ambitious outcome” to raise the plight of low-lying countries in the Pacific region for whom the climate crisis poses an existential threat. “We need to finally elevate some of the issues so important to our Pacific family,” Bowen said. “[Only] 0.2% of the world’s available climate finance goes to small island developing states for adaptation, for countries whose very existence is at stake.”

But climate advocates and more than 500 scientists in Australia said Australia must stop approving coalmines and gas projects if it wanted to escape the charge of hypocrisy.

The summit will have a notable absentee, with the US refusing to send a delegation for the second year in a row. The Trump administration wants no part of “extremist climate policies” embraced by other countries, according to a White House spokesperson.

Donald Trump expressed glee shortly before the US midterm elections about the huge profits made by oil and gas companies due to the Iran war, which he started and has caused an increase in living costs around the world. “I don’t give a damn,” the president said at a recent rally in Georgia. “I’m going to say it: we’re making a frickin’ fortune.”

However, a group of 20 Democratic members of Congress have made the trip to Antalya, buoyed by their party’s stunning success in the US midterms last week that will enable them to stymie Trump’s attempts to dismantle pollution rules and withhold financial support for clean energy.

Developing countries and civil society will seek to put climate finance and justice at the heart of the Cop31 talks. Rukiya Khamis, the east Africa programme manager at the 350.org campaigning group, said: “Across east Africa, people are facing the devastating impacts of a climate crisis they did not cause. From prolonged droughts to destructive floods, we are losing homes, livelihoods and access to food and water. Yet the money needed to respond to these impacts remains out of reach for many of the countries and communities most affected. It is fundamentally unjust that those least responsible are being left to carry the greatest costs.”

This summer more than 50,000 people died in Europe due to heatwaves, severe wildfire smoke shrouded swathes of North America and a glacier collapse in Nepal triggered a landslide that caused more than 1,500 deaths, while the El Niño weather event, described as “staggering” by scientists and still to reach its peak, is gathering strength.

However, while the pace of progress on cutting global emissions has been slow, the Iran war has spurred many countries to see fossil fuels as expensive and vulnerable to shocks, while renewables continue to plummet in price.

Simon Stiell, the UN’s climate chief, said before the talks: “Climate impacts hit every population and every economy harder each year. [But] almost every major economy, and many medium-sized and smaller economies, now see climate action as a central driver of economic growth, jobs, and affordable and secure energy.”

Cop host Turkey also wants more countries to switch to electric technologies, such as electric vehicles and heat pumps, as these are many times more efficient than their fossil fuel counterparts. A target for 35% of global final energy to come from electricity by 2035 will be on the table, but faces opposition from some.

Both presidency countries rely heavily on fossil fuels. Australia is one of the world’s leading exporters of coal and liquefied natural gas. The centre-left Labor government has targets to reach net zero greenhouse gas emissions by 2050, and have more than 80% of its electricity generated by solar and wind by 2030, but is off track to meet them.

Labor also faces a political threat from the resurgent rightwing One Nation party, which dismisses climate science. One Nation and the Liberal and National party coalition want to scrap the net zero goal.

The UK energy secretary, Miatta Fahnbulleh, said: “This summer, we all felt it: climate change is here, in Britain, now. No country can tackle it alone, which is why Cop31 matters. The answer to high bills and climate change is the same – more clean, homegrown power, creating good jobs and warmer homes. Cop31 is about Britain’s national interest.”

text:
Chilgok-gun in North Gyeongsang Province is laying the groundwork to enter the North American market with modular low-speed electric vehicles (LSVs).

A county delegation traveled to Georgia and South Carolina from Oct. 25 to Oct. 31 alongside the Ministry of SMEs and Startups, North Gyeongsang Technopark and special zone operators to discuss technology and commercialization cooperation with local companies and research institutions, the county said Sunday.

The delegation visited Peachtree City, Georgia, where it examined the city's LSV-dedicated road network and safety management systems as a model for community transportation.

The group then visited TAGO EV, an LSV manufacturer and distributor in South Carolina, where North Gyeongsang Technopark and TAGO EV signed an MOU to advance the entry of modular LSVs into the North American market and support local commercialization.

The agreement covers cooperation in vehicle assembly, demonstration, retail and sales.

The delegation also visited Clemson University's International Center for Automotive Research (CU-ICAR) and the International Transportation Innovation Center (ITIC), where discussions covered compliance with US vehicle safety standards, performance verification and the use of local testing facilities.

"Through this visit, we confirmed the potential for modular LSVs to enter the North American market," a Chilgok-gun official said. "We will work with relevant agencies to support local companies in expanding overseas and strengthening their competitiveness."

ANTALYA, Türkiye (November 8, 2026)— The annual U.N. climate talks—COP31—get underway in Antalya, Türkiye tomorrow and will run from November 9-20. The talks must contend with the failure of countries to limit global warming to below 1.5°C and the mounting toll of climate-fueled disasters, which just this year included tens of thousands of lives lost in the deadly floods in Nepal and extreme heatwaves across Europe. At the same time, a fossil energy crisis unleashed by the U.S.-Israel war against Iran is driving up energy costs, leaving people struggling to afford basic necessities.

Transitioning away from fossil fuels, ramping up clean energy and boosting climate finance will be key issues at this COP. The U.N. Environmental Programmes’s 2026 Adaptation Gap report shows that public adaptation finance flows from richer to lower income countries was less than $32 billion in 2024, and even the COP30 aspiration to triple this finance by 2035 would fall well short of developing countries' estimated annual need of at least $305 billion by 2035.

Last week’s election results in the United States will buoy the mood in Antalya, but the country remains on the sidelines at COP31 as the Trump administration exited the U.N. Framework Convention on Climate Change (UNFCCC) and the Paris Agreement.

Below is a quote by Dr. Rachel Cleetus, Climate Program director at the Union of Concerned Scientists (UCS), who will be attending COP31 alongside other UCS experts and has been attending the U.N.’s international climate talks and partnering with the international community on climate and energy policies for over 20 years:

“COP31 comes at a watershed moment with the world staring into the abyss of overshooting 1.5°C of global warming, a result of grossly insufficient action from policymakers and the greed and deception of fossil fuel companies. Global leaders must pull us back from the brink and commit to rapidly transitioning away from fossil fuels and expanding renewable energy, an imperative reinforced by the current energy affordability crisis. With mounting climate disasters harming those who have contributed the least to the climate crisis, richer nations must also fulfill their responsibility to provide funding for adaptation and loss and damage. The glaring gap in climate finance is cruelly exacerbating the injustice of climate change for the lowest income countries; and the unfolding record-breaking El Niño is compounding climate harms, already causing devastating flooding and set to create harsh new challenges for people’s food security, health and livelihoods.

“Ahead of COP31, the resounding rejection of the destructive, corrupt actions of the Trump administration by U.S. voters is a positive signal to the global community. The administration’s illegal war on Iran, tariff wars and attacks on clean energy have driven up costs for everyday people while boosting the obscene profits of fossil fuel polluters. There is a real risk that a beleaguered Trump administration could double down on its authoritarian tactics and continue to disrupt global climate progress and multilateral institutions. But Congress now has the power and responsibility to keep this reckless administration in check and ensure it is held accountable, at home and on the global stage.

“The Trump administration is isolated in shamefully exiting the UNFCCC and Paris Agreement. At COP31 it’s crucial for other world leaders to forge ahead on critical priorities for global climate action, informed by the best available science from the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change and with richer, high-emitting nations living up to their fair share of responsibility. The decisions made here are an issue of profound intergenerational justice and world leaders must commit to building a safer, more just world.”

Read more about COP31 priorities in Dr. Cleetus' recent blogpost, “COP31 in Türkiye: Can Climate Talks Deliver Amid Worsening Disasters, Rising Fossil Fuel Energy Costs and Global Conflicts?” and learn more about the UCS experts that will be present at COP31 and available for media here.

UCS experts have extensive experience doing live and taped TV, radio, podcast and print interviews with major national and international media outlets. Please contact UCS Communications Officer Daela Taeoalii-Tipton if you have questions or would like to arrange interviews with these experts during or after the negotiations. She will be attending the U.N. climate talks in-person and will be in Antalya from November 7-22.

title: US datacenter demand spurs increased fossil fuel pipeline projects as rules are discarded
description:
Datacenters are spurring a boom in fossil fuel pipeline projects at a time when the Trump administration is gutting rules that protect from disasters along the lines, a new review of federal records shows.
Federal records identified almost 200 pipeline projects that are proposed or in the works, and would collectively span 17,000 miles (27,000km).
Meanwhile, the administration has used the Defense Production Act to push through projects over the objections of states.
The Trump administration in January issued a memo stating that it would “refrain from taking any enforcement action” against companies that violated Pipeline and Hazardous Materials Safety Administration regulations.
This also comes as the Trump administration attempts to strip 94% of federal wetland protections.
text:
Datacenters are spurring a boom in fossil fuel pipeline projects at a time when the Trump administration is gutting rules that protect from disasters along the lines, a new review of federal records shows.

The report, compiled by the Environmental Integrity Project, also found pipelines are being built to meet demand for natural gas exports fueled by wars in Ukraine and Iran. Federal records identified almost 200 pipeline projects that are proposed or in the works, and would collectively span 17,000 miles (27,000km).

Not only has the Trump administration targeted laws that protect the environment and human health from pipelines’ risks, it has also pledged not to enforce regulations around them, the report adds.

The findings bring into focus a little-considered environmental threat in artificial intelligence and datacenter proliferation – the US already records about 1.7 pipeline accidents, spills, fires or explosions per day, and these projects would almost certainly lead to more.

The pipelines could help supply the at least 98 gas-fired power plants proposed to serve datacenters, and, if all the lines are completed, they would transport about 40% more natural gas daily than what the system carries today.

“This is the largest boom in a couple decades … and it coincides with all this deregulation,” Alexandra Shaykevich, research manager with the Environmental Integrity Project, said. “That’s concerning because the pipelines do usually operate safely, but they can leak and explode, and so there are big risks for communities across the United States.”

Most of the pipelines would carry natural gas across 42 states, though many of them are concentrated in several fossil fuel-producing regions. About 42 are in or cross Texas, 27 are in Louisiana, and nine each are in Pennsylvania and Illinois.

Advocates say they’re especially worried because of the wide-ranging attacks on foundational environmental protections, from the Clean Water Act to the Endangered Species Act, that until recently have been wielded to stop the riskiest projects, protect from accidents or hold polluters accountable.

The report states that over 25% of the projects have requested an expedited environmental review, and the administration is largely using legally dubious mechanisms to push them through, like invoking the “energy emergency”. That has accelerated permit approvals, reduced the scope of environmental studies, and limited public and community input, the report alleges.

Meanwhile, the administration has used the Defense Production Act to push through projects over the objections of states. In March, it jump-started the Santa Ynez oil pipeline in Santa Barbara, California, despite the state shutting it down in 2015 following a major spill that harmed about 150 miles (240km) of coastline. The act is also being used to attempt to ram through controversial plans for the 125-mile (200km) Constitution pipeline that would run from Pennsylvania to upstate New York, which the latter has opposed.

The Trump administration in January issued a memo stating that it would “refrain from taking any enforcement action” against companies that violated Pipeline and Hazardous Materials Safety Administration regulations. By 2025, it had already cut the average number of enforcement actions initiated in half, recording only 117.

The administration is also raising the risk of accidents and explosions by allowing companies to increase the pressure of pipelines in densely populated areas and letting them conduct fewer pressure tests, the report alleges.

It has made changes like this despite the regularity of accidents, including some that are deadly. The report points to a March 2023 disaster in which a crack in a gas pipeline in West Reading, Pennsylvania, caused an explosion in a chocolate factory that killed seven workers and injured 10 others. Last month, two workers were killed when a New Mexico pipeline exploded.

The pipelines could also destroy thousands of acres of federally protected wetlands. At least 81 of the projects are expected to damage more than 19,000 acres (7,700 hectares) of federally protected wetlands, the report found. This also comes as the Trump administration attempts to strip 94% of federal wetland protections.

The dangers of this are felt in south-west Louisiana, which holds a large concentration of pipelines because of the high number of export terminals along the Mississippi River. These already cut through and harmed sensitive wetlands and fishing grounds, said James Hiatt, executive director of For a Better Bayou.

“The people who live here carry the risks and bear the burden while the profits go elsewhere,” Hiatt said.

title: 8 EVs Now Top 400 Miles of Range, Led by 465 [2026] - shattered.io
description:
The outlet counted eight EVs with EPA or manufacturer ratings of 400 miles or higher at the time of publication.
Second, the suggestion in the headline that 400 miles comes next is posed as a question.
How 300 Miles Became the Baseline To see why 400 miles is even a fair question, look at where the industry started this decade.
Competitive Comparison: Three Routes to 400 Miles The models in the InsideEVs report reach 400 miles in different ways.
Once several cars clear 400 miles, range stops being a differentiator and charging speed takes over.
text:
Eight electric vehicles now carry an EPA or manufacturer rating of 400 miles or higher, according to InsideEVs, which first ran its “300 Miles Of EV Range Is The New Normal. Is 400 Next?” feature on March 24, 2026 and updated the page on November 8, 2026. That count matters because it moves 400-mile electric vehicles from lab curiosity to a short but real shopping list.

The headline makes a claim and asks a question. The claim is that 300 miles has become the floor for a modern EV. The question is whether 400 miles is the next floor. This analysis takes both seriously, separates what the outlet confirmed from what it only estimated, and looks at what the numbers mean for buyers, automakers and charging networks. If you want to see how far a single trip can stretch today, our look at a Model Y road trip across Europe shows the real-world side of long-distance EV driving.

·

Don't miss new tech stories on Google

Add Shattered once in the Google app and our stories show up in your news suggestions.

Add now

What InsideEVs Reported on November 8, 2026

The InsideEVs feature is the anchor for this story, so it helps to be precise about what it says. The outlet counted eight EVs with EPA or manufacturer ratings of 400 miles or higher at the time of publication. It named the BMW iX3 and the Volvo EX60 as vehicles that their makers say are targeting 400-mile estimates when they go on sale later in 2026. It also cited BMW’s statement that the 2027 BMW i3 will deliver 440 miles on the EPA cycle.

The largest number in the piece belongs to the 2026 Cadillac Escalade IQ, which has 465 miles of GM-estimated range from a 205-kilowatt-hour battery pack. That is the highest figure InsideEVs cited, and it comes with an important label. It is a GM estimate, not a number tied to an EPA window sticker in the material we reviewed.

Two details deserve a flag before we go further. First, the line that 300 miles of range is quickly becoming the new baseline is InsideEVs’ characterization of the market. No regulator or standards body has defined a 300-mile baseline. Second, the suggestion in the headline that 400 miles comes next is posed as a question. The outlet did not publish a forecast with a date, and neither will we pretend it did.

That discipline shapes the rest of this piece. Where a number comes from the InsideEVs report, we say so. Where we do arithmetic on those numbers, we label it as our own math. And where the report offers an estimate rather than a fact, we treat it as an estimate.

The 400-Mile Roster: Models and Numbers

The table below collects every vehicle-level figure from the InsideEVs report. Cells that read Not stated mean the report, as summarized for this story, did not give a battery size or price for those models. We would rather show a gap than fill it with a guess.

A few things stand out. The iX3 and EX60 are described as targets, so those two entries represent intent rather than finished window stickers. The i3 figure comes from BMW itself and refers to the EPA cycle, but the car carries a 2027 model year. The Escalade IQ is the only one of the four with a stated pack size, and it is enormous by any standard.

How 300 Miles Became the Baseline

To see why 400 miles is even a fair question, look at where the industry started this decade. Battery-electric vehicles had an average driving range of about 217 miles worldwide in 2021, according to Statista’s figure of 349 kilometers. That is a global average across all types, so it includes small city cars and budget models, but it frames the scale of the climb.

By that yardstick, a 300-mile EV was a long-range outlier only a few model years ago. Statista also noted that the median range of EVs offered in the United States in 2021 came with some models exceeding 300 miles. In other words, 300 miles existed in 2021, but it belonged to the premium end of the lineup.

What changed is where 300 miles sits in the stack. InsideEVs argues it has slid from the top shelf to the middle of the aisle. We cannot verify that statement with a single industry-wide dataset, because the fact base here is one outlet’s reading of the market. The framing is plausible given the 2021 starting point, but treat it as one outlet’s view. Inside Climate News also ran an Oct. 29, 2026 piece headlined “The Slow, Surprising Death of EV Range Anxiety”, which you can find on its Inside Clean Energy page. We cite it as a related read, not as support for any number here.

Industry Data Worth Anchoring On

Three published data points help calibrate the debate. All three come from the Statista Research Department and are older than the InsideEVs update, so read them as historical baselines rather than a snapshot of November 2026.

On consumer expectations, the Statista Research Department reported that “Nearly a quarter of UK consumers said they would need a battery-electric vehicle with a driving range of 300 to 399 miles to consider purchasing one.” The data was collected as of October 2023. It tells us that 300 miles was already a purchase threshold for a meaningful slice of one major market before this year’s models arrived.

On the supply side, Statista’s own summary states that “Battery-electric vehicles had an average driving range of 349 kilometers, or approximately 217 miles, worldwide in 2021.” That figure is our starting line. Every vehicle in the table above beats it by a wide margin, and the 465-mile Escalade IQ roughly doubles it.

On the U.S. market, Statista wrote that “The median driving range of electric vehicle models offered in the United States was reported for 2021, with some models exceeding 300 miles.” Taken together, the three lines show a market that moved from a 217-mile global average and a handful of 300-mile exceptions in 2021 to a point where an outlet can credibly call 300 the baseline and count eight 400-mile models.

The percentages in the right column are our arithmetic, rounded to the nearest whole number. They compare a 2021 global average of all vehicle types with 2026 flagship ratings, so they overstate typical progress. They are still useful as a rough picture of how far the top of the market has traveled.

Cadillac Escalade IQ: 465 Miles From a 205 kWh Pack

The Escalade IQ is the headline number and the clearest example of the brute-force path to range. GM’s estimate of 465 miles comes from a 205-kilowatt-hour battery pack, per InsideEVs. Dividing the first figure by the second gives about 2.3 miles per kilowatt-hour. That is our math, and it uses the nominal pack size, so the real figure on usable energy could differ.

What the ratio says about efficiency

A ratio near 2.3 miles per kWh describes a heavy, large vehicle. It is not a criticism, because buyers of full-size luxury SUVs want space and towing presence, and range has to be bought with energy. The point is that the Escalade IQ reaches 465 miles by carrying a very big pack, not by being unusually frugal with each kilowatt-hour.

Why big packs are a limited path

Bigger packs cost more, weigh more and take longer to fill. They also tie up scarce battery cells in a single vehicle. A strategy built only on bigger batteries works for halo products, and it gets harder to scale to the mass market. That is why the more interesting entries on the roster are the ones where range climbs without a pack that large, but the report did not give pack sizes for them, so we cannot test that claim with numbers.

BMW i3 and iX3: Range From Platform Design

BMW appears twice in the InsideEVs piece. The iX3 is on the list as a vehicle that BMW says is targeting a 400-mile estimate when it goes on sale later in 2026. The 2027 BMW i3 goes further: BMW says it will deliver 440 miles on the EPA cycle. That puts the sedan 40 miles past the 400-mile mark and 140 miles beyond the 300-mile baseline.

Sedans have an aerodynamic advantage over SUVs, and that is a general engineering fact rather than something InsideEVs reported. Less drag means fewer kilowatt-hours spent per mile at highway speed. If BMW is reaching 440 miles in a body style that favors efficiency, the number says as much about design as about cells. We would not push that reading too hard, however, because BMW’s pack size for the i3 was not part of the material we reviewed.

Price is the other open item. BMW has not made the 2027 i3 price public. InsideEVs offered an estimate of about $55,000 and labeled it as an estimate. We treat it as unconfirmed. If that figure ends up close, a 440-mile sedan would land in a price band that many shoppers would consider, but it is premature to build plans around it.

Volvo EX60 and the Mainstream 400-Mile Push

The Volvo EX60 sits beside the iX3 in the report as a model whose maker says it is targeting a 400-mile estimate. Both are positioned as vehicles that go on sale later in 2026, according to their manufacturers. That timing makes them the bridge between the range leaders and the next wave of ordinary premium EVs.

The wording matters. A target is a goal, and an estimate is not a certified rating. When these cars reach showrooms, their final EPA numbers could land above, at or below 400 miles depending on wheel size, tires, drive configuration and battery option. Automakers often sell several trims with different ranges, so the headline figure may apply only to the best-equipped version.

For readers tracking the hardware side, the key question is whether 400 miles can reach vehicles that cost far less than a flagship SUV. The iX3 and EX60 are early tests of that idea. If both ship near their targets, the count of 400-mile models will climb well beyond eight within a single model year. If they miss, the 400-mile club stays a premium-only space for longer. You can follow more of our hardware coverage as ratings arrive.

Competitive Comparison: Three Routes to 400 Miles

The models in the InsideEVs report reach 400 miles in different ways. Sorting them by strategy gives a more useful comparison than ranking them by a single number.

Route one: the big battery. The 2026 Cadillac Escalade IQ pairs 465 miles of GM-estimated range with a 205 kWh pack. It wins on raw range and loses on cost and weight. Its audience is buyers who want a large luxury vehicle that rarely worries about the next charger.

Route two: the efficient platform. The 2027 BMW i3 aims for 440 miles on the EPA cycle. BMW has not said how big its battery is in the material we saw, so we cannot score its efficiency, but a sedan shape and a purpose-built platform are the usual ingredients of this approach.

Route three: the near-term mainstream premium push. The BMW iX3 and Volvo EX60 target 400-mile estimates on sale dates later in 2026. They are the most important products on the list for ordinary buyers because they are closest to a price and size that fit more households. They also carry the most uncertainty, because targets can shift before certification.

Beyond these three, the rest of the eight-vehicle count includes other models that InsideEVs rated at 400 miles or higher. We are not naming them here because the fact base for this story does not list them, and guessing which ones belong would be speculation. The lesson holds regardless of the names: the 400-mile group already spans more than one body style and more than one strategy.

EPA Estimates vs Real Roads

An EPA rating is a standardized test result, and it is the fairest way to compare cars on paper. It is not a promise about any particular trip. Cold weather, high highway speeds, heavy loads, roof boxes and hilly terrain can all cut range below the label. Mild temperatures and steady city driving can push results the other way.

That is why the source of each range number matters. The Escalade IQ figure is a GM estimate. The 2027 i3 figure is BMW’s statement about the EPA cycle. The iX3 and EX60 figures are manufacturer targets. A buyer comparing them should recognize four different levels of certainty rather than treat them as equal facts. Resources such as the Cars.com rundown of all-new and redesigned EVs for 2026 are a handy place to check models as their official specs are published.

There is also a practical argument that range beyond what you drive in a day has diminishing returns. Most trips are short, and a 300-mile car already covers them. The extra 100 to 165 miles show up on long-distance days, in winter, and in the margin of comfort that makes an EV feel like a normal car. That margin is real value, but it is not equal for every driver.

Charging Becomes the Real Constraint

Range and charging are two halves of the same problem. A bigger battery stretches the distance between stops, but it also takes more energy to refill. A car with a 205 kWh pack needs a lot of power delivered to add the same percentage as a smaller pack, so charger speed and availability matter more as packs grow.

Infrastructure is moving in parallel. We recently covered a 12-stall Tesla V4 site that EVgo opened in Chicago, a sign that the public network keeps adding high-power stalls open to a wider set of vehicles. On the lab side, researchers reported an approach in which a Maryland battery reached 80% in 12.8 minutes, which shows where fast-charging science is aiming even though it is not a production car feature.

The trade-off is straightforward. If chargers get faster and more common, buyers can accept smaller packs and still travel far. If they do not, automakers will keep pushing range to make up for the gap. That is part of why the 400-mile question and the charging question cannot be answered separately.

Market Impact: Pricing, Resale and Product Planning

When the top of the market moves, everything below it feels pressure. A 300-mile EV that looked impressive two years ago now has to justify itself next to a growing list of 400-mile cars. Automakers will respond by raising range on refreshed models, trimming price to hold share, or leaning on features other than range.

For used-car buyers, the shift cuts both ways. A 300-mile EV bought today will look ordinary in a few years, which could soften resale values compared with expectations. Yet a 300-mile car also remains more capable than the 217-mile average Statista recorded for 2021, so plenty of existing vehicles will stay useful. We would not predict a collapse. We would expect a gradual repricing as 400-mile models become common.

The wider EV market is also in a restless phase. Our report on the $56.5 billion in charges tied to Ford, GM and Stellantis electric trucks shows that big range numbers do not guarantee big sales. A truck or SUV that carries a large battery can still struggle if the price and use case do not line up. The Escalade IQ sits in that risky category, and the market response will be a useful test.

What Remains Unconfirmed

Good coverage means being clear about what we do not know. The table below separates the claims that the InsideEVs report supports from those that remain open.

Treat the last two rows with the most caution. A baseline is a market outcome, and nobody can declare one by press release. Whether 400 miles earns that label depends on how many models reach it, at what price, and with what real-world results.

Five Predictions for 400-Mile EVs

These are our own judgments based on the facts above. They are not attributed to InsideEVs or any automaker, and none is a certainty.

The 400-mile count grows fast over the next model year. If the iX3, EX60 and 2027 i3 arrive near their stated figures, the list of eight gets longer without any new battery breakthrough.

Marketing shifts from how far you can go to how fast you can refill. Once several cars clear 400 miles, range stops being a differentiator and charging speed takes over.

Sedans make a comeback in EV lineups. The 440-mile i3 target hints that low-drag bodies are a cheaper way to reach long range than ever-larger packs.

The mega-pack SUV stays a niche. The Escalade IQ shows what is possible, yet cost and weight limit how many models follow.

300 miles settles in as the entry point for new premium launches. Not every brand will hit it, but few will advertise anything lower with a straight face.

What Buyers Should Do Now

Start with your own driving. If your longest regular trip is under 150 miles each way and you can charge at home, a 300-mile car already gives you wide margin. Paying extra for 440 or 465 miles buys convenience, not necessity.

If you do drive long distances, wait for certified numbers before you commit to an iX3 or EX60. A target is a good sign, but a window sticker is a fact. Check the range for the exact trim and wheel package you plan to order, since ratings often differ across versions.

Also think about battery wear. Range on the day you buy is not range five years later. Research on longer-lived cells, such as the solid-state coating that kept 82.3% after 300 cycles in one lab report, points to where durability work is heading, though it is far from a showroom feature. Until then, look at warranty terms on the battery as closely as you look at range.

The takeaway: 300 miles is a fair floor for a new EV in late 2026, and 400 miles is a real option on a short list of models. Whether it becomes the next floor is still an open question, exactly as InsideEVs framed it.

FAQ: 400-Mile Electric Vehicles

How many EVs have a 400-mile range? InsideEVs counted eight EVs with EPA or manufacturer ratings of 400 miles or higher at publication. The page was first posted on March 24, 2026 and updated on November 8, 2026.

Which EV has the longest range in the report? The 2026 Cadillac Escalade IQ, with 465 miles of GM-estimated range and a 205-kilowatt-hour battery pack.

What range does BMW claim for the 2027 BMW i3? BMW says the 2027 BMW i3 will deliver 440 miles on the EPA cycle. The price is not public, and the roughly $55,000 figure in the InsideEVs piece is an unconfirmed estimate.

When do the BMW iX3 and Volvo EX60 go on sale? According to their manufacturers, as reported by InsideEVs, both are targeting 400-mile estimates when they go on sale later in 2026.

Is 300 miles now the standard for EVs? InsideEVs describes 300 miles as quickly becoming the new baseline. That is the outlet’s characterization, not a formally defined industry standard.

Will 400 miles be the next baseline? Nobody has confirmed it. The headline poses it as a question, and the report does not present a forecast or a date.

How does the new range compare with a few years ago? Statista put the worldwide average BEV range at about 217 miles in 2021. The 440-mile and 465-mile figures cited for the 2027 BMW i3 and 2026 Escalade IQ are roughly double that, though the comparison mixes a fleet average with flagship ratings.

description:
The big issues were affordability, the Iran war, data centers and the impact of AI.
One important solution is permitting reform.
There is a bipartisan permitting reform bill in Congress called the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act.
Make the changes necessary so Americans don’t need to be rich to have a decent life today.
Pass permitting reform so we can all have a decent life tomorrow.
text:
The election results are in. The big issues were affordability, the Iran war, data centers and the impact of AI. It is clear voters want these issues addressed, as well as a brake on Donald Trump.

I have a niece and nephew who are in college. They share these worries. With AI, they wonder if the careers they are preparing for will be around in another few years. And they’re wondering if even with a job how they’ll afford a house. Heck, gas and groceries are challenging enough.

But you want to know what else they worry about? Climate change.

It wasn’t talked about in the political campaigns, but how livable is Utah going to be as temperatures continue to rise? How are we going to cope with water shortages and worsening wildfires (that also result in skyrocketing home insurance premiums)?

One important solution is permitting reform. We have abundant wind and solar resources, but we lack the transmission lines to bring this energy we desperately need to our homes. Right now solar and wind projects are stalled because we don’t have the infrastructure to bring the power from where it’s generated to where we use it.

There is a bipartisan permitting reform bill in Congress called the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act. It was crafted by our Sen. Mike Lee, with three other senators from both parties. It is this type of cooperation that we need to solve the really hard problems that face our country.

So to our congressional delegation: Keep focused on affordability. Make the changes necessary so Americans don’t need to be rich to have a decent life today. But don’t forget the future. Pass permitting reform so we can all have a decent life tomorrow.

Steve Glaser, Holladay

HINGHAM — Oct. 27, 2026 — Hingham’s Select Board last Tuesday discussed putting a $3.7 million federal tax credit for the Foster School’s geothermal system toward the school’s debt, a move that would need Town Meeting approval in the spring. No vote was taken, and the board also heard early plans for a one-year budget bridge for fiscal 2028.

The Full Story

Foster tax credit. Town Administrator Tom Mayo corrected the agenda’s reference to IRS tax credits, saying the money comes from the federal Inflation Reduction Act. He said the town received a $3.7 million credit for the geothermal work at Foster, and that one option members have raised is paying down the project’s debt.

Board member Julie Strehle credited the town’s sustainability coordinator with pursuing the credit and said the money came in because of Foster’s geothermal system and should be applied back to that project. She proposed adding it to the existing stabilization fund that offsets debt for Foster and the public safety facility, which would require a warrant article at the spring Town Meeting, so homeowners pay less in taxes. Strehle said the money is now in the unassigned fund balance. Strehle later clarified that the 2022 special town meeting put $7 million into that fund.

Board member William Ramsey agreed. Asked by Chair Liz Klein whether the board was voting, Mayo said Town Meeting articles are due Jan. 20 and that a concept would be developed and discussed publicly.

Budget bridge for FY28. The chair said the Sustainable Budget Task Force, meeting since August 2025, is likely to propose a one-year bridge agreement among the Select Board, Advisory Committee and School Committee for fiscal 2028. The 3.5% budget growth caps in the town’s current financial management plan ended with fiscal 2027, while some of its other policies run through 2028; the bridge would address spending caps and unpredictable special education costs.

Mayo said the plan will likely need Town Meeting approval to use some fund balance, plus an article to fund a special education reserve each year with Medicaid reimbursements. Ramsey said reserves should be used tactically to delay any future override as long as possible.

title: Cop31: what is at stake at the UN climate summit and what can it achieve? - The Guardian
description: Delegates from more than 190 countries are gathering in Turkey for climate talks, but the US will be absent
text:
Delegates from more than 190 countries are gathering in Turkey for climate talks, but the US will be absent

As the planet faces unprecedented human-caused global heating, heads of government are meeting for the next fortnight for the latest round of climate talks. We ask why it matters and what is likely to be achieved.

From 9-20 November, world leaders, ministers and high-ranking officials from more than 190 countries are expected to convene in Antalya in Turkey, for the annual UN climate talks . This year, the summit will be hosted by Turkey, but in an unusual twist the negotiations will be presided over by Australia in a compromise deal struck after the two countries vied for the presidency.

While nearly all of the 196 original signatories of the 2015 Paris climate agreement are expected to be present, one glaring absence will be the US, whose president, Donald Trump, has withdrawn from Paris.

Australia will take charge of the formal negotiations where countries thrash out the details of work programmes such as the “just transition”, climate finance and putting the world on track to stick as closely as possible to the Paris agreement goal of limiting temperature rises to 1.5C above pre-industrial levels.

Turkey will take charge of the “action agenda”, the voluntary agreements that work towards the Paris goals but are not legally binding: programmes on cutting waste and achieving a circular economy, cutting methane , improving food security, and – perhaps most important – the electrification of the global economy .

The Paris goal of 1.5C has been breached , but the UN argues that rapid action to cut greenhouse gas emissions would limit the “overshoot” and allow for a return to lower temperatures by the end of this century. For that to happen, countries need to break dependence on fossil fuels and adopt low-carbon technologies faster. The two roadmaps from Brazil – on the “transition away from fossil fuels” and on halting deforestation – will present ways of doing so.

Developing countries are also in dire need of help to cope with the hastening impacts of the climate crisis. After the disaster in Nepal , the country has been granted access to the global fund for “loss and damage” – the rescue and rehabilitation of communities stricken by climate-related disasters. But it is not enough, and poor countries also lack the means to adapt their infrastructure to worsening extreme weather.

Rich countries have been cutting their overseas aid, while rising interest rates have loaded further debt on to the poor.

It was not until 2023 at Cop28 that the final agreement directly addressed fossil fuels for the first time, due to long-term strident opposition from producing countries. The agreement included a resolution to “transition away from fossil fuels” but no deadline or plan for doing so. It is still tricky to get fossil fuels directly on to the Cop agenda, which requires consensus from nearly all parties, but this year the issue will be addressed through a non-binding “roadmap” for the global transition away from fossil fuels.

Given the tense and fragile geopolitical situation – some commentators believe we are already in the midst of an unacknowledged third world war , while inflation and a rising far right are upsetting economies – countries might be tempted to settle for a quiet meeting.

But there are hopes for a better outcome, which could include: acceptance of the plans Brazil has produced and a promise to carry them forward; progress on climate finance for developing countries; a resolution to the row over climate science that has plagued recent meetings of the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change ; and the fleshing out of the “just transition mechanism” designed to help workers reliant on fossil fuels to adjust to a low-carbon economy.

Progress is also possible through Cop-related means outside the formal negotiations. Earlier this year, more than 60 countries, including the UK, the EU and dozens of developing nations, gathered in Colombia to vow to “transition away from fossil fuels” . This “coalition of the willing” could be boosted at Cop31 by new members, as well as fresh impetus from the recent success of political movements in several countries – Brazil, Canada, Serbia, Hungary and the US in states that decisively rejected Donald Trump at the midterms.

Several prominent members of the US Congress may attend, along with businesspeople and US civil society groups, so there will be representation beyond the White House’s absence. Trump appears intent on boosting fossil fuel interests as much as possible in the US, but with oil prices still high after his war in Iran, the economics of low-carbon energy look ever more favourable .

The geopolitics and the technology. Although the winds of conflict have upended international relations, they have also shown countries can benefit from the energy security that results from decentralised renewable generation . China’s oil imports, for instance, are likely to be down about 12% this year owing to a massive uptake of electric vehicles , and its renewable generation capacity has now outstripped coal. This is saving billions of dollars for consumers and businesses as the oil price soars.

Solar is booming in Africa at last , while in Pakistan a consumer-led rooftop revolution now produces about a quarter of the electricity used. Close to half of new cars in countries from Vietnam to some EU members are now electric.

Electrification will be a key focus of Cop31, and the high efficiency of electric technology means it could reduce the amount of primary energy use by half across the world, according to University of Oxford professor Jan Rosenow .

Politically, the re-election of Lula as president in Brazil has also cheered climate supporters . Lula will attend Cop, his first international visit since re-election, and is likely to be a fiery presence, showing progressive parties around the world how to win while championing the climate.

“The results of this week's election have created a historic opportunity to deliver real progress for Pennsylvania families.

“With Democrats now holding a governing trifecta, voters have entrusted us with the heavy responsibility to act on the pocketbook issues that affect their daily lives: lowering costs, strengthening our economy, creating the next generation of careers, and improving quality of life for working people.

“With a majority in both chambers, we now must work quickly to transform those campaign slogans into meaningful legislation that betters people’s lives.

“Few issues are more important to that mission than energy affordability.

“Across Pennsylvania, families are facing rising utility bills and increasing uncertainty about the cost of keeping their homes heated in the winter and cool in the summer.

“For many households, energy costs are not a manageable expense.

“They are a monthly burden that can force difficult choices between paying bills, buying groceries, seeking medical care, and meeting other basic needs.

“As chair of the House Energy Committee, I believe the next legislative session presents a unique opportunity to address these challenges head-on.

Priorities

“Over the past two years, our Committee has advanced meaningful legislation to modernize our energy system, support emerging technologies, regulate large data centers, and strengthen Pennsylvania's electric grid.

“While some progress has been made, much more work remains.

“In the coming session, the Energy Committee will focus on three core priorities: expanding affordable energy supply, modernizing our energy infrastructure, and protecting residents and small businesses from unnecessary costs.

“Pennsylvania must embrace a forward-looking energy strategy that brings more affordable energy onto the grid and ensures we remain an energy leader for generations to come.

“We have an opportunity to accelerate the development of new energy projects, including renewable and next-generation technologies, while leveraging tools such as the Pennsylvania Energy Development Authority to attract investment and create family sustaining jobs.”

A.I. Data Centers

“At the same time, we must recognize that the rapid growth of artificial intelligence, data centers, and other energy-intensive industries is placing unprecedented demands on our electric system.

“Pennsylvania should welcome innovation and economic development, but working families should not be forced to subsidize the infrastructure costs of the A.I. boom.

“Large technology companies and data center operators must pay their fair share, and we must ensure that ratepayers are not left holding the bill for new transmission lines, generation projects, or grid upgrades built primarily to serve corporate demand.

Resilient Energy System

“We also need to think differently about the future of our energy system.

“For too long, our grid has been built around centralized generation and top-down control.

“The future should be more distributed, more resilient, and more empowering for consumers.

“Expanding rooftop solar, battery storage, microgrids, community energy projects, and other distributed energy resources can give Pennsylvanians greater energy freedom while improving reliability and reducing costs over the long term.”

Utility Company Accountability

“Along with infrastructure changes, we must ensure that utility companies are held accountable.

“Pennsylvanians deserve safe and reliable service at a fair price.

“That means examining utility rate structures, preventing predatory practices in the retail energy market, and ensuring consumers are not paying more than necessary to keep the lights on.”

Families Are Paying More, Getting Less

“The challenges before us are significant, but so is the opportunity.

“Citizens are demanding real change from a status quo that has left too many families paying more and getting less.

“We have a chance to build a more affordable, reliable, resilient, and consumer-focused energy system that serves the people of Pennsylvania, not entrenched interests, while creating thousands of good-paying jobs and long-term careers in the industries that will power our future.

“Voters have given us a mandate to tackle the cost-of-living challenges facing working families.

“In the next session, the House Energy Committee stands ready to deliver solutions that lower energy costs, hold powerful interests accountable, and secure an energy future defined by affordability, reliability, and energy freedom.”

They must work with Mr. Trump, or at least attempt to compel him, to change his misguided policies and reverse destructive actions that have harmed Americans — our health, environment, pocketbooks, safety and security.

This is not a choice between nuts-and-bolts governing and holding Mr. Trump and his administration accountable. Democrats must do both.

On the governing side of the agenda, urgent issues abound.

Millions of Americans are losing their health insurance. Congress needs to restore subsidies and work to shore up and improve the Affordable Care Act, which Mr. Trump and Republicans have been gutting over the past two years.

Congress must take a hard look at how public health, and the agencies responsible for protecting it, have eroded under Mr. Trump and Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. It’s unconscionable that measles, once considered eradicated, has resurfaced in multiple states while Mr. Kennedy indulges anti-vaxxers and purges medical bodies of experts.

Congress must reassert its power over tariffs. Mr. Trump’s reckless use of them has driven up costs for farmers, manufacturers, importers and consumers and threatened relations with allies and trading partners.

Advertisement

Article continues below this ad

Congress must also reassert its constitutional authority and responsibility to declare war. That’s a power that presidents over many administrations have been allowed to usurp. Lawmakers must start with an evaluation of Mr. Trump’s flailing approach to the war he needlessly started with Iran, a quagmire that has driven up the cost of oil and harmed American motorists, businesses and homeowners, depleted military resources and weakened the global economy.

Congress must reverse the Trump administration’s assault on the environment, from ending green tax credits to sabotaging offshore wind projects and rolling back pollution rules. They must push to put the country back on a path toward clean energy.

And Congress must impose stronger ethics regulations on every branch of government. Lawmakers must strengthen executive branch guardrails against self-dealing and conflicts of interest. They must impose ethics rules and, perhaps, begin the constitutional process of imposing term or age limits on U.S. Supreme Court justices. And they must fully crack down on insider trading and other means of corrupt self-enrichment in Congress itself. Independent agencies and inspectors general must be better protected against Mr. Trump’s meddling.

On the accountability front, there is much to tackle as well, including the mind-boggling enrichment of Mr. Trump and his family, his abuse of the Department of Justice to persecute perceived enemies, attacks on voting rights, and an immigration crackdown that has led to multiple deaths and widespread reports of civil rights abuses.

Advertisement

But Congress must not rush to impeach Mr. Trump or others in his administration. Lawmakers shouldn’t emulate the president’s practice of picking targets and then looking for evidence to fit the charge. Instead, they must do real oversight, using the investigative powers of their chambers to expose just how Mr. Trump and those around him were able to violate so many laws, crash through guardrails and degrade long-honored norms. That’s how we start fixing the system that Mr. Trump, with the help of an obeisant Republican-led Congress and a conservative Supreme Court, has broken in so many ways.

We realize this is a huge agenda, and even so it’s hardly complete. We’re well aware that Mr. Trump will resist much of it, and doubtless will use the complexities of the judicial system and a frequently compliant high court to thwart and stall efforts to rein him in, expose the depth and breadth of his corruption, and reverse policies that have left so many people struggling just to pay for their gas, groceries, medicine and housing.

But Congress should remind itself of its powers — particularly when it comes to spending and oversight. With those powers and a 100-day plan that includes many of the issues we’ve outlined here, the people’s representatives in Washington could do much to give Americans what they deserve: an honest government that works for them. Mr. Trump and his fellow Republicans would do well to heed that message, too.

name: Louisiana Environment
title: Louisiana is settling major lawsuits over coastal damage. But why are the details secret?
authors: Alex Lubben, Mike Smith, Staff writers, Javier Gallegos, SOPHIA GERMER
description:
John Carmouche, the lawyer who has spearheaded the lawsuits on behalf of the state and coastal parishes, argues the details must remain secret until all cases are final to allow Louisiana to maintain leverage in negotiations.
Total settlement numbers may also not reflect the actual dollar amounts going to coastal restoration if details remain sealed.
To Carmouche, building an enormous spaceport on the coast constitutes coastal restoration in itself.
Coastal advocacy organizations say that environmental mitigation, such as plugging oil wells, and restoration are two separate issues.
“It's not coastal restoration as we have defined the term up to this point.”
text:
Gov. Jeff Landry’s push to settle dozens of lawsuits seeking to hold the oil and gas industry financially responsible for damage to Louisiana’s coast has gained momentum — but the results so far are impossible to judge.

The settlements with major oil companies including Shell, Exxon and BP are being kept secret even though they potentially involve hundreds of millions of dollars or more in public assets, leaving it unclear how much they are worth and to what degree they will benefit coastal restoration.

In refusing to release details, state officials have pointed to court orders sealing the settlements from public view until all the cases are completed, and noted that some of the litigation remains ongoing. But the state did not oppose the oil firms’ request for the court orders, giving tacit approval to keeping them sealed.

John Carmouche, the lawyer who has spearheaded the lawsuits on behalf of the state and coastal parishes, argues the details must remain secret until all cases are final to allow Louisiana to maintain leverage in negotiations. He says he expects the total amount to top $7 billion.

“The public is going to be harmed by this getting out into the public,” he said. “It would minimize the public’s recovery.”

Carmouche said that once the settlements have been finalized, he believes the records will be made public.

“When this thing is over, I think all the settlements, I think everything is public record,” he said. “It’s not just going to be our word … It’s going to be the documents.”

But there are no guarantees for how long that may take or, if the court orders persist or are extended, to what degree the public will ever know the full details. Settlements have already been reached with all major oil companies except one.

Total settlement numbers may also not reflect the actual dollar amounts going to coastal restoration if details remain sealed. Carbon credits and other types of environmental mitigation have formed part of the negotiations as substitutes for cash payments, which some coastal advocates have deemed highly questionable and too advantageous to the industry.

Carmouche’s argument for secrecy has met skepticism elsewhere.

“It’s very common in litigation for parties to want to keep their settlement agreements confidential, and that’s commonly done. The distinction here, though, is that one of the parties is the state of Louisiana and another party is one of the parishes,” said Keith Hall, a professor of energy law at LSU who has previously represented oil and gas companies.

“The public has an interest in knowing how the public business is being conducted. And we’re talking about major money here.”

‘Public needs to know’

The legal battle involving 42 lawsuits, initially filed by Carmouche on behalf of coastal parishes and later joined by the state, stretches back to 2013. Chevron is the last major oil company not to settle, though a number of cases involving smaller companies are also still being litigated.

The Chevron case reached the U.S. Supreme Court earlier this year following a $745 million verdict against it in Plaquemines Parish. The Supreme Court justices essentially sided with Chevron, which argued that the case belonged in federal court.

The latest settlement emerged in October, when Landry and BP announced an agreement but released no details. Landry spokesperson Kate Kelly and Carmouche said that settlement has not yet been finalized.

“As governor I have worked to responsibly and ethically clean up the litigation environment that has impacted one of our largest employers — the oil and gas industry,” Landry said in a statement released by BP on Oct. 23 announcing the agreement. “This is just another step in fulfilling my promise.”

Settlements with Shell, Exxon and others have been finalized, but the details are sealed by the court orders. While some occurred before Landry became governor, he was directly involved at the time as attorney general.

The secret nature of the deals has led to growing concern among coastal advocacy groups, particularly as restoration efforts face a severe funding shortfall in the coming years. For some, it has also played into broader transparency concerns, including the widespread use of nondisclosure agreements in connection with industrial projects.

Louisiana’s land loss crisis is projected to become more complex as sea level rise accelerates, combining with the erosion and subsidence that has already robbed the coast of around 2,000 square miles over the last century — roughly the size of Delaware. The state has been losing a football field of land every 84 minutes on average.

In recent years, the state has used funds related to the 2010 BP Deepwater Horizon oil spill to build large-scale restoration projects. But that money — around $8.5 billion in total — expires by 2032.

The state’s coastal master plan calls for spending at least $1 billion annually on projects, made possible recently only because of the BP dollars.

“If we're going to plan for the future of this coast, we actually need to know what money is in the pipeline,” said Mark Davis of the Tulane Institute on Water Resources, Law and Policy.

“The public needs to know the amount of money the state is getting and what it can use it for. That's pretty basic to functioning government, and it's essential if we're going to know what to do with our coast.”

Haley Gentry, assistant director at the Tulane Institute, said the cases are so unique it’s hard to know whether the protective orders sealing the settlements would survive court challenges. But she noted that payments made to the state are typically considered public information.

‘Should be transparent’

The suits allege violations of a state law that took effect in 1980 guiding coastal permitting and development, saying the companies polluted and damaged the coast without repairing it. The companies deny they were in violation of any laws in effect at the time and say they cannot be held liable for damage. They also say production during World War II was necessary to help the war effort.

A separate 2022 law governs how proceeds from such violations should be distributed, directing 75% to the state’s coastal fund and 25% to local or parish governments after deducting expenses related to enforcement of the statute.

It is unclear if that law will be applied to the settlements or, if it is, how those disbursements will be monitored to ensure compliance given the protective orders sealing the details.

An early settlement in the coastal cases may provide clues to the negotiations in other lawsuits.

Settlement terms announced in 2021 with Freeport-McMoRan were technically worth $100 million, but $76.5 million of it was tied to the sale of “environmental credits" to offset the amount owed. The state was also required to pass laws to enable the full implementation of the settlement, and it is unclear whether that ever occurred.

One aspect of the Exxon agreement has become public because it paved the way for SpaceX to acquire land in the Pecan Island area, on the central Louisiana coast, to build a $100 billion spaceport.

State officials say the $100 million SpaceX paid for the land, previously owned by Exxon, will go to coastal restoration, but details have not been released and questions remain over the arrangement.

To Carmouche, building an enormous spaceport on the coast constitutes coastal restoration in itself.

“They're going to put back land that we don't have right now,” he said, stressing, too, that SpaceX will have to pay mitigation fees for filling in wetlands.

Landry has also suggested that the Exxon deal could include plugging abandoned oil wells — a major problem along Louisiana’s coast. Carmouche asserts that plugging orphaned wells is an appropriate use of settlement funds, arguing that taxpayers would ultimately have to pay for it otherwise.

"Our lawsuit is to restore the property to its original condition," he said, adding that cleaning up old wells could also allow for economic development.

But arguments such as those raise serious concern for others. Coastal advocacy organizations say that environmental mitigation, such as plugging oil wells, and restoration are two separate issues.

Addressing orphan wells, while important, is not in the state’s coastal master plan, and coastal advocates argue the industry should be held separately responsible for that.

“Somebody should have to take care of these orphan wells, and it should be the people who benefited from it,” said Davis, of the Tulane Institute. “It's not coastal restoration as we have defined the term up to this point.”

name: Detroit and Evs
title: It's not just the Cybertruck. America's big electric-truck bet fell apart. - Bundle
description:
"All the capability, status, and desirability of a pickup truck minus that oftentimes poor fuel economy?"
Full-size electric trucks never caught on as automakers predicted, and they are falling even further behind this year.
Even Tesla jumped into the full-size truck party, launching the Cybertruck in 2023.
Plus, "these full-size EV pickup trucks are and were pretty dang expensive," DeGraff added.
An altogether new bet Automakers have a new bet: smaller and cheaper electric trucks that aren't competing with the full-size workhorses.
text:
On paper, EV trucks made sense: Take America's longtime best-selling vehicles — the Ford F-150, Chevy Silverado, GMC Sierra, Ram 1500 — and replace the exhaust pipes with a charging port.

"All the capability, status, and desirability of a pickup truck minus that oftentimes poor fuel economy?" Robby DeGraf, the manager of product and consumer insights at AutoPacific, told Business Insider. "Sounds great, right?"

For many truck buyers, it wasn't.

Full-size electric trucks never caught on as automakers predicted, and they are falling even further behind this year. Cox Automotive data shows that the six EV pickups it tracks sold about 32,500 units through September, down 53% from the same period last year.

The retreat has left behind canceled trucks, production cutbacks, and billions of dollars in EV-related charges.

Since 2025, GM has paid nearly $11 billion in write-downs as it has slowed its EV-building pace; Ford discontinued its electric pickup and recorded a $19.5 billion charge; and the Ram REV never made it to production — but Stellantis still paid $26 billion in write-downs.

On Friday, the electric-truck industry took another major blow: Tesla said it will discontinue the Cybertruck.

So, what happened?

In the early 2020s, Detroit carmakers, inspired by Tesla's surprise success with the Model 3 and Model Y, wanted their own EV options.

Ford launched the all-electric F-150 Lightning in 2022; GM followed with the Silverado EV and Sierra EV for the 2024 model year; and Stellantis planned to release the Ram 1500 REV in early 2025. Even Tesla jumped into the full-size truck party, launching the Cybertruck in 2023.

Those trucks had to compete with cheaper, familiar gas-powered alternatives — and came with compromises.

"Pickup buyers have high expectations, and electrifying a large truck involves real trade-offs," Stephanie Valdez Streaty, the director of industry insights at Cox Automotive, said. "Buyers expect strong towing, payload, range, charging, and overall utility."

Large electric trucks need large, expensive batteries, she said, and towing can also sharply reduce their range.

Plus, "these full-size EV pickup trucks are and were pretty dang expensive," DeGraff added. The Sierra EV, for example, starts around $65,000.

An altogether new bet

Automakers have a new bet: smaller and cheaper electric trucks that aren't competing with the full-size workhorses.

Ford's entry to that market is the Fathom, the first vehicle on its universal EV platform. Ford says the midsize truck will be smaller and simpler to build than the F-150 Lightning, with a starting price under $29,000. It hasn't released key details — including trim levels and range figures — but production starts next fall.

Slate Auto is making an even more radical affordability play. Its bare-bones, two-seat Blank Slate pickup is expected to enter production this month and starts at $24,950.

Whether that formula works remains an open question.

"If a company can offer a smaller electric truck that has at least 300 miles of range, then I think it could work," Seth Goldstein, a senior equity analyst at Morningstar who covers the auto industry, said. "But it's going to be more difficult than building an SUV or a sedan where you don't need as much power."
