title: Critical Raw Materials Act: Guide & EU Rules - CASRAI
description:
The Critical Raw Materials Act (Regulation (EU) 2024/1252) establishes a binding framework to secure the EU’s supply of materials critical for net-zero, digital, defense, and battery technologies.
Common mistakes Compliance teams and project developers navigating the Critical Raw Materials Act should avoid several common pitfalls: Confusing Critical with Strategic Materials: Only the 17 Strategic Raw Materials (Annex I) are eligible for fast-track permitting and 2030 benchmarks.
Related programs The Critical Raw Materials Act coordinates with several European and international policy frameworks: Program Primary Objective Material Scope Target Beneficiaries Key Mechanism Critical Raw Materials Act (Regulation (EU) 2024/1252) Secure EU mineral resilience and set 2030 capacity benchmarks.
EU Batteries Regulation (Regulation (EU) 2023/1542) Enforce life-cycle sustainability and recycled content rules.
The Critical Raw Materials Act is EU Regulation 2024/1252, enacted to secure a diversified and sustainable supply of critical and strategic raw materials for European green, digital, defense, and aerospace sectors.
text:
The Critical Raw Materials Act (Regulation (EU) 2024/1252) establishes a binding framework to secure the EU’s supply of materials critical for net-zero, digital, defense, and battery technologies. For researchers, developers, and battery supply chain operators, the regulation introduces 2030 domestic capacity benchmarks, fast-track permitting for Strategic Projects, and mandatory supply-chain risk assessments for large technology manufacturers.

What it is and who runs it

The Critical Raw Materials Act (CRMA) is codified as Regulation (EU) 2024/1252 of the European Parliament and of the Council of 11 April 2024. Published in the Official Journal on 3 May 2024, it entered into force on 23 May 2024, as described on the official page on 2026-11-08, establishing rules to reduce single third-country import dependencies.

The regulation is administered by the European Commission, primarily through DG GROW. The European Critical Raw Materials Board (Articles 35–37) evaluates Strategic Projects and monitors supply vulnerabilities, while designated national Single Points of Contact (Article 9) coordinate permitting procedures.

The CRMA establishes two statutory material tiers:

Critical Raw Materials (Annex II): 34 materials exhibiting high economic importance and significant supply risk across the EU.

Strategic Raw Materials (Annex I): A prioritized subset of 17 materials vital for clean energy transitions. For battery and energy storage systems, this explicitly includes battery-grade lithium, cobalt, battery-grade nickel, natural graphite, manganese, copper, and permanent magnet rare earths (neodymium, praseodymium, dysprosium, terbium, samarium, gadolinium, and holmium).

Eligibility (summary, with the official source)

Eligibility rules for Strategic Projects are defined in Articles 6 and 7 of Regulation (EU) 2024/1252, as described on the official page on 2026-11-08. Public or private entities undertaking extraction, processing, recycling, or substitution may apply.

Under Article 6(1), applications must satisfy four cumulative criteria:

Contribution to Security of Supply: Directly increases EU extraction, processing, or recycling capacity, or produces verified substitutes.

Technical and Commercial Feasibility: Demonstrates technical maturity and operational viability with a bankable business plan.

Sustainable Operations: Meets high environmental, social, and governance (ESG) standards under EU environmental law.

Cross-Border or Mutual Benefit: Delivers cross-border benefits within the EU, or mutual value for third-country projects while protecting local standards.

Under Article 6(4), host Member States hold sovereign authority over national resources; the Commission cannot designate a project as strategic if the host government objects.

What it funds or requires

Regulation (EU) 2024/1252 combines capacity benchmarks with regulatory obligations, as described on the official page on 2026-11-08:

1. 2030 Union Capacity Benchmarks (Article 5):

Extraction: At least 10% of annual EU strategic raw material consumption mined domestically.

Processing: At least 40% of annual consumption processed within the Union.

Recycling: At least 25% of annual consumption met from domestic secondary recycled waste.

Diversification: No more than 65% of annual consumption of any strategic material from a single third country.

2. Streamlined Permitting (Article 11): Strategic Projects receive overriding public interest status. Permitting durations are capped at 27 months for extraction and 15 months for processing and recycling.

3. Financing Coordination: The CRMA does not disburse direct grant funding. Instead, it provides Strategic Projects with prioritized financing matchmaking through the European Investment Bank (EIB), commercial lenders, and EU programs such as Horizon Europe and the Innovation Fund.

4. Corporate Risk Auditing (Articles 24 and 25): Large companies producing strategic technologies (>500 staff, >€150M turnover) must perform triennial supply-chain stress tests.

5. Circularity Mandates (Articles 27–29): Extractive waste operators must evaluate CRM recovery from mine tailings. Permanent magnet producers must label composition and declare recycled content shares.

Application or compliance steps

Organizations engaging with the Critical Raw Materials Act follow a defined operational workflow, as described on the official page on 2026-11-08:

Classification: Verify proposed minerals against Annex I (Strategic) and Annex II (Critical).

Dossier Submission: Submit technical feasibility, commercial models, and ESG plans via DG GROW’s online portal.

Completeness Screening: DG GROW conducts an administrative screening within 30 days of intake.

Member State Review: The host Member State assesses planning and environmental alignment via its Single Point of Contact.

Board Opinion and Designation: The European Critical Raw Materials Board issues an opinion; the Commission adopts a recognition decision.

Fast-Track Permitting: The promoter submits permit files under statutory caps (15 or 27 months) alongside Environmental Impact Assessments (EIA).

Due Diligence and Material Transfers: Downstream manufacturers incorporate supply tracing and due diligence questionnaires into procurement. Laboratories exchanging materials formalize terms using material transfer agreements.

Typical timeline phases (no calendar dates as facts)

Implementation occurs across structured operational phases, as described on the official page on 2026-11-08:

Phase 1: Intake and Completeness Screening: Dossier intake followed by a 30-day completeness check by DG GROW.

Phase 2: Technical and Intergovernmental Review: Evaluation by the Board and host Member States over a 60- to 90-day window.

Phase 3: Designation and Capital Matchmaking: Formal Commission recognition and structured matchmaking with institutional financiers.

Phase 4: Fast-Track Permitting Execution: National authorities guide permitting under statutory caps: 15 months for processing/recycling or 27 months for extraction.

Phase 5: Operational Monitoring: Operating sites report annual output and recycling metrics to confirm alignment with 2030 Union targets.

Phase 6: Recurring Corporate Audits: Covered manufacturers execute supply-chain stress tests on a rolling 3-year audit cadence.

Common mistakes

Compliance teams and project developers navigating the Critical Raw Materials Act should avoid several common pitfalls:

Confusing Critical with Strategic Materials: Only the 17 Strategic Raw Materials (Annex I) are eligible for fast-track permitting and 2030 benchmarks. Annex II Critical Raw Materials do not qualify automatically.

Assuming Permitting Acceleration Waives Environmental Law: Overriding public interest status does not waive Environmental Impact Assessments (Directive 2011/92/EU); it compresses administrative timelines, not environmental standards.

Overlooking the 65% Single-Country Import Limit: Long-term supply contracts exceeding the 65% single third-country ceiling violate Union resilience benchmarks.

Ignoring Downstream Corporate Duties: Clean tech and battery manufacturers (>500 staff, >€150M turnover) face mandatory triennial risk assessments, alongside EU AI Act compliance for algorithmic supply tracing.

Neglecting Extractive Waste Mandates: Mine operators failing to conduct required preliminary economic assessments of mineral recovery from tailings under Article 27.

Uncoordinated Portal Credentials: Submitting proposals without verified institutional credentials on the EU Funding and Tenders Portal, which requires validated Participant Identification Codes (PIC) and Legal Entity Appointed Representatives (LEAR).

Related programs

The Critical Raw Materials Act coordinates with several European and international policy frameworks:

Program Primary Objective Material Scope Target Beneficiaries Key Mechanism Critical Raw Materials Act

(Regulation (EU) 2024/1252) Secure EU mineral resilience and set 2030 capacity benchmarks. 34 Critical and 17 Strategic Raw Materials (lithium, cobalt, nickel, graphite, manganese, copper, rare earths). Project promoters, waste operators, and large OEMs (>500 staff, >€150M turnover). Strategic Project status, 15/27-month permit caps, priority financing, triennial risk audits. EU Batteries Regulation

(Regulation (EU) 2023/1542) Enforce life-cycle sustainability and recycled content rules. All battery categories (EV, industrial, portable) and active materials (lithium, nickel, cobalt). Battery manufacturers, importers, distributors, and recyclers. Mandatory recycled content minimums, digital battery passports, supply-chain due diligence. Net-Zero Industry Act

(Regulation (EU) 2024/1735) Scale domestic manufacturing capacity for clean energy hardware. Clean technologies: battery cells, solar PV, wind turbines, electrolyzers, heat pumps. Clean technology manufacturers and industrial site promoters. Net-Zero Strategic Projects, accelerated plant permitting, public procurement non-price criteria. US Inflation Reduction Act

(Public Law 117-169) Incentivize North American clean energy manufacturing and mineral sourcing. 50 designated critical minerals and clean energy hardware components. Automotive OEMs, mineral extractors, and clean tech manufacturers in US or FTA countries. Tax credits ($3,750 critical mineral EV credit, Section 45X manufacturing production credit).

FAQ

What is the Critical Raw Materials Act?

The Critical Raw Materials Act is EU Regulation 2024/1252, enacted to secure a diversified and sustainable supply of critical and strategic raw materials for European green, digital, defense, and aerospace sectors.

Who is affected by the Critical Raw Materials Act?

The act directly impacts mineral extraction, processing, and recycling promoters, extractive waste operators, and large downstream manufacturers (>500 employees, >€150 million net turnover) producing strategic clean energy technologies.

What are the 2030 targets under the Critical Raw Materials Act?

By 2030, the EU aims to extract at least 10%, process at least 40%, and recycle at least 25% of its annual consumption of strategic raw materials domestically, while capping single-country import reliance at 65%.

How do projects qualify as Strategic Projects under the CRMA?

Projects must demonstrate contribution to European strategic raw material security, verified technical and commercial feasibility, adherence to high environmental standards, and cross-border or mutual benefit, subject to host Member State consent.

Does the Critical Raw Materials Act provide direct grant funding?

No. The CRMA is a regulatory and permitting framework rather than a grant distribution program. However, Strategic Projects receive facilitated access to capital through the European Investment Bank and EU programs like Horizon Europe and the Innovation Fund.

What are the permitting deadlines for CRMA Strategic Projects?

Under Article 11, national permit-granting procedures are legally capped at a maximum of 27 months for mineral extraction projects and 15 months for mineral processing and recycling projects.

title: Debate Grows Over Effectiveness of Production Tax Credit for Electric Vehicles - Aju Press
description: The government is considering the introduction of production tax credits and the expansion...
text:
The government is considering the introduction of production tax credits and the expansion of their application to strengthen the domestic production base for national strategic industries, including electric vehicles. However, there is growing controversy over the effectiveness of these policies. The structure of the production tax credit requires companies to have tax liabilities to benefit, making it difficult for loss-making firms, which urgently need financial support, to take advantage of these incentives.
◆Production Tax Credits Require Tax Payments...Limits on Immediate Support
According to relevant government departments, discussions are underway to expand the application of domestic production tax credits and support for loss-making companies. Following a meeting on economic issues on October 25, Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Finance Lee Hyung-il met with Hyundai Motor Group on November 2 to discuss the introduction of production tax credits for electric vehicles.
Previously, the government decided to establish domestic production tax credits for six key sectors, including solar power, wind power, secondary batteries, semiconductors, core materials, and artificial intelligence (AI) robot components, as part of the 2026 tax reform plan. From next year until 2036, tax reductions will be provided based on the quantity produced and sold domestically. The amount of the credit will vary by production region, with up to 1.5 times the benefit for areas outside the capital region.
The issue is that the effectiveness of the support varies depending on a company's profitability. The production tax credit deducts a certain amount from corporate taxes that companies must pay. Even if a company produces a large quantity and generates a tax credit, if it is operating at a loss, it will find it difficult to receive any real benefits in that fiscal year.
To address this issue, the government is preparing a plan that allows unused credits to be carried forward for up to 10 years. This means that even if a company records a loss initially, it can utilize the accumulated credits when it eventually turns a profit.
However, the carryforward credits only reduce future tax burdens and do not alleviate current cash flow issues. Companies that face significant initial investment burdens and take considerable time to secure profitability after starting production may experience delayed support effects.
As an alternative to address these limitations, direct subsidies are being discussed. President Lee Jae-myung proposed at a national report meeting on the Korean Green Transition (K-GX) strategy last month that subsidies be provided to loss-making companies upfront, with the amount deducted from future production tax credit benefits. This approach aims to share some of the initial risks with the government rather than waiting for companies to turn a profit.
In other countries, systems have already been implemented to complement the limitations of tax credits. A notable example is the advanced manufacturing production tax credit under the U.S. Inflation Reduction Act (IRA). The U.S. supports local production of certain items, such as batteries and solar and wind-related components, while introducing direct payments and transfer systems that allow companies to cash in tax credits. If companies meet specific criteria, they can receive cash refunds or transfer credits to third parties to secure funding.
◆Rising Electric Vehicle Imports Highlight Need for Domestic Production Support...Calls for Direct Subsidies
There is an increasing need for expanded support at the production stage domestically, particularly for electric vehicles. While electric vehicle purchase subsidies aim to reduce consumer costs and promote adoption, production support focuses on maintaining domestic factories and supply chains while lowering production costs.
Recently, as the electric vehicle market has expanded in South Korea, concerns have arisen that the increasing share of imported vehicles may not directly lead to increased domestic production. Reducing companies' cost burdens through production tax credits could help maintain domestic production facilities and secure work for parts suppliers. However, there are voices suggesting that tax credits alone may not provide sufficient incentives for loss-making companies, and that direct subsidies should be considered in conjunction.
Financial burdens and the selection of support recipients also pose challenges. Direct subsidies can provide funding regardless of a company's profitability, but there is a risk that public funds may be allocated to projects with uncertain outcomes. Therefore, it is essential to establish specific support criteria based on production volume, domestic investment, and job retention, along with mechanisms to assess performance. Ultimately, expanding production tax credits is not enough; designing a system that allows companies to receive benefits when they genuinely need support is crucial.
Park Hoon, a professor of taxation at the University of Seoul, stated, "For loss-making companies, providing subsidies would be the most effective approach," adding, "If financial support can help a company survive, the impact of subsidies will be the greatest."

name: Clean Energy
title: China's Clean-Tech Manufacturing Boom Is Reshaping the Global Climate Fight
description:
But its huge clean tech exports mean it has also become among the biggest global forces in reducing climate-damaging emissions.
The $132 billion figure derived by Reuters for China’s global climate contribution also includes an estimated $40 billion of Chinese foreign direct investment into clean-technology projects in developing countries.
China’s manufacturing boom is creating another pathway: Driving down the price of clean technology through self-interested innovation and scale – until developing countries adopt it for economic reasons.
Export Giant, Diplomatic Mouse Beijing has so far shown little interest in translating its commercial might into diplomatic leadership at global climate talks since President Donald Trump withdrew the United States from international climate cooperation in 2025.
Forcing out Fossil Fuels Meanwhile, China’s manufacturing boom has made renewable energy more affordable in the developing world.
text:
By Lewis Jackson, Valerie Volcovici and Simon Jessop

China sent $132 billion in clean technology and investment to the developing world last year, by far the largest contribution to carbon-dioxide reduction of any country.

In fact, the nation’s green-manufacturing juggernaut, built in part through heavy subsidies from Beijing, nearly matches the current total of grants, loans and private finance that all wealthy countries sent to poorer ones in 2024 to help fight climate change, according to a Reuters analysis.

Those loans and grants stemmed from a climate-finance program the world’s wealthiest nations agreed to at a 2009 United Nations climate conference on the premise that industrialized nations made outsized contributions to the climate crisis – and had outsized means to help poorer countries pay to clean it up.

A Reuters investigation in 2024 found that most global climate finance comes in the form of loans – and sometimes at market interest rates that funnel billions of dollars back to rich countries.

China took a different approach, funneling billions in subsidies into its own green-energy industries, serving its own national interest to dominate next-generation manufacturing domestically and globally.

The result: massive and rapid market-share gains in solar panels, batteries and battery minerals, electric vehicles, wind turbines and other green products.

China remains by far the world’s biggest greenhouse-gas emitter because of its large population, concentration of heavy industry and reliance on coal power. But its huge clean tech exports mean it has also become among the biggest global forces in reducing climate-damaging emissions.

The Reuters analysis used customs data to calculate the value of Chinese exports of clean technologies to countries classified by the Organization for Economic Cooperation and Development as developing nations.

Those exports alone will help the Global South avoid 257 million metric tons of carbon dioxide emissions (MtCO2) per year once deployed – an amount equal to the annual carbon dioxide emissions of France, according to analysis by Lauri Myllyvirta, co-founder of the Helsinki-based Centre for Research on Energy and Clean Air. This year’s exports from China, meanwhile, are on track to avoid 337 MtCO2 in the Global South, the analysis shows.

Reuters was unable to find a reliable single estimate of how much greenhouse gas emissions are avoided as a result of global climate finance from rich to poor countries.

The OECD estimates a fifth of all rich world climate giving in 2024 came from the private sector.

The United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change and the High Ambition Coalition – an informal coalition of nations that has advocated for substantial climate finance – did not immediately comment for this story.

The $132 billion figure derived by Reuters for China’s global climate contribution also includes an estimated $40 billion of Chinese foreign direct investment into clean-technology projects in developing countries. The investment data was compiled by Mathias Larsen and Xiaokang Xue at the London School of Economics.

That brings China’s contribution to nearly equal to the $137 billion in climate finance that wealthy nations provided to poorer ones in 2024 under their UN climate pledges, according to the most recent figures provided by the OECD.

The figures are not directly comparable. China’s total largely reflects commercial transactions focused on clean energy development, while climate finance can also support other types of programs like developing climate-resilient agricultural techniques or cleaning up damage from major storms or floods.

But the comparison illustrates the extraordinary scale at which China’s manufacturing economy is now shaping the energy transition in poorer countries.

The findings point to a potential shift in the mechanics of the global energy transition, according to Li Shuo, a veteran observer of China at UN climate talks who heads the China Climate Hub at the Asia Society Policy Institute.

For years, climate talks focused on how much money and technology wealthy countries would provide to poorer ones to help them decarbonize. China’s manufacturing boom is creating another pathway: Driving down the price of clean technology through self-interested innovation and scale – until developing countries adopt it for economic reasons.

“You can align it to your economic agenda,” he said.

Export Giant, Diplomatic Mouse

Beijing has so far shown little interest in translating its commercial might into diplomatic leadership at global climate talks since President Donald Trump withdrew the United States from international climate cooperation in 2025.

China’s diplomatic role likely will take center stage as nations gather this month for the UN’s COP31 climate conference in Antalya, Turkey.

Bilateral agreements between heavyweights Washington and Beijing have traditionally paved the way for international climate agreements, including the landmark 2015 Paris deal to limit global warming. But Beijing may be unwilling to go on alone without its geopolitical counterweight at the table, according to former climate negotiators.

Beijing may also be worried that taking a bold stance on global carbon reduction would bring unwanted pressure for China to give more climate aid or cut its own fossil-fuel emissions, observers say. China emits about a third of all carbon dioxide emissions and still burns coal for more than half its power.

“How China engages on different levels in the coming years is the most fundamental thing that is going to happen on climate because of both their role in clean-tech deployment… but also because of their emissions profile,” said Jennifer Morgan, Germany’s former climate minister.

China’s Ministry of Commerce said the country is an important contributor to the global green transformation, and that its wind and solar exports have cumulatively reduced global emissions by roughly 4.1 billion tons of CO2 over the past five years – the equivalent of around 80% of the total emissions of the United States in one year.

“Against the backdrop of a global climate governance ‘action deficit,’ China will continue to uphold a responsible attitude, working with other countries to address challenges, overcome difficulties, and jointly promote global green and low-carbon transformation and sustainable development,” it said.

Forcing out Fossil Fuels

Meanwhile, China’s manufacturing boom has made renewable energy more affordable in the developing world.

When Ethiopia banned combustion engine car imports in 2024, for example, it was the first country to take such a dramatic step toward electric vehicles. The decision was less about emissions and more about cutting its fuel import bill, its deputy minister of transport at the time told Reuters.

“No one in Ethiopia is asking COP to pay for any of this; the economics have just switched. It is just the cheapest and best solution,” said Larsen, a senior policy fellow at the London School of Economics, who built the database of Chinese green investment used by Reuters in this story.

China has been by far the world’s biggest supplier of electric vehicles over the past few years, as dozens of subsidized automakers have waged a fierce price war in China and dramatically increased exports.

Nearly two thirds of China’s exports of solar panels, and the cells needed to make them, went to the developing world last year, according to Reuters analysis of customs data.

The picture is different in wealthy countries like the United States and parts of Europe, which in recent years have imposed tariffs and other restrictions on Chinese clean technology to protect their domestic manufacturers from the surge in shipments.

The United States, for example, imposes tariffs exceeding 100% on Chinese electric vehicles and has taken other measures to effectively block them from the market.

“What is striking is that policies originally designed to address climate change are now facing opposition not because of their climate impacts, but because of concerns about trade and competitiveness,” said André Corrêa do Lago, a veteran climate negotiator for Brazil, which hosted last year’s climate summit.

text:
How a Democratic Sweep in the US Could Affect Korean Industry

Subsidies for Samsung and SK Hynix’s US Plants

Payment Procedures Could Lengthen or Be Delayed

No Immediate Hit to Chip Demand Seen

Battery, Solar Sectors Hope for Green Revival

South Korean semiconductor companies are closely watching the fallout from a Democratic “blue wave” that gave the party control of both chambers in the US midterm elections. Samsung Electronics Co. and SK Hynix Inc., which operate plants in the US or are expanding capacity there, could be directly affected by changes to subsidy and tax-credit policies. At the same time, some in and around the chip industry say concerns over a sharp slowdown in artificial-intelligence investment are overstated. Containing China’s push in AI remains a bipartisan priority in the US, leading to expectations that AI investment is unlikely to fall off significantly. In the electric-vehicle, battery and solar industries, hopes are also rising that clean-energy investment will regain momentum.

Subsidy Procedures a Variable as Long-Term AI Demand Holds Up

Industry officials said on Nov. 8 that subsidies are likely to be the first area of impact for Samsung Electronics and SK Hynix after the US midterm elections. Samsung’s foundry plant in Taylor, Texas, is set to receive phased subsidies of as much as $4.745 billion from the federal government and as much as $250 million from the state of Texas under the US CHIPS Act. SK Hynix’s fab in Indiana, where construction began in August, is eligible for subsidies of up to $458 million.

There is also the possibility that subsidy disbursement procedures could expand or be delayed as additional steps, including certification of compliance with environmental regulations, are added. KOTRA, the Korea Trade-Investment Promotion Agency, said in a recent report titled “The 2026 US Midterm Election Results and Implications” that a Democratic Congress would likely tighten oversight of the implementation of existing agreements, the execution of subsidies and the management of funding for research-and-development projects.

Despite concerns over regulation in the US, many in the industry do not expect demand for AI semiconductors to weaken sharply anytime soon. Lee Jong-hwan, a professor in the Department of System Semiconductor Engineering at Sangmyung University, said construction of AI data centers could face a temporary slowdown. But the US cannot afford to retreat from AI investment if it feels threatened by China, he added. While some long-term supply agreements signed by Samsung Electronics and SK Hynix could be affected, he said a major hit remains unlikely.

New data-center investment is expected to become more selective. Democrats have signaled they would charge companies for AI infrastructure costs, including electricity and water. Industry officials also say companies could be pressed to present job-creation measures, given that data centers generate less employment than other large-scale facilities such as factories. If costs rise, lower-margin data-center projects could lose momentum.

Big Tech is already moving to respond. Meta Platforms Inc. is considering expanding existing data centers to avoid complex permitting procedures. Setting up data-center hubs outside the US, including in Asia, is also being discussed. The Wall Street Journal reported that OpenAI Chief Executive Officer Sam Altman told employees after the midterm elections that building data centers in the desert could also be an option.

MASGA Policy Seen Staying in Place

The impact of the blue wave on South Korea’s auto industry is likely to be limited. The 15% tariff imposed on Korean-made vehicles is based on Section 232 of the US Trade Expansion Act. That falls under the executive branch, not Congress.

Instead, a more favorable environment may emerge for electric-vehicle adoption. Democrats are pushing to restore the EV purchase tax credit that expired in September last year. The key variable is whether President Donald Trump exercises his veto power.

Because Democrats are supportive of green industries, the battery and solar sectors have also gained some relief. Republican efforts to move quickly to scale back tax credits for battery production in the US and support for energy storage system, or ESS, investment appear likely to face resistance. Delays in data-center permitting remain a burden, but there are also expectations that Big Tech will increase ESS installations and backup batteries for servers to store electricity against power shortages and blackouts.

The basic direction of MASGA, a South Korea-US shipbuilding cooperation project, is also seen remaining in place. Rebuilding the US shipbuilding industry and strengthening defense capabilities are bipartisan goals.

Roh Yoo-jung and Yang Gil-seong, Hankyung reporters yjroh@hankyung.com

title: Democrats must carefully reframe climate debate to end Trump's unchecked attacks
description:
The dramatic Democratic victory on Nov 3 will end the era of Trump’s unchecked climate rollback.
But don’t expect a dramatic reset on US climate policy for now.
“While majorities across the spectrum accept that climate change is real, it is not a top-tier public priority compared with cost-of-living and reliability concerns,” said Clarence Edwards, executive director of the Washington office for London-based climate policy think-tank E3G.
And the long list of policy priorities facing the Democrats means they will have to choose their next steps carefully.
Democrats can usefully signal that they support a return to more cooperative global climate action and lower-cost green energy.
text:
SINGAPORE – Since returning to the White House, US President Donald Trump has waged a ruthless battle to revoke or strangle US climate regulations, reduce green investment and bully companies into rolling back net-zero emissions pledges.

That is about to change. The dramatic Democratic victory on Nov 3 will end the era of Trump’s unchecked climate rollback. Control of both houses of Congress means the Democrats can stifle any further attempts by Trump to derail renewable energy investment or remaining emissions regulations.

But don’t expect a dramatic reset on US climate policy for now.

“While majorities across the spectrum accept that climate change is real, it is not a top-tier public priority compared with cost-of-living and reliability concerns,” said Clarence Edwards, executive director of the Washington office for London-based climate policy think-tank E3G.

Analysts say the Democrats will have to navigate Trump’s power to veto Bills from Congress. And the long list of policy priorities facing the Democrats means they will have to choose their next steps carefully.

“It will hinge on how the Democrats pick their battles and frame the climate topics to the American public to meet their immediate concerns: economy, energy affordability and jobs,” said Putra Adhiguna, managing director of the Energy Shift Institute, a think-tank focusing on Asia’s energy transition.

Still, given the Democrats’ traditional support for green energy and climate action, their strong performance in the midterms will hearten investors looking for positive signals – and the possibility that the Democrats will win the 2028 presidential election.

And what happens in the United States still matters. As the world’s largest economy and second-largest greenhouse gas polluter after China, the country’s emissions have risen again, thanks to Trump’s support for the fossil fuel industry and energy-hungry data centres – right at a time of record global temperatures and worsening climate impacts around the globe.

For Asia, however, the impacts of renewed climate action will be more nuanced as governments in the region have become more independent of the US in green investments since Trump’s abandonment of climate diplomacy and his use of punishing tariffs.

Trump withdrew the US from the Paris Agreement and the United Nations’ main climate convention and used tariffs to slash clean-tech exports from Asia, such as solar panels made in South-east Asia. Democrats can usefully signal that they support a return to more cooperative global climate action and lower-cost green energy.

Next steps to roll back Trump’s anti-climate policies

A Democrat-controlled Congress can still halt and possibly start to reverse some of Trump’s anti-climate measures.

“The Democrats cannot reverse climate rollbacks outright as they lack the numbers to override a presidential veto. But they can bargain, and funding Bills are likely their strongest lever,” said Will Nichols, Head of Climate and Resilience at risk intelligence company Verisk Maplecroft.

For example, the White House will need Democratic votes to approve funding to keep the government running. They can use this leverage to push for stronger support for renewables, a return to tougher environmental standards, and restoring clean-energy and climate-resilience funding, he said.

And armed with new subpoena powers, the Democrats will be able to scrutinise attempts to roll back federal environmental and climate policies, and force administration officials and business figures to testify.

Specifically, Congress could revisit Trump’s One Big Beautiful Bill Act provisions, which accelerated the phase-out of billions of dollars of wind and solar tax credits, said Edwards.

The Democrats might also target the repeal of most Biden-era power-plant greenhouse-gas standards and the rollback of corporate fleet fuel economy standards, he added.

“Bipartisan agreement remains possible on selected energy issues; the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act of 2026 (introduced in the Senate on Sept 30) is the clearest near-term vehicle,” Edwards said. It would streamline permitting, require large data centres to bear more of their incremental grid costs, and address other affordability and reliability measures.

Reframing climate measures as reducing the cost of living

States are also likely to move the green needle. For instance, Democratic governors in states such as Michigan, Minnesota, Pennsylvania and Texas will likely advance measures focused on lower energy costs.

These include community solar power generation, battery storage, data-centre siting and efficiency programmes. “In the long run, these state experiments will shape the political and technical environment for any federal policies,” said Edwards.

Boardrooms are also likely to appreciate greater regulatory certainty. Many large US companies maintained climate targets despite federal rollbacks, Nichols said. And they will continue to face pressure from shareholders and other investors to address the growing risks and costs of extreme weather linked to climate change.

Framing the debate around how the measures can benefit the population will be key.

“To succeed, Democrats will need to step carefully, framing this as lowering the cost of living rather than as a climate imperative that remains fairly low on voters’ radars,” Nichols said.

Li Shuo, director of China Climate Hub at the Asia Society Policy Institute in Washington, said it would be a mistake to underestimate the extent to which the climate agenda has become politicised.

It is a view shared by others.

“As Trumpism wanes, climate activists would do well to take a page from (the book of) this year’s elections to focus on the costs of global warming: Higher utility bills. Higher insurance premiums. Higher home repair bills. Higher food prices caused by droughts and heatwaves,” commentator Bill Sternberg wrote in Callaway Climate Insights on Nov 5.

What it means for Asia

As Trump slashed climate regulations and funding, China pressed ahead with its dominance of Asia’s clean-tech production: chiefly electric vehicles, solar panels, batteries and wind turbines. The US has dramatically curbed imports of these goods through tariffs or bans, isolating itself from the region.

The Trump administration also ended its support for renewable energy and transition programmes in countries like Indonesia and Vietnam, favouring fossil fuel investments and trade instead .

This means the US is becoming an increasingly irrelevant player in the global clean-tech transition, particularly in Asia, said Li Shuo. “Beyond Tesla, which is not competitive in many sizeable Asian markets outside China, I struggle to name even one American clean-energy company that could play a meaningful role in the region.”

“And do we really believe the US government will deploy its limited public finances for other countries’ energy transition?” he added.

Putra said US allies with deeper ties in clean tech, such as South Korea, might benefit from a Democrat-controlled Congress. But the revival of ASEAN-manufactured solar exports to the US is less likely because US domestic job creation remains a priority, he added.

So, for now, the US remains a weaker player in Asia on clean tech, climate diplomacy and climate research, with Trump also slashing funding support for US institutions’ climate science programmes.

COP31

The midterm results come as delegates from nearly 200 nations gather in the Turkish resort of Antalya for the COP31 climate talks from Nov 9 to 20. There will be no official US delegation, but US politicians and business leaders are set to attend in an unofficial capacity.

For some, the Democrats’ victory is a hopeful sign. For others, it is a reminder of decades of US climate policy flip-flops – from George W. Bush, who rejected binding international caps on emissions and opposed the UN’s Kyoto Protocol, the precursor to the 2015 Paris Agreement, to Barack Obama, who was key to the creation of the Paris pact.

“This US domestic political change may contribute to a more hopeful atmosphere. It will not reverse the US absence, restore US leadership or absolve others from stepping up,” said Edwards. But the strong unofficial presence in Turkey, such as members of Congress, will help to lift the mood at COP31.

“Expect American participants there to say, ‘Wait for us to be back in two years’,” said Li Shuo.

“Some will welcome that and act as though the Trump years never happened. Others will simply say, ‘We have seen this movie many times before’.”

text:
As the rapid growth of AI data centres compounds the world’s energy crisis, engineers in Denmark have found a way to make use of the vast amounts of “waste heat” generated by these centres, which is usually lost to the outside air.

There are more than 12,500 data centres around the world and more are coming online every day, straining global energy infrastructure and resources.

Beyond consuming hundreds of billions of litres of water, these systems not only place a massive demand on the global electrical grid, but are likely to be contributing to global warming on a massive scale as well.

The International Energy Agency (IEA) has reported that, in 2024, data centres used 485 terawatt hours of electricity, the equivalent of 1.5 percent of the world’s total energy supply – or the total electricity generation of Germany.

And this figure will double to 3 percent by 2030, with an exponentially growing proportion driven by AI development. This comes as nations are seeking energy independence and need to drastically cut their CO2 emissions.

Indeed, the United Nations Economic Commission for Europe has warned that the rapid expansion of AI hyperscalers – the large-scale cloud service providers like Google, Amazon and Microsoft – and the vast data centres required to support them – pose a “growing threat to electricity systems worldwide”.

The proliferation of data centres is causing widespread anger. In the Netherlands, police arrested protesters against the construction of a new Microsoft data centre close to Amsterdam on Friday. Meanwhile, Elon Musk has earned the ire of residents of Texas, where he moved his AI and SpaceX operations to take advantage of tax breaks. Texans voted in their first Democratic senator – James Talarico – in nearly 40 years in this week’s midterm elections despite Musk sinking hundreds of millions of dollars into campaigns for the Republican Party.

How capturing wasted heat works

The Bitten supercomputer, which was launched in May this year at the University of Southern Denmark in Sonderborg, is the go-to AI resource for academic research across the country. It provides the AI computing power required for deep data analysis and complex scientific simulations.

But like supercomputers and AI data centres everywhere, Bitten’s capability matches its power consumption. Twenty-four hours a day, its specialised processors generate extreme amounts of thermal energy as they handle the workload.

Now, instead of just allowing that energy to dissipate like AI centres elsewhere, 100 percent of the waste heat is recovered by advanced liquid cooling technology designed by the Danish engineering company Danfoss. This replaces traditional air conditioning and fans that vent to the outside air.

The new system pumps coolant directly over the high-temperature processing chips, completely absorbing the waste heat. That heat can then be channelled directly into Sonderborg’s municipal district heating network to help the town’s 75,000 residents stay warm.

Kristian Strand, president of Danfoss Climate Solutions, told Al Jazeera that whenever we take a picture or upload a document, we activate processing in a data centre.

“That creates heat which we have to remove,” he said. “With the waste heat recovery system, at the end of the process you basically have a tap of hot water coming out of the data centre. That hot water can then be used not only to heat homes but in industrial processes, too.”

Turning data centres into energy sources

Across the world, a colossal amount of energy from industrial processes just vanishes into the atmosphere. Strand told Al Jazeera that Danfoss calculated heat wasted across Europe in one year could power the entire city of Paris for 48 years, while roughly two-thirds of the world’s energy is expelled as excess heat.

The United States hosts more data centres than any other country by far, currently about 4,000. They draw down 5 percent of the nation’s electricity. Yet the US recovers very little heat because it has nowhere to go.

“We should be building data centres where their heat can be used, not just where land is cheapest,” said Jan Rosenow, professor of energy and climate policy at the University of Oxford.

Scandinavia has been leading the way on capturing waste heat, Rosenow said. “Meta’s data centre in Odense in Denmark recovers around 100 GWh a year, enough for 6,900 homes. And Stockholm in Sweden has been feeding data centre heat into its network since 2014.”

At Danfoss, other potential sources of waste heat are being showcased, from supermarket fridge systems, to factories and wastewater treatment plants.

Its engineers recently replaced two carbon-intensive gas boilers at Sonderborg Hospital with a heat pump system that captures waste heat from medical equipment like MRI scanners, and from temperature regulation systems in operating theatres, wards and corridors.

This heat used to be vented outside via cooling towers. Now, the hospital is energy independent for nine months of the year and can feed heat back into the district heating network, saving significant sums on heating bills.

“There was a very good business case for making this happen,” said Lasse Bo Madsen, head of technical services at Sonderborg Hospital. “The project will pay for itself inside two years, and it means we will be able to spend more money on patient care and new equipment, like scanners.”

According to Kristin Strand, this technology is a huge opportunity to save energy and reduce carbon emissions. “We have a vast untapped source of energy in waste heat,” Strand said. “Putting that energy to use reduces reliance on fossil fuels while also making business sense.”

As the AI boom accelerates and new data centres come online, each demanding enough electricity to power a small city, Danfoss believes the scalability of this new waste-heat technology could help ease the soaring demand that is currently stretching global supply.

text:
BANGKOK, Thailand – Thailand’s Finance Ministry is preparing a major overhaul of excise tax rules for electric vehicles (EVs), linking tax rates more closely to domestic manufacturing and the use of locally produced components. The proposed structure aims to encourage foreign automakers to establish production facilities and source more parts from Thai suppliers rather than relying on imported finished vehicles. Under the proposed framework, EV manufacturers operating factories in Thailand and meeting the required local content threshold would qualify for a 10% excise tax rate. Companies with domestic factories but insufficient use of locally made components could face rates of 15–20%, while fully imported EVs would be subject to a 35% rate.

Finance Permanent Secretary Lavaron Sangsnit said the changes are intended to encourage automakers to deepen their investment in Thailand and support the development of a domestic supply chain. The 35% excise tax on imported EVs has already been approved by the Cabinet on November 3, 2026. It will take effect on January 1, 2027, replacing the previous rates of 10% for battery electric vehicles (BEVs) and 15% for range-extended electric vehicles (REEVs). Previous EV 3.0 and EV 3.5 incentive programs helped expand the market and attract manufacturers to establish eight factories in Thailand. However, the relatively low tax on imported vehicles has encouraged some companies to continue importing finished cars rather than investing in local production.

The higher tax is intended to change that balance. One additional company has already expressed interest in investing in Thailand, potentially bringing the number of EV factories to nine, with a tenth also considered possible. The ministry is also preparing to revise the way local content is calculated to ensure that the figures reflect genuine use of domestically manufactured components. The new criteria are expected to take effect within about three years, around 2030, giving manufacturers time to adjust. The Excise Department is discussing the proposed framework with the Federation of Thai Industries and considering the use of the Made in Thailand (MIT) standard to determine local content. Initial details are expected soon, although the minimum proportion of locally sourced components has yet to be decided.

The department is also reviewing tax incentives for the production of high-value EV components, particularly batteries. Many automakers continue to retain control of battery technology and production within their overseas parent companies, making it difficult for Thailand to attract investment in this critical part of the supply chain.

Ratchada Vanichakorn, Deputy Director-General of the Excise Department, said attracting battery manufacturing investment remained challenging because of the strategic importance of the technology. The government is therefore considering incentives that could encourage domestic production of other high-value EV components. One option under study is to add two more tax levels to the existing incentive structure. The current lowest rate of 2% applies to vehicles meeting strategic component requirements, such as using domestically produced batteries. A revised rate of around 10% could be introduced, alongside more flexible conditions covering other important components.

The ministry stressed that the 35% tax on imported EVs has been approved, while the additional tax structure and revised local content requirements remain under consideration. The longer-term objective is to move Thailand beyond vehicle assembly towards becoming a regional production and export base for EVs and their components.

text:
By Matthew Holloway |

The U.S. Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) has given final approval to a Maricopa County air quality rule allowing fleet owners to generate emissions credits by replacing or upgrading higher-emitting vehicles, county officials announced Thursday.

Under Rule 205, qualifying reductions from on-road vehicles can generate credits used to offset emissions from new or expanding industrial facilities. The county said the approval allows its Air Quality Department to begin issuing the credits immediately.

“Rule 205 is a win-win for our residents, demonstrating that Maricopa County can prioritize both cleaner air and a strong economy,” Board of Supervisors Chair Kate Brophy McGee said. “By incentivizing rather than punishing job creators, this approach will deliver measurable improvements in air quality while creating new opportunities for businesses to invest and expand.”

The program connects voluntary fleet improvements with federal permitting requirements for industrial development. Under the Clean Air Act’s nonattainment New Source Review program, new major stationary sources and major modifications to existing major stationary sources must provide offsets for increased emissions.

Fleet owners can submit replacement or retrofit projects to the Air Quality Department for evaluation. Qualifying reductions must be real, quantifiable, surplus, permanent, and federally enforceable before the county certifies them.

Certified credits may then be traded for use as offsets. A facility relying on those credits cannot begin operating until the corresponding vehicle replacements or retrofits have occurred. The required offsets must exceed the facility’s emissions increase under the applicable offset ratio.

The guidance identifies eligibility conditions, including that fleet vehicles be based and operated within the Phoenix-Mesa ozone nonattainment area. Certain projects completed on or after January 1, 2017, may qualify, subject to the rule’s requirements.

The county’s rule history lists an initial adoption date of April 26, 2023, and a revision on May 21, 2025. The county submitted the revised version to the EPA on May 30, 2025.

Vice Chair Debbie Lesko praised EPA Administrator Lee Zeldin’s work with the county.

“I applaud EPA Administrator Lee Zeldin for working with Maricopa County to find Clean Air solutions that fit the unique needs of our region,” Lesko said. “It’s proof we can partner with the federal government to streamline regulations while still protecting the quality of the air we breathe.”

Maricopa County is also pursuing emissions credits for upgrades to railroad locomotives and construction equipment through Rule 204. The EPA proposed approving that rule on October 6, extending the county’s approach to voluntary emissions reductions from nonroad engines.

The EPA said the proposed Rule 204 approval would allow qualifying reductions in nitrogen oxides or volatile organic compounds to generate credits for facilities seeking to build or expand within the county’s ozone nonattainment area.

In its October announcement, the EPA identified portions of Maricopa County as being in moderate nonattainment for the 2015 federal ozone standard. That designation subjects covered industrial projects to additional permitting and emissions-offset requirements.

Rule 205 has received final approval. The county described Rule 204 as remaining at the proposed-approval stage.

title: Energy policy comes into focus after Dems take majorities in Michigan - Yahoo
description:
"Now is the time to deliver on campaign promises to lower costs, hold utilities accountable, protect against data center expansion and advance clean energy solutions."
Data center guardrails In the days following the midterms, Democrats in Lansing have broadly outlined aims to lower costs, without diving too deep into specific policy aims.
In the midterms, they turned into a hot topic politically as residents in communities across Michigan either expressed concern or plainly called to reject new data center development.
On the campaign trail, candidates from both parties embraced data center accountability measures.
Gretchen Whitmer aimed at improving energy affordability in Michigan.
text:
Buoyed by Democrats taking wide majorities in both chambers of the state Legislature and Democratic Secretary of State Jocelyn Benson being elected as Michigan's next governor, energy affordability and climate activists believe the results of the Nov. 3 election have laid the groundwork for new policy to advance through Lansing next year.

Voter frustration with the cost of living in general fueled electoral gains for Democrats nationally and in Michigan. The price of energy, from gas prices to home heating costs, also played a role, analysts and candidates noted throughout the run up to Election Day.

"Michigan families have been clear that their energy bills are too high, and they want leaders who will do something about it," Denise Keele, executive director of the Michigan Climate Action Network said in a statement provided to the Detroit Free Press. "Now is the time to deliver on campaign promises to lower costs, hold utilities accountable, protect against data center expansion and advance clean energy solutions."

Data center guardrails

In the days following the midterms, Democrats in Lansing have broadly outlined aims to lower costs, without diving too deep into specific policy aims. But incoming Senate Majority Leader Darrin Camilleri, D-Trenton, told reporters Nov. 5 he was in favor of a moratorium on new data center projects in Michigan while adding the caveat that the entire Democratic caucus hasn't taken a position on such a policy, yet. Democrats will hold a 23-15 majority in the Senate, although many Republican lawmakers have called for a pause on data center projects, too.

Data centers are the facilities that house computer hardware needed to power various functions on the web. In the midterms, they turned into a hot topic politically as residents in communities across Michigan either expressed concern or plainly called to reject new data center development.

Besides a moratorium, some lawmakers have called for guardrails on water and electricity usage at data centers. Earlier this year, Senate Democrats introduced a series of bills setting parameters for how data centers could operate in Michigan, although the legislation didn't advance. It's not likely the bills are taken up during the lame duck session but data center guardrails are likely to be reintroduced not long after the new Legislature begins its session next year.

Ben Poulson, state government affairs director for the Michigan League of Conservation Voters, said the guardrail package is a "great starting point" for Democrats next year. He pointed to measures adopted by the Michigan Public Service Commission (MPSC), including requiring data centers to pay for the electricity they use, as something lawmakers should codify into state law.

"Ensuring data centers pay their own way is the most important step the Legislature can get done on affordability," Poulson said Nov. 6.

On the campaign trail, candidates from both parties embraced data center accountability measures.

Utility accountability measures get new life

Michigan voters overwhelmingly backed a ballot proposal that bans investor-owned utilities, like DTE Energy and Consumers Energy, along with company executives, from donating to political campaigns. Proposal 2 passed with 81% support, according to unofficial results.

Although DTE and Consumers have challenged the proposal's legality in court on First Amendment lines, advocates believe legislation to hold the companies accountable for spotty service reliability and prolonged outages in recent years hasn't advanced because of the influence of corporate spending in Lansing. Should Proposal 2 withstand legal challenges, its supporters believe the margin it passed by gives lawmakers a mandate to advance policy related to utility service in Michigan.

Poulson said legislation that increases the amount of distributed energy generation local residents and communities can produce (which typically is through community solar projects or battery storage, in some cases) can not only help with energy affordability but also aid Michigan in its goal to have 100% clean energy generation by 2040. Current law places caps on the amount of energy that can be produced locally.

No more annual rate hikes?

Earlier this year, the MPSC presented a series of recommendations to Gov. Gretchen Whitmer aimed at improving energy affordability in Michigan. MPSC Chair Dan Scripps backed a ban on annual rate cases, among other policy tweaks.

More: New Michigan Senate majority leader promises actions to lower costs

Under current law, there is nothing stopping electric and natural gas providers from seeking rate hikes for their customers in consecutive years. The typical rate case takes about ten months to complete and follows a routine formula: Companies will ask to raise their rates by a certain amount and argue the higher prices are needed to invest in the grid. Intervenors, which often include Attorney General Dana Nessel's office and affordability advocates, will argue the hike is unnecessary. The MPSC usually ends up approving a rate increase lower than what the utility first sought. In recent years, Nessel has drawn attention to utilities opening new rate hike requests shortly after their most recent case is settled.

In January, lawmakers in the Michigan House introduced bills to ban utilities from seeking rate increases for at least three years after their most recent case is settled, although it hasn't advanced through the chamber. With new majorities in both the House and Senate, taking up the MPSC's recommendation to stop annual rate hikes could have new life in Lansing.

title: Dems Campaigned on Affordability. But Can They Deliver? | The New Republic
authors: Emma Janssen, The New Republic Staff
description:
Inside Washington “We campaigned as affordability Democrats.
There’s also the issue of President Donald Trump’s veto power, which could thwart Democrats’ affordability legislation during the next Congress.
Even if Trump’s vetoes make affordability legislation tricky, Democrats “have another tool, and that’s oversight,” Owens said.
—Emma Janssen Outside Washington Could Dems’ state-level victories turn out to have a greater long-term impact than retaking Congress?
With four days until the election, Democrats terrified of another disappointment are focused on one big question: Are the polls right?
text:
You’re reading The TNR Blue Book. Get daily scoops, strategy, and developments inside the liberal ideas factory delivered right to your inbox. Sign up for free.

Inside Washington

“We campaigned as affordability Democrats. That was the message of every single candidate across this country,” Representative Katherine Clark, who is poised to be the House majority leader come January, told CNN on Thursday. “And that is exactly how we’re going to govern.” Delivering on this message, however, is easier said than done.

Representative Hakeem Jeffries, who is almost certain to be the next House speaker, likewise said that the party will be united “right out of the gate” to address the cost of living crisis—a topic that Democrats credit for their massive Election Day wins. In a “Dear Colleague” letter on Thursday, he proposed reversing cuts to the Affordable Care Act subsidies that have forced millions of Americans to pay more for health care, undoing cuts to Medicaid and SNAP, reversing tariffs, and stopping the war in Iran—all in the first 100 days of the next Congress.

Some advocates are pushing Democrats to start even sooner. “Government funding runs out on December 11, and I think they should use that must-pass vehicle to demand an end to the war in Iran, bringing down gas prices. And they should ensure that the Medicaid cuts don’t go into effect in January, which would raise health care costs for families,” said Lindsay Owens, executive director of Groundwork Collaborative.

Republicans, of course, might not go along with that while they still hold power in the lame-duck session. There’s also the issue of President Donald Trump’s veto power, which could thwart Democrats’ affordability legislation during the next Congress. Trump has given conflicting messages, telling some journalists that he plans to work with Congress and others that he will become “Mr. Veto.”

Some Democrats want to tailor their agenda to that reality. “How about we spend the majority of our time on stuff that we all agree on,” Representative Adam Gray of California told Semafor. Senator Brian Schatz of Hawaii is similarly cautious: “I do not think it is time to propose things that the president of the United States is guaranteed to veto,” said Schatz, who is in line for a Senate leadership role. “I think that’s a bit of wasted energy.” Progressives like Representatives Greg Casar of Texas and Ro Khanna of California, on the other hand, adamantly disagreed with that sentiment. “Make him veto Medicare for All. Make him veto a $25 living wage. Make him veto free childcare. Make him veto Block the Bombs to Israel,” Khanna wrote on X.

Economists like Josh Bivens, chief economist at the Economic Policy Institute, also want to see Democrats go beyond just addressing the high cost of groceries and gas, which was a major part of the campaign. “In terms of the policy levers that will actually work to make affordability better,” he said, “we have at least as many, probably more, that work on the income and wage side than the price side.”

Raising the minimum wage and passing labor legislation that empowers workers would increase incomes. It would be a way to give Americans more purchasing power without trying to lower the cost of goods directly, which can be more difficult. Jared Bernstein, chair of the United States Council of Economic Advisers under former President Joe Biden, makes a similar argument, and is concerned that Democrats could overpromise and underdeliver on lowering prices. “Nobody should be saying that they can lower the price of everything within the walls of Target and Walmart,” he said. “Trump, of course, made precisely such claims, and to say they redounded against him is a massive understatement.”

One thing that most Democrats and experts can agree on: ending the Iran war as quickly as possible. Even if ending the war doesn’t immediately bring down the price of gas, it would begin the process. The war is deeply unpopular; in a remarkable social media post on Wednesday, Vice President JD Vance admitted that it’s part of why Republicans lost Congress.

Even if Trump’s vetoes make affordability legislation tricky, Democrats “have another tool, and that’s oversight,” Owens said. “Americans are aware that one of the reasons that prices are so high is corporations are charging them more than they need to, taking advantage of the war in Iran, taking advantage of the tariffs to raise prices,”she said. Addressing and exposing corporate corruption, she argued, is also good affordability politics. Ultimately, Democrats will need to think about the full array of tools at their disposal—lowering prices, raising incomes, pressuring Trump to sign their bills, and holding hearings. Perhaps the most important thing they can do is show voters that they are doing whatever they can to make life more affordable.

—Emma Janssen

Outside Washington

Could Dems’ state-level victories turn out to have a greater long-term impact than retaking Congress? While the tally is not yet final, Dems so far appear to have ended Republican “trifectas” in Georgia, Iowa, Ohio, and Texas; built Democratic trifectas in Michigan, Minnesota, Nevada, Pennsylvania, Wisconsin, and possibly Arizona; flipped the North Carolina House, quite possibly the Texas House, and both chambers in New Hampshire; and won the governor’s races in Georgia, Iowa, Nevada, Ohio, and Texas. “Democrats will have the power to rewrite policies on redistricting, abortion, climate, health care, education and taxes,” The Washington Post summarizes in its rundown of state results. That includes taking “meaningful steps on lowering utility costs, expanding access to child care and health care, reproductive rights, safeguarding elections and other issues.” And then there’s the big question that Axios raised this week: Could Dems’ state victories pave the way for getting rid of the Electoral College?

Let’s zoom in on one item in the Post’s list: What do these sweeping Democratic victories mean for climate policy? The party conspicuously sidelined the issue on the campaign trail. But as Steven Rodas and Liza Gross at Inside Climate News pointed out this week, voters consistently backed environmental protection on state and local ballot measures on Tuesday. Perhaps the most striking example: More than 80 percent of Michigan voters chose to ban campaign contributions from utility companies. (The first lawsuit challenging this ballot initiative has already been filed.)

The new Democratic trifecta states in particular now have a lot of options on the climate front. And there are signs of movement at the national level, as well: Chellie Pingree, fresh off a commanding victory delivering her a 10th term in Maine’s 1st congressional district, is ready to rumble, telling Grist’s Jake Bittle this week that she has, in Bittle’s words, “prepared a long list of investigations and subpoenas for Trump administration officials, including EPA chief Lee Zeldin.” Pingree, the top Democrat on the House Appropriations subcommittee that oversees the Environmental Protection Agency and Interior Department, also wants to insert stipulations in funding bills “that would deny agencies core operational funds or restrict travel money for leading officials unless they doled out solar and energy funding as Congress previously instructed them to.” For an administration famously attached to its travel money, that probably counts as shots fired.

—Heather Souvaine Horn

The Ideas Factory

On Monday at 2 p.m., the Brookings Institution will host an online event about “the consequences of the 2026 midterm elections,” featuring David C. Barker, Karen Tumulty, Jonathan Rauch, and Sarah A. Binder.

Also on Monday, at 1 p.m., New America will host a virtual discussion with Better Life Lab’s Brigid Schulte and Haley Swenson about their new research on men and caregiving, as well as insights regarding the barriers that keep some men from being more involved in caregiving, even when they want to be. Mohan Sivalogonath of Dads for All, stay-at-home dad Shannon Carpenter, and elder caregiver Carlos Olivas will join for a panel discussion.

—Heather Souvaine Horn

In Closing

Good Week:

I mean, there’s an obvious answer here: Literally almost every Democrat. But if we think outside the box, then we might have to hand this award to Mike Johnson, who announced after the midterms that he would not be running for minority leader, one of the worst jobs in Washington, perhaps second only to being the majority leader in a GOP-led House. Johnson led a caucus of MAGA-werewolves who routinely brined themselves in right-wing meme slop about as well as anyone could. He will now get to spend more time with his son and their favorite hobby: monitoring each other’s pornography intake.

Bad Week:

Again, obvious answer: nearly every Republican in Christendom! But some Democrats fared poorly, as well. Haley Stevens’s decision to go against the party and endorse Mike Rogers was a shot so poorly taken that even Lin-Manuel Miranda would have been like, “Hales, I’d have holstered that one.” And we must spare a thought for John Fetterman, a senator who exists only to thwart his own caucus, which will now swell to numbers so large as to make him entirely irrelevant. Go ahead and switch parties, pal! (Caveat: A new annoying Democratic senator with swing vote power could emerge at any time.)

—Jason Linkins

Political Trivia Question of the Day

The first Latino governor in the United States was Romualdo Pacheco of California. In what decade did he ascend to that office? (Sign up for The TNR Blue Book to find the answer in tomorrow’s newsletter.)

—Michael Tomasky

You’re reading The TNR Blue Book. Get daily scoops, strategy, and developments inside the liberal ideas factory delivered right to your inbox. Sign up for free.

Inside Washington

“As other states shift left in a brutal cycle, Florida does what we do best—we held the line,” former Florida GOP Chair Christian Ziegler wrote on X on Wednesday morning. “THANK GOD I LIVE IN FLORIDA!” Democrats, on the other hand, are disappointed that the night’s successes didn’t extend to the Sunshine State. On a giddy, “blue wave” evening when even states as improbable as Kansas and Texas elected Democratic senators, both Angie Nixon, Democrats’ Senate nominee in Florida, and David Jolly, the gubernatorial candidate, lost to their Republican opponents. This disappointment, some say, was preventable. And perhaps more importantly, it holds some lessons for 2028.

“We think that Angie could have won with any kind of substantial investment made over the last month,” said Ravi Mangla, press secretary for the Working Families Party, which was the first national organization to endorse Nixon. Ultimately, Nixon came closer than polls predicted, losing to GOP Senator Ashley Moody by less than three percentage points. Jolly’s margin against Republican Byron Donalds was even tighter—he lost by less than two percentage points.

Though Nixon received support from groups like the WFP, which spent more than $200,000 on her race, as well as from national political figures like Senators Bernie Sanders and Chris Murphy, she received very little from the national Democratic establishment. The Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee included the Florida Senate race in its $40 million Win the Senate program but prioritized states like Maine and Texas instead.

Texas and Florida are, to some extent, mirror images of each other. Both are southern states that Democrats have counted out in recent years. Both have large Latino populations. But while Florida stayed red on Tuesday night, Texas’s Senate race, gubernatorial race, and all of its statewide offices flipped blue. “I don’t think there’s any question that Texas received the investment it needed, but we didn’t see that same commensurate investment in Florida,” Mangla said. “And I would hope that had the DSCC chosen to invest and put its resources behind Angie, that we would be celebrating a really historic win today.”

On Wednesday, Nixon expressed sadness about her loss but optimism for the future. “We invested in grassroots organizers and partnered with candidates down ballot. I’m so proud of the work we did helping to flip 17 House Seats,” she wrote on X. “Imagine what would have happened if we had more investment early on.” She also hinted at the possibility of running again in two years, saying “2028 is around the corner” in her concession speech.

While the lack of national spending might be part of why Nixon and Jolly lost on Tuesday, acknowledged Aubrey Jewett, a professor of political science at the University of Central Florida, other factors were at play, as well. For example: Republicans have more than 1.5 million voter registrations than Democrats do, which happened “very rapidly” in recent years. “We had a blue wave,” Jewett explained, but it still wasn’t enough. Republicans didn’t have great turnout, but they “had good solid turnout,” and “that’s all they needed.”

While Latino voters swung toward Democrats in both Florida and Texas, Cuban Americans in Florida ultimately voted for Moody. In contrast, Mexican American voters, who make up 40 percent of the population in Texas, were more likely to swing for Democrats this year in the aftermath of ICE raids targeting their communities.

Looking ahead, some experts share Nixon’s optimism for 2028. Republicans’ “price per vote was a lot higher than Jolly’s price per vote, or Nixon’s,” said Jared Nordlund, the Florida State director at UnidosUS, a Latino civil rights nonprofit, comparing the total spending numbers in the race and laying them against how well each candidate performed. “I think seeing that out there tells you that the Republican vote isn’t guaranteed.”

James Talarico’s success in Texas and the close margins in Florida could spark more investment in 2028. And for some, that’s the big takeaway from this election, regardless of how it played out in individual races: Democrats need to rethink their assumptions about the electoral map. Would more funding have turned the tide? “If you don’t think you can win and you don’t invest, then you almost always don’t win,” Jewett said. “Whereas if you invest, sometimes you might.”

—Emma Janssen

Outside Washington

A year that began with clergy members being arrested en masse in subzero ICE protests is closing with five Democratic ministers headed to a newly blue Congress. In deep-red Kansas, Methodist megachurch leader Adam Hamilton stunned the country by thumping Republican Roger Marshall in their Senate race. In Iowa, Lutheran minister Sarah Trone Garriott and Presbyterian minister Lindsay James flipped the 3rd and 2nd congressional districts, respectively, shrugging off months of right-wing attacks suggesting they weren’t real Christians. In Texas, Friendship-West Baptist Church pastor Frederick Haynes won the 30th congressional district seat. It wasn’t all sunshine and roses for the clergy; Anna Golladay lost in Tennessee, and Robb Ryerse lost in Arkansas. But it’s hard to dispute the prominence of progressive visions of Christianity in some of the biggest flips of this election. Former Presbyterian seminarian and Senator-elect James Talarico quoted both scripture and his grandfather, a Baptist preacher, in his victory speech after becoming the first Democrat to win a statewide Texas election in 32 years. Rob Sand, who won Iowa’s gubernatorial election, also talked extensively about his Lutheran faith on the campaign trail.

What do the results of races across the country mean for Washington, D.C.—the city that President Donald Trump has repeatedly threatened to take over and is doggedly trying to turn into one giant construction site? The Washington Post has outlined a few ways that newly elected Democrats could mess with the construction plans, at least. In addition to two Democrats now joining the review panel that has so far approved Trump’s projects, a newly Democratic Congress could “file suit to block Trump’s most controversial projects” and “also rein in Trump’s spending” on said projects. Meanwhile, D.C.’s socialist mayor-elect, Janeese Lewis-George, has said she’s “willing to work with this administration to the benefit of D.C. residents” but is also “willing to stand up to this administration.”
