Inside Washington

Democrats have won a massive majority in the House, and amid the celebrations, different factions of the party will be clamoring to claim credit for the blue tsunami. Was it the progressives, the centrists, or even the Bernie dogs who carried the party to victory? And which faction will be calling the shots come January?

The answer, to some extent, depends on who you ask. “A Democratic majority is really going to be built on the back of moderate candidates in the House,” said David de la Fuente, deputy director for politics and research at the centrist group Third Way. He pointed to moderate candidates who eventually won on Tuesday night, like Jared Moskowitz in Florida’s 25th congressional district or Bobby Pulido in Texas’s 15th congressional district.

Meanwhile, Usamah Andrabi, the communications director of progressive group Justice Democrats, argued that progressives brought the energy and policy platforms that turned the tide. “The mandate from voters across this country is for this majority to look like what many Democrats finally learned to campaign on, which is taking on corporate interests to deliver on an affordability agenda that actually helps working class communities,” he said. “They finally listened to the left.”

Andrabi pointed to Justice Democrats’ massive wins this cycle; it was their most successful year by far. The group is poised to send at least seven leaders to Congress, including Donavan McKinney in Michigan, Darializa Avila Chevalier and Claire Valdez in New York, and Melat Kiros in Colorado. These electeds will be joining fellow progressive firebrands like Representatives Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, Rashida Tlaib, and Greg Casar in Congress. As it stands, the Congressional Progressive Caucus currently has 101 members, while the New Democrat Coalition, which includes more centrist lawmakers, touts 114 members. While it’s too soon to say definitively how those numbers will change, the Congressional Progressive Caucus PAC suggested that the caucus might be adding “over 20” new members, according to an email the group sent previewing a later press call.

“Typically, the Congressional Progressive Caucus is bigger than the New Dems when Republicans control the House, and the New Dems are bigger than the progressives when the Democrats control the House, and that’s because, essentially, the New Dems tend to be the majority makers,” de la Cruz said. The term “majority maker” comes from former House Speaker Nancy Pelosi, who famously called the moderate-to-conservative Blue Dogs the “majority makers” for their success in unseating Republicans and contributing to the Democratic majority.

But some progressive candidates overturned that orthodoxy on Tuesday. In Michigan’s 7th congressional district, Sunrise Movement co-founder William Lawrence prevailed despite running in one of the most competitive districts in the county, and facing the most Republican spending of any House candidate this cycle—more than $23 million. Similarly, in California’s 22nd congressional district, Randy Villegas declared an early victory over Republican Representative David Valadao, a testament to the size of his win (usually, California results trickle in slowly).

Trying to tally up the number of seats that will soon be held by progressives versus moderates creates another problem: “It suggests that there’s just a kind of monolithic progressive ideology and a monolithic centrist ideology, and in my experience, it’s not quite that simple,” Democratic strategist Oliver Libby said.

This year, that question became even more complicated with the emergence of a number of so-called Bernie dogs—candidates endorsed by both the Blue Dogs and Senator Bernie Sanders. Those candidates include Sam Forstag in Montana’s 1st congressional district, Rebecca Cooke in Wisconsin’s 3rd congressional district, Brian Poindexter in Ohio’s 7th district, and Bob Brooks in Pennsylvania’s seventh district. All four won.

A more useful way of analyzing the Democratic majority—and predicting what they might do come January—could be to look directly at what policies they ran on, regardless of how they identify ideologically. That could help reconcile the simultaneous successes of moderates, progressives, and Bernie dogs, the Progressive Change Campaign Committee suggested in an Election Day memo. These winning policy platforms—including anti-establishment fights against data centers and surveillance tech, oversight of AI companies, and affordable health care—could ultimately provide a roadmap for Dems in 2028 and beyond.

—Emma Janssen

Outside Washington

The humble “I Voted” sticker could turn out to be one of the enduring images of this election. On October 19—the first day of early voting in Texas—Ronaldo Salgado cast a ballot and placed his voting sticker on Houston’s makeshift memorial to his father, who was shot and killed by an ICE officer this summer. Amid a historic rise in early voting, hundreds of other voters proceeded to follow Salgado’s lead, leaving “I Voted” stickers or other messages at the memorial to Lorenzo Salgado Araujo. On Tuesday afternoon, MPR News and other outlets reported that the practice had spread to Minneapolis, with local affiliate Fox 9 reporting “dozens” of “I Voted” stickers at the memorials for Alex Pretti and Renee Good, both of whom were shot and killed by an ICE agents in January.

Elsewhere:

James Talarico, Gina Hinojosa, and Nathan Johnson won the Senate, gubernatorial, and attorney general races in Texas last night—breaking a 32-year Dem losing streak in statewide races. But if we’re talking long losing streaks: No Democrat has held a seat on the Texas Railroad Commission—an underappreciated body with huge and little understood power to regulate the fossil fuel industry—since 1990. On Tuesday, though, Democrat Jon Rosenthal claimed victory over Republican Bo French, a candidate so prone to nakedly racist rhetoric that even Karl Rove denounced him in The Wall Street Journal in September and vowed to vote for Rosenthal.

As of publication time for this newsletter, the race in New Jersey’s 2nd congressional district has not been called. Multiple outlets have reported, however, that four-term Republican Representative Jeff Van Drew has conceded to Democrat Zack Mullock. This is another race that longtime watchers of Democratic politics are going to be talking about today—particularly if a formal winner emerges. You can read more about this race—Van Drew, who used to be a Democrat, “has certainly earned the everlasting animosity of Democrats in the district,” Micah Rasmussen said—in Emma Janssen’s prior TNR Blue Book reporting here. Just a few weeks ago when this was written, analysts that she talked to still thought a Mullock victory was a long shot. Early Wednesday morning, Mullock led by nearly 8,000 votes, with 92 percent in.

—Heather Souvaine Horn

Inside Washington

As votes roll in throughout Election Day, most eyes will be on the balance of the House and Senate. But in some states, voters will be directly deciding on some of the biggest political questions of the decade—including how to run a modern democracy. Ballot initiatives in some states could reduce voters’ rights and power. In others, voters have the chance to enshrine those rights and reject partisan gerrymandering.

“Amid rising authoritarianism, the fight for democracy is also happening through ballot initiatives,” said Chris Melody Fields Figueredo, the executive director of the Ballot Initiative Strategy Center. “This year, we’re seeing more attacks from politicians on voters’ rights,” agreed Hannah Ledford, the executive director at the Fairness Project. “And voters are having to defend those rights at the ballot box more than ever really, in an election.”

Six states are considering voter ID rules, some of which mirror President Donald Trump’s SAVE America Act. Ohio and North Carolina already require identification at the polls, but ballot measures would put that in the states’ constitutions. Nevada, too, is trying to amend its constitution to require photo ID to vote. Arizona has a measure requiring those voting by mail-in ballot to somehow show ID. Even in blue California and Colorado, voters will consider similar measures. Experts say that voter ID laws end up suppressing the votes of Black voters, students, and Native voters, while failing to actually address election fraud (which is exceedingly rare).

In North Dakota, South Dakota, and Utah, voters will decide on measures that would make it harder to pass constitutional amendments in the future. Experts say that could remove a key source of power for voters by making it harder for them to practice direct democracy. In recent years, voters have used ballot initiatives to enact progressive policies like raising the minimum wage or protecting abortion rights—to the chagrin of conservative legislators. “Politicians that are really upset with the progress that voters have made in their backyard, trying to take direct democracy back, they are trying to make it harder to use and harder to pass things at the ballot box,” Ledford said.

Some ballot initiatives, though, give voters the opportunity to enshrine their rights. Missouri’s Amendment 6 would require 80 percent support in both legislative chambers and another statewide vote to change laws approved by voters or enact laws that voters rejected by referendum. That’s crucially important in a state where voters have approved progressive multiple ballot initiatives that the Republican legislature has then altered or outright reversed. “Voters in Missouri just two years ago passed the right to reproductive freedom at the ballot box. The legislature is trying to take it away and install a near-total abortion ban in the state, and voters are going to decide tomorrow whether or not politicians overreached,” Ledford said. Similar things have happened with paid sick leave and raising the minimum wage.

Missouri will also be voting on gerrymandering—specifically, via Proposition A, the redrawn 2025 map that the Supreme Court blocked for this election. “Voters in Missouri, it feels like we are in a battle with our elected officials to have our voices heard, and it’s really frustrating,” said Richard von Glahn, the executive director of People Not Politicians, about the gerrymandered maps. He’s hopeful that voters will reject the Republican maps and, through Amendment 6, will block Republican legislators from reconsidering the maps next year. “Missourians were so angry about seeing our elections really just rigged like this,” he said, “that we actually gathered about three times as many signatures as was needed” to get Prop A on the ballot. “Voters are really indicating that they should be the central focus of our democracy and the ultimate power brokers.”

These battles, which could shape the state of U.S. politics for years to come, will be playing out not just through voting rights and gerrymandering measures, but also through ballot initiatives that address abortion and trans rights. Fields suggests watching these initiatives to get a preview of future strategies to restrict bodily autonomy for women and LGBTQ individuals. “I do think ’26 is a testing ground,” she said, “for what conservatives may go full throttle [on] in 2028.”

—Emma Janssen

Outside Washington

Democrat Josh Turek’s race against Republican Ashley Hinson in Iowa could decide the balance of the Senate. On Monday, the Des Moines Register’s Stephen Gruber-Miller reported on the Republican National Committee’s self-described all-out attempt to sway the outcome. Among the efforts: The RNC and the Hinson campaign have executed the first “coordinated ad buy”—which a Supreme Court ruling made possible this summer—worth $5 million. It’s not the only last-ditch Republican attempt to win the state, but this one sounds a little more organized than President Donald Trump’s off-script remarks at a rally in Dubuque over the weekend, wherein he inexplicably went on a tangent about Hinson’s weight loss. The last New York Times/Siena poll had Turek up by one point, which was well within the margin of error.

Elsewhere:

On Monday, supermarket chains in multiple European countries reported that their cold storage systems had been targeted in a cyberattack overnight, with temps rising as high as 122 degrees, rendering the food unusable. A similar attack occurred in France last month, and the latest cold storage failure in Europe arrived days after Reuters reported, based on anonymous sources, that the Pentagon is treating cold storage failures that happened on military bases in August as a cyberattack, as well. It’s hard to overstate how crucial networks of cold storage facilities (known as the “cold chain”) are to both food and medicine supply chains in the present world—both domestically and for international trade.

Media outlets and experts alike were already facing a difficult balancing act on the topic of threat preparedness. But then last week, news on three separate but related fronts raised further alarms: Pete Hegseth’s “FORTRESS America” initiative instructing U.S. military bases to prepare for 90 days without grid power, former Trump FBI Deputy Director Dan Bongino’s call for nationwide household prepping, and the British government’s new “Be Ready” campaign urging people to stock up on canned goods and emergency radios. Combined, those caused a fair amount of anxiety in certain circles. “The line between giving people solid, grounded, actionable information and stirring panic is incredibly fine,” Texas A&M professor Angela Clendenin told Fox Baltimore when asked about Bongino’s remarks in particular. But, properly executed, “preparedness avoids panic,” she added. Several experts, both in the Fox Baltimore piece and in a Guardian piece published on Monday, noted that the U.S. has long recommended that people keep several days’ worth of supplies on hand—and that Trump-era cuts to federal emergency management, along with everything else, have made this an even better idea.

—Heather Souvaine Horn

The Ideas Factory

In a new report titled “Tracking the Return on Investment of Trump’s Backers,” the Center for American Progress’s Devon Ombers, Ryan Koronowski, and Will Ragland estimate that more than 75 “individuals and entities” have donated almost $1.7 billion to Trump’s pet projects, and in return, they “have reaped or will reap benefits conservatively estimated at approximately $183 billion.”

A new report from Arnav Rao at Open Markets Institute warns that robotaxis could “extend Big Tech’s monopoly power from the digital world into the physical world, putting the future of American transportation under the control of just a few, already-dominant corporations.” Instead of fixating on whether driverless cars are safe, Rao argues, policymakers should be looking at, for example, breaking up vertically integrated monopolies and ensuring that regulators have the tools that they need for this new landscape.

—Heather Souvaine Horn

In Closing

Four Questions For: Tim Grieve, editor in chief of The Washington Sun

Q: Who are you, and what are you working on right now?

A: I’m the editor in chief of The Washington Sun, the news publication formerly known as NOTUS. And here’s a sentence you won’t hear a lot in journalism: I spend most of my time hiring. We dove in when The Washington Post pulled back—expanding our coverage of political Washington and adding coverage of local news and sports. We’re the fastest-growing newsroom in D.C., and maybe the world: We started 2026 with 45 journalists. We’re at 110 today, and we’re just getting started.

Q: The Washington Sun is launching at a time of layoffs, consolidation, and growing billionaire control of the media. What does a news organization have to do differently to build something durable in this environment?

A: Hire the best people, be disciplined about what you do, and find a revenue model to support it. No problem, right?

Q: Washington reporting can be a breed of its own, with its fixation on access, insiders, and the daily churn of politics. What does the D.C. press corps understand well, and where does it still have blind spots?

A: Not surprisingly, the D.C. press corp understands … D.C. We’ll find out this week how well we understand the rest of the country.

Q: What do people outside Washington misunderstand about the way journalism works here?

A: Way too many people think that journalists just make stuff up. There have definitely been a few famous fabulists in journalism history. But I’ve worked in this business off and on for more than 40 years, and I can’t think of a single time one of my colleagues made up a story or fabricated a quote, a source, or a fact. Do we get things wrong sometimes? Sure. But journalists at reputable news organizations try very, very hard to get it right.

Interview by Indigo Olivier

Inside Washington

What if the polls are wrong?

With four days until the election, Democrats terrified of another disappointment are focused on one big question: Are the polls right?

Most polls show Democrats winning the House and, potentially, the Senate—a possibility that seemed improbable even a few months ago. A new CNN poll on Thursday, for example, showed Abdul El-Sayed and James Talarico in strong positions. But the most critical toss-up Senate races are so tight that even a polling error of a few percentage points could shift the outcome from Democratic control to two more years of Republican leadership. FiftyPlusOne modeled how the election would look if polling misses matched those in the 2018 and 2022 midterms, or instead matched 2016, 2020, and 2024—presidential election years when Trump was on the ballot. “The polling errors have been much larger in presidential years than non-presidential years,” explained Guy Molyneux, a Democratic pollster and partner at Hart Research.

If polling averages are off by roughly the same margins that they were in the Trump election years, seats like Michigan and Ohio—critical pickups for Democrats this year—could fall to Republicans. Senator Susan Collins could win Maine by nearly four points, and Senator Dan Sullivan could take Alaska by five. In that case, Republicans could keep the Senate. But if this midterm looks more like other midterms in terms of poll error, Democrats might even be able to pick up seats in red states like Iowa and Kansas.

Molyneux says he’s inclined to believe that this year’s polls will be closer in accuracy to the 2018 and 2022 polls, which would be good news for Democrats’ prospects. Most election-watchers predict that Democrats will take the House, but nobody is sure whether it will be a blue wave or a blue tsunami. If polling is roughly correct, Democrats could take 238 seats (218 seats is a majority), NBC News estimates. But Dems could potentially pick up some 260 seats or win as few as 220. That’s a majority, but a narrow one.

Polls aren’t the only data points people can use to understand the election, stressed Simon Rosenberg, a Democratic strategist. He sees hints of a Democratic advantage everywhere: “We’ve seen it in the candidate fundraising data, where our candidates have raised way more money than their candidates have, which is a far better indication of intensity than the checkbooks of ten oligarchs,” he said—referring to Democrats’ advantage with grassroots donors and Republicans’ advantage with super PAC money funneled from ultrawealthy donors like Elon Musk. Rosenberg also pointed to the fact that Republicans are campaigning in states like Mississippi, South Carolina, Kansas, and Nebraska—areas that ordinarily shouldn’t pose a problem for Republicans. “There’s a lot of inputs here. It’s not just, you know, a handful of New York Times polls in the last few weeks,” he said.

Early voting data also suggests that Democrats are in a strong position. As of Thursday, 43 million Americans have already voted, according to the University of Florida’s Election Lab. Hispanic voters have turned out in higher numbers than they did at the same times in 2022 and 2024, which could be a promising trend for Democrats and help candidates like James Talarico in Texas. (Though Hispanic and Latino voters helped Trump win in 2024, some polls have found that only 24 percent of Latino registered voters approve of Trump’s handling of his job, down from 38 percent at the start of his second term.)

In the final stretch before Election Day, experts stress that voters should view polls as part of a larger picture, rather than overinterpreting any one number (remember J Ann Selzer’s Iowa poll in 2024, which predicted that Vice President Kamala Harris could win Iowa but was 16 points off?). “Both for accuracy and emotional health, I would urge people to focus mainly on the averages, and not the either scary or hopeful news of the day,” said Molyneux.

Though Rosenberg doesn’t like polling averages, he also recommends looking at multiple polls instead of just one, and trying to find a way to live in the uncertainty. “There’s far less certainty in the data that [voters are] being presented than you assume based on how certain it looks when on television you see a graph that has two numbers,” he said. “It’s only a snapshot in time.”

—Emma Janssen

Outside Washington

Last-minute polls are rolling in, along with last-minute attack ads. CNN’s latest poll, published on Thursday, has James Talarico leading Ken Paxton in Texas (49–43), Abdul El-Sayed leading Mike Rogers in Michigan (49–42), and neck-and-neck races in Maine and Kansas. While Troy Jackson and Adam Hamilton appear to be leading their Republican opponents 49–45 on paper, there’s a margin of error of 4.5 percentage points.

Attack ads in Maine—as in other states—are getting increasingly ugly in the final stretch. Republican Senator Susan Collins last week disavowed a new Republican super PAC ad featuring a song about Jackson that goes: “If he’ll screw his own family, he’ll screw yours too.” But as Jackson’s campaign has pointed out, Politico’s Jonathan Martin asked Collins in a video interview last month whether Jackson’s personal life was “fair game,” and she replied, “Well, I’m not going to bring up the fact that the mother of his two children is his second cousin. I don’t know whether people know that or not.”

Meanwhile, in Texas, a super PAC largely funded by Elon Musk recently ran an ad with evangelical influencer Miriam Evans, saying, “Every mom in Texas should be concerned about James Talarico.” The ad (falsely) claims Talarico supports gender-affirming surgeries for minors and jail time for parents who object. In another one of the group’s ads, Tarrant County Sheriff Bill Waybourn opens: “Folks, I’m going to ask you: Where has James Talarico been?” After a pause in which viewers may wonder whether Waybourn’s about to bust the candidate’s alibi in a multiple homicide investigation on Law and Order, Waybourn proceeds to say that Talarico has “been in Austin standing with and donating to a radical group that wants to defund the police”—an apparent reference to Talarico appearing on a video call organized by Texas progressive youth group Texas Rising six years ago. In his own last election in 2024, Waybourn drew scrutiny for the number of people who had died in county custody since he took office in 2017—65 deaths, as compared to 25 in the prior eight-year period—along with a lack of independent investigations as required by law. As of October 18, the number of deaths in Tarrant County Jail during Waybourn’s tenure has increased to 79.

Elsewhere:

Is it time for Democrats to forgive Ralph Nader for the 2000 election and recognize that he was right about a lot of stuff? The Guardian’s Heather Timmons examines the case, speaking not just with Nader but a variety of think tankers and others on the left, including Robert Weissman of Public Citizen (which Nader co-founded), Lindsay Owens of Groundwork Collaborative, Barry Lynn of Open Markets Institute, and—surprise?—Matt Bennett of the moderate Dem group Third Way. Nader, Timmons reports, has recently “been dialing progressive candidates including Michigan’s Abdul El-Sayed and Maine’s Troy Jackson directly, to present his policy plan he thinks would guarantee their midterm success.”

—Heather Souvaine Horn

The Ideas Factory

Alasdair Phillips-Robins, Teddy Tawil, and Sam Winter-Levy penned an interesting report for the Carnegie Endowment of International Peace this week about “how middle powers can survive the AI race.” The fundamental problem, they write, is that the U.S. and China control most of the resources. Other countries, “fearful of missing out on the benefits of advanced AI while still bearing the brunt of its harms, are scrambling to respond.” The right strategy for those governments will depend on both the speed of innovation and “the gap between the best systems and open-source or other cheap alternatives.” But “finding sources of leverage at supply chain chokepoints is valuable in almost every technological future.” Sounds … fun. (Warning: This report is unlikely to make you feel better about the AI-riddled future. But there are fancy graphics, if that’s your jam.)

The Natural Resources Defense Council has issued a statement on the Trump administration’s proposed rollback of methane leak rules. “Methane leaks are the dumbest kind of pollution because the industry is losing the very product it is selling,” David Doniger, a senior attorney and strategist at the NRDC, said in the organization’s press release. “These leaks are not just bad for the climate, they result in more smog and cancer-causing pollution for nearby communities.”

—Heather Souvaine Horn

In Closing

Good Week: Barack Obama

The former president has been making campaign stops as he does for Democrats every election—and is in fine form. His zingers and humor have gotten under Trump’s skin, galvanized Democrats, and made news in the usually slow days right before the end of the campaign.

Bad Week: Darline Graham

Graham, who was appointed to be South Carolina’s senator earlier this year after her brother Lindsey—who previously held the seat—passed, has become the poster child for bad candidates. Other Republicans are blasting her as unqualified and such a terrible campaigner that she’s making it possible for Democrats to potentially win in a state where they almost never do.

—Perry Bacon

text:
Contact: Seth Nelson

Following the release of updated text of the the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act (BAAJA), crucial legislation that addresses longstanding barriers to building out clean energy infrastructure across America, and ahead of a pivotal Senate vote to move this legislation forward, Evergreen Action Executive Director Lena Moffitt released the following statement:

“Voters spoke loud and clear on Tuesday: They want bold action to cut energy costs. And on their first day back to legislating, the Senate can immediately deliver on that mandate. Climate change has been wreaking havoc on our lives, our economy, and our communities, for too long. We know the clean energy transition is required to address both costs and pollution, but we are woefully behind on building out the infrastructure needed to make that transition possible—while fossil fuel projects are getting greenlit left and right. We need federal siting and permitting reform now. We need the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act.

“Congress must take action to build out clean, cheap energy at scale to meet the urgency that the energy affordability and climate crisis demand. This legislation will speed the construction of high-voltage interregional transmission lines, improve the ability of clean energy to plug into our grid, increase oversight on monopoly utilities, advance transformational tools like virtual power plants and grid-enhancing technologies, and require data centers to pay for using and upgrading our grid. All of these changes are necessary to cutting costs and pollution and delivering on the promise Democrats just ran and won on.

“Legislation is always a compromise, and Republicans were able to extract significant concessions in this bill. This bill weakens tools that advocates have used for decades to protect communities from the harms of the fossil fuel industry. The hard truth is that despite decades of advocacy, polluting fossil fuel projects and pipelines are still being built en masse, while transmission lines are not. If the status quo remains, and clean energy projects are not built faster, the toll of the climate crisis will only get exponentially higher. We are committed to working with new Democratic majorities to build on this legislation while America builds the infrastructure we need for the clean energy transition. We cannot afford to wait what could be years for another hypothetical deal to come together.

“Thank you to Senators Martin Heinrich and Sheldon Whitehouse for your leadership in fighting for our clean energy future. We are pleased to see improvements made to the text in this manager’s amendment. The Senate should pass this bill when it comes to a vote, and the House should take it up and pass it immediately after. This moment demands urgent action and we cannot afford any more delays to accelerate the clean energy transition and deliver change now.”

text:
Evergreen Action, the organization I lead, is supporting the Senate’s permitting bill (BAAJA). Here’s why.

Evergreen is dedicated to tackling the climate crisis and building an affordable, inclusive clean energy economy. Our primary focus has been speeding up the deployment of clean energy, because, simply put, switching our homes, buildings and vehicles to run on clean electricity rather than fossil fuels is how we avoid a worsening climate crisis. At the same time, it’s how we can avoid skyrocketing energy prices.

We’re going to have to build a lot of clean energy, fast. And we’ll need to connect it to a grid that can carry it to the major population centers where most people live.

But that’s not what’s happening right now. 2025 was a banner year for clean energy, with nearly 50 GW coming online, but that amount is much less than experts say we’ll need. And our country has built almost NONE of the long-distance transmission lines necessary to carry this power where it needs to go. At the same time, the grid we have is nearly impossible to plug into; according to Lawrence Berkley National Labs, in 2025, 85% of the projects in interconnection queues were clean energy, down from 95% in previous years due to the explosion of gas plant proposals as clean projects struggle to connect without adequate transmission buildout. Thanks to high wait times and interconnection fees, 75% of these projects were ultimately cancelled.

Furthermore, monopoly investor-owned utilities have shackled their customers to expensive and volatile gas and coal power plants, rather than using cheaper clean energy, and standing in the way of the interregional transmission that would threaten their profits.

To make things worse, data centers are demanding an unprecedented amount of power. Our patchy, aging and inefficient grid has been slow to provide it, so many of these data centers are now pursuing dirty “behind the meter gas.”. This reality facing communities around the country is not only horrible for the planet but incredibly harmful for adjacent communities and the air they need to breathe – a status quo that could get significantly worse if improvements to our grid aren’t made.

This bill would take steps to address all of these problems and build a cleaner, cheaper, more reliable power system. Specifically the bill would deliver:

More Interregional Transmission: The bill would make it much easier for interregional transmission lines to be planned, permitted and financed. Right now, a transmission line that crosses multiple states needs to secure a permit from each of those states – allowing each their own veto over a project, regardless of its benefits. The bill would provide the federal government with the authority to approve lines found to be in the public interest. The bill would also require regional transmission organizations (RTOs, such as PJM in the east, MISO in the Midwest and great planes, SPP in the west) to conduct consistent, interregional planning for transmission. And it would allow independent developers to propose their own transmission projects – introducing competition to compel faster and cheaper construction of interregional lines. The bill would also make it clearer and easier to determine who pays for interregional transmission by establishing a standard cost allocation framework that would help us avoid the deadlock we now face where no one wants to pay for a line they perceive as being more beneficial to others. Taken together, these reforms would finally allow our nation to build the transmission infrastructure necessary to power a clean, reliable and affordable 21st century electric grid.

A more efficient grid: The legislation would also make our current grid more efficient by requiring lower-cost advanced transmission technologies to be analyzed and used; and would exempt reconductoring lines or installing these technologies from additional environmental reviews, making efficient upgrades to our current transmission system faster, easier and cheaper. The bill would let groups of home and business-owned batteries and distributed resources sell power or energy demand reduction into wholesale electricity markets; requiring grid operators to remove rules that currently block this within 18 months. And it would make it faster and easier for new energy generation to plug into the grid by requiring the automation of interconnection studies and the standardization of connection fees.

Utility Accountability: The bill would also enable greater federal oversight of exorbitant utility spending that is currently raising families’ electricity bills throughout the country. It would allow states to demand federal regulators investigate if utilities are proposing the construction of costly local transmission lines rather than regional or interregional lines that could deliver more low-cost clean energy. Regulators are also empowered to levy significant penalties if the utility is found to be acting counter to the public interest, including by lowering their return on equity, fines, and requiring the utility to issue refunds or rate credits to their customers.

Data Center Accountability: The bill would also hold data centers accountable, by directing federal regulators to develop rules requiring data centers to pay not only for any necessary upgrades to the grid needed for their facilities, but also for the use of existing grid assets. This would help protect ratepayers from footing the bill for data centers’ energy needs and help ensure data centers are paying to build the better grid we all need. Rates might even decrease as data centers pay in above what they’re using.

All of these changes are essential to enable the clean energy transition we know is needed to keep energy costs down over the long haul and stave off a spiraling climate crisis. But they are not sufficient – we will need to keep fighting to ensure that clean energy projects are permitted (many of which are currently held up or blocked by local siting and permitting) and that the law is followed by regulators, states and utilities. But it gives us that chance. It provides a critical step forward — and an opportunity for us to accelerate progress currently constrained by our aging and outdated grid.

At the same time, I am clear eyed about the necessity of keeping up the fight to rein in fossil fuels. I spent more than a decade of my life directly fighting fossil fuel projects – from the Keystone XL and Dakota Access pipelines, to oil and gas drilling in the Arctic, the Permian and Marcellus. The demands the Republicans made in exchange for the very good transmission and utility components of the bill were steep and weigh heavy on my heart. And this bill will not create a “fair market” or a “level playing field.” We will have to keep battling the deeply entrenched fossil fuel industry and the incumbency that these companies enjoy in our economy.I am committed to working with new Democratic majorities to come back and build on this bill and fix many of these giveaways while we work to unrig this system that has singularly favored billionaires while working people suffer. But, as a climate advocate, I fear that if we keep for a better deal the status quo will just deliver more pollution and a deepening climate crisis will mean more lives lost.

These changes have been too long delayed, already. Despite the monumental election, I do not believe that a better deal is around the corner. The time to act is now. We have to start building clean at scale. The planet and its most vulnerable populations can’t afford to wait.

I encourage Congress to pass and the president to sign the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act.

title: The Watch: Coal-Fired Power Plants Often Located in Disadvantaged Communities
description:
Coal-fired power plants often located in disadvantaged communities People living near U.S. coal-fired power plants are more likely to be in disadvantaged communities, potentially adding to the health risks they already face, a new study finds.
Residents of disadvantaged communities already experience higher rates of chronic illness and other health problems, raising concerns about additional health harms from power plants.
They found coal-fired power plants were rarely located near neighborhoods with low levels of disadvantage, which are typically wealthy and well-resourced.
The findings come amid changes to federal environmental protections that could increase exposure to pollution from coal-fired power plants.
Earlier this year, the Trump administration rejected findings that served as the scientific basis for federal limits on greenhouse gas emissions and weakened restrictions on pollutants released by coal-fired power plants.
text:
Coal-fired power plants often located in disadvantaged communities

People living near U.S. coal-fired power plants are more likely to be in disadvantaged communities, potentially adding to the health risks they already face, a new study finds.

Nearly a third of the nearly 2.8 million people who lived within three miles of coal-fired power plants in 2023 were in communities considered to be disadvantaged, according to the November 5 research in JAMA Network Open.

Previous research has found living near coal-fired power plants can increase exposure to harmful air pollutants, including mercury, nitrogen dioxide, sulfur dioxide and fine-particle matter, also known as PM2.5. Exposure to pollution from the plants has been linked to respiratory diseases, increased risk of death and pregnancy-related problems.

Residents of disadvantaged communities already experience higher rates of chronic illness and other health problems, raising concerns about additional health harms from power plants.

Researchers gauged neighborhood disadvantage based on the Area Deprivation Index, which looks at income, education, employment and housing quality. They found coal-fired power plants were rarely located near neighborhoods with low levels of disadvantage, which are typically wealthy and well-resourced.

About 12% of people living within three miles of a coal-fired power plant lived in the nation’s most severely disadvantaged neighborhoods, compared with less than 1% in the most well-off neighborhoods.

Compared with the overall U.S. population, people living within three miles of the plants were more likely to be American Indian and Alaska Native or white.

The findings come amid changes to federal environmental protections that could increase exposure to pollution from coal-fired power plants. Earlier this year, the Trump administration rejected findings that served as the scientific basis for federal limits on greenhouse gas emissions and weakened restrictions on pollutants released by coal-fired power plants.

The changes could increase exposure to particle pollution in communities already facing significant health and economic disadvantages, the study said.

EPA abandons work to estimate farm air pollution, drops cancer risk estimates

The Trump administration has scrapped long-in-the-works plans to assess air pollution from the nation’s thousands of animal feeding operations.

An October 30 announcement from the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency ended a 20-year effort to develop methods for estimating harmful emissions from large livestock and poultry farms, which can pose health risks to nearby communities.

Animal feeding operations release a range of pollutants, including ammonia, hydrogen sulfide and fine-particle matter, also known as PM2.5. A 2025 University of Michigan study detected elevated levels of PM2.5 near cattle and hog feeding operations. Exposure to pollution from feeding facilities has been linked to asthma and other respiratory problems, particularly among children.

The operations also release methane and nitrous oxide, greenhouse gases that contribute to climate change.

EPA’s decision ends an initiative launched in 2005 after the National Academy of Sciences called for better ways to measure pollution from animal feeding operations. About 2,600 operations, representing about 14,000 livestock and poultry farms, voluntarily agreed to be part of the effort.

The initiative included a national study that collected emissions data from 2005 to 2007. That data is now too outdated to produce reliable estimates, EPA said in last week’s announcement, citing that as a reason to cancel the work.

The new decision is the latest Trump administration action to curtail information about air pollution and its potential health risks to Americans.

In April 2026, EPA released its most recent update on the Air Toxics Screening Assessment, known as AirToxScreen. While the update included information on emissions and concentrations of pollutants, it omitted estimates that help people understand their potential cancer risks.

On October 27, the Environmental Protection Network and Union of Concerned Scientists called on EPA to explain the omission and restore the cancer information, which had been available for more than 20 years.

AirToxScreen was designed to help communities, researchers and public health agencies learn about toxic air pollution that may pose elevated dangers. Without the cancer estimates, members of the public will have to analyze complex pollution data on their own to understand their risks, the groups said.

States facing greatest climate health threats often have weakest protections

People who live in the Southern U.S. will face some of the worst health harms of climate change in coming years. But states in the region are lagging on policies that can help protect their residents, new findings show.

The gap is especially pronounced in the Southeast, where states have experienced high levels of heat-related deaths, severe storms and other climate hazards but have relatively weak policies to help residents prepare and recover from them, according to research published in the November issue of Health Affairs.

Louisiana, North Carolina, South Carolina and Texas are among the states with high climate-related health burdens and weaker protections. In contrast, states along the West Coast and in the Northeast generally have stronger policies, the study said.

Climate change is making heat waves, wildfires, floods and severe storms more frequent or intense, threatening health and lives. People who lack affordable housing, reliable healthcare or money to pay energy bills may have greater difficulty protecting themselves, researchers said.

The study looked at state policies on issues such as wages, nutrition, health, housing, energy and transportation. States received higher ratings for policies that provided substantial benefits, reached more residents and were enforceable.

California, Oregon and Washington were among the leaders, with all three boasting workplace protections that address extreme heat and wildfire smoke, two growing threats associated with climate change. California and Oregon also use Medicaid programs to provide cooling equipment and housing-related assistance to at-risk people with chronic illnesses.

Southern states have made less progress. North Carolina, for example, has introduced Medicaid initiatives addressing some health-related social needs, but other forms of assistance remain largely disconnected from its climate preparedness planning, the researchers said.

The Southeast is particularly vulnerable because its high burden of heat-related deaths coincides with weaker wage, housing and energy assistance policies.

Other recent public health news of note:

• Rural Americans who have heart attacks are nearly three times as likely to die before reaching a hospital as people in large cities, new research shows. The findings, presented at the American Heart Association’s Scientific Sessions 2026, found rural residents were also 89% more likely to die at home and 58% more likely to die in emergency or outpatient care settings than residents of large metropolitan areas.

• A chemical commonly found in fertilizers could be contributing to serious heart defects in newborns, new research in Frontiers in Public Health suggests. The study linked higher levels of nitrate in Utah drinking water to an increased risk of congenital heart defects. Rates of the defects jumped 88% between 2016 and 2023 in the state. During the same period, nitrate levels in drinking water rose 65%, researchers said. Nitrate is commonly used in agricultural fertilizers but can also enter drinking water through sewage, septic systems and decaying organic matter.

• Losses of homes, buildings and other structures from wildfires could triple by 2060, a new study in Nature Communications warns. As many as 449,000 U.S. structures could be damaged or destroyed by wildfires over three-plus decades if current development patterns continue without new protections, the study projected. The Western U.S. would remain the hardest-hit region, with California facing particularly high losses. However, wildfire risks are also growing in the Central and Eastern U.S., the study said. Climate change, expanding development in fire-prone areas and longer fire seasons are driving the growing threat.

The Watch is written by Michele Late, who has more than two decades of experience as a public health journalist.des of experience as a public health journalist.

title: 'Step up and lead': All eyes on Australia as it takes the reins of UN COP31 climate negotiations
description:
Speaking from Antalya, Dr Simon Bradshaw, COP31 Lead at Greenpeace Australia Pacific, said: “The world is in a moment of flux.
We know it is in moments of huge upheaval that era-defining progress can happen — but only when countries step up and lead.
“As Australia takes control of COP31 Negotiations, we have an opportunity and responsibility to shepherd global climate cooperation through this moment of interlocking crises.
That means backing Pacific leadership and priorities, and leading by example at home to end fossil fuels and deliver new, multi-year climate finance commitments.
“In Antalya, the COP31 Presidency must respond to the accelerating climate crisis and defend the 1.5°C goal based on the law and the science.
text:
ANTALYA, Türkiye, Saturday 7 November 2026 — As leaders and delegates gather for the UN COP31 climate summit, Greenpeace Australia Pacific is calling on the Australian government in its role as President of Negotiations to ensure the just transition away from fossil fuels is central to negotiations, rigorously defend the 1.5°C temperature goal, and significantly scale up climate finance commitments.

This year’s climate talks take place amidst a deepening global energy shock, and grim reports that the world will barrel past the 1.5°C temperature goal. They also follow a deadly summer of extreme weather disasters that swept the northern hemisphere, with fears that a severe El Niño will see similar dangerous impacts in Australia.

But recent election wins by progressive candidates in the United States and Brazil are set to breathe energy and optimism into the negotiations as people around the world, bearing the brunt of soaring cost of living and climate disasters, shun regressive and divisive politics.

Speaking from Antalya, Dr Simon Bradshaw, COP31 Lead at Greenpeace Australia Pacific, said: “The world is in a moment of flux. We know it is in moments of huge upheaval that era-defining progress can happen — but only when countries step up and lead.

“As Australia takes control of COP31 Negotiations, we have an opportunity and responsibility to shepherd global climate cooperation through this moment of interlocking crises. That means backing Pacific leadership and priorities, and leading by example at home to end fossil fuels and deliver new, multi-year climate finance commitments.

“As a major coal and gas exporter, Australia plays an outsized role in fuelling the climate crisis, and has approved 38 new, extended and expanded fossil fuel projects since first elected in 2022. More than half the world’s coal export project pipeline is in Australia, and the Albanese Government is poised to make decisions on massive new gas projects. Australia must reckon with this reality.

“Domestically, we have made significant strides on ramping up renewables and the global ‘35 by 35’ electrification goal is welcome and necessary. But electrification must end fossil fuel dependence, not be an end in itself — its ultimate success depends on ensuring electricity comes from renewable sources that displace fossil fuels and align with a 1.5°C pathway.

“In Türkiye, the Australian government can rise to the occasion and show what true climate leadership looks like, but we can not move the world towards a clean energy future while expanding the industry we need to leave behind.”

Speaking from Antalya, Shiva Gounden, Head of Pacific at Greenpeace Australia Pacific, said: “As leaders meet in Türkiye amidst warnings that we will pass the 1.5°C threshold, the stakes have never been higher. Every heatwave, every flood, every storm is being unleashed on communities with the deadly force of accumulated emissions and gives a warning of what is to come.

“In Antalya, the COP31 Presidency must respond to the accelerating climate crisis and defend the 1.5°C goal based on the law and the science. 1.5°C is a non-negotiable survival line for Pacific communities and climate-vulnerable nations facing rising seas, extreme weather disasters, food insecurity and soaring economic costs. It is a fundamental component of the Paris Agreement and enshrined as a binding legal benchmark by the world’s highest court, the International Court of Justice.

“Australia must arrive at COP31 with more than meaningless speeches. The Pacific and the world need concrete dates, credible plans to deliver roadmaps away from fossil fuels built on the best available science, and a commitment to put people, energy security and the planet ahead of fossil fuel interests.

“We need real action to advance multilateral climate cooperation, ensure the just transition away from fossil fuels is high on the agenda, and back longstanding Pacific priorities — including keeping 1.5°C alive and significantly scaling-up climate finance.”

text:
Federal and local police surrounded several properties in Midlothian on Nov. 6.

Midlothian Police Department officials directed WFAA to the FBI for comment on the law enforcement presence in the city.

An official with the FBI would only confirm that it was at the properties conducting court-authorized activity.

Law enforcement officers were at the following locations Friday:

4000 block of Wisteria

500 block of S. 9th Street

2900 block of Eagles Nest

2500 block of Springer Road

Chopper video showed police entering the Springer Road property.

A company called West Texas Crude Energy LLC sits at 2520 Springer Road, Midlothian, Texas. Public records also show the address is tied to someone named Robert Curry III.

Brett Michael Kemp, who lists himself on LinkedIn as the CFO, CRO and CCO of West Texas Crude Energy LLC, has an address in the 4000 block of Wisteria in Midlothian, according to public records.

Both Kemp and Curry III, along with West Texas Crude Energy LLC, are defendants in multiple lawsuits in which investors allege they were defrauded through oil and gas investment offerings.

There are at least three lawsuits against the company and people affiliated with it. Several investors claim in the suits that they provided the company with nearly $2 million for oil and gas projects that did not materialize in the way the company claimed they would.

One investor, Chris Daubitz, told WFAA that he was initially receiving payments for the company. However, eventually, those payments stopped.

A group of 10 investors claim it gave the company $1.45 million. They received $866,965 in return but are still owed another $588,000, according to the suit.

The FBI did not say what court-authorized activity was taking place and did not indicate whether it was related to the civil lawsuits. No criminal charges connected to the allegations reviewed by WFAA were publicly known as of Saturday, Nov. 7.

In the latest suit, filed Nov. 4, investor Lawrence V. Brackett alleges the projects and representations made to investors were fictitious, writing that "all of it was a sham."

WFAA emailed the company for comment and called numbers listed for Kemp and Curry III, but has not heard back as of publication.

text:
Electric vehicle owners in downtown Albuquerque can now charge up considerably faster, after Bernalillo County leaders unveiled a new Level 3 charging station this week. County officials say the fast-charger can take many EVs from empty to full in about 30 minutes, a dramatic improvement over standard chargers that can take hours.

According to KRQE, Bernalillo County leaders gathered at the Mid-Region Council of Governments on Copper to unveil the new station. The outlet reports the charger is a Level 3 station, which allows many electric vehicles to fully charge in 30 minutes. Separately, citizenportal.ai has described the planned station as being located on Fourth Street at Alvarado Square, so the precise address has not been reconciled between the two accounts.

The project was funded through a $500,000 grant from the New Mexico Department of Transportation, per the station's report. A partial Bernalillo County blog post, representing the county's own account of the opening, describes the new equipment as a Level III, 200-kilowatt charger with built-in capacity to add a second port when needed, according to Bernalillo County.

Funding and Cost Breakdown

Beyond the state grant, the downtown project carried a total estimated cost of about $607,000, according to citizenportal.ai. That reporting indicates the county planned to cover the remaining balance with a $56,900 local bond match and a $50,000 rebate from PNM. The same account noted the station was expected to meet a June 30, 2026 activation deadline, though the evidence available does not establish exactly when the charger became operational or confirm current public availability.

More Chargers Planned Countywide

The downtown station is not a standalone project. The county currently operates 24 EV charging ports and plans to add 14 more at four additional county facilities, the station's report notes. Details on timing and exact locations for those additional ports have not yet been established.

For now, the new downtown fast-charger stands as the county's latest step toward expanding EV infrastructure in the Albuquerque metro area, giving drivers another option for quick charging without needing to wait for a lengthy session at a standard station.

text:
Senators write: “…The definitions proposed by the SNPRM [Supplemental Notice of Proposed Rulemaking] would remove federal protections for 80 percent of streams in the United States and 95 percent of individual wetlands, which makes a mockery of the congressional intent behind the Clean Water Act.”

November 7, 2026 - Washington, D.C. – U.S. Senators Adam Schiff (D-Calif.), Ranking Member of the Senate Environment and Public Works’ Fisheries, Water, and Wildlife Subcommittee, and Ed Markey (D-Mass.) are calling on the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) and the U.S. Army Corps of Engineers (USACE) to abandon their new proposal that threatens to harm public health and leave communities vulnerable to flooding and loss of access to clean drinking water.

The EPA’s new proposal to revise the definition of the Waters of the United States (WOTUS) rule replaces the proposed November 2025 standard with an even more extreme one, defining “relatively permanent” to mean “perennial” waters, stripping federal protections for hundreds of bodies of waters. Previously, in January 2026, the Senators urged the agencies to reverse this proposal.

“As we explained then, excluding these waters from federal protection threatens drinking water, increases downstream pollution and flood risk, and shifts substantial costs onto states, communities, and ratepayers. We are disappointed that your agencies have not only chosen to disregard all of these concerns, but have put out a second, more extreme proposal that does even more harm. We urge you to abandon this effort altogether and remember your statutory responsibilities to protect drinking water, public health, and the environment,” the Senators wrote in a letter to the EPA.

EPA’s latest proposal goes further to eliminate safeguards on bodies of waters that were already reduced by the Supreme Court’s 2023 decision in Sackett v. EPA. Additionally, the Senators raise concern with the subsequent harms this proposal will have on state and tribes’ capacity to manage waters, as well as on American households, who will bear the financial costs.

“…Pollution does not respect the arbitrary boundaries laid out in these proposals. When upstream waters lose federal protection, downstream communities do not cease experiencing their effects of that loss…the costs of additional pollution, degraded drinking water sources and the associated health risks, diminished flood protection, and lost aquatic habitat are shifted to states, Tribes, municipalities, water utilities, and ultimately the American taxpayer,” the Senators wrote.

“The Clean Water Act was enacted to “restore and maintain the chemical, physical, and biological integrity of the Nation’s waters.” Proposing to systematically exclude waters known to be critical to that integrity ignores science and defeats the purpose of the Act…We urge you to abandon this disastrous SNPRM as well as the 2025 proposal and leave the 2023 conforming rule in place,” the Senators concluded.

The EPW Committee’s Ranking Member, U.S. Senator Sheldon Whitehouse (D-R.I.), also signed the letter.

The full text of the letter can be found here and below.

Dear Administrator Zeldin and Mr. Forsgren:

We write to express our serious concern regarding the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) and U.S. Army Corps of Engineers’ September 9, 2026 Supplemental Notice of Proposed Rulemaking (SNPRM) that proposes to further narrow which waters would receive federal protections under the Clean Water Act. On January 28, 2026, we urged the agencies to abandon the proposed 2025 waters of the United States (WOTUS) rule. As we explained then, excluding these waters from federal protection threatens drinking water, increases downstream pollution and flood risk, and shifts substantial costs onto states, communities, and ratepayers. We are disappointed that your agencies have not only chosen to disregard all of these concerns, but have put out a second, more extreme proposal that does even more harm. We urge you to abandon this effort altogether and remember your statutory responsibilities to protect drinking water, public health, and the environment.

The core proposal of the SNPRM is to define “relatively permanent” waters to include only perennial waters, which the proposal suggests defining as “having standing or continuously flowing water every day of the year during ordinary conditions.” The SNPRM includes limited exceptions for drought, dry spells, and low tides, and allows only a single interruption of no more than 30 consecutive days annually. The SNPRM also considers a definition of “continuous surface connection” that would require even perennial surface water within a wetland to be continuously connected to a jurisdictional water in order to merit protection as WOTUS.

Limiting “relatively permanent” waters to perennial and interconnected waters would be scientifically indefensible and would put downstream water quality at risk. EPA’s own scientific record demonstrates why. EPA’s review of more than 1,200 peer-reviewed studies concluded that streams are connected to downstream waters regardless of their size or frequency of flow and strongly influence downstream physical, chemical, and biological conditions. That review, and numerous other independent scientific studies, found that perennial, intermittent, and ephemeral tributaries transport water, sediment, nutrients, contaminants, organic material, and organisms through river networks and collectively affect larger downstream waters. Further, the definitions proposed by the SNPRM would remove federal protections for 80 percent of streams in the United States and 95 percent of individual wetlands, which makes a mockery of the congressional intent behind the Clean Water Act.

Your agencies acknowledge these concerns in the SNPRM and recognize the functions served by ephemeral streams. The agencies also acknowledge that the majority of wetlands would not satisfy the supplemental definition of “continuous surface connection,” because most wetlands do not contain perennial surface water. Even more, your agencies concede that the 30-day threshold is not “scientifically-grounded” and is proposed only because it is “easy to administer.” Given these acknowledgements, it appears the entirety of the SNPRM is contradictory— proposing changes that go against the very scientific findings cited in the notice. “Easy to administer” does not justify the neglect of waterways that contribute on average 55% of the water found in larger rivers – the protection of which is the mission of your agencies and the Clean Water Act.

The SNPRM also includes an arbitrary five-year cutoff for waters impacted by drought conditions, a policy that would cause particular harm to more arid regions like the West. After five years of dry conditions, such drought conditions would be treated as the new baseline. As American Rivers explains in its public comment, this would “convert a growing share of currently ‘relatively permanent’ waters to non-jurisdictional status over time, particularly in the West, as droughts lengthen and recur more frequently.”

The agencies justify these contradictions and known harms in part by claiming that the proposal allegedly provides regulatory clarity, giving landowners clearer notice of Clean Water Act obligations. But administrative simplicity cannot provide cover for a scientifically and legally indefensible interpretation of the Clean Water Act, as its primary purpose is to protect waters from pollution. Moreover, this SNPRM would not provide clarity, as it would inevitably lead to litigation and overwhelm state and tribal capacity to manage waters. The agencies acknowledge in the supplemental proposal that “Tribes may disproportionately rely on the Federal Government for water program implementation and enforcement of water quality violations” and “many Tribes are still building capacity and may lack resources to create a Tribal water program.” This SNPRM will remove federal protections for many waters Tribes may care about, thus pulling the rug out from under them.

As we emphasized in January, pollution does not respect the arbitrary boundaries laid out in these proposals. When upstream waters lose federal protection, downstream communities do not cease experiencing their effects of that loss. And states are not going to be able to fill the gaps left by the SNPRM. One state’s hypothetical capacity to regulate their own waters, absent federal law, does not mean as much when an under-resourced, upstream state exports the cost of their water quality remediation downstream. Instead, the costs of additional pollution, degraded drinking water sources and the associated health risks, diminished flood protection, and lost aquatic habitat are shifted to states, Tribes, municipalities, water utilities, and ultimately the American taxpayer. Our previous letter warned that narrowing WOTUS in this manner would transfer responsibility and costs downstream rather than eliminate them. The recent supplemental proposal fails to heed that warning and would multiply these costs to the American people.

description:
On September 30, 2026, Senate negotiators released the text of the proposed Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act of 2026 (“BAAJA”).
For distributed energy resources (“DERs”) and virtual power plants (“VPPs”), the bill comes at a critical moment.
A VPP is a group of DERs that a VPP provider controls through software to act like a single power plant.
Section 2108, titled “Dispatchable energy systems market access,” instead defines a “qualifying behind-the-meter distributed energy system facility” (a “qualifying BTM DES facility”).
