title: What Happens When The Wind Stops In A Wind-Powered State - World Atlas
description:
On the evening of September 6, 2023, wind generation across Texas dropped off at the worst possible moment.
The Grid Must Replace Missing Wind Generation The September 2023 emergency reflects a basic constraint of wind power.
Turbines produce electricity only when wind conditions permit, so a state with substantial wind generation still needs other sources of supply.
Batteries Supply Electricity During Short Wind Lulls Battery storage provides another response when wind generation falls.
In its 2025 State of the Market report, SPP recorded average wind generation equivalent to 37% of electricity demand in its real-time market.
text:
On the evening of September 6, 2023, wind generation across Texas dropped off at the worst possible moment. Temperatures were high, electricity demand had reached a September peak of 82,705 megawatts, and solar output was fading toward sunset. At approximately 7:25 p.m., the state's grid operator declared an emergency. Grid frequency slipped below its normal 60-hertz target, and reserves were running low. Texas is one of the country's leading wind-producing states, so a calm evening is more than a passing inconvenience there. What happened over the following hour, and what happens anywhere the turbines go still, comes down to everything else the grid has in reserve.

Texas Shows What Happens When Reserves Run Low

The emergency that the Electric Reliability Council of Texas (ERCOT) declared that evening was an Energy Emergency Alert Level 2, issued after operating conditions deteriorated during the evening peak. Grid frequency dropped to approximately 59.77 hertz. The declaration allowed ERCOT to access additional reserves and activate demand response. The operator brought available generation online, coordinated with market participants to secure additional capacity, and deployed participating load resources to reduce electricity demand. ERCOT stepped down to a lower emergency level at 8:27 p.m. and returned to normal operations at 8:37 p.m. No grid-related controlled outages were necessary.

At the time, ERCOT's Level 2 reserve threshold was 1,750 megawatts. In November 2023, the operator raised that threshold to 2,000 megawatts, providing an earlier opportunity to respond as operating reserves decline. An emergency declaration is a warning that grid conditions require intervention, but it does not automatically mean customers will lose service.

The Grid Must Replace Missing Wind Generation

The September 2023 emergency reflects a basic constraint of wind power. Turbines produce electricity only when wind conditions permit, so a state with substantial wind generation still needs other sources of supply. According to the US Energy Information Administration (EIA), wind generated approximately 464 million megawatt-hours of electricity nationwide in 2025, accounting for about 10% of utility-scale generation. Texas, Iowa, Oklahoma, Kansas, and Illinois were the five leading wind-producing states.

When wind output falls by 1,000 megawatts for one hour, it creates a 1,000-megawatt-hour energy gap, and over 24 hours that gap reaches 24,000 megawatt-hours. Grid operators can close it by increasing generation, discharging batteries, importing electricity, or reducing demand, depending on which resources are available and how quickly they can deliver power.

Natural Gas And Other Generators Increase Output

Natural gas plants are a major source of replacement electricity in Texas. During a February 2025 cold snap, wind and solar generation across the ERCOT region fell by 52% between February 18 and 21. EIA reported that natural gas generation supplied 73% of the remaining electricity requirement on February 21.

Coal and nuclear plants also contribute, although their ability to change output depends on plant design and operating conditions. The Comanche Peak Nuclear Power Plant near Glen Rose, Texas, generates electricity regardless of local wind conditions, covering part of overall demand while more flexible resources handle shorter-term changes. According to EIA, natural gas, coal, and nuclear plants collectively supplied 75% of US utility-scale electricity generation in 2025.

Batteries Supply Electricity During Short Wind Lulls

Battery storage provides another response when wind generation falls. The DeCordova Energy Storage Facility near Granbury, Texas, has a rated output of 260 megawatts and an energy capacity of 260 megawatt-hours, enough for approximately one hour of discharge at full output, or longer at lower output. It operates alongside the DeCordova natural gas generating facility, giving the site two sources of electricity.

Across the wider Texas grid, EIA reported that batteries delivered an average of approximately 4,000 megawatts during the 8 p.m. hour in the summer months of 2025, helping replace solar generation as it declined toward sunset. Batteries respond quickly, but their contribution is limited by their stored energy, so extended shortages require additional generation, demand reductions, or opportunities to recharge.

Regional Grids Share Electricity Across State Lines

Wind shortages can affect more than one state simultaneously. Oklahoma and Kansas participate in the Southwest Power Pool (SPP), which coordinates wholesale electricity markets and transmission operations across a multistate region. In its 2025 State of the Market report, SPP recorded average wind generation equivalent to 37% of electricity demand in its real-time market. During one five-minute interval, wind production reached the equivalent of 83% of demand.

The report also recorded 35,934 megawatts of registered wind capacity at the end of 2025. SPP monitors wind conditions across locations including Amarillo and Lubbock in Texas and Hays in Kansas. When output falls in one part of the network, the operator can dispatch available resources elsewhere in the region, subject to transmission limits.

Businesses May Be Asked To Reduce Electricity Use

Demand response, one of the tools ERCOT used in September 2023, can help stabilize an electricity grid without disconnecting entire communities. Large electricity customers that have agreed to provide this service can curtail selected operations when called upon, narrowing the gap between generation and demand.

For businesses in the Houston area and other parts of the ERCOT region, the consequences depend on whether they participate in such arrangements and how severe the shortage is. A participating industrial facility might temporarily reduce electricity consumption, while other customers continue to receive normal service. If available generation and voluntary or contracted demand reductions cannot restore adequate reserves, grid operators may direct utilities to implement controlled outages.

Fuel Supplies And Water Infrastructure Also Matter

Replacement generation has operating requirements beyond installed capacity. Natural gas plants depend on sufficient fuel delivery, while some generating stations require large cooling-water supplies. At DeCordova, the operator has reported diesel backup arrangements for its gas-fueled generating units, providing an alternative fuel supply for up to seven days under its published specifications.

The nearby Brazos River also supports electricity infrastructure. The Brazos River Authority completed DeCordova Bend Dam in September 1969, creating Lake Granbury. The reservoir has 136,326 acre-feet of conservation storage and supports industrial water uses associated with power generation, including the Comanche Peak Nuclear Power Plant. Fuel and water are most important when replacement generators must operate for extended periods.

Longer Wind Shortages Require A Different Response

A lull lasting several hours creates different operating requirements from one lasting several days. Batteries can handle short intervals, while fuel-powered generators can run as long as they have adequate fuel and remain available. A prolonged period of unusually low wind and solar output is sometimes called a dunkelflaute. In wind-producing states such as Iowa, Kansas, Oklahoma, and Texas, a brief reduction can be handled through routine grid operations, while a longer shortage during periods of high demand can place greater pressure on generation reserves and transmission networks.

As of 2026, that balancing is taking place alongside growing electricity demand, with ERCOT's hourly load reaching a record 91.1 gigawatts on July 22, 2026, according to EIA. During any wind lull, generation, storage, and available demand reductions must together match consumption closely enough to maintain grid stability. When they do, customers can keep receiving electricity even while wind turbines produce very little.

Tesla’s Cybertruck, the hulking, stainless-steel pick-up that inspired devotion and derision with its science-fiction looks, will cease production next year.

Elon Musk announced the model’s demise Friday with a curt post on X, his social media site, simply noting production of the vehicle “will be winding down” around the middle of 2027 at its facility outside Austin, Texas. Musk said the move was to allow increased production of its Cybercab robotaxi.

For the Cybertruck, a pet project of Musk, who insisted it was Tesla’s best product, it marks an unceremonious end to one of the auto industry’s most ballyhooed debuts.

“Few vehicles in history have generated as much attention,” said Armen Hareyan, whose Torque News site covers autos. “The Cybertruck became a cultural symbol – loved, mocked and impossible to ignore.”

The Cybertruck rolled onto the scene in a dramatic unveiling in 2019, when a Tesla designer hurled a metal ball at the vehicle to demonstrate its supposedly unbreakable glass, only to see it shatter. He repeated the stunt on another window of the truck only to shatter that one, too.

Tesla gives the world a look at its new electric pickup truck, the Cybertruck.

Even as some critics scoffed, Musk was steadfast.

“I just wanted to make a futuristic battle tank — something that looks like it could come out of Blade Runner or Aliens or something like that but was also highly functional,” he told Automotive News. He called it “a better sports car than a Porsche 911” and “a better truck than an F-150”.

It struck some as the perfect vehicular reflection of the brash, convention-busting Musk.

“A really controversial vehicle unveiled by a controversial individual into a market where none of the electric trucks have been able to really capture demand,” said Spencer Penn, a former Tesla executive who left the company before the Cybertruck’s launch and now heads software developer LightSource.

Penn remembered watching the unveiling and feeling initially revolted by the sight of the Cybertruck, calling its appearance “madness.” But the more he looked at it, the more his opinion changed. He signed up for a pre-sale reservation, though ended up not getting a Cybertruck when Musk’s promises of a price tag under $US40,000 went unmet and the first trucks sold for double or more. Penn called the Cybertruck part of Tesla’s adventurous spirit that drives innovation.

“Some of these bets work and some of these bets don’t,” he said.

While the decision to end Cybertruck production may be driven by sales realities, it’s also a reflection of Tesla’s shift to autonomous vehicles, on which Musk is betting the company’s future.

Musk once forecast he’d make 250,000 Cybertrucks a year. US vehicle valuation and automotive research company Kelley Blue Book estimated Tesla sold just 20,237 of the vehicles last year, down about half from the year prior. Sales through the end of September this year were down another 28 per cent, according to Kelley.

If the imposing, sharp-angled, dystopian appearance of the Cybertruck wasn’t enough to turn many potential buyers away, Musk did so himself by allying with a panoply of right-wing figures, most notably US President Donald Trump.

He alienated some customers as his image morphed from eccentric innovator to polarising force trading his billions for political influence.

Once-passionate Tesla drivers rushed to sell off their cars, or slapped stickers on the bumper declaring, “I bought this before Elon went crazy.”

Organisers staged demonstrations outside Tesla showrooms and urged investors to dump shares of the company’s stock. Anger spilled into violence, with Molotov cocktails hurled at Tesla vehicles, charging stations set ablaze, and dealerships covered in graffiti.

text:
Sen. Martin Heinrich announced a substitute amendment to the landmark Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act on Saturday amid growing demonstrations against it.

Heinrich said the amendment reflected feedback lawmakers have received since the bill's introduction in September.

"I've worked hard to incorporate the feedback we've heard from Tribes and New Mexicans into this Substitute Amendment," said Heinrich in a statement, adding that it makes "targeted changes" to the proposed bill.

RELATED: Haaland outlines priorities after historic New Mexico governor’s race

Heinrich released the statement together with a bipartisan panel of lawmakers working on the bill amid demonstrations by environmentalists and concerns by New Mexico tribal leaders.

Among the outlined changes are elevating tribal leaders and governments in permitting and environmental review processes and establishing a Data Center Community Assistance Program. The program would provide state, local and tribal governments with information on the energy, water, infrastructure, economic and community impacts of data center development upon request.

The changes came after Pueblo governors joined environmental activists and lawmakers this week in opposing the bill, citing its potential impact on sacred lands and federal protections.

The legislation proposes changes to the federal environmental review process, creates ratepayer protections for large data centers, and limits the scope of the National Historic Preservation Act.

These provisions have drawn criticism from the All Pueblo Council of Governors, which represents 20 nations.

The council relies on the National Historic Preservation Act and other federal protections mentioned in the bill to ensure it has a voice in major federal decisions affecting its sacred lands.

"If this is really about green energy, there's an opportunity over the next two years, and over the next four years certainly with the next presidential cycle in there, to get profound changes to policy on energy that doesn't do it at the expense of sacred sites," said National Congress of American Indians President Mark Macarro.

Heinrich, meanwhile, reiterated his support for the bill, highlighting its intended benefits.

"When you look at it as a whole, it dramatically increases clean energy on the grid, it brings down prices, it is designed to create 20,000 New Mexican jobs, and it reduces emissions," said Heinrich.

Heinrich also acknowledged that Democratic lawmakers compromised with Republicans to pass the bill but declined to specify on which parts of the legislation those compromises were made.

title: GM Steps On Tesla's Cybertruck Toes With EV1 Celebration - CleanTechnica
description:
In a move that shocked and surprised nobody, last week Tesla CEO Elon Musk pulled the plug on his much-hyped Cybertruck.
It may be small consolation, but at least the Cybertruck sold more units than another notorious flop in modern automotive history, General Motors’s ill-fated EV1 sedan.
In sales, yes, but GM wants everyone to know that the EV1 beat Tesla to the electrification punch in key technology milestones.
Alas, EV1, We Barely Knew Thee GM actually sold few, if any, EV1 units, preferring to lease the car with a focus on drivers in California.
This year marks the 30th anniversary of EV1 production, and GM is using the occasion to celebrate.
text:
Support CleanTechnica's work through a Substack subscription, on Patreon, or on Stripe. Help us produce all of the high-quality, original content we publish week after week despite the challenges of content-scraping AI, antisocial media, inflation, and other hurdles.

In a move that shocked and surprised nobody, last week Tesla CEO Elon Musk pulled the plug on his much-hyped Cybertruck. Production will end sometime next year. It may be small consolation, but at least the Cybertruck sold more units than another notorious flop in modern automotive history, General Motors’s ill-fated EV1 sedan. Was EV1 really a flop, though? In sales, yes, but GM wants everyone to know that the EV1 beat Tesla to the electrification punch in key technology milestones.

Alas, EV1, We Barely Knew Thee

GM actually sold few, if any, EV1 units, preferring to lease the car with a focus on drivers in California. Production began in 1996 but that didn’t last long. In 2003 GM pulled the plug, recalled the vehicles, and sent them to the crusher, having produced barely more than 1,000 units overall.

Only a scant few escaped the junkyard. One of them was rescued by US filmmaker Alex Gibney, leading to his advisory role in the searing 2006 EV1 documentary “Who Killed the Electric Car?” (btw, Gibney ‘s newly released “Musk” documentary is available on streaming now).

This year marks the 30th anniversary of EV1 production, and GM is using the occasion to celebrate. Rather than shoveling all memory of the EV1 debacle into the memory hole, GM has embarked on sort of under-the-radar public relations campaign, seeking to position the car as a necessary, albeit short lived, step along the vehicle electrification journey.

In not so many words, GM also draws attention to the fact that its work on EV1 predates the launch of Tesla Motors, which came on the scene in 2003. The automaker’s Senior Writer and Editor at GM News, Chris Perkins, ran down the particulars in March, noting that EV1 was the first EV to deploy heat pumps for climate control, energy efficiency, and battery temperature management.

Perkins also takes note of the car’s regenerative braking system. “Engineers developed a system for the car that translated a driver’s brake-pedal input into an electronic signal that blended regenerative and friction braking,” Perkins wrote.

“It’s a precursor to the braking systems used in GM’s modern EVs, which also add One-Pedal Driving1 and paddle-actuated Regen-On-Demand2 capability,” he added.

EV1 also eschewed mechanical actuators in favor of fully electronic (aka by-wire) controls for the accelerator pedal, brake pedal, parking brake, and gear selector, with the power steering featuring electro-hydraulic control.

Additionally, Perkins elaborated on the regenerative braking angle in a follow-up article in August, by way of demonstrating a through line between the 1990’s technology and the automaker’s current EV lineup.

“Conceptually, the EV1’s braking system operates exactly like the braking systems in GM’s modern EVs,” Perkins wrote. “Press the brake pedal, and the car’s computers decide how much friction and regenerative braking to actuate. Should the electronic system fail, it’s connected to a mechanical backup, just as in the EV1.”

GM Seeks To Elbow Tesla Aside

As part of the PR campaign, GM is also putting its 1994 concept sedan on display, the 1994 Impact (pictured above). “As one of the first modern, purpose-built electric vehicles from a major automaker, the Impact was a critical learning tool that shaped the final production version of the EV1,” GM emphasizes.

If you blink, you’ll miss it. The Impact is on display at the GM-sponsored Test Track at EPCOT, the Disney theme park in Bay Lake, Florida, until mid-December.

As for why all this fuss, why now, that’s a good question. Over the past several years, GM has put a jolly spin on its inability to catch up to Tesla in sales, let alone surpass it. As recently as last year, GM vigorously touted itself as #2 in EV sales in the US, second only to Tesla as a badge of honor.

Still, by August of 2025 the competition was beginning to take on a different tone, with GM pitching low-cost LFP (lithium-iron-phosphate) batteries as a near-term pathway to meeting, then beating Tesla.

The 2026 EV1 celebration elaborates upon the technology angle, underscoring GM’s claim on the pre-Tesla, 1990’s roots of innovation in the vehicle electrification field.

The new emphasis on technology also comes at a pivotal moment for EV sales in the US. The US market nosedived last fall after US President Trump and his Republican allies in Congress prematurely eliminated federal tax credits for EVs. However, activity continued to stir in some quarters, and Trump himself made the case for EVs more attractive when he decided to bomb Iran in February.

Nine months later, the price of gas remains stubbornly high, sparking renewed hopes that EV sales will rebound more quickly than first anticipated. In addition, a fresh round of innovation is on the horizon, with GM banking on its forthcoming LMR (lithium manganese-rich) battery formula to push costs down without sacrificing performance.

Life After Cybertruck

While Tesla is not the only competition in town, beating the startup at its own game would be a feather in GM’s cap, and Elon Musk made the effort a little easier when he canceled the Cybertruck, leaving Tesla without a foothold in the hot market for pickup trucks in the US. The automaker still has sedans, SUVs, the new Semi Class 8 truck, and the “flying” Roadster in its pocket, but the demise of the Cybertruck has left the pickup field wide open.

Meanwhile, Ford is on track to produce its new Fathom electric pickup next year starting at under $30,000, far less than the Cybertruck’s most recent starting price of $77,000 plus change. The Jeff Bezos-backed startup Slate Auto is also aiming at the affordability market with a stripped-down electric pickup starting at a base price of $26,000 and change, before accounting for add-ons.

On its part, GM is aiming for the middle ground with the 2027 Silverado electric pickup, starting at around $56,000 and reaching close to Cybertruck range at around $72,000.

Meanwhile, Rivian is also aiming upscale at close to $80,000 and up for its RIT pickup. The startup is on the move, having somehow managed to squeeze a loan guarantee of up to $4.5 billion out of the Trump administration. The funds are earmarked to expand Rivian’s production capacity with a new factory in Georgia.

Readers, what do you think? Does GM — or any other automaker — have a snowball’s chance in hell to catch up to Tesla in the US market? Drop a note in the discussion thread…

text:
President Donald Trump is previewing battles to come with a new Democratic majority in Congress, saying he’s ordered the Justice Department to “look into” lawmakers who are seeking investigations and potential impeachment votes for members of his administration.

As Republicans take stock of a capital upended by the Democrats’ sweeping midterms blue wave, change is coming to the White House, too.

Trump is moving on to his sixth chief of staff across two terms, replacing Susie Wiles with immigration hardliner Stephen Miller. He also said Saturday that he offered the White House press secretary job to Dana White — though a source familiar with the matter says the UFC CEO declined the unorthodox idea.

West Wing aides describe a post-election workplace filled with tension and infighting, likening it to the “knives out” days of Trump’s first term.

Catch up on other headlines here:

Balance of power: Vote counting continues in Mississippi and Alaska, where Senate races have yet to be called. There are 20 House races that CNN has not yet projected, out of a total 435 seats. These include tight contests in Arizona, Colorado, Florida and Minnesota. See more of what we’re still watching here.

On the ground: CNN is in Mississippi, where Annie Grayer spoke to a voter who described her relief upon learning her ballot was finally accepted. A local election official also explained why the majority of provisional ballots at Jackson State University had to be rejected.

New Senate leader: Minority Leader Chuck Schumer has expressed confidence that he will continue to lead the caucus in the next Senate, but several incoming Democrats have vowed not to support him. We heard from Sen. Chris Van Hollen and Sen. Elissa Slotkin today, who each suggested the next leader is far from a foregone conclusion.

On “60 Minutes”: In an interview with CBS, which was taped on Friday, Trump said he could “very easily” stop attacking Democrats for six months if it allowed the two parties to reach a deal on policy. He also expressed confidence in embattled Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth.

War in Iran: Iranian hardliners are seizing on Trump’s midterm losses to demand he pay a steeper price for an exit from the conflict.

CNN’s Aaron Blake, Catherine Nicholls, Xiaoqian Lin, Mostafa Salem, Patrick Svitek, Logan Schiciano, Kaitlan Collins and Molly English contributed to this report.

Mississippi voter recounts stress of not knowing whether ballot was counted

Mississippi voter recounts stress of not knowing whether ballot was counted

0:19

One of thousands of Mississippi voters who had to fill out an affidavit ballot told CNN Saturday that her experiencing on Election Day was “disappointing,” after she encountered challenges that day she’d never faced before.

Tachana Hurst told CNN she voted the last seven years without issues. But this year, after not being allowed to vote absentee, she arrived at her polling place only to be told she had to report to a different precinct, where she was informed because she had been moved to an inactive voting status. She eventually had to fill out an affidavit ballot that was accepted a few days later.

“I’m just glad that I refused to give up because I could have just left when they couldn’t find me in the system, but that wouldn’t be exercising my right to vote,” she recalled. “I’ve never had this experience before.”

While Democratic candidate Scott Colom has grown his narrow lead over Republican candidate Cindy Hyde-Smith, the race is still too close to call, and Mississippi’s Republican Party has claimed there are still thousands of affidavit ballots left to be counted.

Hurst cautioned that some affidavit voters may not have their vote counted “because they might not have the resources or the people that’s telling me what to do and how to go forward.”

CNN’s Piper Hudspeth Blackburn contributed to this report.

NAACP officials in Mississippi set up a booth at the Jackson State University football game tailgate today to help voters ensure their ballots are being counted in the US Senate race that remains too close to call.

Democrat Scott Colom maintains a slight lead over GOP Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith, but the race will likely come down to thousands of provisional ballots, known in the state as affidavit ballots, that voters had to cast because they lacked photo ID or were not showing up in their precincts’ poll books.

“We came to the Jackson State game because that’s where our community is” NAACP President Derrick Johnson said in a statement to CNN. “Helping them check their ballot status and recruiting volunteers to serve as election monitors. We remain committed to seeing this process all the way from ballots cast, to ballots counted, to elections certified.”

Pennsylvania’s Democratic Gov. Josh Shapiro has been cagey about his 2028 ambitions, saying for much of the year that he’s been focused on his reelection campaign and other races at home.

Now, with a blowout reelection victory four days behind him, Shapiro is opening up a bit more, saying he wants to help ensure his party nationally “is looking at doing big things again.”

It was hardly an acknowledgment of interest in the presidential contest but comes after months of dodging questions about his national ambitions.

“All I have been focused on is these midterms,” Shapiro told CNN’s Jake Tapper earlier this week, following the election.

The 2028 Democratic primary is expected to be crowded. Earlier at Crooked Con, Sen. Chris Van Hollen of Maryland acknowledged to CNN that he is “kicking the tires” on a potential run. And Sen. Elissa Slotkin of Michigan told the crowd she expects a “busy, robust primary.”

“We should accept it,” she said. “It’s going to be big and messy, and that’s fine.”

President Donald Trump said he would have the Department of Justice look into threats of “Impeachment and many other forms of punishment” by Democrats against certain members of his administration, companies and donors to his ballroom project as he grapples with a new reality in Congress.

“The Democrats are going around threatening a lot of people, including the Attorney General of the United States, and others, with Impeachment and many other forms of punishment, even though they admit they have no reason to do so, and there have been no impeachable acts committed, or even thought of, by the victims of this illegal process,” Trump wrote on Truth Social on Saturday, adding that it was “extortion at the highest level.”

“The imprisonment should be against these EXTORTIONISTS, and Republicans should get smart, fast! Threatening letters have been sent to many people, all innocent, from Democrat Political Leaders,” Trump continued. “By copy of this statement, I am ordering the Department of Justice to look into this criminal act, immediately!”

CNN has reached out to the White House and the DOJ for comment.

Sen. Richard Blumenthal, who is expected to chair a key Senate investigative panel when Democrats take control of Congress in January, sent letters to a slew of companies and Trump administration officials on Thursday asking them to cooperate with potential investigations.

Among those who received letters were Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin, Federal Communications Commission Chair Brendan Carr, and several White House ballroom donors, including Amazon, Apple and Google. Crypto companies World Liberty Financial, Binance and Tether also got letters.

Blumenthal warned that the subcommittee will look into “alternative measures to obtain compliance” if the companies and officials do not provide information that the panel requested by January 4, a day after the new Congress convenes. People and companies who received the letters are not obligated to reply until the new Congress is officially in power.

Sen. Elissa Slotkin declined today to rule out running for Senate majority leader after Democrats’ far-reaching wins in the midterms.

The Michigan Democrat, who has long pushed for new leadership inside her party, said it was up to Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer to convince Democrats that he has a plan for how they should wield their new power. Asked if she would run for the job, she did not say no.

“I’m not ruling anything out,” she added.

Slotkin was being interviewed at Crooked Con, a post-midterms Democratic conference in Washington, DC.

Schumer has expressed confidence he will continue to lead Senate Democrats.

Earlier today, Sen. Chris Van Hollen of Maryland told the crowd at Crooked Con that there should not be a “coronation” for the next Senate Democratic leader. However, Van Hollen suggested he was unlikely to run for the job, telling CNN it is “not my focus.”

While it is clear that Democrats have flipped control of the House of Representatives, the party is awaiting calls in several key races that will determine the size of its majority.

There are 20 House races that CNN has not yet projected, out of a total 435 seats. These include tight contests in Arizona, Colorado, Florida and Minnesota.

Democrats are on the verge of exceeding the 257 House seats at the start of Barack Obama’s presidency and the 258 at the start of Bill Clinton’s tenure.

Senate: Democrats have also secured a majority in the upper chamber, but votes are still being counted in Mississippi and Alaska’s Senate races to determine the final balance of power.

CNN Sightline rates the Mississippi Senate race as neutral. Democratic nominee Scott Colom has grown his narrow lead over Republican Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith as counties bring their counts closer to completion. Several advocacy groups have called for greater transparency in the ballot-counting process.

In Alaska, Sightline favors Democrat Mary Peltola, who has a very slight edge over Republican incumbent Sen. Dan Sullivan as of Saturday afternoon. The race has been roiled by a federal investigation into an alleged Democratic scheme to stack the ballot and confuse voters.

Days before the midterms, federal prosecutors ordered Gerald Heikes, a longshot Senate hopeful in Alaska, to appear before a grand jury with any records he has related to political groups and other candidates in the race, according to documents reviewed by CNN.

It’s hard to overstate how factionalized the West Wing has become in the last several days.

Aides have described a workplace filled with tension and infighting, likening it to the “knives out” days of President Donald Trump’s first term. The president announcing Susie Wiles’ departure yesterday will only accelerate the shift in the balance of power in his inner circle.

As the scrutiny on Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth grew following the GOP’s midterm losses, it only highlighted how fractured his relationship with Wiles had become.

For months, people familiar with the matter said, Wiles had raised concerns about his leadership inside the Pentagon and his role in Trump’s Cabinet. Shortly after the president announced her departure, Hegseth was one of the first senior aides to celebrate Stephen Miller’s ascension to chief of staff.

President Donald Trump said he can work with Democrats without insulting them, in an interview that comes as he prepares for the last two years of his presidency with Republicans no longer in control of Congress.

In the interview with “60 Minutes,” which was taped on Friday to air Sunday, Trump said he could “very easily” stop attacking Democrats for six months if it allowed the two parties to reach a deal on policy.

But just seconds earlier in a clip released by CBS News, the president reverted to one of his familiar labels for members of the opposing party.

“I also call many of them ‘Dumbocrats,’” Trump said.

Trump in recent days has signaled that he’s open to working with Democrats on issues like immigration and economic development.

“I think we can do a lot of things together, actually,” Trump told reporters on Friday. “You know, a lot of them are about common sense, also. And I think you’ll see that.”

Trump has also pledged to use his veto power to push Democrats into bipartisan deals.

Salgado said he left his own “I voted” sticker at his father’s memorial shortly after he cast his ballot and noticed two other people doing the same. By the end of the week, hundreds of stickers covered the memorial.

They include one belonging to James Talarico, the state’s incoming Democratic senator.

Reacting to the Democrats’ rout of the Republican state government in Texas, and pledges by city leaders in Houston to now limit some cooperation with ICE, Salgado said he believes immigrants in the city “will be able to live a little bit more freely, a little bit more at peace.”

Democratic Sen. Chris Van Hollen said today that there should be “no coronation” of the chamber’s next Democratic leader after the party’s sweeping gains in the midterms — though he suggested he was unlikely to seek the post himself.

Looking to the coming days, Van Hollen said it was “really important that people withhold commitments” until they can speak to newly elected Senate Democrats and learn lessons from them. The Maryland Democrat said his highest priority was understanding how the party will use its new power in the Senate to end the war in Iran.

Van Hollen told CNN after he spoke at the event that running for majority leader himself was “not my focus” and that he was instead “seriously kicking the tires on the presidential race.”

Some context: Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer has expressed confidence that he will be reelected as majority leader. But several incoming Senate Democrats have vowed not to support him, and Van Hollen’s comments show not every returning member is immediately onboard.

Iranian hardliners who believe Tehran has already emerged victorious in its war with the United States are seizing on President Donald Trump’s midterm losses to demand that he pay a steeper price for an exit from the conflict: a “new world order” that favors the Islamic Republic.

The influential group of conservatives intensified their rhetoric this week, publicly demanding that Washington not be offered compromises in ongoing negotiations.

After the midterm elections saw Trump’s Republican Party suffer a major defeat, Supreme Leader Mojtaba Khamenei warned in a message Wednesday against the “slightest inclination towards submission” – a caution hardliners believe was directed to Iran’s negotiators.

Trump acknowledged in a call with Fox News that the war in Iran was partly to blame for the Republicans’ midterm losses but Vice President JD Vance was more explicit, saying in a lengthy X post Wednesday that “the reason we lost is the war.”

Those admissions appear to have galvanized Iranian hardliners with conservative politicians and media outlets celebrating Trump’s midterm loss as a win for Iran. A hardline outlet, Raja News, published a column saying the US should not be given a “way out” before it “pays the price” for attacking Iran, and Trump should not be allowed to “escape with a rushed agreement.”

The Democrats’ upcoming simple majority in the Senate will enable them to take actions on environmental issues. But the lack of a veto-proof majority means that Democrats’ power will still be somewhat limited, given the need for President Donald Trump’s signature on legislation.

Here are some of the concrete actions that a Democrat-led Senate could take to advance their environmental priorities.

Investigate the war on wind: The Senate has the authority to launch investigations of the Trump administration’s actions. The White House’s energy policies and extensive regulatory rollbacks of clean air, climate and species protection regulations are likely to be targets.

The budget process: Senate Democrats could seek to prevent the administration’s environmental actions through the appropriations process by attaching language to bills that would prohibit any money from being spent to keep coal-fired power plants open, something that the Energy Department has used emergency orders to do. Democrats could also prohibit spending money to build data centers on public lands or only allow their construction after soliciting extensive local public input, Michael Gerrard, an environmental law professor at Columbia University Law School, said.

Since the Democrats will lack a veto-proof majority in the Senate, however, if Trump vetoes such bills, they will serve more as a signal to voters about Democratic priorities rather than becoming laws.

Roll back rollbacks: Democratic senators can also work to pass bills that would accomplish environmental goals, regardless of whether the president signs it. This could include bills aimed at fully staffing environmental agencies after DOGE reduced headcounts.

Read more here about the impact Dems could have on environmental legislation.

As the dust settled on Election Night, Democratic operatives working to elect James Talarico were surprised by the breadth of his victory across Texas’ 254 counties. But even then, one area stood out.

Kaufman County, southeast of Dallas, is the site of two massive data center projects that have sparked local backlash. The largest city in the county, Forney, is already working to outlaw new data centers within its city limits.

The solidly red county was one of 55 counties where a pro-Talarico super PAC, Lone Star Rising PAC, targeted voters within 5 miles of a proposed or approved data center project. The PAC sent them a series of mail pieces and digital ads blaming the project on the Republican nominee, Ken Paxton.

Talarico carried Kaufman County by 1 percentage point as he notched a striking 12-point victory statewide, helping lead Democrats to statewide victory in Texas for the first time since 1994.

It was one of many examples where backlash to data centers fueled Democrats’ staggering victories in the midterms. From statewide races to local ballot initiatives, voters demonstrated sweeping support for a tougher stance toward data centers, if not outright opposition to their continued development.

About a quarter of voters said AI and data centers were “crucial” to their vote in the midterms, trailing higher priorities such as the cost of living and corruption, according to CNN’s Voter Poll. But when voters were asked about building data centers in their communities, they were overwhelmingly opposed by a roughly 3-to-1 margin.

ALBUQUERQUE – New independent analyses released this week from the Solar Energy Industries Association (SEIA) , Rhodium Group , and Grid Strategies LLC find that Ranking Member of the U.S. Senate Energy and Natural Resources Committee U.S. Senator Martin Heinrich’s (D-N.M.) Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act (BAAJA) would lower household electricity bills by $50 to $78 annually by 2040, reduce power sector emissions by approximately 20 percent, and avoid $54 billion in cumulative public health damages.

The analyses also find that the legislation would accelerate the connection of clean energy projects to the grid and require data centers to pay billions more toward the transmission infrastructure needed to serve their electricity demand.

“Americans are tired of paying more in utility bills while projects that could lower costs sit stuck in the planning phase for years,” Heinrich said. “These independent analyses show exactly what we stand to gain by fixing our broken permitting system: lower electricity bills, cleaner air, healthier communities, and more reliable energy infrastructure. BAAJA will help get more affordable energy connected to the grid while making sure massive energy consumers like data centers pay up. We should be building the infrastructure America needs, not making families foot the bill for permitting delays.”

BAAJA will deliver lower costs and cleaner air for Americans:

Lower electricity bills: Reduce household electricity bills by $50 to $78 annually by 2040, representing a 3–5 percent decrease in electricity prices, according to Rhodium Group.

Reduce pollution: Cut cumulative power sector CO₂ emissions by approximately 20 percent between 2028 and 2035 compared with current law, according to SEIA.

Save billions in health costs: Reduce cumulative public health damages by an estimated $54 billion, according to SEIA.

Accelerate clean energy: Enable an additional 167 Gigawatt Alternating Current (GWac) of net solar capacity additions between 2028 and 2035 compared with current law, according to SEIA.

Connect more clean energy to the grid: Drive an additional 17–249 Gigawatts (GW) of clean energy resources to connect to the grid through 2040, according to Rhodium Group.

Increase clean energy generation: Increase solar and wind generation to 37.4 percent of total power generation, compared with 19.6 percent under the current permitting regime, according to SEIA.

Avoid massive amounts of emissions: Avoid as much as 1.5 gigatons of cumulative emissions through 2040, according to Rhodium Group — equivalent to almost 35 million gasoline-powered cars off the road or taking 39 coal plants offline for a decade.

BAAJA will also make data centers pay their fair share:

Recover $55 billion in transmission costs: Grid Strategies estimates that changes to federal transmission pricing policy under BAAJA could result in data centers contributing approximately $55 billion toward transmission costs over the next decade.

Collect $35 billion more from data centers: That represents approximately $35 billion more than data centers would otherwise pay under current policy.

text:
Legal challenges are mounting against Proposal 2 just days after voters overwhelmingly passed the campaign finance measure.

Big picture view:

Two separate federal lawsuits have been filed, one on Election Night by a conservative policy group, and a brand-new lawsuit filed by major utilities DTE and Consumers Energy.

The message of getting big money out of politics clearly resonated with voters this week, but opponent action was immediate.

On Election Night, the Mackinac Center for Public Policy filed the first federal lawsuit, claiming Prop 2’s campaign finance rules and donor privacy requirements are unconstitutionally broad and vague.

Then yesterday, DTE Energy and Consumers Energy filed a joint federal lawsuit of their own, arguing the measure's ban on political contributions by utilities, their executives, and their family members violates their First Amendment rights to free speech and equal protection.

Both lawsuits name Secretary of State Jocelyn Benson and Attorney General Dana Nessel as defendants.

Prop 2 was written specifically to curb utility spending after years of voter frustration over rising rates and power reliability.

What they're saying:

FOX 2 spoke with an attorney for the Mackinac Center about their Election Night filing.

"The new rules that are created, they gather a lot of speech, a lot of vague definitions of what’s covered and what isn’t," said attorney Patrick Wright. "A lot of reporting requirements, they can lead to criminal prosecutions and so we are concerned this could be a nasty tool in a partisan hunt and to keep people from participating in discussions about politics, policy and elections."

"You know honestly, I think it’s probably got a pretty good chance of being able to block the proposition," said Oakland University Professor Dr. Peter F. Trumbore. "The Supreme Court, really since 2010 with the Citizens United decision, has essentially said two fundamental things. The first is that corporations are people and, therefore, they have the same rights that you and I have as individuals, and second, that money equals speech."

The other side:

In their new lawsuit filed yesterday, DTE issued this statement to FOX 2:

"DTE has long supported the right of Michiganders to lawfully participate in the political process and engage on issues that affect their families and communities regardless of their job. Our company is made up of 10,000 Michiganders whose fundamental right to free speech is under attack. They deserve the same rights as their friends and neighbors to support the candidates and issues they care about."

authors: Everlyn Tan, Jeremie Eliahou Ontiveros, Xiaopeng Laoban, Dylan Patel

text:
Stargate Abilene has become the symbol of America’s AI buildout. It is a gigawatt-scale campus on the Texas plains built for OpenAI. China has campuses on a similar scale, though few people outside the country have had a look inside. In September, we visited one, and we found the speed, scale, ultra low cost, and deep vertical integration astonishing.

During the trip, we toured Inner Mongolia, China’s fastest-growing AI datacenter region. It's the “West Texas” of China, but while the Lone Star State faces its highest ever anti-datacenter sentiment, Inner Mongolia is accelerating and faces no such backlash.

Our main stop was Galaxy, a campus in Ulanqab planned for up to 800MW of IT capacity.

Galaxy is about the size of Abilene’s core campus. Its first 120MW phase was delivered within a year at a fifth of US costs. All four phases are built-to-suit for two internet giants.

When we visited, the rest of the campus was still a busy construction site, and the surrounding Chahar High-tech Zone had nearly 30,000 construction workers on site across 22 datacenter projects according to a local report. As we noted in our primer on the China datacenter market, with this much labor available, Chinese datacenters rarely take a fully modular approach, yet construction costs keep falling. We take a closer look at why in this report.

The datacenter is owned by Envision Group, a renewable systems integrator with more than 100GW of wind turbines installed worldwide. It came to datacenters from energy management, a path many others are taking today. Yet it is one of the most vertically integrated players we have ever seen.

Beyond running the datacenter, Envision builds its own wind farms and a dedicated power line to supply it. Its blade factory sits just across the road from the Galaxy datacenter campus, with finished blades stacked in the yard.

Inside the campus, it designed and integrated the low-voltage power modules and the 800V system, manufactured the battery storage that smooths the load, and co-designed the prefabricated substation.

In one 5MW hall, we saw the 800V system at work. Solid-state transformers (SSTs) take 10kV AC from the grid and convert it straight to 800V DC for the racks. This removes the low-voltage transformers, UPS and rectifier stages in between. The same architecture is still on the US roadmap, as we outlined in our 800V DC deep dive.

In China, datacenters have been running on DC power for almost two decades, from China Telecom’s 240V DC pilots in 2007 to Alibaba’s Panama power system in 2018. Today, roughly a quarter of Chinese datacenters built in the past decade run on DC, while about 97% of US datacenters still use AC UPS. An SST is a natural next step on that path, and we cover the evolution and the pilot in detail later in this report.

On cooling, Galaxy uses a design common in Inner Mongolia. Liquid- and air-cooled servers share one water loop, with no central chiller plant. Nvidia says Vera Rubin can run on 45°C water without chillers, yet most datacenters in the US keep one for air-cooled equipment and for the flexibility to shift between the two. Galaxy drops the central chiller and keeps much of that flexibility, a design that has been running at scale in northern China for years.

In this report, we use what we saw on the site visit to show how China builds hyperscale datacenters today, with a deep dive on each of the topics above. Many questions still open on the US roadmap find a reference point here.

Our next report will take a wider view of Inner Mongolia’s datacenter market. The region has lined up 25GW of announced datacenter projects, including several gigawatt-scale campuses. Many reports picture it as a land of empty datacenter halls. Our data tells a different story. Few have asked what limits datacenter development there. We look at each constraint, from power to land and water. Stay tuned.

The SemiAnalysis China Datacenter Model

This trip was part of our ongoing fieldwork for the SemiAnalysis China Datacenter Model, the China counterpart to our global SemiAnalysis Datacenter Model.

It tracks over 1,000 facilities across 70+ operators, with quarterly delivery curves through 2032, a lease signing and delivery tracker, and EDWC hub and cluster analytics. Every project in our report is tracked in the model.

Contact sales@semianalysis.com for more information.

China’s Stargate campus

Envision comes to datacenters as a renewable systems integrator. Beyond building wind turbines, it designs, integrates, and manages power systems across the full chain, from generation and storage to computing loads. Its affiliate, Envision AESC, develops and integrates batteries, energy storage systems, and the power electronics and software that link them.

Inner Mongolia has far more wind than its existing industry and population can use, so policy encourages bringing new demand to where the renewable resources are. In Chifeng, Envision built a 2GW off-grid wind, solar and storage system that feeds a green ammonia plant. The system runs entirely on power electronics, with no synchronous generator. A small pilot datacenter built with Tencent’s modular T-Block units runs on the same system. Galaxy is a larger application of the same idea.

This is a pattern we see across China right now. Industrial groups with an edge in energy, construction or electrical equipment are pivoting into AI infrastructure. Project returns are thin, with IRRs squeezed hard, so the reward often comes from elsewhere. For Envision, datacenters create new demand for the power and equipment it already produces. For many listed companies, the draw is the stock market.

Of these newcomers, Envision is one of the most ambitious. Its datacenter plans in Inner Mongolia add up to 3GW. Galaxy is the first. Its initial phase was delivered in August 2026, and the full campus is expected to be completed by the end of 2027.

The scale of the campus invites comparison with Stargate’s flagship campus in Abilene, Texas. Crusoe began building Abilene in mid-2024 and leased it to Oracle, which runs it for OpenAI. Crusoe describes the eight-building campus as 1.2GW of power, which comes to about 820MW of critical IT capacity, on par with the 800MW planned at Galaxy. That makes Galaxy one of the largest single campuses in China. Our SemiAnalysis Datacenter Model also tracks an expansion phase that Crusoe plans to add, powered behind the meter, which takes the whole Abilene site to 1.5GW of IT capacity. Galaxy also has room to grow. If the wind turbine factory next to the campus is converted, a later expansion phase could take the campus to ~1GW.

In addition to scale, the two share a starting point. Both are developed by companies with roots in energy, and both were planned around their own power. Abilene draws on the grid and on gas turbines on site, while Galaxy relies largely on wind.

What sets Galaxy apart from Abilene, and what draws our attention, is its vertical integration.

Own wind for its own load

Galaxy’s power comes through a model China calls source-grid-load-storage (”SGLS”). Under this model, a project builds its own wind and/or solar farm, battery storage and datacenter, and links them through a dedicated line instead of the public grid.

For hyperscalers, the appeal of an SGLS project is long-term power at a largely fixed cost. Power from wind and solar also counts toward green targets.

Inner Mongolia holds about 57% of China’s usable wind resources. A wind farm here runs on average about 2,800 full-load hours a year, a capacity factor of roughly 32%. Ulanqab is windier, with a capacity factor of 35–40%. That sets the starting point for how much of an SGLS project’s power can come from wind.

For Galaxy, Envision aims to supply over 60% of the first two phases’ power use with its own wind farms. Three factors make this possible:

Siting. Envision chose windy sites, even though they sit about two hours’ drive from the campus. The two wind farms are about 80km apart, which cuts the hours in a year when neither has wind.

Scale. The wind farms have a combined 420MW of installed capacity, about 1.75 times the 240MW datacenter load. With this oversizing, even light-wind hours can still cover much of the load.

Storage. A 4-hour battery storage system shifts power from windy hours into calm ones. Most SGLS projects add storage too, but Envision makes its own storage systems and runs them on its own software, which we detail in the next section.

The chart below shows how each factor raises the wind share, using illustrative curves.

Panel 1 starts with a simple case: 1MW of wind for every 1MW of datacenter load. A good site in Ulanqab produces as much power in a year as running flat out for about 3,500 hours. To keep it simple, the panel shows the farm at full output for 3,500 hours and at zero for the rest of the year. Wind covers 40% of the year’s power.

Panel 2 shows a more realistic picture. Wind output goes up and down, so the panel sorts every hour of the year from windiest to calmest. The farm is the same size as the load, so it never produces more than the campus uses. All its power gets used, and wind still covers 40%.

Panel 3 doubles the wind farm. Output in every hour doubles too, so even light-wind hours now cover much of the load, and wind’s share rises to about 55%. The cost shows in the gray area. In windy hours, the farm produces more than the campus can use, and that power must be stored or curtailed.

Panels 4 and 5 show what can be added on top. A 4-hour battery moves some surplus into the hours after the wind drops, though it cannot help much when the wind stays calm for days. Better matching between wind output and load can push the share even higher.

The table at the bottom shows how the result changes with wind quality, the size of the wind farm relative to the load, and how fully the datacenter is used.

Inside the campus: developer, designer and integrator

Beyond pairing energy production with consumption, Envision is also integrated inside the campus, acting as more than a developer and operator. The chart below shows its three roles, in three colors.

The first is as a manufacturer. Envision designs its own turbines and develops the converters and control software. The battery energy storage systems (BESS) at both the datacenter campus and the wind farm come from its affiliate AESC, which builds every major part in-house, from cells to power conversion and software, so the whole system can be tuned and tested together at the factory before shipping. Most vendors cover only one part of the system (high voltage, low voltage or generators), so getting the parts to work together falls to on-site commissioning, which can take 3–6 months. Envision’s factory pre-configuration has become its core selling point.

The second role goes beyond Envision’s traditional business into the datacenter space. For Galaxy, Envision designed and integrated the low-voltage power modules and the 800V SST system.

800V DC is the architecture that Nvidia is pushing for its next generation of high-density racks, as Kyber racks at around 600kW cannot be served efficiently at today’s voltages. In the US, the industry is still early on this path. SSTs that convert medium-voltage AC straight into 800V DC are the final step. Galaxy’s SST pilot is only 5MW, but it already runs 800V DC all the way to the rack at a live hyperscaler site. We discuss this in detail shortly.

Lastly, Envision co-designed the prefabricated substation sitting inside the campus. The substation is built and tested as modules in the factory while civil work goes on at the site, then shipped and connected on site. This takes less than 3 months, versus about 6 months for a conventional indoor substation.

Today, vertical integration on its own does not lead to hyperscaler orders, but two trends suggest it could matter more over time.

First, access to power is becoming central to datacenter development. In the US, developers bridge the power gap with on-site gas turbines, fuel cells and batteries. In Southeast Asia, governments have been pushing developers to bring their own power this year. Malaysia now requires datacenters to source at least 30% of their power from renewables and encourages on-site generation. In China, approvals increasingly favor projects that pair compute with green power, under the national push for “Compute Power Coordination.” Across different markets, access to energy is becoming part of what a datacenter developer sells.

Second, the power architecture from the grid connection to the rack is being redesigned. In the US, the industry is moving toward higher-voltage DC power, while battery backup units (BBUs) and BESS are starting to take over the role of UPS. The technology roadmap is not settled yet, but the shift looks set to continue, giving integrated players room to compete differently from traditional developers.

These trends have drawn other players onto a similar path. The closest case is the tie-up between VNET, CATL and Zhongheng Electric.

VNET is a leading colocation operator, CATL is the world’s largest EV battery maker, and Zhongheng Electric is China’s largest supplier of HVDC power systems for datacenters, working with both Alibaba and ByteDance.

In 2026, CATL became VNET’s largest shareholder and announced a deal to take a 49% stake in Zhongheng Electric’s controlling shareholder. It has since agreed with VNET to jointly develop gigawatt-scale datacenter campuses, and separately with Zhongheng to work on datacenter power systems. Between them, VNET covers the datacenter side, CATL leads green power and storage, and Zhongheng brings power conversion inside the hall.

CATL is also one of DeepSeek’s largest outside investors, which extends its reach downstream to the model layer.

Where Envision builds most of the pieces in-house, CATL links them through partnerships and equity stakes.

China’s datacenter market is highly competitive. Rents have roughly halved over the past five years, to about $40/kW/month excluding power. Capex has fallen about 25% over the same period, to less than $3mm per MW. Power in Inner Mongolia costs about $0.055/kWh all-in, among the lowest in the world.

In a market like this, owning more of the value chain is one way to differentiate, a playbook familiar from China’s EV market, where players like BYD make much of what goes into their cars.

It is too early to say whether vertical integration will become a meaningful advantage in China’s datacenter market. For now, it gives integrated players more control over cost and schedule, but hyperscalers still choose vendors mainly on resources and track record. That could change as power becomes harder to secure and the power system inside the datacenter is redesigned.

Behind the paywall, we walk through how Galaxy was built and designed in detail.

On speed and cost, we follow Galaxy from land auction to customer acceptance and explain why capex keeps falling.

On power, we trace how China took a different path from the US, adopting 240V DC in its datacenters years ago, and walk through Galaxy’s live 5MW pilot. A larger version is planned for the next phase.

On cooling, we take apart a design common in northern China that offers one answer to the chiller debate in the US.

text:
Blue-wave politics could lift the renewable-energy outlook for investors

The midterm elections gave climate-friendly Democrats control of both chambers, raising expectations for a revival of the clean-energy policy agenda. Industry executives and investors say the result could reduce political interference in renewable-energy incentives and extend the long-term economics of wind, solar and battery storage.

Barclays analysts said the shift potentially reduces the risk of further political interference and supports the long-term economics of U.S. wind, solar and storage investments. The note also points to the possibility of more constructive bipartisan energy policy discussions.

Policy mechanics remain unsettled. A bipartisan permitting-reform bill awaits Senate action, with some progressive Democrats signaling a desire to delay votes until the new Congress convenes in January to rewrite provisions favoring renewables over fossil fuels. The outcome could influence the pace of project approvals and the flow of incentives.

Investment and funding trends point to continued interest in climate solutions. GIIN’s 2026 survey found that 56% of impact funds are invested in clean energy and 25% plan to increase those allocations over the next five years. That framework, in combination with a broader push into climate infrastructure, underpins investor interest in the sector.

"There are many different approaches that could lead impact investors to be thinking about clean energy investments," said Amit Bouri, retiring as CEO of the Global Impact Investing Network. The GIIN survey results reflect a broad appetite across asset classes for climate-aligned opportunities.

Hannah Hess, director of energy and climate at Rhodium, noted that "investment has consistently been very strong in solar and storage at the utility scale," aided by evolving tax-credit timelines. She described the current environment as one where policy design and project timelines increasingly align to support utility-scale deployments.

Goldman Sachs offered a perspective on data centers and renewables, saying that "While U.S. data-center development faces increasing political and community opposition, project data and our updated capacity estimates suggest that the growth outlook through 2027 remains largely unchanged." The firm frames data-center demand as a potential tailwind for grid upgrades and renewable-energy integration.

Market and project metrics cited in the context reinforce the momentum. In the second quarter, investments in clean energy and transportation totaled about $75 billion, a quarterly high that rose 22% from the prior quarter. Over the four quarters ending in mid-year, investment across renewable-energy manufacturing, deployment, non-fossil-fuel vehicles, building electrification and carbon-management technology totaled roughly $277 billion.

The supply chain for renewables has expanded, with manufacturing capacity for solar modules, wind blades and nacelles up about 50% by the third quarter from the first quarter of the previous year, according to industry reporting. Across the past year, funding has supported a broad mix of public markets, private credit and infrastructure investments in climate solutions.

On the policy horizon, the One Big Beautiful Bill Act altered the sunsets and deadlines for federal clean-energy credits, hastening some provisions compared with the Biden administration’s Inflation Reduction Act. The shift in timing increases the likelihood that projects can claim credits if construction or completion milestones are met within revised windows.

Despite the policy ambiguities and potential shifts in state-level approvals, the overarching trend suggested by the involved investors is that the midterm results could create a more predictable environment for clean-energy capital. The combination of advancing projects, resilient supply chains and a continuing flow of capital supports a constructive outlook for renewable-energy assets and related technologies in the coming years. The balance of incentives, rate structures and project timelines will likely determine the pace of deployment as the sector navigates a dynamic political landscape.

In this context, climate-tech investing remains active across multiple streams, including public-equity funds, private markets and project-based financing, with ongoing attention to grid resilience, storage and advanced generation technologies.
