title: The Crunch Time Changes to the Senate Permitting Deal, Explained - Heatmap News
description:
We now have the updated final text of the bipartisan Senate permitting deal.
First, transmission projects will now be able to use the bill’s cost allocation formula even if they don’t use the federal backstop authority.
Under the new bill text, agencies will be explicitly allowed to revoke or alter permits “in response to an order by a court”.
The Wilderness Society, whose president is Tracy Stone-Manning, Biden’s former director of the Bureau of Land Management, released a statement shortly after the new bill text was released reaffirming its opposition.
“Americans deserve permitting reform that isn’t crafted behind closed doors and rushed to the Senate floor,” Manning said in a statement.
text:
We now have the updated final text of the bipartisan Senate permitting deal. Will it be enough to get the bill across the finish line?

On Saturday morning, senators released a reworked version of the Bipartisan Affordability and American Jobs Act. This version, known as a “manager’s amendment” under parliamentary procedure, aims to address many of the concerns and criticisms raised about the bill and will become the official legislative text that ultimately gets a vote in the Senate. There’s something in these changes for everyone – environmentalists, tribes, utilities – but it remains to be seen if they put the bill into a Goldilocks zone.

Let’s walk through some of the most significant changes. There are a lot of changes, and we’re sure people will spend the coming weeks poring over them, but here are a few key ones.

Transmission and Utilities

The amendment preserves — and even strengthens — many of the bill’s most important (and praised) transmission provisions, while addressing and easing some of the loudest Republican criticisms of the bill.

The new text leaves the bill’s core transmission mechanisms intact: Every grid region will have to run a long-term planning process with its neighbors, overseen by the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission, focused on how it can build more interregional lines. The bill lays out how these new power lines should be paid for, via a cost allocation formula that says customers who benefit from the lines need to pay for them. And it creates a new federal siting backstop, which allows the federal government to step in and approve the route for a line if a state has refused to do so.

The amendment deals with one of the provisions that faced the most criticism from former Republican regulators and ends one — but not all — of the bill’s mandates for vertically integrated monopoly utilities, which are largely in the Southeast.

In return, it strengthens the bill’s federal backstop siting provision for transmission lines, and it makes the overall bill more useful for transmission developers. It also clarifies that transmission developers can use some of the bill’s expedited powers without needing to use all of them.

“I think there’s some really good improvements in [the new text], and they provide more flexibility for more types of projects to go through,” said Rob Gramlich, a longtime advocate of federal transmission reform and the president of Grid Strategies, a power sector consulting firm.

In the original bill, a transmission developer could apply for state permits and the FERC federal backstop permit at the same time. A former Republican FERC Commissioner Mark Christie had savaged that provision, arguing recently in Utility Dive that it “effectively renders the state proceeding meaningless, and states will perceive it exactly that way.”

Now, for some advocates, rendering the state process moot was the whole point. But it also wasn’t clear whether developers would ever actually go to FERC and states simultaneously. Doing so would shove a finger in the eye of state regulators, essentially telling them, “We can do this the easy way or the hard way.” The amendment removes the possibility of a simultaneous process; now developers must go to states for a year before they apply for the federal backstop.

The new version of the bill also exempts vertically integrated utilities that aren’t in an electricity market from an otherwise mandatory new process that will require utilities to plan their long-term transmission and their power plant expansion at the same time. That new process is inspired by the planning process used in the Southwest Power Pool, a Midwestern electricity market Midwestern grid.

The Southeast’s monopoly utilities, which are vertically integrated and don’t participate in a regional transmission organization, had disliked that provision, and it wasn’t clear the bill as written actually worked for their operations. That requirement has now been removed from the bill. Utilities won another victory by preserving existing rights of first refusal to build transmission infrastructure in federal law.

But they didn’t win every fight. These utilities will still be subject to the mandate requiring them to participate in an interregional planning process for transmission.

And the utilities will remain subject to a provision, particularly praised by anti-monopoly advocates, that allows states and FERC to exercise oversight over local transmission projects that can drive up electricity costs. The new bill clarifies that state public utility regulators are responsible for asking FERC to investigate these types of projects, and that a utility can invite scrutiny even if it’s replacing an old line, not just building a new one.

“I am relieved that the section survived generally, given what a target this was for utility lobbying. It was strengthened significantly by covering replacement of local facilities in addition to new-build,” David Pomerantz, the executive director of the utility watchdog the Energy and Policy Institute, said in a statement.

In return, Democrats secured a few big changes in the bill that could benefit transmission developers. First, transmission projects will now be able to use the bill’s cost allocation formula even if they don’t use the federal backstop authority. Second, transmission developers will be able to use the bill’s cost allocation formula for only part of their projects.

This makes the bill better in a few ways for transmission developers. First, a developer could get a route entirely approved by the states without having to come up with a new way to pay for it — they can use the formula that’s already in the bill. It also means a power line could use the formula to monetize one of its benefits to the grid without using them all. That could sweeten the economics for projects meant to, say, arbitrage power between two regions, allowing it to make money off its reliability benefits without altering its broader economics.

The amendment also clarifies that the new federal backstop siting authority applies to state-owned land. That closes a potential loophole in which a state government could acquire land from a property owner in order to block a federally approved project from getting built.

The bill also makes some technical changes to the 230-kilovolt floor for projects that can use the federal backstop. It establishes that a line using advanced conductoring technology — which generally allows more electricity at lower voltage — can use the backstop even if it’s not at least 230 kilovolts. But it must have a throughput roughly similar to what a conventional line of 230 kilovolts would have.

The amendment also makes it clear that a utility can’t decline to upgrade a piece of infrastructure — even one at lower voltage — in order to block a transmission line. In 2021, the utility NextEra had fought a major power line in Maine because it required the utility to upgrade a single power circuit at its Seabrook nuclear plant in New Hampshire.

These provisions broadly strengthen the most popular parts of the bill and may address some concerns from southeastern utilities, which could have torpedoed the bill in the House of Representatives.

Certainty, Preservation and Data Centers

At the same time, new text attempts to assuage opposition in both the environmental and tribal advocacy spaces, and it’s undeniable that on first blush, the manager’s amendment does address complaints from those camps about the bill. But as we’ll explain however, it’s unclear if this will be good enough for either community to lay down their arms.

First, Senate negotiators clearly took complaints about the “project certainty” provision seriously, including by dealing with language that would allegedly protect unlawful actions. Under the new bill text, agencies will be explicitly allowed to revoke or alter permits “in response to an order by a court”. The prior text of the bill did not grant federal agencies this explicit jurisdiction and said it could only rely on court orders to make those permit changes if a judge required it. As our colleague Emily Pontecorvo recently wrote, some environmental lawyers were concerned that this original text would inadvertently protect individual permits granted under policies that violated the law.

Other changes are similarly geared towards addressing complaints in the environmental legal space. The original text of the bill allowed companies to sue the federal government for “disparate treatment” against their industry, which would theoretically assist renewable energy companies gain legal leverage against the Trump administration’s permitting freeze. However, the old text used a 5-year baseline of past projects for determining “disparate treatment,” which could mean the president’s anti-wind and pro-fossil actions weren’t built into the baseline. The new bill extends that baseline to 10 years, potentially diluting the influence of Trumpian permitting practices over the next administration.

New language would explicitly stipulate that court settlements brought under these lawsuits must be approved by a court, an apparent nod to claims from critics that this provision could encourage more offshore wind buyouts.

The new text also cuts out or modifies reforms to the National Historic Preservation Act geared towards addressing complaints from Native American tribes. It strikes a controversial attempt to define “property of traditional religious or cultural importance” that was in the original text, and it eliminates a much-maligned provision that would let the Interior Secretary assume the role of a tribal historic preservation officer in certain cases.

These changes were insufficient to thaw the bloc of tribes opposed to the bill. The 106 Coalition, a group of tribal organizations including the National College of American Indians, sent a statement to media saying they’ll still oppose the bill and want the entire section of NHPA changes removed. The leader of the Coalition of Large Tribes, which has pushed for technical fixes to the bill but not opposed it outright, said in a statement it was “grateful to see many positive changes for tribes” but added there was “still room for improvement.”

Lastly, the new version of the bill adds another provision to address concerns that it doesn’t do enough to address the national backlash to data centers, which opponents have argued is necessary.

As we’ve explained, the bill already would create the toughest measure against data centers ever enacted – a ratepayer protection program that would let states and utilities require data centers to pay full freight for system upgrades. And now the bill would additionally create a new federal Data Center Community Assistance Program within the Energy Department whereby local communities could request assistance from agencies to get information and technical expertise on how data centers work and what impacts specific projects could have on their areas. The language mirrors legislation introduced last month by Sens. John Curtis of Utah and Lisa Blunt Rochester of Delaware.

Such a program could be a big deal. But it’s important to emphasize that the text leaves a lot of details to be worked out. It does not say how this program would be set up within the Energy Department and the provision does not explicitly lay out funding authorization language.

The amendment also closes a loophole that might have allowed data centers with behind-the-meter natural gas power plants to profit by selling excess power to the grid. The original bill contained a provision meant to force grids to allow more residential batteries or the creation of virtual power plants. But that provision, as written, could have applied to behind-the-meter gas plants at data centers. The new text clarifies that the requirement only applies to resources below 5 megawatts, which is smaller than a data center power source.

What’s Next

It remains to be seen whether these changes and the myriad other tweaks to the bill’s project certainty and historic preservation titles will win over lawmakers previously hesitant to vote yes.

The Wilderness Society, whose president is Tracy Stone-Manning, Biden’s former director of the Bureau of Land Management, released a statement shortly after the new bill text was released reaffirming its opposition. “Americans deserve permitting reform that isn’t crafted behind closed doors and rushed to the Senate floor,” Manning said in a statement. Meanwhile, House Natural Resources Jared Huffman provided comments to Punchbowl News reacting to the text that said some of the changes to the permit certainty provision represented an “improvement” but “we could improve it further in this and other areas with a hearing and a more open negotiation process with more Democrats in the room.”

It’s unclear these voices would ultimately ever support this bill. “Manager’s [amendment] does a good job of accounting for the stated concerns of anybody looking to get to yes,” Liam Donovan, a veteran GOP political strategist, wrote on the social network X.

description:
An October University of Houston poll cited by Reuters found that 79% of likely Texas voters supported limits on the number of data centers.
Also read: Oracle, Bloom in focus after Trump's data center power push The split screen is the story.
NTT DATA shows Bloom Energy can follow the builders So the overseas win is bigger than the stock's reaction suggests.
More Bloom Energy: Another AI power stock plunges 11% despite earnings beat Morgan Stanley spots 3 game-changing Bloom Energy opportunities Bloom Energy CEO delivers stark warning on America's power demand Capital may move before the politics settle.
Bloom Energy stock now trades below a cautious target Bloom is a $51 billion company whose stock has become shorthand for how fast data centers can get electricity.
text:
Most people never think about where the internet physically lives. In Texas this year, voters had to, as server farms spread faster than officials could track them. Their answer hangs over Bloom Energy (BE), a company that sells power systems to exactly those buildings.

That unease found a candidate. Democrat Gina Hinojosa ousted Gov. Greg Abbott on Tuesday, November 3, 2026, after pledging to crack down on data center growth, Reuters reported. An October University of Houston poll cited by Reuters found that 79% of likely Texas voters supported limits on the number of data centers.

Two days later, NTT DATA agreed to deploy 900 megawatts of Bloom fuel cells, Bloom's largest international project to date, according to a press release. Yet the stock finished down about 15% in a week.

Also read: Oracle, Bloom in focus after Trump's data center power push

The split screen is the story. Bloom is winning abroad as Texas turns against the buildings its fuel cells serve.

Texas hearings showed the fight was never just about power

The backlash reached the state Capitol months before Election Day. On Monday, July 27, 2026, the Texas Senate Finance Committee held a hearing on the state's data center sales tax break.

Lawmakers once expected that break to cost about $14.6 million over the 2014 to 2015 budget cycle, Texas Public Radio reported. Projections now put it near $3.3 billion for the 2028 to 2029 budget cycle, turning a tax question into a trust question.

The hearing exposed a bigger blind spot. Officials acknowledged that the state does not regulate where data centers are built.

Brad Reynolds, the comptroller's chief revenue estimator, was asked if more projects existed than the state knew about. "We don't really know what's going on," he said.

On Monday, August 3, Abbott halted new data center grid connections and ordered an audit expected to wrap up by year-end, Reuters reported. Hinojosa promised something broader: a ban on all data center approvals until the Legislature passes new laws.

Bloom Energy's onsite pitch answers the wrong question

For Bloom, that difference matters. Its fuel cells generate electricity on a customer's own site. Chief Commercial Officer Aman Joshi said in the NTT release that fast power offers an "accelerated path to revenue."

On paper, a freeze on grid hookups is the problem Bloom exists to solve. ERCOT, the state's grid operator, was tracking more than 400 gigawatts of data center connection requests, according to Reuters. Self-powered data centers can sidestep much of that line.

However, Hinojosa's promise works differently. A ban on approvals decides whether a data center gets built at all, not where its power comes from. Nothing in her pledge, as Reuters described it, exempts projects that make their own electricity.

The release seems aware of that. It stresses minimal water use and quiet operation, language aimed at the communities now deciding elections.

NTT DATA shows Bloom Energy can follow the builders

So the overseas win is bigger than the stock's reaction suggests. The release says the partnership is designed to reach gigawatt scale across NTT DATA's global data center portfolio.

More Bloom Energy:

Another AI power stock plunges 11% despite earnings beat

Morgan Stanley spots 3 game-changing Bloom Energy opportunities

Bloom Energy CEO delivers stark warning on America's power demand

Capital may move before the politics settle. Alpha Compute CEO Brittany Kaiser said developers without signed contracts and financing are more likely to look elsewhere, including Canada, Mexico and Europe, Reuters reported. A supplier that ships wherever builders go is better placed than one tied to a single state's permit office.

Even so, the release gives no dollar value and names no sites. Shipments start in 2027, which may help explain why investors shrugged it off.

Bloom Energy stock now trades below a cautious target

Bloom is a $51 billion company whose stock has become shorthand for how fast data centers can get electricity. The shorthand took a beating, sliding from $222.30 on Thursday, October 29, to $167.52 on Thursday, November 5.

Shares bounced 3.4% on Friday, November 6, 2026, to close at $173.24. The close leaves them about 51% below their 52-week high of $351.28, yet more than double the 52-week low of $75.70.

Wall Street has not walked away. The 29 analysts tracked by StockAnalysis rate Bloom a Buy, with an average price target of $283.85, about 64% above Friday's close.

Yet one cautious call stands out. Wells Fargo analyst Praneeth Satish kept a Hold rating on Monday, October 26, 2026, while raising the price target to $182 from $176. The stock trades below even that mark.

Here the NTT deal earns its keep. It will not change this year's results, but it gives the stock a growth path beyond Austin's reach.

The bigger question arrives in January, when Hinojosa takes office and lawmakers return to Austin. Investors will watch whether a Texas moratorium treats self-powered data centers like any other project. If it does, the next chapter of onsite power may be written far from Texas, and Bloom just signed its biggest one abroad.

description:
Well, it’s now time for another energy focused campaign to capture our attention – The 35 by 35 pledge.
The 35 by 35 electrification pledge was announced recently by the United Nations’ COP 31 Presidency, alongside Australia’s Minister for Climate Change and Energy and COP31 President of Negotiations Chris Bowen.
The 35 by 35 pledge plans to increase electricity’s share of global final energy consumption from just over 20 per cent today to 35 per cent by 2035.
There is a lot of upside in meeting the 35 by 35 electrification target.
And to feed this growing demand we must step up the expansion of least cost renewable energy and storage.
text:
It's almost 100 years since consumers were captured by the ‘Now you’re cooking with gas’ campaign.

Almost half a century later, the electricity industry in Australia had a go with its own ‘Switched on Living’ drive, while who could forget the natural gas ‘Living Flame’ ads on rotation across Australian TV screens throughout the 1980s.

Well, it’s now time for another energy focused campaign to capture our attention – The 35 by 35 pledge.

The 35 by 35 electrification pledge was announced recently by the United Nations’ COP 31 Presidency, alongside Australia’s Minister for Climate Change and Energy and COP31 President of Negotiations Chris Bowen.

The 35 by 35 mantra was also adopted by the Electrify Now campaign in Australia with the support of 30 industry bodies, consumer groups, and trade unions.

It was part of the global Electrify Now campaign, launched during London Climate Action Week.

35 by 35 is memorable in its phrasing, but also timely in helping to focus our attention on the productivity potential of electrification here in Australia.

The 35 by 35 pledge plans to increase electricity’s share of global final energy consumption from just over 20 per cent today to 35 per cent by 2035.

For Australia, it’s hoped that it will mobilise action to accelerate electrification across transport, industry – including the resources sector and data centres, as well as residential and commercial buildings.

Australia’s mining sector consumes about 10 percent of the country’s energy, yet it only sources about one third of that energy from electricity.

Demand for critical, strategic and rare earth minerals is expected to drive continued growth in the sector, meaning there are significant opportunities to increase electricity’s share of total energy use.

There are also large gains to be made in the electrification of transport in Australia. The sector accounts for about 22 percent of the country’s carbon emissions, but that has started to fall with the rapid uptake of electric vehicles.

The growth in energy use from data centres in Australia is expected to outpace every other sector by a long way. Data centres currently use about three percent of all electricity use across the National Electricity Market. That share is expected to increase seven fold by 2050.

There is a lot of upside in meeting the 35 by 35 electrification target.

Roughly 90 percent of all the oil and diesel used on our roads, farms and across industrial processes in Australia is imported. In a volatile world, this leaves us vulnerable to shortages, price spikes and the associated economy-wide impacts.

Increasing the use of electricity generated on shore across these sectors improves our energy security and independence.

It’s also cheaper. According to a report recently released by the International Energy Agency, greater electrification could cut the world’s energy import bills by more than USD 500 billion every year.

Lastly, as we replace carbon intensive sources of energy with electricity made from renewable sources, there is a comparable reduction in carbon emissions and pollution. That’s good for human health, and the health of the planet.

The environmental impacts of a warming planet are very real issues for Australia’s neighbours in the Pacific, and this forms a key part of its policy platform at COP 31.

This includes improving Pacific nations’ access to climate finance and putting more focus on resilience and oceans as a critical pillar of climate action.

According to the Green Building Council of Australia, on our existing trajectory, electricity will account for around 25% of final energy demand by 2035.

To reach 35%, we need to electrify around four times faster than we are today.

And to feed this growing demand we must step up the expansion of least cost renewable energy and storage. However, as we were reminded recently by the Australian Energy Market Operator, we won’t be successful without the support of a bigger and stronger electricity grid.

This grid expansion plays two equally essential roles. It connects new sources of renewable generation and storage with the cities and regions that need it.

Secondly, it strengthens our electricity system through more interconnection.

Australia’s renewable energy and storage credentials are well known.

According to the Clean Energy Council, Australia’s utility scale and home storage market is one the largest in the world, with only China and the United States higher up the list.

Rates of household solar installations in Australia are the highest in the world, and the commercial and industrial solar market is expected to hit new heights following new government programs and support.

Renewables are consistently supplying around 50 percent of our national energy demands, with states like Tasmania and South Australia increasingly supplied by 100 percent renewable generation.

Interestingly, new data released this month from Rystad Energy also showed that wholesale electricity prices in Australia were lower than almost every other major economy for the first three quarters of 2026.

However, to achieve greater electrification, keep a lid on prices, and reduce carbon emissions we need our grid to step up.

The National Electricity Market is one of the world’s longest interconnected power systems, stretching around 44,000 kilometres and connecting with a distribution network spanning 764,000 km.

However, it lacks connection between states and from new generation heavy regions.

It’s estimated that only 5-10% of total generation in the NEM is traded across state borders each year. This means network faults, demand spikes or generation shortfalls can leave states vulnerable to higher prices or reliability concerns.

AEMO has now forecast that more than 6,000 km of new electricity transmission lines will be required across the country by 2050 – a 14 percent expansion. It has highlighted 20 critical projects that are required – eight of those are currently underway.

About 40% of the additional length is needed to strengthen the connection between states, adding reliability and stability to electricity supply across the NEM.

The other 60% connects new capacity in state based Renewable Energy Zones to energy-intensive industries in regional hubs, or demand centres in big cities.

A more connected grid means less curtailment and more sharing of existing renewable generation. It means we won’t have to over-build local generation.

A modern and more connected electricity grid also comes with new grid forming capabilities, which adds system strength and builds greater resilience.

So this grid expansion in Australia is not just critical to meeting the COP31 35 by 35 electrification target, it’s also key to realising energy security, affordability and sustainability benefits for the country.

text:
The chancellor has said "some of the best innovation anywhere in Britain" happens in Rotherham.

John Healey was speaking on a visit to a global manufacturer in the town where he also met some of the country's first "AI apprentices".

Since becoming chancellor he has also highlighted the Advanced Manufacturing Park, built on the site of the Orgreave Colliery and home to big global brands like Rolls-Royce and Boeing, as an example of how the north could be reindustrialised.

He said the success of the park also means young people are able to find skilled jobs close to where they live.

A recent report raised concerns that Rotherham has the fewest suitable entry-level jobs for young people in Britain.

The findings, published by the Institute for Public Policy Research (IPPR), said the town had 46 online vacancies for every 1,000 young people, while the Cotswold district council area, for example, had 288.

On a visit to ASSEAL, a global manufacturer of seals based in Rotherham, Healey said supporting young people into work was a focus of the government.

"This area of South Yorkshire will be the first to develop a new local apprentice service matching those youngsters who can't get a start with potential employers and work placements," he said.

Rotherham had a rich heritage of coal mining and steel production, but large numbers of jobs were lost when those industries ended.

Twenty-five years ago the redevelopment of the former Orgreave site provided a blueprint for how heavy manufacturing can be replaced by something greener and more sustainable.

The vision to develop the site began in 2001, when landowners Harworth Group partnered with anchor tenant the Advanced Manufacturing Research Centre (AMRC) to bridge the gap between university research and factory floors.

It is the UK's first technology park dedicated to high-value manufacturing and production. Sheffield and Rotherham councils have been heavily involved in the transformation of the brownfield site.

Now a new generation of workers whose families worked in heavy industry is employed at the AMP.

Sean Delaney, 26, is the son of a miner who retrained as a plumber after the closure of Harworth Colliery in Nottinghamshire.

Delaney left school in 2019 before a chance meeting in a pub with one of the AMRC's founders, Adrian Allen, led to a tour of the site off the A630 between Rotherham and Sheffield.

He said: "I knew Sheffield was a world centre of industry, but I never had any idea of what sort of companies and what sort of industries were on this site only half an hour's drive from my home.

"People were already seeing the jobs market was more difficult for university graduates, so I thought it was worth taking an opportunity to be an apprentice here."

Delaney started a degree apprenticeship as a machine technician, which gives him secure employment and a qualification without student debt. The University of Sheffield partners with the research centre.

"A lot of 'levelling up' exists to help people from areas like mine, former coal mining villages, former steel towns, particularly for young people who don't go to university.

"It's been brilliant for the local area. During my apprenticeship I've met loads of different young people who have jobs, some with family backgrounds similar to mine."

Since becoming chancellor, Healey has highlighted the innovation in South Yorkshire in numerous speeches.

He is MP for Rawmarsh and Conisbrough, and pointed to the AMP as symbolising the "new age of industrialisation".

He described it as "one of the most concentrated areas of innovation anywhere in Britain" where "young people are working with high-tech systems, making things that their grandparents could never have dreamed of".

He went on to announce that Rolls-Royce would invest an extra £300m in its UK factories - including its plant in Rotherham.

Healey has also announced that the National Wealth Fund will create and support a further 130,000 jobs across the UK by 2030 across sectors including AI and technology, defence and clean energy.

The director of the park's research centre, Matthew Farnsworth, said the chancellor had shone a spotlight on the AMP because it could be difficult to illustrate economic growth in the post-industrial age.

"For the AMRC it has meant £350m inward investment, creating an opportunity for 2,500 jobs and 2,220 apprentices. Around 1,858 of them are from Rotherham and Sheffield, which means young people securing training and jobs in the local area."

Part of the old colliery is now the Waverley housing estate, with 4,000 homes and a growing community. Local schools focus on STEM subjects and Farnsworth believes there is a visible path from growing up on Waverley to a training place at the research centre and a career.

In 2005 the centre employed 20 people, it now has a workforce of more than 700.

The eventual goal is for the AMP to provide 4,000 jobs - eight times the number of people who were employed at Orgreave when the colliery closed in 1990.

description:
A datacentre company that said it would power a massive AI development near Glasgow with renewable energy has admitted that the scheme will be entirely served by the National Grid.
DataVita says the power it draws from the grid will be largely renewable energy.
Under the former prime minister Keir Starmer, Britain’s AI strategy was to build massive datacentres in zones across the country.

text:
A datacentre company that said it would power a massive AI development near Glasgow with renewable energy has admitted that the scheme will be entirely served by the National Grid.

DataVita, a key plank of the UK’s AI strategy, had promised that the Lanarkshire project would draw 1GW – the equivalent output of a small nuclear reactor, or Britain’s largest windfarm – from green sources. But when the Guardian raised questions about the pledge, it said the arrangement was “subject to final commercial agreements, planning, grid and consenting processes”.

Now, the company, which says its proposals would transform the economy of the village of Chapelhall, outside Airdrie, has quietly revised the plan. It now says the datacentres will be “fully grid served” with the possibility that solar and windfarms “could connect in the future”.

DataVita says the power it draws from the grid will be largely renewable energy. The company remains in receipt of £202m of public money in the form of wealth guarantees from Britain’s national wealth fund.

While the shift may appear to have been inevitable given the implausibility of the claimed renewables provision, it could present a problem for both DataVita and Britain’s AI strategy.

Under the former prime minister Keir Starmer, Britain’s AI strategy was to build massive datacentres in zones across the country. Their developers would get incentives – including, potentially, discounts on energy and expedited planning approvals. DataVita was to build one of the key developments associated with this strategy, an “AI growth zone” in Lanarkshire.

But this strategy began to founder just over a year after it was announced, when the Guardian’s investigations demonstrated that there was little solidity behind many announced plans.

AI datacentres are some of the most energy-intensive structures humanity has ever built, and energy costs are higher in Britain than in most of Europe. There is a years-long wait for the UK developments to connect to the grid.

Two key UK AI investments – announced with great fanfare by Starmer’s government – are on shaky ground after questions emerged over their ability to power themselves, or pay the high energy costs necessary to realise their stated ambitions. Now DataVita, which was supposed to bring 3,400 jobs to Lanarkshire by building a 500MW datacentre, also appears to be backtracking on its energy plans.

In a response to the Guardian, the company said it had not misrepresented its intention to supply renewables to the site earlier this year. “Our commitment to renewable energy is unchanged,” said a spokesperson. However, they added: “Our datacentres are being designed to be grid served … Our grid supply will be through a renewable power purchase agreement.”

This appears to contradict an earlier announcement, in which the company said: “More than 1GW of renewable energy capacity, including wind, solar, and battery storage, will be delivered through private wire connections directly linked to the datacentres.”

DataVita left open the possibility that its datacentres would connect to renewable energy in the future, through a wind and solar park it proposes to build in North Lanarkshire.

Kat Jones, the director of the Edinburgh-based charity Action to Protect Rural Scotland, said DataVita’s apparent change in direction was “emblematic of the hyperbolic claims being made by datacentre developers in Scotland”.

“Hyperscale AI datacentres simply cannot run on renewable power alone, they absolutely need a highly reliable source of grid power,” she said. “It is not surprising that the goalposts have now changed.”

text:
Ghana’s Energy and Green Transition Minister John Abdulai Jinapor has called on African countries to develop domestic solar manufacturing, arguing that the continent’s renewable energy ambitions must extend beyond installing imported equipment. Speaking at the International Solar Alliance Assembly in India, he identified technology transfer, local industrial capacity and affordable long-term finance as requirements for building an African solar industry.

Ghana has more than 150MW of utility-scale and floating solar capacity connected to its national grid, according to Energy and Green Transition Minister John Abdulai Jinapor, who wants the continent to capture a greater share of the industry behind the technology.

Addressing the ninth session of the International Solar Alliance Assembly in India on 5 November, Jinapor argued that Africa’s solar ambitions should extend beyond deployment to the manufacture of equipment and the development of local supply chains.

The minister said recent disruption in global energy markets had reinforced the importance of reducing dependence on imported fuels. Developing domestic solar production, he argued, would give African countries a greater degree of energy security while creating opportunities for industrial development.

“This will require technology transfer, local industrial capacity and, critically, affordable long-term financing,” Jinapor said.

Ghana is pursuing several strands of solar deployment, including solar streetlighting, rooftop installations and policies to transition critical public facilities to solar power. Jinapor also cited off-grid systems supplying electricity to island communities.

The distinction between installing solar capacity and manufacturing the equipment used to generate electricity is central to his argument. A growing market for solar installations does not automatically create a domestic manufacturing industry, particularly where equipment, technology and financing continue to depend on external suppliers.

Building that capacity would require investment in production facilities, skills development and the transfer of technology, alongside financing that allows manufacturers to compete.

Jinapor said Africa should become a producer of solar technology rather than remain a consumer of it, describing the continent’s solar resources as an opportunity to support industrialisation and employment.

“Our abundant sunshine must become a catalyst for industrialisation, job creation, economic resilience and energy sovereignty,” he said.

text:
In a state where gas hovers around $4 a gallon, skipping the pump sounds like a fantasy, and 54-year-old Paul Gillespie is living that dream.

Gillespie’s Chevy Bolt and Rivian R1T are among the over 450,400 registered electric vehicles, or EVs, in Florida. He’s driven an electric car since 2018.

“The EV driving experience, it’s a completely different feel than driving a gas car,” he said. “You get a lot more bang for your buck out of an EV.”

His only complaint about his EV is the towing range. A fisherman in his free time, Gillespie regularly towed his boat from Gainesville to Steinhatchee in search of scallops this summer. Although his car had no problems towing the boat, he found the battery losing charge faster, and its range was effectively cut in half from 300 miles to around 130.

As fuel prices continue to average almost $4 in Alachua County, Gillespie and other EV drivers are dodging gas gripes, and market data shows how some drivers are considering the switch to electric.

In January 2025, Gainesville received an $11.65 million grant from the federal government to build almost 50 EV charging stations across the city. Many of the new stations, which would have added to the nearly 130 existing ones, were planned to be built in East Gainesville’s lower-income communities.

But construction slated for late 2027 has been put on an indefinite hold after President Donald Trump signed an executive order, nicknamed "Unleashing American Energy,” that eliminated several other state waivers and subsidies.

The Trump administration’s One Big Beautiful Bill Act also ended three tax credits for EV purchases, including the $7,500 clean vehicle credit for new vehicles and the $4,000 credit for used EVs.

The tax credit sweetened the pot during Gillespie’s first EV purchase, but today he would still buy one without it, he said.

Florida has over 4,500 public charging stations, the fourth-most in the U.S. after California, New York and Massachusetts, according to the U.S. Department of Energy. The growing network has made it easier for those without at-home charging setups to own an EV.

A rebounding market

Last year was rocky for the EV market, but market data from the first three quarters of 2026 shows a steady recovery.

The end of the tax credits inflated the third quarter of 2025 as drivers rushed to capitalize on the impending expiration, buying almost 440,000 vehicles over three months, according to Cox Automotive’s EV market report. But sales halved in the fourth quarter after the tax credit ended.

But the market has proven its resilience so far this year, increasing every quarter. The third quarter saw over 260,000 EVs sold in the U.S., accounting for about 6% of all new-vehicle sales — the highest in a year.

As of Oct. 13, around 725,000 EVs had been sold in 2026, a 30% dip from the same time in 2025, according to the market report.

At the same time, almost 50,000 used EV sales were reported as of September, a 20% increase from the same month last year. Tesla vehicles accounted for more than half of all EV sales in the U.S.

Enrique Maldonado, a 59-year-old car salesman at Main Street Motors in Gainesville, has noticed slightly higher used EV demand in 2026 than last year. Depreciation, which is the amount of value a car loses over time, on Tesla and Kia models has led to lower prices, he said.

Of the EV sales he’s made in the last two months, the average price was in the low $20,000s – a considerable decrease from the vehicles’ original $60,000-$70,000 range.

“If it’s accessible in price, savings will be big on gas immediately,” Maldonado said. “But you need to consider time to recharge, too.”

For customers who dislike frequent recharging, he wouldn’t recommend short-range EVs with ranges of 100 or fewer miles, he said. Even quick charging stations mean a 20- to 30-minute stop. For those with at-home setups, like Gillespie, charging can be as simple as an overnight plug-in.

But Alex Clark, a 21-year-old salesman at Davis Gainesville Chevrolet, hasn’t seen as much demand for EVs at his dealership. Most of his customer base is larger pick-up truck owners, he said, many having driven trucks for decades.

The 10 EVs currently on his lot make up a small fraction of the dealership’s total inventory of more than 150 new and used cars, he said, and Clark has only sold one EV in the last month.

“There is definitely a market for EV customers within our dealership,” he said, highlighting affordable options like the Chevrolet Equinox and the GMC Hummer.

But options under $20,000 are still scarce, at least in the U.S. EV market.

The international market

Chinese EVs have taken the world by storm, accounting for two-thirds of the EVs sold globally in 2025. Affordable options like the BYD Seagull and Geely EX2, which generally sell for under $15,000, are the most popular in China.

But drivers are unlikely to see them on roads in the U.S. anytime soon.

Chinese EVs enjoy low manufacturing costs and price points because of direct government investment in EV and battery manufacturing companies, according to Alex Settles, an associate professor at UF’s Warrington College of Business.

If brought to U.S. markets, he said, there’s a fear that domestic manufacturers wouldn’t be able to compete.

Tariffs on Chinese-made EVs and lithium-ion EV batteries were raised significantly in 2024, effectively doubling the price of the vehicles in the U.S.

Data privacy concerns have also been associated with Chinese software in EVs, including cameras, microphones and sensors used for telematics and automated driving.

The Connected Vehicles Rule acts as a barrier to entry for Chinese EVs. It bans the import and sale of Chinese or Russian vehicles with Wi-Fi, Bluetooth, radio or other related hardware and software due to “national security risks,” according to the U.S. Department of Commerce. The rule went into effect March 17, 2025, and applies to vehicles and parts made in 2027 and after.

Chinese EVs could eventually hit U.S. markets, Settles said, but not before big changes in market conditions and geopolitics.

As for U.S. interest in EVs, he said it’s a natural pivot for consumers as the affordability of gas-powered vehicles decreases.

“The question is whether or not consumers think this is a temporary shift in prices or a long-term shift in prices,” he said.

November 3, 2026

The Nature Conservancy (TNC) in Utah with other partners of the Great Salt Lake Sentinel Landscape announced today an award of $8.2 million in federal funding from the USDA Natural Resources Conservation Service (NRCS) to launch the Great Salt Lake Agricultural Easement Program, the first effort of its kind in Utah. A win-win solution for agricultural producers and Great Salt Lake, the program seeks to sustain working farms, ensure that agricultural return flows reach Great Salt Lake, and strengthen economic and ecological resiliency across the Great Salt Lake watershed. Project partners are providing a required non-federal match of $8.6 million, for a total investment of $16.8 million in agricultural preservation, watershed health and community resilience.

Working with partners and producers, the program will identify farm-specific water conservation actions while supporting long-term production amid increasing pressure to convert agricultural lands. By focusing on lands with high conservation value, the program will help preserve vital wetland habitat created by agricultural return flows that support some 12 million migratory birds every year.

To implement this innovative program, TNC will collaborate with other Great Salt Lake Sentinel Landscape partners across the region. These partners include the Great Salt Lake Watershed Enhancement Trust, National Audubon Society, Ducks Unlimited, Bear River Land Conservancy, Utah Department of Agriculture and Food, Office of the Great Salt Lake Commissioner and Utah State University.

“Protecting Great Salt Lake requires collaboration at an unprecedented scale, and this program is only possible because of the extraordinary commitment of many dedicated partners,” said Danna Baxley, TNC’s water and agricultural strategy director in Utah. “Together, we have assembled one of the largest and most diverse partnerships focused on delivering water to the lake. This funding will allow us to pilot a new approach, learn from producers and continue working toward solutions that demonstrate how agriculture and Great Salt Lake can thrive together.”

The Great Salt Lake Sentinel Landscape focuses on enhancing military readiness and national security through nature-based solutions, such as safeguarding agricultural land around Utah’s military installations to preserve critical open space buffers for testing and training. The Great Salt Lake Sentinel Landscape also supports securing water for Great Salt Lake to conserve vital wildlife habitat and mitigate hazardous dust events that threaten community health and disrupt military operations.

By pairing agricultural land protection with farm-specific water management, this pilot has the potential to become a model for other Western watersheds where agricultural production and water security align to provide significant benefits to lakes, rivers and wildlife as well as agricultural producers and local communities.

“Keeping agricultural lands in production is essential to the long-term resilience of the landscapes we all depend on,” said Travis Mote, Acting State Conservationist for the USDA Natural Resources Conservation Service. “This project is a demonstration of how the Regional Conservation Partnership Program promotes strategic partnerships to turn shared priorities into lasting conservation benefits for Utah’s farm families and future generations.”

text:
Just a few years ago, the United States was developing new hydrogen hubs to support energy diversification and help achieve a green transition. However, the development of these fuel hubs has not proceeded as expected, with several major projects stalling and political support faltering.

The Biden administration showed broad support for hydrogen production, aiming to massively expand the sector and advance green hydrogen development. In November 2024, the Biden administration announced up to $2.2 billion in award commitments for two Regional Clean Hydrogen Hubs (H2Hubs) – the Gulf Coast H2Hub in Texas and the Midwest H2Hub in Illinois, Indiana, Iowa, and Michigan, out of a total of $7 billion in federal funding for seven H2Hubs.

Hydrogen can be used for a wide range of applications and, under Biden, was seen as having the potential to decarbonise hard-to-abate industries, such as shipping and steel production. Several countries around the globe began to rapidly expand their hydrogen industries about half a decade ago, with a particular focus on zero-carbon green hydrogen.

One of the H2Hubs being developed – the Mid-Atlantic Regional Hydrogen Hub (MACH2) – was in Philadelphia, which was expected to become an important region for energy diversification. The Appalachian Hydrogen Hub (ARCH2), meanwhile, is based in West Virginia and covers parts of West Virginia, Ohio, and Pennsylvania. In 2023, Pennsylvania Governor Josh Shapiro said the hubs would "ensure Pennsylvania continues to be an energy leader for decades to come."

MACH2 was expected to support the development of more than 20,000 jobs in the Delaware Valley region and help the U.S. accelerate the development of its green hydrogen sector with a $750 million award from the Department of Energy (DOE). Meanwhile, ARCH2 was expected to receive $925 million to manufacture blue hydrogen from fossil fuels, incorporating carbon capture and storage (CCS) technology to reduce emissions.

However, under the Trump administration, progress has stalled amid funding uncertainties. The federal government has reportedly gone back and forth on funding promises over the last year. This has led to the halt in development of both MACH2 and ARCH2 as operators await news on financing. "Until I see significant evidence to the contrary, I just don't think the hubs are happening," stated Tom Torres, chief of staff at the Ohio River Valley Institute, an Appalachia- focused think tank.

Meanwhile, last year Shapiro said that losing the funding would "harm Pennsylvania". "It's going to mean we're producing less energy. I have no idea why the president of the United States would want to do that."

In Louisiana, plans for hydrogen development have also stalled. Gas and chemicals company Air Products cancelled its $4.5 billion Louisiana Clean Energy Complex, which was expected to be one of the world's largest blue hydrogen and ammonia projects. The company reported approximately $2.9 billion in pretax charges associated with exiting the Louisiana project, an Arizona hydrogen project, and other initiatives. Air Products said the Louisiana project no longer met its financial expectations.

Hydrogen was expected to be produced at the facility using fracked gas, with plans to install the world's largest CCS equipment to reduce emissions. Throughout development, environmentalists argued that using fracked gas for production could not be considered "low-carbon" and that the operators were greenwashing with plans to use CCS.

By 2024, Air Products was already seeking partners to take over the ammonia and CCS components of the project, entering negotiations with the Norwegian fertiliser firm Yara in 2025. The two companies decided to abandon the project this year, citing financial worries and an inability to find customers for a speculative market. While local opponents of the project were happy to hear of the cancellation, it is just another example of U.S. hydrogen development stalling.

Meanwhile, in November last year, Exxon Mobil paused the development of a major hydrogen production facility in Baytown, Texas, with the firm's CEO, Darren Woods, citing weak customer demand for the fuel. The project had previously experienced delays. The cancellation reflected a broader shift in the U.S. energy industry, as several oil and gas companies backtracked on plans to diversify operations and invest heavily in clean energy.

The facility was expected to produce up to 1 billion cubic feet of blue hydrogen per day once operational. While hydrogen is much more expensive than alternative fossil fuels, the introduction of far-reaching green energy and cleantech subsidies by the Biden administration was expected to encourage adoption in hard-to-abate industries. However, it seems that operators may have been overly ambitious in their target to produce affordable, low-carbon hydrogen.

Financing uncertainties and cuts to several green energy grants and loans under the Trump administration have dampened interest in clean fuels over the last year. In addition, the industrial slowdown and economic uncertainty in Europe crimped demand, according to Woods. Exxon and its partners, including Abu Dhabi National Oil Company, had already invested around $500 million in the project, which is estimated to cost several billion dollars to complete and can recommence at any time if the market permits, Woods said last year.

Several hydrogen projects have stalled over the last two years, as operators face greater uncertainties in federal financing and see a lack of interest in the U.S. market. So long as the government continues to oppose the development of the country's green energy sector, this is unlikely to change.

The appointment brings an executive with experience in automotive manufacturing, greenfield plant development and electric vehicle production to Exide. Khare has worked on manufacturing projects in India and overseas, including battery cell manufacturing and electric vehicle assembly facilities.

At Agratas, where he worked from October 2023 to November 2026, Khare was involved in developing the company’s battery gigafactory at Sanand, Gujarat. His responsibilities included land acquisition, recruitment, onboarding design and construction partners, and overseeing the development of the facility. In a recent LinkedIn post announcing his departure, Khare said process equipment was being commissioned at the site, marking an important stage in the project’s development.

Before joining Agratas, Khare served as Head of Manufacturing Operations at Lucid Motors from August 2022 to September 2023. During his tenure, he was involved in establishing the luxury electric vehicle manufacturer’s manufacturing operations in Saudi Arabia, including preparations for the commencement of vehicle production.

Khare brings nearly three decades of experience across automotive manufacturing, plant operations, supplier development and quality management. Earlier in his career, he held senior manufacturing responsibilities at Ford Motor Company, including managing vehicle production operations at its Sanand facility, where he led a workforce of more than 1,800 employees. His responsibilities covered production, quality, safety, cost management and operational improvements.

He also worked with Airbus as Director, Procurement Quality, and held engineering roles at Caterpillar. His career spans automotive, aerospace and industrial equipment manufacturing, with experience in production management, supplier quality and manufacturing operations.

Khare’s appointment comes as Exide continues its expansion into lithium-ion battery manufacturing through its subsidiary, Exide Energy Solutions. His background in developing battery manufacturing facilities and managing automotive production operations is particularly relevant to the company’s ongoing investments in advanced battery manufacturing.

American voters have spoken. And in our 250th anniversary year, it’s encouraging to know that our constitutional order has survived another election.

Yes, we finalize our political battles in the private voting booth.

It appears yet again that the majority of American voters prefer a divided government to coerce political consensus.

As Congress prepares to return for a postelection legislative session, there are major items on their agenda, and hopefully, personal agendas can be set aside on behalf of some needed reforms for their constituents.

The Senate will vote on Monday, Nov. 9, to consider the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act. This bill proposes to reform the federal environmental review and permitting processes with the goal of delivering cheaper energy, more jobs and responsible growth across the United States.

BAAJA has been introduced by the Republican chairmen and ranking Democratic members of the Senate Environment and Public Works Committee and the Senate Energy and Natural Resources Committee. Despite this high-level support from Democratic committee leaders, it’s not certain that Democratic senators will provide enough support to reach the 60-vote threshold necessary under Senate rules to proceed to consideration of the bill.

After running a midterm elections campaign in which Democrats repeatedly professed their concern about affordability, it’s time to transform their campaign rhetoric into votes to proceed to Senate consideration of this legislation and final passage in both houses of Congress before the end of 2026.

As an advocate for limited government and free market economic policies, I joined Americans for Tax Reform president Grover Norquist and other coalition leaders in calling on the Senate to pass this legislation expeditiously. Our call points out that BAAJA will “lower energy costs, speed up approval of critical infrastructure projects, curb superfluous litigation and give builders and investors the certainty they need to commit capital.”

Urgently needed energy and infrastructure projects currently spend years under review before they can even begin. Approvals can be delayed by redundant paperwork, blocked by a single state for political reasons or tied up in litigation long after a permit is issued. Left-wing activists, who oppose entire categories of American energy production, use these tedious review processes to stall or stop projects.

These delays discourage investment and reward obstruction, leaving America more dependent on foreign energy sources. The costs are passed on to families and businesses through higher energy costs and fewer jobs.

The North American Electric Reliability Corporation has warned that 13 of 23 regional assessment areas will face resource adequacy challenges over the next 10 years. Other data show that electricity demand is growing at its fastest pace since 2000 and that residential prices are up nearly 5% this year.

The Americans for Tax Reform coalition letter to Senate leaders points out that “With these growing problems, lawmakers must act to ensure more growth to keep up with rising demand. Otherwise, Americans will see even higher energy bills and face a less reliable grid.”

As data centers drive demand for more power, BAAJA will require them to pay for all of their associated transmission costs. It will also ensure that the centers pay their fair share of the grid updates they require.

The postelection legislative session colloquially known as a lame-duck session of Congress includes members who have run for other offices, decided to retire or just lost their campaigns. Attendance and attentiveness can become challenging, but most members recognize that they have an obligation to serve their constituents and the nation during the remaining weeks of this term.

Permitting reform is one of several issues that will be addressed in the lame-duck session. There is important work to be done, and the American people deserve a bipartisan commitment toward delivering cheaper energy, more jobs and responsible growth.

We don’t want lame excuses from the lame-duck Congress. It’s time to put the election behind us and get our economy firing on all cylinders.

Democrats can’t seem to decide whether they want higher or lower gas prices. On the one hand, they promised that if they won a majority in Congress, they would work to bring down prices at the pump. On the other hand, they can’t bring down prices in their own blue states.

Imagine your child’s school receives a suspicious message, a small-business owner notices someone lingering on security camera footage or you see a concerning post in a community Facebook group.

In 2014, President Barack Obama, during the last midterm of his presidency, was 53 years old. He did seven rallies, four of which took place in October.

Manufacturing is our second-largest industry. It contributes $20 billion a year to our economy. Every day, over 97,000 Nebraskans don their hard hats, lace up their steel-toed boots and get to work.

In 2010, President Obama described those midterm elections as a “shellacking” for Democrats, who lost 60 seats in the House. Then, as now, the economy was the top issue.

Communities in Northeast and North Central Nebraska often demonstrate their strength in ways that go beyond population figures or economic statistics. They show it when residents come together around a common goal and invest in the next generation.

PENDER — Veterans Day is Wednesday, Nov. 11, a time to honor and remember those who have served in our nation’s armed forces. While military service comes with immense sacrifices, there is some encouraging news to report regarding veterans’ well-being. In September, the U.S. Department of Ve…

Thriving communities need businesses that build lasting relationships and entrepreneurs who are willing to take a chance. Northeast Nebraska is fortunate to have just that.

Listen, let’s get one thing straight — lest anyone jump to conclusions relative to my interest in defending a rational politician who served both her state and her country well in challenging times.

description:

text:
Quick Read

Federal EV tax credits, including the $4,000 used-car credit, ended for vehicles acquired after September 30, 2025, so outdated online advice misleads buyers.

Without the credit, a modest driver saves roughly $650 a year on fuel, so it takes about six years to match the lost $4,000.

Pay with cash savings rather than IRA money, since withdrawals are taxed as ordinary income and can raise Medicare premiums; check state and utility incentives first.

The biggest 401k decisions tend to get made once and never revisited: when to roll it over, what to hold inside it, and when to start taking money out. That is exactly what the report: 401k & IRA Tips and Answers was created to address, and it is free today. Read more here. (Sponsor)

She'd saved an old article about the used EV tax credit, the one that took up to $4,000 off a pre-owned electric car. At 67, retired and driving mostly around town, she walked into the dealership expecting that discount. The sales rep told her the credit was gone.

This happens to a lot of people right now. Plenty of articles about the credit are still online, and they read like current advice, but the truth is that they're out of date.

When the Federal EV Credits Actually Ended

The used-car credit paid the lesser of $4,000 or 30% of the sale price. The One Big Beautiful Bill Act, signed July 4, 2025, moved its end date from December 31, 2032 to September 30, 2025. Today, the law says no credit for any used EV acquired after September 30, 2025. The new-car credit ends on the same date.

The home charger credit is finished too. It covered 30% of the cost, limited to $1,000 for personal use, and it doesn't apply to anything installed after June 30, 2026.

Can Fuel Savings Replace a Missing $4,000?

The credit was her buffer against the risks of an older battery. Now the savings at the pump have to carry the whole load.

------

Now Available: The 401k Answers Nobody Gives You.

For many Americans, funding a 401(k) only leads to more retirement questions. Should you roll your 401k into an IRA, and when? What's the tax impact if the rollover check gets made out to the wrong name? When do required withdrawals begin, and how much do you have to take?

Fisher Investments put the answers in one place. 401k & IRA Tips and Answers is free, and it covers rollovers, contribution limits, required withdrawals, and what actually belongs inside the account once the balance gets serious. Read More Here ›

------

Here are simple assumptions for a modest driver: 7,500 miles a year, a gas car getting 30 miles per gallon, and an EV going 3.5 miles per kilowatt-hour (a kilowatt-hour is the unit on your electric bill), charged at home. Regular gas averages about $4.15 a gallon. The federal government's energy analysts expect home electricity to average 18.2 cents per kilowatt-hour in 2026.

On those numbers, gas costs about $1,040 a year and electricity about $390. She saves roughly $650 a year. It would take about six years of savings just to equal the lost credit.

Both prices move. Gas rose from about $4.01 in August to nearly $4.48 in late September, then fell. Home electricity prices are expected to rise about 5% in 2026.

Fuel is only one line. EVs skip oil changes, so routine maintenance usually runs lower. Insurance often runs higher, and some states add an annual EV registration fee. Get an insurance quote and check your state's registration fee before you sign.

Be fair about the battery. A used EV's battery has already lost some capacity, so the range printed for the new model exaggerates what she'll get. Ask for a battery health report and check what's left on the original battery warranty.

Cash, a Car Loan or IRA Money

For most retirees, paying cash from regular savings is the clearest move. A loan only makes sense if its interest rate is lower than what her savings earn after tax. That's rare with used-car loans.

IRA money is where people get hurt. At 67, the 10% early withdrawal penalty no longer applies because she's past 59½. Every dollar is still taxed as ordinary income. Someone filing alone in 2026 sees the 12% bracket run up to $50,400 of taxable income, and 22% applies above that.

A $20,000 withdrawal costs $2,400 in federal tax if it all lands in the 12% bracket and $4,400 if it lands at 22%. A big withdrawal can also raise Medicare premiums. Once an individual's income tops $109,000, Part B jumps from about $203 to about $284 a month (that IRMAA surcharge is one of several traps we mapped in a free Medicare guide).

If the IRA is her only source, splitting the withdrawal between December and January spreads it across two tax years. We walked through the same withholding and tax-bill trap with a 60-year-old pulling $40,000 from a 401(k) for a truck.

State and Utility Money That Still Exists

Some states still pay, usually with strings attached. Vehicle Exchange Colorado gives a point-of-sale rebate, so the discount comes off the price at the dealership. It's income-qualified, and you have to turn in a working car that failed an emissions test or is at least 12 years old. California's Clean Cars 4 All offers grants to income-qualified buyers of new or used EVs.

These incentives can change quickly. Colorado's separate Innovative Motor Vehicle Credit, for example, dropped to $750 in 2026 for qualifying new EVs, although certain lower-priced vehicles qualify for an additional $2,500. Many electric utilities run their own charger or rate programs, so check yours as well.

What to Do Before You Sign

Ask one question first. What incentives do my state and my utility still offer, what are the income limits, and are they paid at the dealership or later? Get the answer in writing before you talk price.

Pay for the car on its own merits. The common mistake is accepting a sticker or monthly payment built around a $4,000 credit that ended more than a year ago. If the EV still beats a gas car after fuel, insurance, and registration, buy it with cash savings. If you have to use IRA money, keep the withdrawal inside the 12% bracket.

title: Energy policy comes into focus after Dems take majorities in Michigan - Detroit Free Press
description:
"Now is the time to deliver on campaign promises to lower costs, hold utilities accountable, protect against data center expansion and advance clean energy solutions."
Data center guardrails In the days following the midterms, Democrats in Lansing have broadly outlined aims to lower costs, without diving too deep into specific policy aims.
Data centers are the facilities that house computer hardware needed to power various functions on the web.
On the campaign trail, candidates from both parties embraced data center accountability measures.
Gretchen Whitmer aimed at improving energy affordability in Michigan.
text:
Buoyed by Democrats taking wide majorities in both chambers of the state Legislature and Democratic Secretary of State Jocelyn Benson being elected as Michigan's next governor, energy affordability and climate activists believe the results of the Nov. 3 election have laid the groundwork for new policy to advance through Lansing next year.

Voter frustration with the cost of living in general fueled electoral gains for Democrats nationally and in Michigan. The price of energy, from gas prices to home heating costs, also played a role, analysts and candidates noted throughout the run up to Election Day.

"Michigan families have been clear that their energy bills are too high, and they want leaders who will do something about it," Denise Keele, executive director of the Michigan Climate Action Network said in a statement provided to the Detroit Free Press. "Now is the time to deliver on campaign promises to lower costs, hold utilities accountable, protect against data center expansion and advance clean energy solutions."

Data center guardrails

In the days following the midterms, Democrats in Lansing have broadly outlined aims to lower costs, without diving too deep into specific policy aims. But incoming Senate Majority Leader Darrin Camilleri, D-Trenton, told reporters Nov. 5 he was in favor of a moratorium on new data center projects in Michigan while adding the caveat that the entire Democratic caucus hasn't taken a position on such a policy, yet. Democrats will hold a 23-15 majority in the Senate, although many Republican lawmakers have called for a pause on data center projects, too.

Data centers are the facilities that house computer hardware needed to power various functions on the web. In the midterms, they turned into a hot topic politically as residents in communities across Michigan either expressed concern or plainly called to reject new data center development.

Besides a moratorium, some lawmakers have called for guardrails on water and electricity usage at data centers. Earlier this year, Senate Democrats introduced a series of bills setting parameters for how data centers could operate in Michigan, although the legislation didn't advance. It's not likely the bills are taken up during the lame duck session but data center guardrails are likely to be reintroduced not long after the new Legislature begins its session next year.

Ben Poulson, state government affairs director for the Michigan League of Conservation Voters, said the guardrail package is a "great starting point" for Democrats next year. He pointed to measures adopted by the Michigan Public Service Commission (MPSC), including requiring data centers to pay for the electricity they use, as something lawmakers should codify into state law.

"Ensuring data centers pay their own way is the most important step the Legislature can get done on affordability," Poulson said Nov. 6.

On the campaign trail, candidates from both parties embraced data center accountability measures.

Utility accountability measures get new life

Michigan voters overwhelmingly backed a ballot proposal that bans investor-owned utilities, like DTE Energy and Consumers Energy, along with company executives, from donating to political campaigns. Proposal 2 passed with 81% support, according to unofficial results.

Although DTE and Consumers have challenged the proposal's legality in court on First Amendment lines, advocates believe legislation to hold the companies accountable for spotty service reliability and prolonged outages in recent years hasn't advanced because of the influence of corporate spending in Lansing. Should Proposal 2 withstand legal challenges, its supporters believe the margin it passed by gives lawmakers a mandate to advance policy related to utility service in Michigan.

Poulson said legislation that increases the amount of distributed energy generation local residents and communities can produce (which typically is through community solar projects or battery storage, in some cases) can not only help with energy affordability but also aid Michigan in its goal to have 100% clean energy generation by 2040. Current law places caps on the amount of energy that can be produced locally.

No more annual rate hikes?

Earlier this year, the MPSC presented a series of recommendations to Gov. Gretchen Whitmer aimed at improving energy affordability in Michigan. MPSC Chair Dan Scripps backed a ban on annual rate cases, among other policy tweaks.

Under current law, there is nothing stopping electric and natural gas providers from seeking rate hikes for their customers in consecutive years. The typical rate case takes about ten months to complete and follows a routine formula: Companies will ask to raise their rates by a certain amount and argue the higher prices are needed to invest in the grid. Intervenors, which often include Attorney General Dana Nessel's office and affordability advocates, will argue the hike is unnecessary. The MPSC usually ends up approving a rate increase lower than what the utility first sought. In recent years, Nessel has drawn attention to utilities opening new rate hike requests shortly after their most recent case is settled.

In January, lawmakers in the Michigan House introduced bills to ban utilities from seeking rate increases for at least three years after their most recent case is settled, although it hasn't advanced through the chamber. With new majorities in both the House and Senate, taking up the MPSC's recommendation to stop annual rate hikes could have new life in Lansing.

title: Tesla Cybertruck Discontinued: Why BMW Never Built A Pickup Truck - bmwblog
description:
Why Is Tesla Really Ending Cybertruck Production?
What BMW Designers Told Us About The Cybertruck When we spoke with some BMW designers off the record in the past, they appreciated the Cybertruck’s daring, unconventional design.
Then-R&D chief Klaus Fröhlich said in 2019 that a proper pickup needs a ladder-frame architecture BMW doesn’t have.
Its tailgate-style rear seating was about as close to a pickup bed as BMW was willing to get.
BMW’s designers can keep their soft spot for the stainless steel wedge, but the people who approve BMW’s product plan were never going to see a business in those numbers.
text:
Elon Musk said on X on Friday that production of the Tesla Cybertruck will start winding down at Gigafactory Texas around the middle of 2027, “to make room for increased Cybercab production.” If that holds, the stainless steel pickup will have been on sale for about three and a half years.

Tesla sized the line for 250,000 trucks a year, but Kelley Blue Book estimates it sold 20,237 Cybertrucks in 2025, down from 38,965 in 2024. Cox Automotive counts 11,586 US sales through September of this year.

Why Is Tesla Really Ending Cybertruck Production?

Musk blames floor space for the Cybercab robotaxi, but Electrek notes that Giga Texas has more than 10 million square feet and the Cybertruck line already runs at about a quarter of its installed capacity. Tesla promised a $39,900 starting price in 2019, listed the cheapest truck at $60,990 when sales began in late 2023, and was charging $74,990 for the entry Dual-Motor AWD after an August increase. That trim can no longer be ordered at all.

Nearly every Cybertruck on the road was recalled in March 2025 over an exterior panel issue, the truck can’t be sold in Europe or most right-hand-drive markets, and last month Tesla canceled reservations in Australia and New Zealand nearly seven years after opening them.

What BMW Designers Told Us About The Cybertruck

When we spoke with some BMW designers off the record in the past, they appreciated the Cybertruck’s daring, unconventional design. Most designers like strange things, and few production vehicles are stranger. Tesla design chief Franz von Holzhausen has said the truck’s hard lines came from the stainless steel Musk handed his team, and a shape dictated by a material rather than a customer clinic is something designers rarely get to do. Admiring it was as far as it went, though: there was never an intention for BMW to chase a segment like that.

Has BMW Ever Seriously Considered Building A Pickup Truck?

No, and its executives keep saying so. Then-R&D chief Klaus Fröhlich said in 2019 that a proper pickup needs a ladder-frame architecture BMW doesn’t have. Adrian van Hooydonk, BMW’s design chief at the time, told BMWBLOG in 2023 that a pickup is “not an obvious fit for the BMW brand,” and last year Bernd Koerber, senior vice president of BMW brand and product management, told us: “Pickup is not a segment we look at.” Mercedes-Benz showed what happens when a German luxury brand tries anyway: its Navara-based X-Class sold 15,300 units worldwide in 2019 and was out of production by May 2020.

BMW’s pickups have stayed one-offs: the 1986 E30 M3 Pickup that hauled parts for BMW M until 2012, its E93 M3-based successor that doubled as a 2011 April Fools’ joke, and the X7 Pick-up built by Munich plant trainees in 2019.

Why The Canceled BMW Rugged Was The Closest BMW Came

The closest BMW came was the G74 “Rugged,” a true off-road vehicle with big tires, a spare wheel on the back, and real off-road hardware. The rumor is that the idea grew partly out of BMW’s evaluation of the Rivian R1T, so BMW studied an electric pickup and came away wanting an SUV. It started as an electric model on the Neue Klasse NA5 platform, then moved to CLAR alongside the next-generation G65 X5, with Spartanburg production and a 2029 launch target. Its tailgate-style rear seating was about as close to a pickup bed as BMW was willing to get.

In July, we reported the Rugged failed to clear final approval, as a bespoke luxury off-roader struggled to justify itself against the G-Class and Range Rover. The Land Rover Defender alone hit a record 115,404 deliveries in 2025, and BMW still judged that segment too small to enter from scratch.

The Cybertruck, built on a line sized for 250,000 trucks a year, never topped 40,000 in a year by Kelley Blue Book’s estimates. BMW’s designers can keep their soft spot for the stainless steel wedge, but the people who approve BMW’s product plan were never going to see a business in those numbers.
