title: UN climate talks start in a year of disasters, energy price shocks and fast rising temperatures
description:
Three stories about climate change are playing out like popular movie genres as United Nations climate negotiations begin in Antalya, Turkey.
But renewable energy is capturing some of the world's attention because it's cheaper and cleaner than fossil fuels.
This isn't helping curb climate change.
A key issue this year is the implementation of promises to transition away from fossil fuels.
One important sideline initiative this year is Turkey's goal of increasing electricity's share of global energy use from 21% to 35% by 2035, preferably by using renewable power.
text:
Three stories about climate change are playing out like popular movie genres as United Nations climate negotiations begin in Antalya, Turkey.

There's the horror story. Many scientists believe global warming is accelerating. Two months ago, the U.N. readjusted its decade-old goal of limiting global temperature rise to 1.5 degrees Celsius (2.7 degrees Fahrenheit) because the world is blowing past that threshold. The fallout from rising temperatures is felt globally, with Europe's deadly summer heat waves and Nepal's devastating flooding as stark examples.

There's the love triangle. For more than a century, the world has been powered by coal, oil and gas. This love affair spurred economic development, as well as the emissions warming the planet. But renewable energy is capturing some of the world's attention because it's cheaper and cleaner than fossil fuels. Instead of switching from one to the other, the world is using both to meet demand from power-hungry artificial intelligence and ever-growing economic development. This isn't helping curb climate change.

Then there's the war movie. Russia's 2022 invasion of Ukraine triggered a European energy shock. This year the United States and Israel bombed Iran. The conflict closed the Strait of Hormuz and sent fossil fuel prices skyrocketing, forcing nations to rethink their energy systems.

These stories are colliding as the 31st Conference of Parties, or COP31, starts Monday with speeches from world leaders and will later dig into how to follow through on past climate pledges.

A key issue this year is the implementation of promises to transition away from fossil fuels. Co-host Turkey is also pushing a separate plan that would help do that by shifting more global energy use — including transportation — to electricity generated from solar and wind power. Negotiators also will hash out how to provide promised funds to poor countries to switch to renewables, adapt to a warmer world and recover from climate-induced damage.

“It’s really the moment that we place a magnifying lens on what’s happening in the world on climate change, both good and bad,” David Waskow, international climate chief at the World Resources Institute, said.

While the U.S. is the world’s largest historic carbon polluter, it skipped last year's COP and isn't expected to participate this year.

“There’s always two topics in the climate negotiations that are relevant and difficult,” said Niklas Höhne, co-founder of Germany’s NewClimate Institute. “The first one is who produces emissions (and) how much. That is difficult enough. But what is even more complicated is the other issue, and that is who pays. And on this one, we are particularly in a difficult situation because the U.S., as the largest contributor, has dropped out. And there’s no other player who can jump in.”

Global climate efforts are off track

Eleven years ago, the world was on track to hit 4 C (7.2 F) of warming above preindustrial levels by the end of the century. In 2015, nations set the goal of keeping warming to below 2 C (3.6 F), but with a preferred limit of 1.5 C (2.7 F), as measured over a multi-year period.

Now, the world is at 1.4 C (2.5 F) of warming and is hurtling toward 2.6 C (4.7 F), the U.N. found.

October 2026 was the hottest October on record, and 2026 is virtually certain to end up as the second year to exceed the 1.5 degree Celsius level, behind 2024, the European climate agency Copernicus announced Friday.

“We have failed so far,” said Johan Rockström, director of Germany’s Potsdam Institute for Climate Impact Research.

Rockström said Earth will likely experience more extreme weather, such as floods, droughts and storms, and may soon reach “tipping points,” such as ocean currents changing and the Amazon rainforest collapsing.

It comes down to fossil fuels

Even though burning fossil fuels is the main cause of warming, it has rarely been targeted in final documents agreed upon at the conference, mostly because those decisions require consensus.

“The reason we are seeing the breach of 1.5 degrees Celsius of warming is because we avoided the absolutely fundamental question of how climate change happened and what’s responsible, the source of the problem and that’s fossil fuels,” said Harjeet Singh, founding director of Satat Sampada Climate Foundation. “Unless and until we resolve the issue of fossil fuel phase out, we will not be able to deal with the problem.”

Brazil, which hosted COP30 last year, this month released a detailed voluntary roadmap for how countries could transition away from fossil fuels.

The roadmap is meant to turn the “big problem” of reducing fossil fuels into “smaller actionable solutions,” Ana Toni, who served as CEO of last year's climate talks, said. One key thing nations must do is stop subsidizing fossil fuels, she said. The U.N. estimates fossil fuel subsidies globally hit $1.1 trillion this year.

“What’s standing in the way is not so much technology as governments and incumbent industries,” said Bill Hare, CEO of Climate Analytics. “One cannot underestimate the power and influence of the fossil fuel industry in slowing down action.”

Climate talks bring hope and frustration

Barbados youth activist Ashley Lashley's first COP was five years ago. She was frustrated by the lack of progress then, but hopeful because there was urgency to keep the 1.5-degree goal alive.

Lashley still attends negotiations with some hope, but she is more frustrated than ever. She said “the science has become more alarming, but yet politically we seem to be negotiating how much failure we are prepared to tolerate.”

Qiyun Woo, a Singaporean youth environmentalist, said her generation is tired of “seeing their present and futures blanketed in wildfire smoke, in devastating floods (and) landslides."

What gives most experts hope is how cheap solar and wind energy are, along with electric car growth, strengthening the economic argument for transitioning away from fossil fuels.

“It has never been as easy to reduce emissions as it is today because, again, this year, renewable energy has been developing faster than before,” Höhne said.

Hope for progress on the sidelines

Much of the work at climate negotiations happens on the sidelines, where not everyone has to agree and some nations do more than others.

One important sideline initiative this year is Turkey's goal of increasing electricity's share of global energy use from 21% to 35% by 2035, preferably by using renewable power.

Mohamed Adow, a veteran COP observer and director of Power Shift Africa, said the conference is taking place at a time when the world is deeply fragmented.

“The closure of the Strait of Hormuz has intensified economic and energy security pressures," he said. "We don’t expect this particular conference to be able to sufficiently respond to the present day challenge ... that is affecting livelihoods and economies.”

The climate talks are hindered by the continued absence of the U.S., Adow said, adding that it wasn't fair to nations like Nepal, which have to face catastrophic destruction alone while the world's wealthiest country and biggest polluter sits on the fence.

“A time will come when we will have to hold the U.S. accountable for the climate harms that it’s caused,” he said.

text:
Just a few years ago, the United States was developing new hydrogen hubs to support energy diversification and help achieve a green transition. However, the development of these fuel hubs has not proceeded as expected, with several major projects stalling and political support faltering.

The Biden administration showed broad support for hydrogen production, aiming to massively expand the sector and advance green hydrogen development. In November 2024, the Biden administration announced up to $2.2 billion in award commitments for two Regional Clean Hydrogen Hubs (H2Hubs) – the Gulf Coast H2Hub in Texas and the Midwest H2Hub in Illinois, Indiana, Iowa, and Michigan, out of a total of $7 billion in federal funding for seven H2Hubs.

Hydrogen can be used for a wide range of applications and, under Biden, was seen as having the potential to decarbonise hard-to-abate industries, such as shipping and steel production. Several countries around the globe began to rapidly expand their hydrogen industries about half a decade ago, with a particular focus on zero-carbon green hydrogen.

One of the H2Hubs being developed – the Mid-Atlantic Regional Hydrogen Hub (MACH2) – was in Philadelphia, which was expected to become an important region for energy diversification. The Appalachian Hydrogen Hub (ARCH2), meanwhile, is based in West Virginia and covers parts of West Virginia, Ohio, and Pennsylvania. In 2023, Pennsylvania Governor Josh Shapiro said the hubs would “ensure Pennsylvania continues to be an energy leader for decades to come.”

ADVERTISEMENT

MACH2 was expected to support the development of more than 20,000 jobs in the Delaware Valley region and help the U.S. accelerate the development of its green hydrogen sector with a $750 million award from the Department of Energy (DOE). Meanwhile, ARCH2 was expected to receive $925 million to manufacture blue hydrogen from fossil fuels, incorporating carbon capture and storage (CCS) technology to reduce emissions.

However, under the Trump administration, progress has stalled amid funding uncertainties. The federal government has reportedly gone back and forth on funding promises over the last year. This has led to the halt in development of both MACH2 and ARCH2 as operators await news on financing. “Until I see significant evidence to the contrary, I just don’t think the hubs are happening,” stated Tom Torres, chief of staff at the Ohio River Valley Institute, an Appalachia- focused think tank.

Meanwhile, last year Shapiro said that losing the funding would “harm Pennsylvania”. “It’s going to mean we’re producing less energy. I have no idea why the president of the United States would want to do that.”

In Louisiana, plans for hydrogen development have also stalled. Gas and chemicals company Air Products cancelled its $4.5 billion Louisiana Clean Energy Complex, which was expected to be one of the world’s largest blue hydrogen and ammonia projects. The company reported approximately $2.9 billion in pretax charges associated with exiting the Louisiana project, an Arizona hydrogen project, and other initiatives. Air Products said the Louisiana project no longer met its financial expectations.

Hydrogen was expected to be produced at the facility using fracked gas, with plans to install the world’s largest CCS equipment to reduce emissions. Throughout development, environmentalists argued that using fracked gas for production could not be considered “low-carbon” and that the operators were greenwashing with plans to use CCS.

By 2024, Air Products was already seeking partners to take over the ammonia and CCS components of the project, entering negotiations with the Norwegian fertiliser firm Yara in 2025. The two companies decided to abandon the project this year, citing financial worries and an inability to find customers for a speculative market. While local opponents of the project were happy to hear of the cancellation, it is just another example of U.S. hydrogen development stalling.

ADVERTISEMENT

Meanwhile, in November last year, Exxon Mobil paused the development of a major hydrogen production facility in Baytown, Texas, with the firm’s CEO, Darren Woods, citing weak customer demand for the fuel. The project had previously experienced delays. The cancellation reflected a broader shift in the U.S. energy industry, as several oil and gas companies backtracked on plans to diversify operations and invest heavily in clean energy.

The facility was expected to produce up to 1 billion cubic feet of blue hydrogen per day once operational. While hydrogen is much more expensive than alternative fossil fuels, the introduction of far-reaching green energy and cleantech subsidies by the Biden administration was expected to encourage adoption in hard-to-abate industries. However, it seems that operators may have been overly ambitious in their target to produce affordable, low-carbon hydrogen.

Financing uncertainties and cuts to several green energy grants and loans under the Trump administration have dampened interest in clean fuels over the last year. In addition, the industrial slowdown and economic uncertainty in Europe crimped demand, according to Woods. Exxon and its partners, including Abu Dhabi National Oil Company, had already invested around $500 million in the project, which is estimated to cost several billion dollars to complete and can recommence at any time if the market permits, Woods said last year.

Several hydrogen projects have stalled over the last two years, as operators face greater uncertainties in federal financing and see a lack of interest in the U.S. market. So long as the government continues to oppose the development of the country’s green energy sector, this is unlikely to change.

title: Why The Democrats' Next Climate Agenda Will Look Different - TIME
description:
Even though explicit mention of climate change was far from the heart of midterm discussions, Democrats have a history of taking big swings to cut emissions.
James Talarico, Texas’s Democratic senator-elect, has promised to protect oil-and-gas jobs as part of an all-of-the-above energy strategy.
Kansas Democratic Senator-elect Adam Hamilton has also called for “all-of-the above-energy production” as part of an energy affordability strategy.
But that doesn’t mean that there is no prospect of climate policy.
In fact, a slew of factors mean that energy and climate policy will be on the agenda—even if it’s not labeled as such.
text:
After two years of the most anti-climate presidential administration in U.S. history, Tuesday’s election results have many climate advocates feeling a sense of hope. Even though explicit mention of climate change was far from the heart of midterm discussions, Democrats have a history of taking big swings to cut emissions.

But even with Democrats on the rise, don’t expect a return to the old climate order where the Green New Deal dominated Capitol Hill chatter, and the big-spending Inflation Reduction Act served as a watered down compromise. Over the next two years, elected officials in Washington will forge the next wave of climate policy, and there’s a good chance it may look pretty different from what we’ve seen in recent history.

The biggest indicator of what this might look like may just be a quick survey of how the new crop of Democratic senators have talked about climate and energy issues. James Talarico, Texas’s Democratic senator-elect, has promised to protect oil-and-gas jobs as part of an all-of-the-above energy strategy. Kansas Democratic Senator-elect Adam Hamilton has also called for “all-of-the above-energy production” as part of an energy affordability strategy. And South Carolina Senator-elect Annie Andrews has called for a suspension of the federal gas tax. All three, along with virtually every newly elected Democrat, have also put a spotlight on the role data centers are playing in the power system, calling on big tech firms to pay more for the costs they incur.

Green New Dealers calling for a rapid end to fossil fuels this batch is not. But that doesn’t mean that there is no prospect of climate policy. In fact, a slew of factors mean that energy and climate policy will be on the agenda—even if it’s not labeled as such. The energy affordability crisis, the war in Iran, the rise of power-guzzling data centers, and competition from China all mean that climate will be top priorities for the coming national political dialogue.

title: As COP31 comes to Turkey, satellites reveal landfill methane problem - The New Arab
description:
Turkey hosts COP31 in Antalya from November 9 to 20 and has made methane reduction a priority for the climate summit.
Turkey's waste sector illustrates both the potential and the difficulty of achieving rapid cuts.
Gas capture is widespread at Turkey's larger municipal landfills, indicating that collection systems alone do not prevent large releases.
ISTAC benefits economically from efficient methane capture to produce electricity, the Environment Ministry said.
In 2021, the Global Methane Pledge (GMP) was launched at COP26, seeking a collective 30% cut in methane emissions from 2020 levels by 2030, with more than 30 countries later backing national targets.
text:
In the countryside west of Istanbul, trucks line up to empty mixed household waste from the city of 16 million people onto a vast landscape of decomposing rubbish, where landfill gas is captured to generate electricity at a nearby plant.

But far above the seagulls circling the waste, satellites detect what the plant has failed to capture: methane escaping at a rate that ranks it among the world’s largest recorded landfill emitters.

Turkey hosts COP31 in Antalya from November 9 to 20 and has made methane reduction a priority for the climate summit.

Methane is the biggest cause of climate change after carbon dioxide (CO2) and is over 80 times more potent than CO2 in its first 20 years in the air. Sharp cuts could therefore slow warming relatively quickly.

Turkey's waste sector illustrates both the potential and the difficulty of achieving rapid cuts.

The country is the world's fifth-biggest emitter of methane from solid waste behind China, the United States, Russia and Brazil, according to data from non-profit emissions tracker Climate TRACE.

Satellite observations analysed by researchers at the University of California, Los Angeles (UCLA) identified 70 plumes from Turkey’s 10 highest-emitting waste sites, where average detected rates ranged from 841 kg to 7.4 metric tons an hour. Three were around Istanbul, while others were near Ankara, Izmir and Antalya, where COP31 is being held.

Gas capture is widespread at Turkey's larger municipal landfills, indicating that collection systems alone do not prevent large releases.

'Huge potential'

Tia Scarpelli, waste sector lead for emissions-monitoring non-profit Carbon Mapper, said cutting landfill methane requires diverting organic material before it reaches dumps, while improving rates of capture.

Because Turkey’s largest detected emissions were concentrated at a few sites, addressing those landfills could deliver disproportionate gains, Scarpelli said.

“There is this huge mitigation potential by just addressing the largest landfills to reduce their national emissions,” she said, suggesting better-designed collection systems and repairs to cracked covers or faulty gas wells.

The UCLA analysis used public Carbon Mapper data from the Tanager-1 satellite between January 2025 and end-May 2026.

It showed an average detected rate of about 7.4 tons an hour from the landfill west of Istanbul near Seymen — just below the highest-emitting landfill on a global list from 2025.

“What stands out is how big its emissions are and how persistently large they are,” said Scarpelli.

In response to a request for comment, Turkey's Environment Ministry said the data were not from continuous measurements and could not be used to measure annual emissions at the Seymen landfill.

It said Turkey's Zero Waste Initiative, a government scheme to promote recycling, aims to reduce waste going to landfills, thereby lowering methane emissions, adding that the national "recovery rate" for waste had risen to 37.53% in 2025 from 13% in 2017.

At the Seymen landfill, municipal operator ISTAC collects gas produced as buried organic material decomposes, while an energy company burns the gas to generate electricity at a plant opened in 2020.

The facility produces about 22,000 megawatt-hours of electricity a month, according to a 2025 report by energy news website Enerji Gunlugu.

ISTAC benefits economically from efficient methane capture to produce electricity, the Environment Ministry said.

ISTAC official Aysen Erdincler disputed whether the satellite observations were representative of the landfill’s emissions, saying they typically ranged between 4 and 6 tons per hour, while a satellite reading of 12 tons per hour on one day had raised the average. ISTAC head Fatih Ugur said about 30 hectares of the landfill had been left uncovered on the day of that measurement while work was carried out on methane-collection pipes, and that low atmospheric pressure had also contributed to a higher concentration of methane.

The Seymen site takes some 8,500 tons of household waste daily, from Istanbul's average total of 20,000 tons, according to ISTAC. It is unclear to researchers how much of the landfill's methane the system captures, but Erdincler said methane leaks at the site were usually around 25%.

Turkey absent from methane pledge

Methane emissions from waste in Turkey rose nearly 25% in the decade to 2024, compared to a global rise of 6.5% over the same period, according to World Bank data based on the European Commission’s EDGAR emissions database. Turkey's waste emissions have remained around 21 million tons of CO2 equivalent annually since 2020.

In 2021, the Global Methane Pledge (GMP) was launched at COP26, seeking a collective 30% cut in methane emissions from 2020 levels by 2030, with more than 30 countries later backing national targets. Turkey is not listed among the pledge’s participants.

Selim Yildirim, chief climate policy researcher at Ankara-based D84, a non-profit policy and media platform, said Turkey had more developed waste disposal than poorer countries but less effective management, recycling and value recovery than much of Europe.

Turkey could still join the GMP during COP31, he said, but that would not guarantee results.

"The issue is whether you can effectively turn it into action and implement it,” he said, adding that regulation was needed to push operators to capture and reuse methane.

In Seymen, about 5 km (3 miles) from the landfill, residents have another concern — the smell. Methane itself is odourless, but the decomposing organic waste can also release pungent compounds.

In summer, it enters through windows left open against the heat, said Soner Duz, a 46-year-old barber.

“Around four or five in the morning, the smell suddenly comes," he said. "It wakes you up.”

title: What could the blue wave mean for economic policy in Michigan?
authors: Stateside Staff, Sam Beaubien, www.michiganpublic.org, stateside-staff, sam-beaubien
description:
AI investment has helped drive overall economic growth, but Stevenson questioned whether that growth is creating enough jobs or raising wages for everyday Americans.
Attracting innovative companies and long-term employment opportunities could be more valuable than the temporary construction jobs associated with new data centers, Stevenson said.
Another major economic question is the rapid expansion of artificial intelligence and the data centers needed to support it.
Investment in AI has helped fuel economic growth, Stevenson said, but that growth hasn't necessarily translated into more jobs or higher wages for American workers.
All of that is to say that yes, we could risk slowing economic growth.
text:
Economist Betsey Stevenson said Democrats have gained voters' trust on economic issues — an area where Republicans have traditionally held an advantage.

Stevenson said newly elected Democrats should focus on affordability, tariffs, and health care costs rather than getting distracted by efforts to hold the Trump administration accountable.

AI investment has helped drive overall economic growth, but Stevenson questioned whether that growth is creating enough jobs or raising wages for everyday Americans.

Attracting innovative companies and long-term employment opportunities could be more valuable than the temporary construction jobs associated with new data centers, Stevenson said.

Democrats won major victories in Michigan and across the country in Tuesday's midterm election.

In Michigan, voters elected Jocelyn Benson as governor and Abdul El-Sayed to the U.S. Senate, while Democrats secured majorities in both chambers of the state Legislature.

But with affordability and the economy among voters' top concerns, what will Democrats need to do to deliver on their campaign promises?

Betsey Stevenson, a professor of public policy and economics at the University of Michigan's Ford School, joined Stateside to discuss what the election results reveal about voters' economic priorities and what they could mean for Michigan's future.

Stevenson said one of the biggest developments is a shift in which political party Americans trust to manage the economy.

For decades, she said, Republicans maintained an advantage on economic issues, even when their policies weren't necessarily producing better outcomes. But recent surveys have shown a growing belief that Democrats can do a better job.

"That was a really tough nut for Democrats to crack," Stevenson said.

Now, she argued, Democrats need to demonstrate that they can address the economic concerns that helped bring them into office.

Stevenson said newly elected lawmakers should prioritize measures aimed at reducing costs for consumers, including rolling back tariffs, and restoring Affordable Care Act subsidies. She also pointed to the economic impact of the war in Iran and its effect on oil prices.

While voters may also want greater accountability from the Trump administration, Stevenson cautioned that Democrats risk losing sight of the issues that helped them win.

Another major economic question is the rapid expansion of artificial intelligence and the data centers needed to support it. Investment in AI has helped fuel economic growth, Stevenson said, but that growth hasn't necessarily translated into more jobs or higher wages for American workers.

Although constructing data centers can create jobs in the short term, Stevenson said the facilities provide relatively few permanent positions once completed. Instead, she suggested Michigan should focus on attracting companies and industries capable of sustaining employment for decades.

"You know what some of those San Francisco companies should do? They should relocate to Detroit," Stevenson said.

With new leadership preparing to take office in Lansing and Washington, Stevenson said the challenge will be turning voters' demands for economic stability into policies that create lasting opportunities.

Scroll up to listen the full conversation, or read the transcript below:

April Baer: What a big flex the election was for the power of pocketbook issues this week, as voters in Michigan and elsewhere expressed a tsunami-sized wish for change. The stock market has been up and down like a yo-yo this week, with election-driven surges of investor confidence followed by losses for stocks that are tied to the build-out of AI data centers.

Also, what now? Will new Democratic leaders wish to rein in Trump's excesses, reach the factors that have made life less predictable and more expensive in Michigan?

With me now is Betsey Stevenson, a professor of public policy and economics at the University of Michigan's Ford School. She is also a former chief economist for the U.S. Department of Labor.

Betsey, welcome back to Stateside. Great to have you.

Betsey Stevenson: Great to talk with you.

AB: So, through an economic lens, what is your read on this? How much of the vote and the blue wave nationwide had to do with the economy and the way we all experience it?

BS: Well, you know, I want to start by pointing out that the Republicans, for decades, many, many decades, have had the upper hand with voters when it comes to trust over managing the economy. You ask people, who do you think is going to do a better job with the economy? And, you know, voters were more likely to say Republicans.

And frankly, that continued even when there wasn't really a lot of good economic evidence that Republicans were actually better for the economy. For many decades, you know, Republicans often did things that were harmful to the economy, but they still maintained a belief with voters.

And what happened was that belief has been cracked. And in fact, we saw that in survey data in 2026, when you started to see voters and Americans more generally saying that they think Democrats have an edge in handling the economy.

So that's the first step, was that they now believe Democrats will do better with the economy. And that was a really tough nut for Democrats to crack, to be able to convince voters that they could do it.

AB: We know that the agenda for many of the newly elected congressional reps and senators, Abdul El-Sayed, people like Sean McCann in the Michigan House delegation, they've talked a lot about trying to address some of these economic factors on the campaign trail.

But also, we know that there is a hunger among Dems in D.C. to try to rein in a president who's consistently pushed back on the boundaries of executive authority, maybe look at some of the leaders who are part of the Trump cabinet.

If you're newly elected, what problems would you say voters want to fix first from that economic standpoint?

BS: I think you are laying out that there's two things that voters are asking for. One is more accountability, and the other one is just basic pocketbook kitchen table issues. Like, are we, you know, can you bring prices down or at least slow the rate of increase of prices?

I think that's what they're asking for. The biggest risk Democrats have is they get distracted by the accountability and they go too far to trying to hold people accountable.

I think the first step, what I would do and what I recommend Democrats newly elected do, if you're elected on pocketbook issues, Congress has the power of the purse, and you need to take that back. And that means the first thing that any newly elected person should do when they're sworn in in early January is reassert Congress's power to tax and spend.

And by doing that, they can show that, first of all, Congress matters. Even if they've got Trump there ready to veto it, I think that voters will still reward Democrats if they're out there passing bills that say end the president's ability to impose tariffs. So they get rid of the tariffs. They're going to show that they are doing something to try to bring prices down.

If they do what they, you know, a very first step thing would be to put the subsidies back for the ACA. Americans have seen an enormous increase in the cost of health insurance, and that cost has come really from two direct things Republicans did: got rid of the subsidies and have had cuts to Medicaid. They can reverse those things immediately.

And then, of course, they need to try to check the president's war powers and see if they can bring the Iran war to, you know, a reasonable close so that we can get some stability in oil prices.

Those four things are really the immediate things that show that they're addressing pocketbook issues. And I think the risk is the distraction of there's so much corruption that they've been witnessing in D.C. But if you focus too much on that, you're not addressing the mandate the voters sent Democrats there to address their pocketbook issues.

AB: Betsey, when you think about the factors that affect inflation, is it enough to eliminate the tariffs? Is it enough to finish the war in Iran? Are these things that are going to move the needle in a way that the average person will feel?

BS: Well, you know, another thing that is driving up prices in the short run is the enormous demand for data centers and AI spending.

And voters also delivered quite a rebuke to data centers on Tuesday's election around the country.

And so slowing down and being more thoughtful about where we want data centers to go, how they're going to impact the community, and what's the responsibility of the companies that are going to be using those data centers to the communities that they're building them in, that slowing that down will bring, will also help slow the rate of price increases.

AB: So I got to tell you, I mentioned that the markets seem a bit nervous about what's, you know, what the election repercussions may be for AI.

I have been trying to think if I have ever experienced an election in which an emerging technology, in this case AI, has ever been so tied up in the politics of the moment and also at the center of so much market investment and exuberance.

Do you see any potential pitfalls for anyone who's trying to change course right now?

BS: I mean, there are pitfalls because this, you know, AI and AI enthusiasm has been propping up the economy.

If you look at, we've had this enormous GDP growth that's come from AI enthusiasm. But if we ask what that has meant for ordinary families, it hasn't meant that much because the job growth hasn't come from there.

If we look at where the job growth has been over the last year, it's basically from healthcare. We're not seeing this AI enthusiasm do much besides boost our GDP numbers in terms of it's not adding a lot of jobs, it's not raising people's wages.

All of that is to say that yes, we could risk slowing economic growth. But as long as it only slows a little, that's not so bad.

Could we push us into a recession? That, of course, is something that every politician has to be aware of and has to navigate. But I think no one's talking about ending AI or stopping AI. What we're talking about is slowing it down so it's a much more purposeful set of choices we're making.

And I think if you look at the mandate that Democrats have, one of their biggest swings was from young men, a bloc who had swung towards the Republicans and now swung back even harder towards the Democrats. And what these young men are saying is, "This world we're entering, it doesn't seem fair. It seems like wealth is being randomly distributed based on crypto or influencers or corruption. And I don't know what to do next. And I want someone who's going to help give us a little bit more security and reduce some of this uncertainty."

AB: Betsey, I want to take a minute to address something that is relevant to the big change in state leadership that we just got.

Michigan has had a Democratic governor for two terms and will continue to have one in the person of Jocelyn Benson.

And the legislature just went through this change with Democrats catching majorities in both the Michigan House and the Senate.

Typically, the state profile reacts to federal policy for sure, but also tax receipts right here in Michigan.

Is there anything, keeping in mind what you said about job growth and wages, is there anything we can say for sure about the outlook that Michigan's leaders will be dealing with by the time that these new crews swear in in January?

BS: I mean, you were right to point out that these things are just very connected with federal policy as well as with state policy.

You know, Michigan, we did just have Democrats take over, but it is a moderate state. It is a state that wants to see sensible policies that sort of play by the rules of people should be able to work hard and have a job that they trust that delivers an income.

The problem that the state has is that we're not 100% sure anymore how to achieve, you know, that promise in, you know, our modern era, right?

We saw a Trump administration throw a whole bunch of tariffs on, which should have helped our auto industry, but actually ended up hurting us because of the challenges with trade with Canada, the integration that we have. And so it's no longer a simple set of policies like, let's protect all the Michigan jobs, but we have to actually think sensibly about how we build not just jobs for the short run.

And I think that's what data centers are about. Data centers lure us into, okay, we'll get some jobs for the next few years as we build the data center, but there's no real jobs there after it's built.

So what we need to be thinking about is how do we bring in industry and how do we attract people who want to do the innovative kind of work that is going to continue to grow for decades.

You know, if you look at a place like San Francisco, it's a very expensive place to operate. You know what some of those San Francisco companies should do? They should relocate to Detroit. Detroit's been being revived. It's a great place to be.

And if we could bring some of those Palo Alto and Silicon Valley jobs to Detroit, that's the kind of job growth that could sustain us, not a data center.

AB: Betsey Stevenson is an economist at the Ford School at the University of Michigan. Betsey, thank you always for your time and your insights.

text:
WASHINGTON, D.C. – Today, U.S. Senators Mike Lee (R-Utah), Chairman of the Senate Energy and Natural Resources (ENR) Committee; Shelley Moore Capito (R-W.Va.), Chairman of the Senate Environment and Public Works (EPW) Committee; Martin Heinrich (D-N.M.), Ranking Member of the ENR Committee; and Sheldon Whitehouse (D-R.I.), Ranking Member of the EPW Committee, released a substitute amendment to the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act of 2026 (BAAJA). The substitute amendment includes clarifying, conforming, and technical edits to reflect feedback received since BAAJA’s introduction in September.

“We have spent months working across party lines on both sides of Capitol Hill and with President Trump to deliver permitting reform that makes it easier to build in America. This substitute amendment reflects that work and brings us closer to getting the job done. Our permitting system takes too long, costs too much, and leaves too much uncertainty for the people trying to build what our country needs. We have an opportunity to lower costs for American families, and get America building again. It’s time to finish what we started,”ENR Committee Chairman Lee said.

“This substitute amendment preserves the foundation of the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act, while making targeted changes based on feedback from our members and stakeholders to further build support. I’m thankful for my colleagues’ efforts to strengthen this legislation, the contributions from members of the House, and the support of countless organizations from across the country. I urge the swift passage of BAAJA to make life more affordable for American families,” EPW Committee Chairman Capito said.

“I’ve worked hard to incorporate the feedback we’ve heard from Tribes and New Mexicans into this Substitute Amendment, and I’m proud to join my colleagues in releasing it today. The Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act will help lower energy costs, strengthen Tribal consultation, and create more good-paying jobs. It also makes sure data centers pay for the energy they use and the grid upgrades they cause, instead of passing those costs on to New Mexico families. Americans can’t afford to wait for lower electricity prices. We need to pass this bill now,” ENR Committee Ranking Member Heinrich said.

“I’m grateful for the input throughout this process from Senate and House colleagues, environmental and labor organizations, and Tribal leaders. Our manager’s amendment improves BAAJA and addresses the thoughtful feedback we have received. Now’s it’s time to pass this bill so we can lower costs, juice the clean energy economy, build big things again in America, reduce pollution, and create tons of new well-paying union jobs,” EPW Committee Ranking Member Whitehouse said.

text:
Industrial processes emit vast quantities of carbon dioxide, and a new perspective article argues that the gas should be treated less as a waste product and more as a raw material. Writing in the journal Discover Catalysis, J. González-Arias, J. J. Villora-Picó and T. R. Reina survey the state of catalytic CO2 valorization, the family of technologies that use catalysts to convert captured CO2 into fuels and chemicals. Their assessment, published on 11 November 2025, weighs recent technical advances against the economic, regulatory and infrastructure barriers that still stand between laboratory demonstrations and routine industrial deployment.

The authors frame the problem in familiar terms: industrial activity contributes substantially to greenhouse gas emissions, and climate pressures are pushing companies toward sustainable practices. Catalytic valorization, they argue, offers a dual payoff. Capturing and reusing CO2 can reduce net emissions associated with industrial operations, while the converted products feed a circular economy in which waste carbon becomes a resource. The field has grown visibly: the authors compiled Scopus publication counts from 1998 to 2024 using the keywords catalysis, CO2 and industrial, and the resulting curve shows steadily rising attention to the topic over that quarter-century.

Technologically, the perspective organizes the field into four mainstream routes. Chemical or thermochemical conversion transforms CO2 into methanol, formic acid, dimethyl ether and hydrocarbons through catalytic processes. Electrochemical reduction uses renewable electricity to convert CO2 into carbon monoxide, hydrocarbons and alcohols. Biological conversion enlists microorganisms such as bacteria and algae to produce biofuels and bioplastics, integrating naturally with bioenergy systems. Photocatalytic reduction harnesses sunlight to drive the formation of fuels like methane and methanol. Each pathway occupies a different point on the maturity curve, and the authors stress that readiness varies widely across the portfolio.

Beyond the mainstream, the article catalogs emerging approaches that could serve specific industrial niches. Plasma-assisted processes activate CO2 under mild bulk conditions and respond quickly to intermittent renewable power, making them candidates for flexible operation. Mechanochemical methods such as ball milling have recently achieved nearly quantitative CO2 methanation at temperatures as low as 65 degrees Celsius, offering low-energy alternatives to conventional routes. Solar thermochemical redox cycles use concentrated sunlight to split CO2 directly into carbon monoxide, bypassing electricity-intensive steps. Accelerated mineralization locks CO2 permanently into stable carbonates while simultaneously valorizing industrial wastes such as steel slag or recycled concrete. More exotic media, including liquid metals, molten salts and radiolytic systems, enable unusual CO2-to-solid conversions that resist catalyst deactivation. All of these remain at low technology readiness levels, but the authors argue they broaden the landscape and could complement established routes.

The chemistry itself is demanding. CO2 is a thermodynamically stable molecule, so direct conversion into useful products faces a steep energy barrier, and catalysts are the tools that lower it while improving efficiency and selectivity. The perspective highlights work on CO2 hydrogenation with renewable hydrogen, conversion into C2+ hydrocarbons via bifunctional routes, and methanation over supported metallic catalysts, with nickel the most prevalent active phase. Converting CO2 to ethanol is singled out as harder than methanol synthesis because it requires direct carbon-carbon coupling. Cascade thermochemical methods are attracting growing interest: bifunctional catalysis combining a metal or metal oxide with a zeolite has shown promise for producing high-value compounds in gas-phase CO2 hydrogenation. Catalyst design advances matter too, and the authors cite work showing that hydrophobic surface modification can suppress water-induced side reactions during syngas conversion, cutting CO2 selectivity from nearly 50 percent to below 15 percent and improving overall carbon utilization efficiency.

Deactivation emerges as a central technical challenge, and the article grounds it in quantitative case studies. Catalysts can fail physically through thermal degradation, contamination or attrition, and chemically through impurities poisoning active sites or composition changes. Wolf and colleagues showed that nickel-aluminum catalysts exposed to just 5 parts per million of hydrogen sulfide lost most of their activity within hours, while manganese- and iron-promoted variants extended lifetime by 10 to 20 percent by acting as sacrificial sulfur traps. Song and colleagues demonstrated that iron-based catalysts deactivate mainly by coke accumulation: one catalyst retained 34 percent CO2 conversion and 16 percent C5+ selectivity at 100 hours but fell to 20 percent and 2 percent at 550 hours, as roughly 3.5 millimoles per gram of graphitic carbon deposited on iron carbide sites. Complementary work by Ahmed and colleagues confirmed that particle morphology controls the dominant mechanism, with smaller particles deactivating by carbon deposition while larger ones suffered fragmentation and re-oxidation. The lesson, the authors write, is that nickel and iron catalysts are extremely sensitive to trace poisons and coke buildup, making promoter doping, impurity traps and carbon management strategies essential for industrial operation.

Economics may be the decisive filter. The perspective assembles techno-economic comparisons across three product families. Methanol synthesis currently shows the lowest operating costs, roughly 310 to 590 euros per ton, with a capital expenditure estimate of about 19.27 thousand euros per ton of daily product capacity, reflecting its higher technology maturity; hydrogen production for CO2 hydrogenation can account for up to 73 percent of total cost, and each ton of methanol requires approximately 550 kilowatt-hours and 0.48 to 1.16 tons of steam. Formic acid production is less mature, with capital expenditure estimated at 770 thousand euros per ton of daily product and operating expenses near 770 euros per ton, largely because energy requirements make up 70 to 85 percent of operating costs. Synthetic natural gas sits in between, with a capital expenditure estimate of 970 euros per ton of daily product and production costs of 70 to 160 euros per megawatt-hour, two to seven times higher than fossil natural gas, and viability highly sensitive to electricity prices for renewable hydrogen. On these numbers, the authors conclude, methanol is closest to economic competitiveness, while formic acid and synthetic natural gas need major advances in energy efficiency and capital reduction before large-scale deployment becomes viable.

Policy is beginning to close some of those gaps. In the United States, the Inflation Reduction Act of 2022 expanded the 45Q tax credit to up to 85 dollars per ton for CO2 storage and 60 dollars per ton for utilization. In Europe, the Innovation Fund, worth roughly 40 billion euros by 2030, and the ReFuelEU Aviation mandate, which requires synthetic e-fuels made from CO2 by 2030, create both funding opportunities and guaranteed markets. Meanwhile the EU Emissions Trading System and the new Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism raise the cost of carbon-intensive imports, incentivizing low-carbon production pathways. Hydrogen costs remain a sticking point: gray hydrogen is cheapest at 1.5 to 2.5 dollars per kilogram but increasingly constrained by carbon pricing, blue hydrogen runs 2.0 to 3.5 dollars per kilogram, and green hydrogen, at 3.5 to 6.0 dollars per kilogram, is dominated by electricity costs that make up about 70 percent of its price. Competitiveness, the authors note, requires renewable electricity below 20 to 30 dollars per megawatt-hour and electrolyzer capital costs, currently 800 to 1700 dollars per kilowatt, falling by 30 to 50 percent as systems scale beyond 100 megawatts.

What distinguishes this perspective from earlier reviews, the authors say, is its emphasis on moving beyond laboratory-scale progress in individual processes toward multidisciplinary collaboration and knowledge transfer. They point to concrete examples: the EU-funded eForFuel project combines electrochemistry, microbiology and chemical engineering to convert CO2 into formic acid that is then transformed into hydrocarbons; the a-leaf consortium is building an artificial photosynthesis platform for solar-to-chemical energy conversion; Sunfire, within the German Kopernikus P2X program, commissioned a 220-kilowatt high-temperature co-electrolysis unit with efficiency above 85 percent on a lower heating value basis, now integrated at the Karlsruhe Institute of Technology to synthesize fuels; and Carbon Recycling International has scaled CO2 hydrogenation from pilot plants to commercial methanol production exceeding 100,000 tons per year. Additional initiatives include Norsk e-Fuel’s renewable aviation fuels partnership, the STORE&GO methanation pilots across Europe, the LEILAC project decarbonizing cement and lime production, and the ongoing Air2Chem project led by Fraunhofer UMSICHT with RWTH Aachen, which integrates direct air capture with carbonate electrolysis to convert atmospheric CO2 into syngas and ethylene.

The authors close with stakeholder-specific priorities. Academia should design robust catalysts with quantifiable lifetimes under realistic feeds and impurities while exploring underexplored routes such as mechanochemical, plasma-assisted and mineralization-based utilization. Industry should scale up integrated systems, particularly in hard-to-abate sectors like steel and cement, implement impurity management and regeneration strategies, and demonstrate multi-megawatt pilot and commercial plants. Policymakers should establish harmonized life cycle assessment and techno-economic assessment standards, effective carbon pricing and clear regulatory frameworks. Computational modelling has a role throughout: the article cites reactor optimization for CO2 methanation at wastewater treatment plants that showed high efficiency and stability, life cycle evaluation of a pilot plant producing light hydrocarbons via methanol, and an integrated methane dry reforming and methanol production scheme at pilot level that lowered costs and reduced the carbon footprint compared with conventional methods. The overall message is that catalytic CO2 valorization is technically real and increasingly well funded, but its transformation of industry depends on solving catalyst longevity, hydrogen affordability and regulatory alignment at the same time.

text:
At 2 p.m. this afternoon the Senate Democratic caucus meets to talk about the big “permitting reform” bill that is supposed to be voted on next week. That meeting is a reflection of pre-election politics, when the GOP had all the power; it will be held in the wake of Stephen Miller’s appointment as prime minister yesterday, which effectively ends the week of good feelings that came from the election. I’m going to write about permitting reform in a minute—but damnit, I refuse to surrender so quickly the long and beautiful night of the election. So many worked so hard not to savor it.

Sometime around midnight on Tuesday I could suddenly feel a great soft weariness—not sleepiness, I was fully wired and hope-scrolling with the best of them, but instead a kind of welcome fatigue settling into my bones. Partly it was an after-effect of the fall’s endless travel back and forth across the country to organize with my Third Act colleagues, but there was something more. I think some part of me was relaxing for the first time since election night 2024, some part of me that had been tensed up against the constant assault of ugliness, cruelty and stupidity that has marked this grotesque period.

Tuesday was…wonderful. Americans just spit out the poison. It turns out, thank heaven, that most people didn’t like the division and hate, the corruption and the constant provocation. It doesn’t end the problem, of course—Trump and his crew remain firmly in power. It will take another election to remedy that, and even then there’s much that may never be fixed—the world’s opinion of our country, for one; the scientific and educational systems broken for the sheer delight of anti-intellectual vandalism; the lives ended or ruined by deportations; the time lost in the climate fight. But at least the spell has broken.

So, on the other side, let’s talk about permitting reform, and today’s Democratic caucus meeting. Because the bill’s proponents are trying to rush it through, that meeting will be taken up with talk of “manager’s amendments” to fix technical clauses. But that’s not the fundamental problem.

Permitting reform, you will recall, is the rubric for a 417 page piece of legislation officially known as the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act, or BAAJA. It was announced last month by two Democratic Senators (Sheldon Whitehouse and Martin Heinrich) and two of their GOP counterparts, and fashioned as a grand bargain that would give both Big Oil and Biggish Cleantech some of what they each want, essentially by making it much easier to build stuff: electric transmission corridors, gas pipelines, you name it. And it largely does this by allowing them to sidestep environmental laws that opponents have used to slow projects down.

It is, in essence, legislation derived from the argument in Abundance, Ezra Klein and Derek Thompson’s bestseller about the need to make it easier to build. I am largely persuaded by their argument—and heartened, for instance, to see YIMBY’s ablest legislative advocate, Scott Wiener, winning Nancy Pelosi’s old seat in Congress. It is much too hard to build stuff we badly need—housing, transit, energy. But in the case of energy there’s a problem, and that problem (as so often) is climate change. Building more housing produces…more housing. But if you take climate change seriously, you have to build more clean energy and less dirty energy, or otherwise you don’t get anywhere.

And so the relevant questions about BAAJA are: what does it give up, and what does it produce? These have become at least a little clearer over the last few weeks as analysts have dug into the byzantine text.

So—What does it give up?

Quite a bit, as you would expect—it is, after all, a compromise with the Republicans, who at the time the bill was drafted were the majority in both the House and Senate, and with the White House, which still holds cards. David Bookbinder, former chief climate counsel at the Sierra Club who has helped argue crucial cases before the Supreme Court, compiled a long list, but it begins like this:

It makes fossil fuel infrastructure permitting even easier than it has already become, binds future administrations to the energy permitting policies of the Trump administration, seriously weakens the Clean Water Act, and effectively repeals the National Environmental Policy Act (NEPA) and the Endangered Species Act.

Those are the things the bill means to give away—they’re the stuff the oil industry wants. But as it turns out, the people drafting the bill on Democrats’ side (a tiny crew, since Whitehouse and Heinrich were telling no one negotiations were underway) managed to make some drafting errors that one analyst after another has noted give away even more than they probably intended to. Bookbinder argues that Title IV of the bill, “Project Certainty,” “beggars belief.”

It effectively insulates not only the construction, but “the operation at full capacity” of all existing fossil fuel infrastructure from any future regulatory action of any sort. That means, for example, no increased stringency in federal environmental regulatory requirements under any statute – the Clean Air Act, the Clean Water Act, etc. can ever be applied to such projects. But it goes well beyond that – the clause barring the federal government from “tak[ing] any other action to interfere with or prevent” construction or operation means these facilities are immune from enforcement of any federal law that would “interfere with” the construction or “operation at full capacity” of any such infrastructure. (Nor is this provision limited to fossil fuel infrastructure; it applies just as well to steel mills, highways, etc.) In other words, a single federal permit or authorization under any one federal law effectively immunizes that project from adverse effects from changes in (1) that federal law; (2) any other federal environmental law; and (3) any federal law at all.

Lots of people—not just environmentalists—are worried about these provisions. For instance, the organizations fighting new detention centers for immigrants put out a call to action saying it would effectively eliminate

the very tools communities have used to fight detention expansion in states including Arizona, Maryland, Michigan, New Jersey, and Texas. Taking them away would leave communities with fewer ways to stop new facilities and challenge the harm they cause.

The same logic applies to data centers. EarthJustice, the most important nonprofit law firm for the planet, has been putting out a series of reports explaining exactly how their drive to slow data center expansion, and with it a truly enormous spread of natural gas turbines, would be impacted. First they have an October report calculating just how much gas is lurking out there that might be hooked up

Building on work from Global Energy Monitor, the Environmental Integrity Project, and Cleanview, we estimate that gas will power approximately 80% of energy generation from BYOP projects coming online in the next five years. In total, we identify 177 GW of planned gas capacity, equivalent to 23% of the entire U.S.’s peak demand in 2025 and enough to power 65% of all U.S. homes.

And then on Thnursday EarthJustice president Abigail Dillen (who you can see in action on David Fenton’s podcast) put out a powerful account of what will happen to anyone’s ability to block any of this:

With its extremely targeted provisions for gas pipelines, BAAJA delivers a precision strike for developers of dirty data centers. Here’s the package: gutting federal environmental review, including an outright exclusion for pipeline expansions, rubber-stamping permits under the Clean Water Act, blocking interference from States and Tribes, and prohibiting courts from issuing injunctions and other meaningful remedies. What this combination gives to the gas industry is an ultra fast-track for new and expanded gas pipelines that is insulated from court challenges and the kind of public opposition to data centers that is now expanding to associated pipeline projects.

As she points out, the timing couldn’t be worse:

Why does the fast-track matter so much? Some of the industry’s biggest players are poised to bring gas from hubs like the Marcellus Shale and the Permian Basin to fuel bigger and bigger data center complexes with gas. From the perspective of AI hyperscalers, piping in gas for on-site power is the fastest, cheapest path to lock in power on a timeline and on terms that are most in their control. The only risk they have now is reliable gas capacity. BAAJA’s pipeline package would solve that problem for them immediately, sealing many deals that would enable the dirtiest version of the data center build-out to move even faster, while the transmission provisions that could enable more clean energy will take years.

That’s what you give up to get this deal. It’s a lot. It more or less means laying down most of the tools that we’ve used over the years to markedly improve the nation’s environment.

But—the biggest threat to that environment now is the rapid heating underway on planet earth, and the only scalable tool we have to slow that down is the even-more-rapid deployment of clean energy, as long as it displaces dirty energy. You could argue that it’s therefore worth it to give up those hard-won things if it produces a real return.

So—what do we get in return?

This bill is extraordinarily complex, and therefore hard to model, especially on the tight deadlines imposed by the decision to push it through in the lame duck session. But the benefits are real, especially in making it easier to build the electric transmission corridors badly needed to bring clean power long distances. (It’s possible that need is lessening a bit as we get better at deploying batteries, but it’s still important). The question is, what kind of change will it produce?

And the answers are…uninspiring.

Some modelers—Kevin Kircher at Purdue, say—forecast that it will actually increase greenhouse gas emissions

With at least 75% probability in this modeling framework, BAAJA increases all of the following: Revenues and jobs in both clean electricity and fossil fuel industries, with larger increases for fossil fuels; domestic energy-related greenhouse gas emissions; domestic mortality attributable to air pollution from fossil fuels; and fossil fuel exports

That is a depressing forecast. But let’s make the very best argument that one can, the one that the bill’s proponents have been hailing. That comes from modelers at the Rhodium Group, who tried to figure out how the interlocking parts of the bill would work. They left some things out—for instance the very likely increase in exported natural gas, which, no matter where it’s burned still ends up in our shared atmosphere (and if you want to hear a few choice words about BAJAA and LNG, here is my old friend Roishetta Ozane, telling some home truths from Louisiana)—but even so here is the conclusion they came to, as explained by Robinson Meyer and Emily Pontecorvo at Heatmap:

In the best case scenario, the bill could cut U.S. economy-wide emissions by 4%, reduce energy bills by $78 per year, and drive more than 200 gigawatts of new clean energy capacity by 2040, compared to status quo policy. In a worst case scenario, greenhouse gas emissions would remain unchanged on their current trajectory.

Read that again. Over the next fifteen years, the absolutely crucial years for anything we’re planning to do to rein in climate change, this bill will do…essentially nothing.

And, just as bad, as we’ve seen above, it will essentially lock in “doing nothing.”

Bottom line: if what this bill’s proponents envision comes true, then America will not have slowed the heating of the planet over the next 15 years. Since the rest of the world is on a very different course, the U.S. will be a massive outlier.

Here’s what it looks like on a graph. The light blue line is where we need to go under the Paris accords. The dark blue, green, and purple lines are where the Rhodium Group’s different scenarios project we’re going, and the dotted lines are where we’re going with BAAJA. If you say to yourself “they’re almost exactly the same,” then you’ve figured out the problem.

If this bill simply mandated those reductions, without destroying environmental laws, it would still be a painful idea. But since we get essentially nothing and give up an awful lot, it’s like the kind of trade that sixth graders pull off on their four-year-old brothers the day after Halloween: “this box of Milk Duds has eight pieces in it, so you should give me eight Reeses cups. And I’ll throw in this Charleston Chew.”

All of this is made worse by the third factor here, which is the timing.

When negotiators put the grand bargain together, we were still in a world ruled by Donald Trump and the GOP, and Whitehouse and Heinrich regarded this as the best possible deal that could be made. But now we’ve had the biggest single shift in political power in this country since the post-Watergate year of 1974.

We don’t know all the factors that drove that great victory—disgust with the Trump regime above all, I think. But one of its distinctive factors was revulsion at data centers. People had many reasons to oppose them, from water use to energy prices to fear of AI to disgust with oligarchs. But they only had one way to oppose them, which were the set of laws BAAJA sets out to sideline. There seem to have been forty ballot measures around the country to restrict data centers, and 39 of them appear to have passed.

As Abigail Dillen noted, to the degree that we can discern anything about voter’s views on rapidly cleaning up our energy system, they’re in favor:

Democrats won control of the Georgia Public Service Commission and appear to have won two seats on the Arizona Corporation Commission, narrowing the Republican majority from 5-0 to 3-2. In Texas, Democrats won a seat on the Railroad Commission, which regulates the oil and gas industry. With these seats, there is an opportunity to usher in clean energy for people who are struggling with soaring energy costs. These were the opposite of sleepy races: Voters are understanding the connection between data centers, utility rates, and regulatory bodies.

And, in the midst of a rush to drill more oil and gas and entrench our fossil fuel dependence, voters rejected a ballot measure to establish a constitutional “right to gas” in Colorado, a major oil-and-gas-producing state. The oil and gas industry presented voters with a false choice between prosperity and policies aimed at reducing greenhouse gas emissions. Voters know better.

As Emily Atkin pointed out, “the U.S. oil and gas industry spent at least $182 million trying to elect Republicans in last night’s midterm elections,” second only to the AI barons. Hell, in the single most expensive House race in the entire country, the oil and gas industry threw everything they had at young Will Lawrence, a founder of the Sunrise Movement, and he beat the incumbent and flipped the seat. As Atkin points out

In perhaps the most stunning blue flip in Texas, Democrat Jon Rosenthal won the race to oversee the Texas Railroad Commission, the agency that oversees the state’s massive oil and gas industry—and his did it despite his Republican opponent receiving $1.8 million from oil-linked donors. While Rosenthal hardly portrays himself as a climate champion, he’s campaigned on ending routine flaring and venting, requiring modern leak detection, and enforcing pollution rules.

So maybe it wouldn’t be the best idea to hand data center proponents an immediate win. If you wonder, by the way, how the AI industry and its hydrocarbon enablers think about BAAJA, the Revolving Door Project has a helpful catalogue of their reactions, which basically boil down to—”please and thank you.” Here’s the Williams pipeline company:

“AI, electrification and the onshoring of manufacturing are creating unprecedented growth in power demand. […] We need to build the power facilities and linear infrastructure necessary to meet this growth or we will surely fall behind. And America’s energy security depends on our ability to supply our allies with American natural gas.”

In the face of all that, BAAJA’s proponents have started talking less about emissions reductions and more about “affordability,” arguing that it will reduce utility costs. Sadly, As Kate Aronoff points out, the same Rhodium Group modeling indicates that the savings for an average savings by 2040 of somewhere around (it seems to be the magic number) 4 percent compared with what they would have been without the law.

If you think it’s just tired old environmentalists saying this, take it from this tired old environmentalist: people sprightlier than me are saying the same thing. Jared Huffman, for instance, who will be running environmental policy in the House after the Democrats take control of the chamber in January. He was responding, the day after the election, to Chuck Schumer’s promise that it would not be a “supplicant Senate” that Trump now faces.

The first chance to show that the days of Trump's "supplicant Senate" are over is Nov. 9th. Dems can demand a hearing and amendments to improve the deeply flawed BAAJA bill before it moves forward. Or, they can cave to Trump and agree to jam through his 400-page MAGA wish list - the most sweeping environmental/energy bill in decades - without a single hearing. If that happens after last night's Blue Tsunami, the word "supplicant" would be far too kind.

The bill’s proponents know that it’s in trouble—the Sierra Club, for instance, came out against it yesterday. Hakeem Jeffries said last night that the bill needed attention from the House—but he focused on relatively small issues with tribes and National Environmental Policy Act provisions that presumably can be sanded behind closed doors, without resolving the larger problems. That may work, or it may not. As Keith Goldberg at Law360 reported, DC energy lobbyists, even on the fossil fuel side, aren’t sure. One, Scott Segal, noted what I was saying above about data centers:

“You’ve got an increasing realization that the second section of the bill is somewhat in service to data centers..an issue that was at play in the midterm elections.”

Look, all of this is hard, and only the oil companies and their harem of politicians have bad intentions; Sheldon Whitehouse and Martin Heinrich are trying to be of service, and they’re navigating a political landscape that suddenly shifted. (Partly thanks to them—by most accounts Whitehouse was one of the people who recruited Mississippi’s Scott Colom to run for the Senate!) We definitely need ways to build out more energy; abundance, all things equal, is abundant! But we also need ways to honor and harness the political energy unleashed on Tuesday, a vital force that we don’t yet fully understand.

My bottom line: I desperately don’t want to get to 2040 (and here I use the metaphorical I, since 2040 is pushing my lifespan) and find that our emissions have gone down a measly four percent.

I think that if this deal had been made thirty years ago, it might have made sense—we’d be reaping the benefits now. But the fossil fuel industry made sure we didn’t. And this bill, which they’re backing with great enthusiasm, seems an awful lot like a hedge to make sure they can string their business model out for a few more decades—a way to lock in the fruits of their decades of political obstructionism.

Gambling on something better is indeed a gamble—maybe the political moment will never come again. But gambling that these kind of reductions are anywhere near sufficient is not a gamble against politics. It’s a gamble against physics. Even after Tuesday I’m not feeling that lucky.

And I think that Trump, after a few days of uncharacteristic meekness, made entirely clear yesterday that we’re not going to be living in a world of anything like normal politics the next two years. Anointing Stephen Miller as, in essence, acting president while he sundowns about ballrooms and arches should be all the signal that the Democrats meeting this afternoon—he is the single most vile character I’ve ever seen on our national scene, a man with blood on his hands and a literal errand boy for the fossil fuel industry. John Podesta explained that BAAJA would be like handing Trump a “loaded howitzer.” Handing Stephen Miller a loaded howitzer is not something any Senator should even contemplate. Period.
