In other energy and climate news:

+Emily Atkin again, with an excellent account of why Democrats should quickly move to tax the “disgusting” profits that American oil companies have made off the Iran war. She draws on a Times analysis of just how disgusting that bonanza has been. As Rebecca Elliott and Keith Collins document

The war with Iran has been very lucrative for American oil companies, which have earned more than $130 billion in profit as people pay much higher prices for gasoline, diesel and other fuel.

That is a conservative estimate based on the performance of more than 50 large U.S. oil and gas companies, most of them producers or refiners, in the six months from April through September. It does not reflect profits earned in March, the first month of the war, or in October…

United Refining, a privately held fuel maker in western Pennsylvania, plans to use this year’s windfall to pay down debt, said John Catsimatidis, the company’s chief executive and a longtime Trump ally. Or, perhaps, to buy a new corporate plane.

“I am serious,” Mr. Catsimatidis said in an interview. “You know why? I’m 78 years old. If I don’t buy a new airplane now, when am I going to buy it? When I’m dead?”

And as Atkin points out, a windfall profits tax is not a radical idea. Jimmy Carter imposed one in the 1970s, only to watch Ronald Reagan shut it down as a favor to his friends at Big Oil. Meanwhile,

After Russia invaded Ukraine in 2022, governments across Europe taxed windfall profits.

According to the European Commission, European Union countries collected more than €26 billion from emergency taxes on fossil fuel companies’ windfall earnings in 2022 and 2023. Much of that money went toward helping households and businesses struggling with high energy prices.

The EU-wide measure expired at the end of 2023, but some countries have kept their own windfall taxes in place. The United Kingdom, for example, imposed its own windfall tax on oil and gas companies in 2022—and they did it under a Conservative government.

That tax is still in effect, and raised £2.6 billion in the last fiscal year alone. In fact, Britain has since extended the tax through 2030, with plans to replace it with a permanent tax on oil and gas companies whenever prices get unusually high.

If you think it’s a good idea, here’s a petition from Make Polluters Pay that you might want to sign

+The rest of the world is gearing up for COP 31 in Turkey later this month (the U.S., of course will not be there because climate change is a hoax). Akshat Rathi has a particularly useful preview, on the ways that electrification is emerging as a path forward

One of the main goals of the organizers of the United Nations climate conference starting next week in Antalya, Turkey, is to have countries party to the Paris Agreement to sign up to a goal to increase the global share of final energy demand coming from electricity to 35% by 2035, from about 20% today. So far, however, the ambition remains only a voluntary one for countries to commit to.

“I would like to see a strong outcome on electrification in our presidency-led decision,” said Chris Bowen, Australia’s climate change and energy minister and COP31’s president of negotiations, on the Zero podcast. That decision would have to be signed off by all countries attending the summit, which starts on Nov. 9.

“Electrification is an unquestionably good thing,” Bowen said. “Even if your grid is powered by coal and you don’t have solar panels at home, if you’re just charging [an electric car] off a coal-fired grid, you are reducing emissions by something like 60%.”

+China has figured out that if you’re going to build data centers it makes eminent sense to pair them with clean, cheap energy. As Andrew Liu explains

Its vast wind, solar and battery industries could help power those facilities with cheaper electricity and bring them online faster by reducing reliance on conventional grid connections.

Envision Energy, the world’s second-largest wind turbine supplier, offers a glimpse of China’s approach. In August, the company began operating a data center campus in Ulanqab, Inner Mongolia, powered by renewable electricity supplied directly to the site. Envision says the facility could become the world’s largest standalone AI data center, with plans to expand beyond 2 gigawatts of capacity. The company also says customers can lock in electricity rates 20 percent below grid prices for a decade.

The project highlights the contrasting strategies China and the United States are pursuing to meet AI’s soaring energy demands. The Trump administration has scrapped a requirement that AI data centers built on federal land be paired with clean energy generation. China is taking a different path, targeting renewable sources for more than 80 percent of the electricity used by new data centers in its major computing hubs.

+Important new book from the venerable Peter Gleick. When the Well Is Dry highlights “the relationship between water and violence, and how we can move from conflict to cooperation and peace.”

The first major water war erupted around 2500 BCE, when the Sumerian city-states of Lagash and Umma fought for a century over irrigation canals from the Tigris River. A few thousand years later, both Athenians and then Spartans were accused of poisoning the water supply of their enemies, in pursuit of victory. From the ancient Sumerian, Babylonian, and Assyrian empires to the present day, access to and control over freshwater has been entwined with human conflict, violence, and war. As a fundamental resource for survival, ecosystems, and the stability of civilizations, water and its scarcity or intentional manipulation have long played a pivotal role in power struggles and geopolitical tensions.

This book will let you understand the rest of the century more easily.

+With his retirement only weeks away, Dana Nuccitelli has a summation of Mitch McConnell’s climate “legacy.”

During his tenure, McConnell exerted his power to halt or overturn climate action in Congress, at the Supreme Court, and in the White House. Over a decades-long career, he joined a short list of individuals most responsible for stymying political efforts to address climate change.

Over his 40-year tenure in the Senate, McConnell received over $4 million in donations from the oil and gas and coal industries – the fifth-most of any senator.

+Just in case you were feeling sorry for the tech barons who lost tens of billions in Thursday’s stock market rout, Evan Halper and Kevin Schaul document how these guys—who once made extensive climate promises—have become some of the world’s biggest emitters.

To support their data centers, tech firms are driving construction of a new generation of supersized, gas-fired power plants that could lock in hundreds of millions of tons of climate pollution for decades to come, according to corporate disclosures and an analysis conducted for The Post by a researcher at the Harvard T.H. Chan School of Public Health.

Industry estimates show these projects have put the tech sector on course to grow from a modest driver of industrial carbon pollution into one of the world’s biggest emitters of greenhouse gases. Some anticipate that its share of global carbon emissions will increase as much as fivefold from 2020 to 2030. That would leave the tech industry churning out more than half the climate pollution created by global aviation or shipping — sectors long associated with driving warming.

“AI may feel completely digital, immaterial, but its infrastructure is very physical. It needs land, power plants, transmission, water and fuel, and those choices can last for decades,” said the Harvard researcher, Gianluca Guidi, who based his analysis on air permits, corporate disclosures, community presentations and other materials collected largely by the research firm Cleanview.

+Climate science suffered a real loss, with the death last week of Lonnie Thompson who in a half century at Ohio State led the world in its understanding of how climate change was melting the frozen areas of our planet. As Mark Bowen wrote in Thin Ice,

In his efforts to obtain ice cores, Thompson has spent an enormous amount of time at elevations above 5,500 meters. High-altitude climbers typically tackle a peak by spending time in a series of camps at lower elevations to acclimatize and then making a final rushed push for the summit. But Thompson and his loyal band of colleagues, students and mountain guides spend literally months at a time working at altitude... Thompson and his colleagues have managed to drill into tropical glaciers with nothing more to rely on than a combination of modest funding, low-tech equipment, ingenuity and sheer muscle power. Because the thin air at high altitudes precludes the use of helicopters, all of the drilling equipment and supplies must be carried up and down the slopes by yaks, mules, horses or humans…

+China is deploying airships to capture high altitude wind power, and just running the electricity back to earth on a long cord. I still want blimps for transit, but you have to admit this one comes with an interesting twist:

The demonstration focused on deployment under real operating conditions near a city, following the system's completion of a full flight verification at an altitude of 4,000 meters in Northwest China in August, according to the company.

Beyond sending electricity to the ground, the company is experimenting with taking computing equipment closer to its power source. Dun Tianrui, CEO of Linyi Yunchuan, told the Global Times that the S4000 has space reserved for graphics processing units (GPUs), and that related experiment have already been conducted.

"The S4000 already has enough space reserved for computing GPUs, and we have carried out related experiments," Dun said. He estimated that deploying GPUs on an airborne platform could cost less than $10 per kilogram, compared with about $10,000 per kilogram for deployment in space.

The idea is to supply the hardware directly with wind-generated electricity while using cold air at high altitudes to reduce cooling requirements. Dun said mounting computing boards on the platform could also reduce the need for conventional buildings and cabinets used to house computing equipment.

title: Energy Security Starts at Home: More Than a Slogan – Now Critical for Business and ...
description:
For a decade, energy policy often pitted fossil fuels against clean energy as political identity markers.
Voters in 2026 prioritized affordability and inflation; energy prices were a dominant issue.
Intermittent resources plus storage and existing gas capacity have delivered measurable benefits under ERCOT’s energy-only market design.
Renewables can scale quickly and cheaply at the margin when paired with storage, transmission, and firm capacity.
One thing missing in the United States Democrat party right now is any discussion on reducing energy costs to consumers.
text:
For years, “energy security starts at home” served as a catchy talking point in policy debates. The Iran war and the resulting disruptions around the Strait of Hormuz, combined with the 2026 midterm “blue wave,” have turned it into a practical requirement for businesses, investors, grid operators, and voters. Reliability, affordability, and deliverable supply now outweigh ideological purity in political and commercial decisions. Stu Turley, Energy News Beat podcast host has been saying that for years, and added “Your Energy Dominance is displayed through your Exports.”

Robert Rapier’s November 6, 2026, OilPrice.com analysis captures the shift clearly. For a decade, energy policy often pitted fossil fuels against clean energy as political identity markers. Governments announced phase-out timelines; investors bet on which technologies would lose favor. The Iran conflict exposed the limits of that approach. Roughly one-fifth of global oil and LNG trade previously moved through Hormuz, giving a single chokepoint outsized leverage. When supplies are interrupted and prices rise, governments prioritize fuel availability, electricity reliability, and cost management over ideological consistency.⁠Oilprice

Geopolitics Forces Pragmatism

Rapier details the response. Saudi Arabia and the UAE are expanding bypass pipelines. HSBC’s CEO has suggested alternative routes could largely sideline Hormuz for oil within five years. Saudi Aramco plans crude storage at Singapore’s Jurong Rock Caverns starting in 2027. QatarEnergy signed a 20-year deal for up to 3 million metric tons annually from Woodside’s Louisiana LNG project (deliveries from 2030). Canada approved Phase 2 of LNG Canada, doubling capacity to 28 million metric tons annually and adding Pacific diversification for Asian buyers. The U.S. Gulf Coast benefits from geography and existing infrastructure that avoids Hormuz entirely.⁠Oilprice

Europe provides a cautionary lesson. After reducing Russian gas dependence via U.S. LNG following the Ukraine invasion, European gas prices still exceeded €100 per megawatt-hour in late October 2026—the first time since 2022—due to colder weather and tight storage amid Middle East disruptions. Nuclear is also returning to the reliability conversation: the U.S. Department of Energy announced a $5 billion loan for uprates adding 1.1 gigawatts at Constellation Energy plants. Grid and transmission upgrades, storage, distributed generation, and demand response are now treated as core security investments because a barrel or electron that cannot reach the customer has little value.⁠Oilprice

The core insight is pragmatic: the transition continues, but it must incorporate redundancy, geographic diversification, dispatchability, and multiple routes to market. Redundancy adds upfront costs, yet the economic value of avoiding disruptions is higher. Solar, wind, batteries, nuclear, natural gas, pipelines, and transmission are evaluated by their contribution to a resilient system rather than by political category.

The Blue Wave and Renewables Discussions

The November 2026 midterms delivered a Democratic sweep of the House and Senate (with Democrats flipping multiple Republican seats, including in Texas and other energy-relevant states). This has revived wind and solar discussions after years of Trump administration hostility, permit challenges, and tax-credit uncertainty. Ørsted’s shares jumped nearly 10% intraday and closed about 5% higher as investors saw reduced risk of further federal interference in offshore wind. Other developers saw more modest gains. Industry voices, including American Clean Power Association CEO Jason Grumet, framed the result around “affordable, reliable power.” Democratic control strengthens defenses of remaining tax credits (especially storage) in budget negotiations, increases scrutiny of executive actions against projects, and opens more state-level opportunities in places that flipped or tightened.⁠The Guardian

Permitting reform is the near-term flashpoint. A bipartisan package (Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act) is scheduled for a Senate procedural vote around November 9. Proponents argue it can cut NEPA and related delays (often 4.5+ years for clean energy projects and longer for transmission), unlock tens or hundreds of billions in investment, expand interregional transmission, and lower electricity costs by several percent—hundreds of billions in consumer savings over time—while adding capacity. Some analyses project meaningful GDP and emissions benefits. With a Democratic Congress and a Republican White House, outcomes will require compromise; full restoration of prior wind and solar credits is unlikely, but blocking further rollbacks and advancing infrastructure is plausible.⁠Realclearenergy

Will It Move the Bar on Dependable, Lower-Cost Energy?

Discussions are increasing, but the bar is set by physics, economics, and customer demand more than by election results. Electricity demand is rising from data centers, manufacturing, electrification, and population growth. Voters in 2026 prioritized affordability and inflation; energy prices were a dominant issue. Businesses require power that is available when needed at predictable costs.

Texas (ERCOT) offers a real-world counterpoint to pure ideology. The state has added large volumes of solar and battery storage while maintaining competitive markets. Reliability metrics improved dramatically (blackout risk falling sharply from earlier projections), and average electricity prices remain well below the national average. Solar and storage have helped suppress wholesale prices and manage peaks even as load grows, according to market analyses and operator data. Intermittent resources plus storage and existing gas capacity have delivered measurable benefits under ERCOT’s energy-only market design. At the same time, gas remains critical for evening ramps and firm capacity, and full system costs (backup, transmission, curtailment, and utilization rates) matter. High-renewable European systems continue to show elevated retail prices in many cases, underscoring that headline generation costs are not the full picture.⁠Utilitydive

The demand for dependable energy at lower system costs is structural. Data centers and AI loads are large, relatively inflexible, and sensitive to both price and reliability. Geopolitical shocks raise the premium on domestic, diversified supply. Nuclear provides firm, low-carbon power without continuous fuel imports. Natural gas offers flexible dispatch and existing infrastructure. Renewables can scale quickly and cheaply at the margin when paired with storage, transmission, and firm capacity. Energy efficiency and distributed resources reduce the volume that must be imported or transmitted long distances—literally starting security at the home or facility level.

Political control influences incentives, permitting speed, and which technologies receive support. It does not rewrite engineering or the requirement that systems near capacity fail expensively during disruptions. A Democratic Congress may protect and modestly expand certain clean-energy pathways and accelerate infrastructure, but sustained results will still require pragmatic mixes, realistic cost accounting, and domestic supply chains. Businesses and capital allocators are already prioritizing projects that clear reliability and cost hurdles rather than political narratives.

Energy security starts at home because undeliverable energy has limited value, because global chokepoints remain real, and because American consumers and industries will punish policies that raise bills or risk outages. The post-Hormuz and post-midterm environment rewards technologies and infrastructure that deliver, not slogans. The mix that succeeds will be the one that keeps the lights on, the factories running, and the costs manageable—regardless of which party holds which chamber.

One thing missing in the United States Democrat party right now is any discussion on reducing energy costs to consumers. Buckle up, get some popcorn and enjoy the show as the try to go for revenge, and I do not believe that the can control the Democrat Socialists Members in their party. Their party is just being used by foreign interests, and I am not sure they see that.

text:
When Kosovo-based Besam Group undertook the renovation of the Ministry of Culture building in 2017, it was a major task for the family-run business. Founded in 1992, the company had decades of experience, but mostly on smaller-scale projects. The Ministry renovation, together with several other public buildings in Pristina, brought more demanding energy-efficiency requirements. Meeting them meant learning new techniques, undergoing specialized training, and adapting the way the company worked.

“It was then that we understood what energy efficiency work was about,” Fejza Haliti, CEO of Besam Group, recalled. Employees attended courses, visited trade fairs, and received factory training. As the company began competing for larger energy efficiency contracts, it expanded its machinery, hired more workers, and has since moved to larger premises. By 2026, Besam Group had completed work on more than 200 buildings, including hospitals, schools, university buildings, and kindergartens.

Insulating buildings, replacing old windows and heating systems, and introducing more efficient technologies can reduce the amount of energy needed to keep homes, schools, and hospitals warm. This is crucial for the energy security of the Western Balkans, a region where heating accounts for around 40% of final energy use — the actual energy in terms of processed fuels and electricity used by consumers.

But Besam's experience points to a broader transformation.

As energy efficiency investments expand, spurring renovations that reduce energy consumption and lower electricity bills, they are also creating new markets, supporting business growth, and generating demand for specialized skills and labor across the economy.

That is why the World Bank Group has made supporting energy efficiency efforts a priority in the region, offering both project financing and technical assistance that demonstrate tangible results in energy savings and job creation. Kosovo's experience shows how a new ecosystem of private businesses and jobs can emerge around public sector renovations, while in Serbia the focus has been on household demand to scale investment. In North Macedonia, training and renovation programs are helping prepare a workforce for the next generation of energy efficient buildings.

From building retrofits to an emerging market that spurred local jobs

Kosovo's experience stretches back more than a decade. Approved in 2014, the World Bank-supported Kosovo Energy Efficiency and Renewable Energy Project combined public-building renovations with energy audits, technical studies, training for firms, and policy and regulatory support intended to strengthen the conditions for continued investment.

By its completion, the investments were projected to deliver 1.14 million MWh in lifetime energy saving — enough to supply energy for 10,000 households for 20 years — and 27% above the project’s initial target.

The project also helped build the skills, institutions, and experience needed for energy efficiency investments to continue beyond individual building renovations.

Approved in 2014, the World Bank-supported Kosovo Energy Efficiency and Renewable Energy Project combined public-building renovations with energy audits, technical studies, training for firms, and policy and regulatory support intended to strengthen the conditions for continued investment.

By its completion, the investments were projected to deliver 1.14 million MWh in lifetime energy saving — enough to supply energy for 10,000 households for 20 years — and 27% above the project’s initial target.

The project also helped build the skills, institutions, and experience needed for energy efficiency investments to continue beyond individual building renovations.

The investments generated work across the energy efficiency value chain: from architects, engineers and energy auditors to construction crews and installers, while also creating demand for building materials and heating and cooling equipment.

An important part of that legacy was the establishment of the Kosovo Energy Efficiency Fund (KEEF) as a financially sustainable institution. By capturing and reinvesting energy cost savings, the Fund can continue financing energy efficiency improvements, helping sustain demand for energy efficiency services and products beyond individual projects and giving local firms greater opportunities to build experience and grow.

For Petrit Ahmeti, Director of Operations at the Kosovo Energy Efficiency Fund, who has worked in energy efficiency since 2007, the sector has completely transformed.

“At first, we didn't have experts who could evaluate the state of buildings and their energy consumption. Now we have specialized companies that can calculate potential savings, and around 300 energy auditors in Kosovo, which is sufficient for our territory.”

Petrit Ahmeti, Director of Operations, Kosovo Energy Efficiency Fund

Ahmeti says professional capacity has improved too. Energy audits and designs have become more detailed, contractors more experienced, and works such as window replacement and insulation faster to implement as firms have become more familiar with technical requirements.

The local supply chain has also been evolving, creating more products and jobs within the country. While earlier energy efficiency projects relied heavily on imported materials, contractors today say more commonly used products can and are being increasingly sourced locally. Mihrije Baloku, a construction engineer who managed energy efficiency renovations in four schools in 2025, has seen the market growing, with only some specialized items imported to meet technical specifications.

“External wall insulation materials like Styropor and Styrodur are produced and supplied in Kosovo. It is not only one producer, but there are many. It is an open market, where solutions can be found. The quality of materials is improving all the time.”

Mihrije Baloku, construction engineer.

Households help take energy efficiency demand and job creation to scale

Serbia shows another shift: thousands of households making their own investments in energy efficiency to cut heating and electricity costs.

Through the World Bank-supported Scaling Up Residential Clean Energy Project (SURCE), national and local government subsidies have helped households invest in measures such as insulation, cleaner heating, and rooftop solar. By May 2026, more than 18,000 households across 149 municipalities had participated in the program.

Homeowners themselves are putting substantial money into the upgrades. Of the €58.7 million invested through the program, households contributed more than half, while the rest came from the national government and municipalities.

For participating homeowners, the support can make larger upgrades easier to afford. Branko Cankovic, a homeowner in Kragujevac, received a subsidy for rooftop solar after previously investing in insulation and a heat pump. His 11 kW solar system cost about $10,000, with the program covering 40% of it. “With those upgrades, our monthly electricity and heating bills combined will be slashed to 3,000 or 4,000 dinars (about $29-38), from almost 25,000 dinars (about $239),’’ Branko explains. He is also considering buying two 5 kW batteries to help maintain power during potential outages.

Old trades, new skills for a changing market

Energy efficiency creates additional construction, engineering and installation work, but it also changes the skills existing occupations require. Architects and engineers build expertise in energy auditing and high-performance design; façade workers learn new insulation systems; heating technicians adapt to heat pumps and controls; and companies gain experience meeting increasingly demanding technical standards.

For Ljube Kjosev, who works at Idadija Polyclinic in Skopje and has spent some 25 years in construction, learning new ways of doing familiar work has become the norm.

As his team replaced outdated windows at the polyclinic, he reflected on how much the job has changed over the course of his career.

“New materials and new techniques require that we constantly learn. I am sure that while we are speaking, some new insulation materials are being developed, and we will need to retrain again,” Ljube says with a smile.

The renovation is part of North Macedonia's World Bank-supported Public Sector Energy Efficiency Project. By May 2026, 15 renovations of central government buildings had been completed. The project had also trained 51 energy auditors, technical designers, contractors and supervisors, including 14 women.

The need for new skills is also being felt by suppliers. Engroup, a Kosovo-based producer and distributor of energy-efficient heating and cooling equipment, is developing a dedicated training center for installers and technicians.

Kushtrim Fetahu, a managing partner at the company, said poor installation can undermine how well the equipment performs. “We are directly interested in making sure qualified people are installing our machines.”

Building the workforce for an energy-efficient future

As renovation programs expand, finding enough people with the right skills may become as important as financing the work itself. Nearly 18 million people were employed in energy efficiency worldwide in 2024, but labor and skills shortages remain a constraint.

Kosovo is seeing some of those pressures already. A recent KEEF survey of contractors working on energy-efficiency projects identified shortages of insulation and window installers, as well as technicians able to commission modern heating and cooling systems.

At the same time, Petrit Ahmeti sees growing interest in the field. More people are seeking training and certification, he says, while students at the university where he teaches energy efficiency and building physics are increasingly choosing the subject for diploma work and looking for advanced programs abroad.

For Vesa Berisha, a student at the University for Business and Technology in Pristina, the energy efficiency course helped connect classroom learning with practical applications.

“The course helped me understand the importance of energy efficiency in architecture and how we can make buildings more sustainable. I got to put what I learned into practice, which helped me see how these concepts work in real-life projects. It made me more interested in this field and opened my eyes to new career opportunities.”

Vesa Berisha, student.

text:
FORT MILL — Silfab Solar gave state officials a required 72-hour notice on Nov. 6 that the company will begin solar cell manufacturing at its Fort Mill plant next week.

The company has been limited to panel assembly since opening in early 2026, then agreed not to phase into chemical manufacturing following two leaks in March.

Silfab entered into an agreement with the S.C. Department of Environmental Services to have an independent contractor review policies and safety measures at its site before starting chemical manufacturing.

In addition to the review, the SCDES agreement required Silfab give a 72-hour notice before operations begin.

“At a time when strengthening America's energy independence is more important than ever, resuming full operations supports domestic manufacturing, creates additional high-tech jobs in South Carolina, strengthens our nation's energy security, and helps reduce reliance on foreign supply chains,” the company said.

Meanwhile, Silfab Solar, York County and many Fort Mill residents are still assessing the legality of Silfab’s operations.

The county filed to seek a declaratory judgment on whether Silfab can operate in its light-industrial zone in October, following a court decision that concluded solar cell manufacturing didn’t belong in that category.

The Fort Mill School District and long-time Silfab foe Wally Buchanan are requesting intervenor status in that court case. That will allow attorneys for both to make filings and presentations in the court cases.

The school district filed for intervenor status on Oct. 30, followed by Buchanan on Nov. 2.

Buchanan’s opposition to Silfab has spurred much of the legal battles over the last couple of years

In 2024, he requested the York County Board of Zoning Appeals assess the county’s conclusion that solar cell manufacturing qualified as a light-industrial use. The board voted unanimously against the county’s conclusion, which set off a lawsuit by Silfab against the zoning board.

Over the summer, a judge heard the case and sided with the zoning board. County officials have said the BZA ruling affected only businesses applying to operate after the May 2024 decision. The judge’s summer ruling prompted the York County Council to seek the declaratory judgment.

Buchanan was also an intervenor in that case. His home is on property adjacent to the business park on Logistics Lane where Silfab operates.

“Buchanan has a direct and substantial interest in the changed land use now in operation at the Silfab site,” his attorney, Cameron Halford, wrote in the intervenor filing. “Disposition without permitting Buchanan to Intervene would materially impair his ability to protect his home and neighborhood interests.”

Silfab is also located next to two schools, Flint Hill Elementary and Flint Hill Middle, which opened in 2025 and last summer, respectively.

“The health and safety of Fort Mill School District students and staff has always been and remains the district’s highest priority,” said attorney Daniel Ballou, representing the district.

description:
The license for Northfield Mountain, a pumped-storage power plant dug into a mountain in Franklin County, Massachusetts, expired on April 30, 2018.
So how do you run a power plant for more than eight years on a license that’s expired?
FirstLight, which runs the plant, applied for a new license on April 29, 2016, two years before the old one ended.
We’ve looked at this kind of plant before: the Ludington plant in Michigan lifts water 363 feet, and Grand Coulee’s pumps manage 280.
Regulators call that “entrainment,” and you or I would call it getting sucked into a power plant.
text:
Let your driver’s license lapse and you’ve got a problem. You might get away with it for a while, but the first time you get pulled over, you’re in for an awkward conversation.

Federal hydropower licenses work a little differently. The license for Northfield Mountain, a pumped-storage power plant dug into a mountain in Franklin County, Massachusetts, expired on April 30, 2018. The plant’s been running ever since, it’s all perfectly legal, and on November 2 it got a new owner.

So how do you run a power plant for more than eight years on a license that’s expired?

Basically, the law expects the paperwork to run late. Under the Federal Power Act, if a new license isn’t ready when the old one ends, the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission (FERC) has to give the operator a one-year license on the old terms. FERC’s 2018 notice for Northfield Mountain says that first one ran through April 30, 2019, and after that it gets “renewed automatically” until the agency acts.

That’s eight automatic renewals so far, by my count. Frankly, that’s a long run for anything with the word “annual” on it. But there’s nothing shady going on here. FirstLight, which runs the plant, applied for a new license on April 29, 2016, two years before the old one ended. FERC’s still keeping an eye on the place too, and inspected it on July 15.

So what’s inside that mountain?

If you haven’t run into pumped storage before, think of it as a rechargeable battery that runs on river water. When there’s power to spare, the plant pumps water up to a high reservoir. When the grid needs more, that water falls back through the same machines and makes electricity.

Northfield’s bottom reservoir is the Connecticut River, specifically the 20 or so miles backed up behind Turners Falls Dam. Its top reservoir is man-made and sits on the summit, covering 286 acres when it’s full, with a main dam about a mile long and up to 140 feet high. Apparently that dam also has an intake built in case anyone ever wanted to send water over to the Quabbin Reservoir, one of Boston’s main water sources, which is a pretty fun thing to have lying around.

Engineers call the drop between the two reservoirs the “head,” and here it runs from 753 to 824.5 feet depending on water levels. So “about 800 feet” is a fair shorthand. We’ve looked at this kind of plant before: the Ludington plant in Michigan lifts water 363 feet, and Grand Coulee’s pumps manage 280.

The star of the show is the powerhouse. It’s a cavern measuring 328 by 70 feet, so a little longer than a football field without the end zones. Going by the elevations in FirstLight’s amended application, it’s about 134 feet from the floor of the valve gallery to the roof. Four reversible machines live in there, and they spin one way to pump and the other way to generate.

One thing I can’t give you is a clean number for how deep the cavern sits. FirstLight’s application doesn’t state one, and I haven’t found it in what I’ve been able to read of FERC’s environmental statement. The closest thing I’ve got is that ventilation and emergency shaft. I’d really rather not find out how long those stairs take.

The top reservoir holds 12,318 acre-feet of usable water, or about 4 billion gallons by my math. An acre-foot is just what it sounds like, enough water to cover one acre a foot deep. FirstLight says that’s equal to about 8,729 megawatt-hours of stored energy.

I ran the plant’s maximum flows against the reservoir, and at full tilt you’re looking at about seven and a half hours to drain it and just under 10 to fill it back up. FirstLight’s website says up to 7.5 hours, so that checks out.

You’ll also see a few different figures for the plant’s output. FirstLight’s sale announcement says 1,168 megawatts, FERC’s listing says 1,166.8, and FERC’s final environmental statement recalculates that to 1,166.6. The 1,168 does show up in the application, in a table that gives the capacity at 820 feet of head and then falls to 840 megawatts at 768 feet. So that’s arguably a best-case number, but the gap between those three figures is under 2 megawatts.

Why would you burn more power than you make?

On paper, this plant looks like a terrible idea. From 2011 through 2019, it generated an average of 889,845 megawatt-hours a year and used 1,189,640 megawatt-hours a year for pumping. That’s 34% more power going in than coming out.

It works for the same reason a store can make money on stuff it bought wholesale. The plant pumps during the slow hours when power’s cheap, then generates when demand’s high and power’s expensive.

An earlier version of FirstLight’s application breaks this down for 2013, which is the most detailed year I’ve been able to read. Northfield sold its power at $85.17 per megawatt-hour that year and paid $40.01 per megawatt-hour to pump. Even after losing about a quarter of the energy on the round trip, that’s a pretty healthy spread.

The energy trade apparently wasn’t the biggest check, either. That same breakdown leaves about $26.1 million after pumping costs, compared with $35.5 million in capacity payments and $14.9 million for reserves. Those last two are basically the grid paying Northfield to be ready. FirstLight puts the annual plant factor at about 9%, meaning it makes about 9% of what it could if it ran flat out all year. You don’t judge a fire extinguisher by how often it’s in use.

FirstLight’s earlier application also points to blackouts. It says grid operator ISO New England reconnected to New York’s grid at Northfield after the August 2003 blackout. It also says a September 2010 failure to recover from a lost power source likely wouldn’t have happened if the plant hadn’t been out of service. FirstLight isn’t exactly a neutral witness here, admittedly. But FERC’s staff also credits Northfield and Turners Falls with fast ramping and black start capability, meaning they can help restart a dead grid.

So why’s the new license taking so long?

Mostly, it’s the river. FERC’s staff released its final environmental statement on January 30, 2026, and it recommends relicensing both Northfield and the smaller Turners Falls hydro plant nearby. It also lists shoreline erosion, swings in water levels, fish passage, protected species and cultural resources as the main issues.

Fish are the easiest one to picture. Young American shad and American eels get pulled in when the plant pumps. Regulators call that “entrainment,” and you or I would call it getting sucked into a power plant. The plan on the table hangs a barrier net in front of the intake every year, from June 1 to November 15.

FirstLight also wants more room in the top reservoir, with a maximum drawdown of 84.5 feet instead of today’s 62.5. As I read it, FERC’s staff wouldn’t let that extra water be used for generating, and it’d limit pumping in the spring to protect spawning shortnose sturgeon.

Some locals would rather see the plant shut down for good. The Greenfield Recorder, citing FERC’s statement, reported that 49% of the comments FERC received opposed giving it a new license. Comment counts aren’t votes, but that’s still a lot of unhappy people.

Then there’s Massachusetts. Under the Clean Water Act, a state gets to sign off on water quality before FERC licenses a project like this. That sign-off is called a 401 certification. The state issued its certification in April 2025, and groups including the Franklin Regional Council of Governments, the Connecticut River Conservancy and American Rivers appealed it.

The latest I can find is that the appeal’s still unresolved, though that’s from earlier this year. Andrea Donlon, a planner at the council, told the Recorder in February that a license could be “another couple of years” away. She pointed to Bear Swamp on the Deerfield River, which got its license in December 2025 after a FERC environmental analysis in 2020.

All of that now belongs to Hull Street Energy, a Maryland private equity firm that closed on FirstLight’s US fleet on November 2, and the announcement doesn’t say what it paid.

I went through FERC’s online docket for the project, and as of November 5 there’s no new license in it. The most recent entry is FirstLight’s October 23 statement of generation for annual charges. Unless that changes, by my reading Northfield Mountain’s current annual license runs through April 30, 2027, and then it renews itself again.

title: Energy Department offers $237M to strengthen U.S. power grid - The North State Journal
description:
Some large power transformers can take years to obtain, delaying construction projects, electrical upgrades and the expansion of industrial facilities.
According to the Energy Department, imported equipment accounts for approximately 80% of U.S. power transformers and half of the distribution transformers used to deliver electricity to homes and businesses.
Reconditioning existing equipment can reduce purchasing expenses and shorten delivery times, although the Energy Department acknowledges that domestic refurbishment capacity remains limited.
Energy Secretary Chris Wright said the investment is intended to strengthen American manufacturing while improving electricity reliability and affordability.
“The Energy Department is investing in American-made technologies and modernizing our grid to reduce reliance on foreign suppliers and deliver affordable, reliable electricity,” Wright said.
text:
WASHINGTON, D.C. — The equipment that keeps America’s electricity flowing has become increasingly expensive and difficult to obtain, creating problems for utilities and manufacturers trying to keep pace with growing demand. The U.S. Department of Energy announced a $237 million funding opportunity last Friday aimed at expanding domestic production of critical electrical equipment, reducing dependence on foreign suppliers, and addressing shortages that have complicated efforts to maintain and expand the nation’s power grid.

The initiative comes as utilities face rising prices and extended delivery times for transformers and other essential components. Some large power transformers can take years to obtain, delaying construction projects, electrical upgrades and the expansion of industrial facilities. Unlike equipment that can be ordered off the shelf, many large transformers are built to meet the specifications of the utility purchasing them. Replacing one is not always a matter of finding another supplier. The federal government estimates the investment could save utilities $125 million annually while keeping another $50 million each year in the American economy that would otherwise go to overseas suppliers.

For North Carolina, where energy infrastructure has become an increasingly important part of the state’s manufacturing economy, the initiative comes amid significant private investment in electrical equipment production. In February, Siemens Energy announced a $421 million expansion across North Carolina, expected to create 500 jobs statewide. The investment includes expanding large power transformer manufacturing in Charlotte, where the company is increasing production capacity to meet growing domestic demand. The Charlotte operation is one piece of a much larger national supply chain, one that has struggled to keep up with demand for equipment essential to the nation’s electrical infrastructure.

According to the Energy Department, imported equipment accounts for approximately 80% of U.S. power transformers and half of the distribution transformers used to deliver electricity to homes and businesses. Shortages of domestically produced electrical steel, copper and other materials have further complicated manufacturing. Transformers perform a basic but essential job: changing voltage so electricity can travel long distances and then be delivered safely to customers. When a utility cannot obtain a replacement or order equipment for a new project, the consequences can reach construction schedules, industrial development and the cost of providing service.

The new funding will be divided between two areas. Up to $50 million will support projects that refurbish and reuse existing grid equipment, allowing utilities to extend the useful life of transformers and other components rather than purchase replacements. Another $187 million will support manufacturers developing alternatives to imported materials and components, with an emphasis on products sourced and manufactured in the United States. The department wants companies to find more domestic options for parts and materials that have traditionally come from overseas.

The refurbishment effort could offer a practical solution for utilities dealing with high replacement costs. Reconditioning existing equipment can reduce purchasing expenses and shorten delivery times, although the Energy Department acknowledges that domestic refurbishment capacity remains limited. Expanding that work would also give utilities another option when they cannot afford to wait for newly manufactured equipment.

“America should never have to rely on foreign suppliers to keep the lights on,” said Katie Jereza, assistant secretary for the department’s Office of Electricity.

Energy Secretary Chris Wright said the investment is intended to strengthen American manufacturing while improving electricity reliability and affordability.

“The Energy Department is investing in American-made technologies and modernizing our grid to reduce reliance on foreign suppliers and deliver affordable, reliable electricity,” Wright said.

The funding opportunity, called Grid Supply Chain Alternatives to Lead Energy Dominance, is the first under a federal program authorized to provide up to $375 million for domestic electrical equipment manufacturing. Additional funding announcements are expected in 2027, including support for newer transformer technologies and efforts to standardize equipment designs, potentially making manufacturing more efficient. Standard designs could allow manufacturers to produce more equipment without making as many changes between orders, an issue that becomes more significant when demand is high.

Companies and other eligible applicants must submit concept papers by Nov. 20 to qualify for consideration. Full applications are due Feb. 8, 2027. The money has not yet been awarded, and the projected savings will depend on which projects receive funding and how widely the resulting equipment and manufacturing practices are adopted.

title: Diwali celebrations coincide with worsening air. Here's how to stay safer - Audacy
description:
An estimated 1 billion people worldwide celebrate Diwali, a holiday of Hindus and Jains with ties to ancient epics such as the Ramayana.
Air pollution monitors have reached the maximum reading they can display multiple times in recent years.
When many households set off fireworks, their combined emissions can worsen air quality across neighborhoods and entire cities, exposing people who are not taking part.
Electric lights can be another way to celebrate Diwali, avoiding toxic gases and smoke from firecrackers.
Damp-mopping floors and wiping dusty surfaces, instead of dry sweeping, can avoid stirring up particles that worsen air quality.
text:
BENGALURU, India (AP) — For people across South Asia, especially in northern India, Diwali celebrations coincide with the return of hazardous winter air, raising concerns about how to celebrate safely.

Winter also brings severe smog to parts of Pakistan and China, where warmer air can act as a lid, trapping colder air and pollution near the ground. In eastern Europe, burning coal and wood to heat homes also adds to winter pollution. Western Hemisphere countries, meanwhile, face their own seasonal air-quality problems, as summer wildfires send smoke across vast areas of the United States and Canada.

Experts say no matter where you live or when you face pollution, simple steps such as checking the air quality index, wearing a well-fitting mask and using air purifiers can reduce exposure to harmful pollutants.

An estimated 1 billion people worldwide celebrate Diwali, a holiday of Hindus and Jains with ties to ancient epics such as the Ramayana. Fireworks traditionally set off during the holiday, which starts Sunday, can make polluted air more dangerous.

As Diwali approaches, here are ways to reduce exposure to polluted air.

Check the air before heading out

Fireworks add a sharp burst of pollution to a much bigger problem. Across India, Pakistan and other parts of South Asia, traffic, factories, dust from construction and burning of crop residues and waste foul the air. Weak winds and stagnant winter air allow that pollution to build up.

“Poor air quality is our all-year-round problem in our country,” said Shweta Narayan, a public health expert at the Global Climate and Health Alliance. Narayan said firecrackers add to the problem.

India’s air quality index turns pollution measurements into a health warning. AQI readings of 201–300 mean “poor,” 301–400 “very poor” and 401–500 “severe.” Severe levels can harm even healthy people.

Check pollution levels on government or privately run websites before heading outdoors. Look for data from a nearby monitoring station and the time of its last update. A citywide average can conceal a polluted neighborhood.

The problem is especially bad in Delhi, where fine particle pollution averaged about 19 times the World Health Organization’s annual guideline last year. Air pollution monitors have reached the maximum reading they can display multiple times in recent years.

City authorities have responded with temporary construction, industrial and vehicle restrictions. Public health experts said such measures often fail to address the root causes. The city of more than 20 million people is also implementing a long-term plan to promote use of electric vehicles.

Make your mask fit

Dr. Arvind Kumar, a chest surgeon at Medanta hospital near Delhi and founder trustee of the Lung Care Foundation, recommends using properly fitted N95 or N99 masks outdoors during periods of heavy pollution. These masks are available at pharmacies, hardware stores and online retailers.

N95 filters are designed to capture at least 95% of airborne particles; N99 filters are made to capture at least 99%. The particle respirator masks do not filter harmful gases.

Cover your nose, mouth and chin. Shape the nose clip and check the seal every time. Facial hair can break that seal. The aim, Kumar said, is to ensure “all the breathing is through the mask and not around the mask.”

Replace disposable masks when dirty, damaged or hard to breathe through. Never put a mask on a child younger than 2. People with heart or lung disease should seek medical advice about mask use.

Loose surgical masks, cloth masks and scarves offer unreliable protection against fine particles.

Kumar said pollution can cause persistent coughing, inflame the airways and trigger asthma-like attacks. He also cited increased risks of pneumonia, heart attacks and strokes, while linking prolonged exposure to impaired lung development in children and lung cancer.

Kumar said people should avoid strenuous exercise outdoors during heavy pollution, including early mornings, when pollution levels can be high.

Match the purifier to the room

Using the right air purifiers indoors can help. The devices draw in air to filter out pollutants, then recirculate the cleaner air.

A purifier needs enough capacity to clean the air of the room where it runs. Look for a high-efficiency particulate air, or HEPA, filter. Then check its clean air delivery rate, which is the volume of filtered air it supplies.

Place the purifier where you spend the most time, such as the bedroom. Keep its airflow clear and run it consistently.

HEPA filters trap particles. Substantial activated-carbon filters can remove some gases. No purifier removes every pollutant. Avoid machines that deliberately produce ozone, which irritates the lungs.

Cleaner indoor air reduces exposure, but a purifier cannot eliminate pollution’s health risks, Kumar said.

Celebrate with less smoke

Kumar said it’s important to avoid incense, mosquito coils and candles. Their particles can linger indoors for hours, especially in poorly ventilated rooms, while fireworks pollution can persist overnight, depending on the weather. When many households set off fireworks, their combined emissions can worsen air quality across neighborhoods and entire cities, exposing people who are not taking part. Electric lights can be another way to celebrate Diwali, avoiding toxic gases and smoke from firecrackers.

“If one wants to celebrate and really enjoy the festival of Diwali, avoid bursting firecrackers,” said Narayan, the public health expert.

India’s health ministry also recommends reducing smoky cooking and using a kitchen exhaust that vents outdoors. Damp-mopping floors and wiping dusty surfaces, instead of dry sweeping, can avoid stirring up particles that worsen air quality.

Personal precautions have limits. Narayan said people who earn their livelihoods outdoors cannot simply stay home. Many families also cannot afford air purifiers.

She called for sustained action on pollution sources and affordable health care for those already suffering. Masks and filters can reduce exposure, but lasting protection requires governments to clean the air.

“It’s our responsibility to hold our governments accountable,” Narayan said. “There’s no other way about it.”

title: What midterm election blue wave rebuke of Trump means for renewable energy - CNBC
description:

And following the midterm elections that gave climate-friendly Democrats control of the House and Senate, the prospects of reviving the clean energy agenda suddenly brightened.

The U.S. is on pace to add a record 89 GW of clean energy capacity by the end of 2026, with installations projected to exceed that level in 2027, according to BloombergNEF’s latest US Clean Energy Market Outlook.
text:
As recently as 2022, many leaders in corporate America and the investment community were singing the praises of ESG — environmental, social, governance — as the foundation of stakeholder capitalism. It didn’t take long for that tune to change, for understandable reasons.

President Trump didn’t just make “ESG”, “sustainability” and “climate change” dirty words in his “green new scam” rhetoric. The Trump administration’s rollback of environmental regulations, elimination of clean energy subsidies and tax credits, defunding and halting of wind and solar projects, and embrace of the fossil fuels industry accelerated the backlash.

But renewable energy investing remains alive and well, notably among public and private funders of infrastructure projects and clean technology innovation. And following the midterm elections that gave climate-friendly Democrats control of the House and Senate, the prospects of reviving the clean energy agenda suddenly brightened.

Clean energy and solar stocks rallied the day after the election results, which “potentially reduces the risk of further political interference with renewable energy incentives and provides greater protection for the long-term economics of U.S. wind, solar and battery storage investments,” Barclays analysts led by Peter Crampton wrote in a note.

While Trump can veto legislation to restore subsidies and credits and revive projects, and continue to issue executive orders on energy policy, some Republicans may be more inclined to help Democrats override the president in order to appeal to voters outraged over high energy prices — a sentiment expressed in the passage of multiple state initiatives to impede the build-out of electricity-hungry data centers.

The blue wave also shines a spotlight on a bipartisan permitting-reform bill awaiting Senate approval. Several progressive Democrats want to put off the vote until the new Congress convenes in January, giving them time to rewrite provisions favoring renewables projects over fossil fuel ventures.

Ultimately, the midterms could improve the outlook for investors focused on clean energy. That is likely to start with impact investors who specifically seek to generate a competitive financial rate of return alongside positive, proactive social and environmental impact. Opportunities can be found through public equity investments like mutual funds and ETFs that are constructed to invest in clean energy companies. But many investors also seek out pure-play clean energy positions offered through fixed income, private equity, private credit, venture capital, real assets and community-focused investments.

“There are many different approaches that could lead impact investors to be thinking about clean energy investments,” said Amit Bouri, who’s retiring as CEO of the Global Impact Investing Network at year’s end. GIIN’s 2026 survey of impact investors found that 56% have funds invested in clean energy and 25% plan to increase those investments over the next five years. The survey was conducted prior to the midterms.

“Clean energy infrastructure can be really compelling from an investment standpoint, because the financial thesis and impact thesis are mutually reinforcing,” said Justina Lai, chief impact officer at LNW, a wealth management advisory firm. LNW has about $3.5 billion of its total $12.1 billion assets under management invested in impact strategies. She added that it’s challenging to break down the number of clients who are specifically focused on clean energy and clean tech. “Climate change or climate action writ large is likely the most common impact priority that we encounter with our clients,” she said.

While it might be hard to focus on the potential in the renewable energy sector in 2026 with energy commodities leading all sectors of the market as crude oil prices surged, some of the factors Lai cites should be on the radar of investors beyond the impact investing space.

She pointed to the nation’s growing electricity demand — partly tied to data centers — its aging and constrained grid infrastructure, the increasing need for energy storage, the effects of geopolitics on energy security and rising energy costs as major factors driving clean energy investing. Simultaneously, though, because of declining costs and continuing maturity of many clean technologies, “we know that renewables are the lowest cost form of new-build generation, even on a fully unsubsidized basis,” she said.

The proof is in the gigawatts. The U.S. is on pace to add a record 89 GW of clean energy capacity by the end of 2026, with installations projected to exceed that level in 2027, according to BloombergNEF’s latest US Clean Energy Market Outlook. In just the first half of this year, the Environmental Defense Fund and Atlas Public Policy recently reported, 11.5 GW of solar, 8.3 GW of battery storage and 6.3 GW of wind power were installed.

U.S. investment in clean energy and transportation alone totaled $75 billion in the second quarter of 2026, the second-highest quarterly figure on record and up 22% from the previous quarter, according to the Clean Investment Monitor, a joint project of Rhodium Group and MIT’s Center for Energy and Environmental Policy Research.

The supply chain has amped up, too. By the third quarter of this year, manufacturing capacity for solar modules, wind blades and nacelles had expanded by roughly 50% from the first quarter of 2025, reflecting new facilities that have come online, the CIM reported in October. And over the past four quarters, $277 billion was invested across the country in the manufacture and deployment of renewable energy, non-fossil fuel vehicles, building electrification and carbon-management technology.

“Investment has consistently been very strong in solar and storage at the utility scale,” said Hannah Hess, director, energy and climate at Rhodium. That makes sense from a bottom-line perspective, she said, “particularly when some of the deadlines for these projects have changed for them to be eligible for tax credits.”

Hess is referring to provisions in the One Big Beautiful Bill Act, which significantly hastened the sunsets and deadlines for federal clean energy tax credits compared to the original timeline set by the Biden administration’s Inflation Reduction Act. Solar and wind projects had to begin construction by July 4 of this year or be placed into service by December 31, 2027, to claim standard investment or production tax credits.

‘A rich time to be looking at this space’

Meanwhile, even with the Trump administration’s concerted efforts to rescind much of the $1.6 trillion set aside for clean energy under Biden’s Bipartisan Infrastructure Law and the IRA, nearly $600 billion remains available, according to a Politico analysis. Keeping that third of the funding pipeline open bodes well for clean energy developers and investors, especially considering the midterm results.

“Despite the gutting of the IRA, our long-term thesis and our clients’ long-term views on clean energy remain the same,” said Roraj Pradhananga, chief investment officer at Veris Wealth Partners, an advisory firm that specializes in impact investing. “If we look at the volatility and risk-adjusted returns of the traditional energy sector, in the long run, shifting to renewable energy makes the most [economic] sense,” even when taking the tax credits out of the equation, he said.

Veris manages $3 billion across asset classes, Pradhananga said, using various vehicles, including public markets, private debt and infrastructure funds. “Climate solutions tend to be the largest allocation for our clients. We recently allocated to strategies from GPs like Closed Loop Partners, Streetlife Ventures, SJF Ventures, New Energy Capital and Sunwealth.”

The proliferation of AI data centers was a hot-button issue in the midterms. Voters in 10 states weighed in on 41 local initiatives, which included complete bans on new construction, pausing ongoing and planned facilities and restrictions on energy consumption. All but one passed. And although newly elected governors in three states — Ohio, Texas and Georgia — ran on platforms critical of data centers, they’re not calling for permanent bans.

For instance, Gina Hinojosa, governor-elect of Texas, said during a CNN interview on November 5, “We will have laws to protect Texans, and we need to stop what we are doing with data centers until we have those protections.” She also emphasized giving local communities a meaningful say in whether and how facilities operate. That echoes Pennsylvania Governor Josh Shapiro’s cautious approach to data center development in that state. In August, he issued an executive order that places a host of restrictions on developers.

The upshot for AI companies may be a slowdown in new data center construction, increased input from local residents and officials, and self-financing for electricity and water usage. Yet they are not expected to change their long-term expansion plans. A few days before the election, Goldman Sachs said, “While U.S. data center development faces increasing political and community opposition, project data and our updated capacity estimates suggest that the...growth outlook through 2027 remains largely unchanged.” The Wall Street firm forecast data center power demand to grow 38% or 12 GW in 2026 and 38% or 17 GW in 2027.

On Friday, OpenAI’s CFO told CNBC the company will not be changing its investment plans despite the election results. White House economic advisor Kevin Hassett expressed a similarly optimistic view of continued investing on CNBC on Friday. “We respect the localities that decide that’s what they want to do,” Hassett said. “But America is a big place, and right now, the data centers scheduled over the next couple of years aren’t affected by these ballot initiatives.”

From another perspective, the risks associated with AI and data centers could be beneficial to renewable energy investments. “If anything, sustainability concerns around AI actually reinforce their interest in climate action,” Lai said. “The growth in AI and data centers could drive significant new fossil fuel generation, so our clients are motivated to ensure that more of that [electricity] demand is met by renewables.”

That’s true for many of Veris’ clients, too, Pradhananga said. But he also acknowledged that because natural gas is a prominent fuel source for large-scale utilities, as well as behind-the-meter LNG turbines that power many data centers, “there are some [of our] clients who view this as part of the transition” from fossil fuels to renewables, espousing the often-mentioned “all of the above” approach to the changeover. “This is where we do have exposure to utilities in [our] public markets portfolio.”

Public consternation over data centers, a Democratic-controlled Congress come January and, at least for now, a voting map across the country that has swung significantly towards the Democratic Party ahead of the 2028 presidential election, could create a trifecta of tailwinds for investors in renewable energy and clean-tech. And while any moratorium on data centers could impact renewable project development on a case-by-case basis, it might also promote investments in transmission grid upgrades that allow utility-scale solar and wind installations to tie into existing and proposed data centers.

It could also speed up research and development of emissions-free power generation, energy-efficiency and other technologies that climate-tech VCs are funding. Due to the AI boom, renewable energy companies have faced stiffer competition in recent years for venture capital dollars previously targeting climate change and decarbonization. But climate-tech VC hit $26 billion in the first half of 2026, a 55% increase year over year, according to market-intelligence firm Currence.

“There are very interesting infrastructure opportunities in [climate investing], including advanced fusion ventures, floating offshore wind turbines and solar plus storage operations,” said Adam Wolfensohn, a clean-energy investment advocate and advisor. “All of these technologies keep getting better and cheaper, unlocking so much more potential for renewables and new financial structures. It’s a rich time to be looking at this space.”

Among the guiding resources the GIIN offers to its 350 member organizations in 40-plus countries, including 126 in the U.S., is a recently launched climate solutions investing framework. “It’s designed to help investors make sense of the landscape of climate solutions and to ensure they have rigor around the actual climate impacts underpinning an investment strategy,” Bouri said. “A lot of things have green labels on them, but what we are really focused on is what drives real results for people and the planet.”

name: Detroit Environment
title: Diwali celebrations coincide with worsening air. Here's how to stay safer - ClickOnDetroit
description:
An estimated 1 billion people worldwide celebrate Diwali, a holiday of Hindus and Jains with ties to ancient epics such as the Ramayana.
Air pollution monitors have reached the maximum reading they can display multiple times in recent years.
When many households set off fireworks, their combined emissions can worsen air quality across neighborhoods and entire cities, exposing people who are not taking part.
Electric lights can be another way to celebrate Diwali, avoiding toxic gases and smoke from firecrackers.
Damp-mopping floors and wiping dusty surfaces, instead of dry sweeping, can avoid stirring up particles that worsen air quality.
text:
BENGALURU – For people across South Asia, especially in northern India, Diwali celebrations coincide with the return of hazardous winter air, raising concerns about how to celebrate safely.

Winter also brings severe smog to parts of Pakistan and China, where warmer air can act as a lid, trapping colder air and pollution near the ground. In eastern Europe, burning coal and wood to heat homes also adds to winter pollution. Western Hemisphere countries, meanwhile, face their own seasonal air-quality problems, as summer wildfires send smoke across vast areas of the United States and Canada.

Experts say no matter where you live or when you face pollution, simple steps such as checking the air quality index, wearing a well-fitting mask and using air purifiers can reduce exposure to harmful pollutants.

An estimated 1 billion people worldwide celebrate Diwali, a holiday of Hindus and Jains with ties to ancient epics such as the Ramayana. Fireworks traditionally set off during the holiday, which starts Sunday, can make polluted air more dangerous.

As Diwali approaches, here are ways to reduce exposure to polluted air.

Check the air before heading out

Fireworks add a sharp burst of pollution to a much bigger problem. Across India, Pakistan and other parts of South Asia, traffic, factories, dust from construction and burning of crop residues and waste foul the air. Weak winds and stagnant winter air allow that pollution to build up.

“Poor air quality is our all-year-round problem in our country,” said Shweta Narayan, a public health expert at the Global Climate and Health Alliance. Narayan said firecrackers add to the problem.

India’s air quality index turns pollution measurements into a health warning. AQI readings of 201–300 mean “poor,” 301–400 “very poor” and 401–500 “severe.” Severe levels can harm even healthy people.

Check pollution levels on government or privately run websites before heading outdoors. Look for data from a nearby monitoring station and the time of its last update. A citywide average can conceal a polluted neighborhood.

The problem is especially bad in Delhi, where fine particle pollution averaged about 19 times the World Health Organization’s annual guideline last year. Air pollution monitors have reached the maximum reading they can display multiple times in recent years.

City authorities have responded with temporary construction, industrial and vehicle restrictions. Public health experts said such measures often fail to address the root causes. The city of more than 20 million people is also implementing a long-term plan to promote use of electric vehicles.

Make your mask fit

Dr. Arvind Kumar, a chest surgeon at Medanta hospital near Delhi and founder trustee of the Lung Care Foundation, recommends using properly fitted N95 or N99 masks outdoors during periods of heavy pollution. These masks are available at pharmacies, hardware stores and online retailers.

N95 filters are designed to capture at least 95% of airborne particles; N99 filters are made to capture at least 99%. The particle respirator masks do not filter harmful gases.

Cover your nose, mouth and chin. Shape the nose clip and check the seal every time. Facial hair can break that seal. The aim, Kumar said, is to ensure “all the breathing is through the mask and not around the mask.”

Replace disposable masks when dirty, damaged or hard to breathe through. Never put a mask on a child younger than 2. People with heart or lung disease should seek medical advice about mask use.

Loose surgical masks, cloth masks and scarves offer unreliable protection against fine particles.

Kumar said pollution can cause persistent coughing, inflame the airways and trigger asthma-like attacks. He also cited increased risks of pneumonia, heart attacks and strokes, while linking prolonged exposure to impaired lung development in children and lung cancer.

Kumar said people should avoid strenuous exercise outdoors during heavy pollution, including early mornings, when pollution levels can be high.

Match the purifier to the room

Using the right air purifiers indoors can help. The devices draw in air to filter out pollutants, then recirculate the cleaner air.

A purifier needs enough capacity to clean the air of the room where it runs. Look for a high-efficiency particulate air, or HEPA, filter. Then check its clean air delivery rate, which is the volume of filtered air it supplies.

Place the purifier where you spend the most time, such as the bedroom. Keep its airflow clear and run it consistently.

HEPA filters trap particles. Substantial activated-carbon filters can remove some gases. No purifier removes every pollutant. Avoid machines that deliberately produce ozone, which irritates the lungs.

Cleaner indoor air reduces exposure, but a purifier cannot eliminate pollution’s health risks, Kumar said.

Celebrate with less smoke

Kumar said it’s important to avoid incense, mosquito coils and candles. Their particles can linger indoors for hours, especially in poorly ventilated rooms, while fireworks pollution can persist overnight, depending on the weather. When many households set off fireworks, their combined emissions can worsen air quality across neighborhoods and entire cities, exposing people who are not taking part. Electric lights can be another way to celebrate Diwali, avoiding toxic gases and smoke from firecrackers.

“If one wants to celebrate and really enjoy the festival of Diwali, avoid bursting firecrackers,” said Narayan, the public health expert.

India’s health ministry also recommends reducing smoky cooking and using a kitchen exhaust that vents outdoors. Damp-mopping floors and wiping dusty surfaces, instead of dry sweeping, can avoid stirring up particles that worsen air quality.

Personal precautions have limits. Narayan said people who earn their livelihoods outdoors cannot simply stay home. Many families also cannot afford air purifiers.

She called for sustained action on pollution sources and affordable health care for those already suffering. Masks and filters can reduce exposure, but lasting protection requires governments to clean the air.

“It’s our responsibility to hold our governments accountable,” Narayan said. “There’s no other way about it.”
