title: A 'geologic freak' called the Smackover may end America's lithium dependence on China
description:
“It’s a geologic freak with its very high lithium concentrations,” Standard Lithium CEO David Park told Fortune.
“It’s critically important to bypass the Chinese bottleneck,” said Park, of Standard Lithium.
Once the first phase of SWA is complete, Standard Lithium plans to double capacity to 45,000 tons a year.
“They’re waiting for EnergyX or Standard Lithium to go build the first commercial plant and see it proven commercially.
Its acreage is at least triple that of Chevron or Standard Lithium.
text:
The problem is the U.S. produces little more than 1% of the world’s lithium supplies, largely from Albemarle’s Silver Peak mine in Nevada. The world relies primarily on China for refining, as it does for many other critical minerals and rare earths.

That may be about to change. About 1,500 miles from Silver Peak lies the oddly named Smackover Formation in southern Arkansas and East Texas. Crude oil was discovered there a century ago. Now industry is fixated on its unusually large lithium concentrations in its massive underground aquifer. Early French settlers called the area “Sumac Couvert,” meaning “covered in sumac bushes,” and the name evolved into Smackover.

“It’s a geologic freak with its very high lithium concentrations,” Standard Lithium CEO David Park told Fortune. “We believe that our lands alone have the potential for over 150,000 tons per year of production.”

The contenders

Standard Lithium is, well, the standard bearer for the Smackover—the region with the most potential to turn the U.S. into a major lithium player. It is slated to authorize its South West Arkansas Project (SWA) late this year and start construction on the first 22,500-ton phase in the first quarter of 2027.

Its brash challenger is Austin, Texas-based EnergyX (short for Energy Exploration Technologies), which is led by Elon Musk acolyte Teague Egan, 38. EnergyX could break ground on its 15,000-ton Project Lonestar commercial facility by the end of 2027. A 250-ton pilot plant came online earlier this year.

Big Oil is following. ExxonMobil established its position three years ago and now holds more than 400,000 net acres, the largest in the formation. It plans to start building a pilot project there next year. Chevron also bought a lot of land, announcing a 125,000-acre position last year.

The U.S. lacks the traditional resources of leading producers Australia, Chile, Argentina, and China. It has few open-pit, hard-rock deposits or economically viable evaporation ponds, such as Silver Lake.

The reason Exxon and Chevron bought in is because the Smackover instead requires newer direct lithium extraction (DLE) technology. Operators drill wells much like oil and gas producers do, pump out the brine water, process and refine the lithium, and return more than 90% of the brine underground. No hydraulic fracturing, or fracking, is needed, limiting any seismicity concerns.

Evaporation ponds can take two years to extract the lithium. DLE only requires about two days, though most of its costs come up front in the facility and well construction.

“You extract the lithium, and then you reinject the remainder of the brine so that it leaves the ecosystem the same as it was before,” EnergyX’s Egan told Fortune. “There are no huge pits or huge ponds. It takes basically one-hundredth of the land footprint.”

Making the business case

Max Yerrill, a critical minerals analyst at BMO Capital Markets, is both skeptical and optimistic. DLE remains unproven at a commercial scale and must compete in a global market vulnerable to Chinese price manipulation. The Trump administration also has eliminated EV tax credits, weakening the domestic market.

Regardless, Yerrill said, “I think DLE is the only way. It’s more out of necessity. The geology is what the geology is in a particular region.”

“In theory, there are huge amounts of lithium in the Smackover. It’s yet to be proven if it’s economic to do so,” he said. “But I think it makes sense. You’re not planning for one year out. These are 25-year projects. You have to look way down the road.”

Even in a bad year, he added, lithium is still a market that’s growing at close to 20% or more a year.

The nascent self-driving vehicle and robotaxi industry is being built up almost entirely on EVs. Tesla this week said it is discontinuing the costly Cybertruck to make way for the self-driving Cybercab, while Waymo, Avride, and Zoox are all betting on robotaxis. Egan sees them daily. “Living in Austin is seeing the future, and that is only going to spread.”

Lithium is now about much more than just cars, medical devices, and electronics, including mobile phones, Egan emphasized. Utility-scale battery storage is the biggest growth area in the U.S. right now.

“Batteries are the future, and lithium batteries have the most robust infrastructure, and that’s what we need for robotics,” Egan said. “That’s what we need for grid storage, for energy resiliency, for data center backup, and redundancy. It’s what we need for everything.”

The U.S. buildout

Similar to rare earths, lithium isn’t actually rare. The challenge is economically extracting its nearly invisible ions from brine. Lithium doesn’t exist as a shiny metal in nature. It’s typically either in the salty brine aquifers or locked inside off-white or pinkish rock ore.

China isn’t the top lithium miner, but it is the top refiner and battery manufacturer.

The Smackover projects build refining on site, so the lithium doesn’t have to go to China for processing. U.S. battery manufacturing is also on the rise.

“It’s critically important to bypass the Chinese bottleneck,” said Park, of Standard Lithium. “We’ve seen them weaponize other critical minerals. We’re strategically exposed. If they want to cut us off, they can.”

The challenge is building up the necessary financing and customer contracts to start construction, Park said. In the past, China has used price dumping to prevent potential competitors from getting off the ground. For Standard Lithium’s SWA Project, that work is already done.

“I feel very good about things,” Park said. “It’s taken longer than I would have liked, but there were a lot of people to convince along the way.”

That included both the Biden and Trump administrations for a lithium industry that has bipartisan support, even though many Republicans oppose EV subsidies. Biden’s Department of Energy gave SWA a $225 million grant, and the Trump administration fast-tracked project permitting.

Norway oil and gas giant Equinor is also a 45% joint venture partner. Major offtake agreements are signed with global commodity trader Trafigura and battery manufacturer LG Energy Solution, which is growing its U.S. operations.

Once the first phase of SWA is complete, Standard Lithium plans to double capacity to 45,000 tons a year. It’s also advancing the Franklin Project in East Texas, for up to 70,000 tons, and two more East Texas facilities. “As we move into East Texas, the lithium concentrations get higher,” Park said. “Arkansas is more advanced technically and from a regulatory perspective than East Texas, but East Texas is catching up quickly.”

In October, EnergyX inked a 10-year offtake deal with Trafigura for its Project Lonestar, near Texarkana, and its Project Black Giant in Chile. EnergyX is focused on U.S. and South American growth.

Egan said the deal covers 100,000 tons and nearly $2 billion in lifetime value. He called it the largest DLE offtake in history. Trafigura will take 30% of Lonestar’s output, so more dealmaking remains.

“This will cause a lot more dominoes to fall, and I’m excited for the next three to six months,” Egan said. He plans to expand Project Lonestar from 15,000 to 50,000 tons by 2031.

With most of the critical minerals focus on rare earths and tungsten, Egan said he wants lithium to become an “unsexy commodity” like copper. “We want to be in an unsexy business that just produces a white powder that’s used in batteries.”

Big Oil and big goals

Lithium Americas may lead the U.S. lithium industry with Thacker Pass in Nevada, a 40,000-ton, open-pit clay mine that could be completed by the end of 2027. It’s much larger than Silver Peak and could eventually reach 160,000 tons. But analysts said the Smackover has more potential as few places have similar geology.

Exxon made big waves in 2023 when disclosed a 120,000-acre position—now much larger—in southern Arkansas. Egan said that pushed a risk-adverse industry toward DLE.

Egan would even like the oil majors to move faster. “They’re waiting for EnergyX or Standard Lithium to go build the first commercial plant and see it proven commercially. That kind of sucks because you would want those companies to make investments into the industry and push the innovation forward and help us.”

Exxon told Fortune it plans to start building its Pine pilot project in Arkansas next year. Its acreage is at least triple that of Chevron or Standard Lithium. Exxon has drilled exploration and appraisal wells and is focusing on its technology at a Houston pilot plant.

“The Smackover has the potential to become a significant source of domestically produced lithium, and ExxonMobil is uniquely positioned to help unlock it,” Exxon said in a statement.

Slower U.S. EV sales are not reflective of the rest of the world as Chinese EV manufacturers such as BYD surge globally, Park said. And U.S. is recovering, helped by record-high fuel prices from the Iran war. “Demand is not the constraint at this point. The real question is, will supply be able to keep up?” Park said.

He credited the Trump administration for helping get SWA started but said it could do more. “The administration may have thought they could focus on rare earths and deprioritize lithium a little bit,” Park said. “I think what they’re realizing right now is the industry could use another little shot, another catalyst.”

Regardless, Standard Lithium is just about to commence construction on the first major Smackover project. “We’re near the finish line or, I should say, we’re near the starting line.”

title: We Energies customers face another rate hike — but smaller, as regulators push back on utility
authors: Paul Kiefer / Wisconsin Watch, Paul Kiefer, Wisconsin Watch, Alexander Shur, Hope Kirwan

text:
Reading Time: 9 minutes

We Energies customers are in for another round of rate hikes over the next two years, although not as steep as the utility first proposed.

Wisconsin’s Public Service Commission voted Thursday to approve a roughly 7% increase in We Energies’ electricity rates spread across 2027 and 2028 — the utility’s sixth consecutive rate hike. The utility expects an average residential customer’s monthly bill to rise between $7 and $8 per month in 2027 and again by between $6 and $7 the following year.

The utility will direct much of the new revenue toward emerging renewable energy, natural gas and battery storage projects. It comes after We Energies, which serves more than a million customers in Wisconsin and parts of Michigan and Illinois, touts a roughly $10 billion increase to its capital spending plans over the next five years.

The company initially proposed a roughly 9% overall electricity price increase, including a 16% hike for residential customers, over the next two years.

We Energies’ rate increases have outpaced inflation for the past three years, and commissioners sought to pump the brakes during Thursday’s 10-hour hearing.

“I do not believe we can ignore the cumulative impact of years of increases simply because each individual increase can be explained by a particular investment or expense,” Commissioner Kristy Nieto said at the hearing’s outset. “When customers are experiencing some of the highest rates in the region” and the utility is delivering strong returns for its shareholders, she added, “we have to ask whether the scales are properly balanced.”

The commission pared back the increase on multiple fronts, including by lowering the utility’s guaranteed “rate of return” — the amount We Energies shareholders earn on each dollar they invest, passed along to ratepayers on their electricity bill. Market forces also play a role: We Energies’ fuel costs are also set to dip next year, as are those of Wisconsin’s other major utilities.

Their rewrite came two days after Wisconsinites voted to send a Democratic trifecta to Madison in 2027, with a new governor and legislative majorities poised to steer the largest energy buildout in Wisconsin’s living memory. The commission’s chair made clear on Thursday that she wants lawmakers to overhaul the state’s utility regulation rules.

What is We Energies’ new rate of return?

We Energies’ shareholders typically earn a 9.8% return on their investment, though that rate rises to roughly 10.5% or more for dollars spent building infrastructure to power data centers.

The company asked the commission this year to bump its rate of return to 9.9%, which it was as a “conservative” increase needed to attract new capital.

The request prompted outcry from — among other critics — Walmart. In testimony filed with the Public Service Commission in September, the retail giant called the request “unjustified,” saying it would push We Energies shareholders’ profit margins above the national average — and even higher when accounting for profits from new data center customers.

Walmart did not propose an alternative, but the Wisconsin Citizens Utility Board called for lowering the rate by nearly a percentage point.

Commissioners split the difference Thursday, setting the rate at 9.5%. The decrease from We Energies’ original ask will save ratepayers roughly $60 million over the next two years as the utility ramps up construction.

Do the rate increases include data center-related costs?

We Energies proposed the rate increase in March, when the utility still awaited commission input on a pitch to bill ratepayers for a quarter of the costs of building new power plants for new data center customers. The utility offered to offset those costs for non-data center ratepayers with revenue from selling the plants’ surplus electricity on the wholesale market.

Commissioners rejected that plan a month later, instead ordering We Energies to assign the power plant construction costs directly to its current and future large data center customers.

A pending agreement between We Energies and Oracle, a partner in the Project Lighthouse data center campus in Port Washington, could also save ratepayers millions.

The tech giant reached an agreement with We Energies last month to “subscribe” to a share of the Point Beach Nuclear Plant’s electricity output. Fueling that plant – Wisconsin’s largest — is increasingly expensive; the price of a megawatt of Point Beach electricity will rise more than 7% under We Energies’ current contract with the plant’s operator. The utility estimates that granting Oracle rights to a share of the plant’s output would spare other ratepayers roughly $300 million in fuel costs over the next five years. The commission has yet to approve the agreement.

Ratepayers could still pay for a portion of transmission infrastructure built to serve data centers. Transmission cost sharing is mostly outside the Wisconsin Public Service Commission’s authority.

Those powers rest with the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission, which is considering a proposal from the American Transmission Company — the utility that owns and operates most of Wisconsin’s grid — to charge data center operators based on their projected transmission needs.

Microsoft, the operator of the sprawling new data center in Mount Pleasant, has pushed back on that plan, arguing the transmission company could overbill it for infrastructure without providing an opportunity to protest.

How did regulators respond to We Energies’ cost overruns?

Commissioners attempted to clamp down on We Energies’ recent overspending on renewable energy projects by limiting its shareholders’ profits from a southeast Wisconsin solar and battery project.

The commission allowed We Energies in 2022 to purchase a large planned solar farm and battery storage facility in Kenosha County from an independent developer for $433 million.

The solar farm went online in late 2024; the battery facility followed less than a year later. Their final price tag exceeded the commission-approved figure by nearly 40%.

WEC Vice President of Regulatory Affairs Richard Stasik attributed the overrun to inflation, component shortages and delays tied to a then-new law requiring customs officers to confirm that the project’s solar panels weren’t made using forced labor in China’s Xinjiang Uyghur Autonomous Region.

Commissioner Marcus Hawkins noted that the labor law — and many of the other economic forces behind the overspend — existed before We Energies sought permission to buy the facilities. Hawkins argued that the utility’s leaders “chose to put their head in the sand” instead of identifying those risks in their purchase request, leaving ratepayers to absorb any unexpected spending.

While the commissioners allowed We Energies to bill ratepayers for the full cost of the projects, they barred the utility from earning a profit on the $166 million in unapproved spending.

“We need to deny something,” Hawkins said, explaining the decision would pressure utilities to be more transparent about the risks of budget overruns when proposing to build or buy new infrastructure.

The commission plans to revisit two other multimillion-dollar overspends in the utility’s next rate case. We Energies’ Darien Solar Energy Center in Rock and Walworth counties is 35% over budget; the utility’s Koshkonong Solar Energy Center in Dane County is 42% over budget. Neither project is fully online as of November.

Unlike the Kenosha County facility, the commission approved the Darien and Koshkonong projects on the condition that We Energies cannot bill ratepayers for any amount above their original price tags.

How did regulators try to ease the burden of retired power plants on ratepayers?

We Energies’ customers still owe roughly $1 billion for the utility’s “stranded assets” — power plants and generators retired before the utility’s customers fully paid off their value. When the utility pulled the plug on its once-mighty Pleasant Prairie coal plant in 2018, for instance, ratepayers still owed $775 million toward We Energies’ investment in the plant, plus a return for shareholders.

“Retiring these plants saves customers millions of dollars in avoided operations and maintenance costs and hundreds of millions of dollars in additional costs for ongoing capital investments when compared to their original expected retirement dates,” Stasik testified earlier this year.

With more retirements on the horizon, consumer advocates pushed the commission to lighten the financial burden the now-demolished generators place on ratepayers.

The commission took a moderate approach on Thursday, extending the timeline for We Energies to recoup its investments in the “stranded assets.” The longer payment period will reduce customers’ monthly payments on the remaining balance by spreading those costs over six additional years. Commissioners also voted to limit shareholder profits on the defunct plants. The Wisconsin Industrial Energy Group, which represents manufacturers and other large electricity customers, estimated those changes will save ratepayers at least $30 million by 2028.

While forcing the utility to write off the plants as a loss was out of the question, Nieto argued that treating the plants “as though they were used and useful” is unfair to ratepayers.

The problem isn’t new, Hawkins added. But the looming retirement of coal generators at We Energies’ Oak Creek plant in Milwaukee County — which the utility pushed back from 2024 to 2027 — and the construction of new renewables and natural gas projects increased pressure to spare ratepayers from a double whammy.

“Now we have the confluence of the replacement costs hitting along with more stranded asset costs piling up,” he said.

Public Service Commission Chair Summer Strand described extending the payment timeline as the best option in the limited pool available under state law, slipping in a critique of state lawmakers for limiting commissioners’ flexibility.

“We do not have any action from the policymakers in this state to help with stranded assets,” she said.

Some neighboring states allow utilities to “securitize” the remaining value of a retired plant — converting the value into a specialized bond, similar to refinancing a mortgage. Customers still pay back the bond, but its interest rate on the bond may be lower than the utility’s profit margin.

Will We Energies bill ratepayers to pay for its board of directors?

We Energies sought permission to bill ratepayers for roughly $5.3 million to cover a portion of its board of directors fees, arguing that the board’s oversight of budgets, capital plans and risk management “helps ensure utility resources are used prudently and in customers’ interests.”

Commissioners weren’t convinced. The board provides a “shareholder benefit, not a customer benefit,” Strand said. “If you benefit from an expense, you should pay for it.”

We Energies also asked to bill ratepayers roughly $4 million over the next two years for its membership in industry associations. Several of those groups, especially the Wisconsin Utilities Association, the Metropolitan Milwaukee Association of Commerce and the national Edison Electric Institute and American Gas Association, run extensive state and federal lobbying operations.

The commission typically allows utilities to recoup only a portion of their membership dues from ratepayers — a share meant to match the ratepayer benefits of those memberships. That practice will continue over the next two years. Commissioners called the justifications in the latest request for billing customers for some membership dues “flimsy” and urged the utility to be more transparent about whether the memberships benefit customers in any future requests.

“I don’t know how else to send the message that we’re serious about this,” Strand said.

How much will We Energies’ customers pay to restore service when the utility disconnects them for missing bills?

We Energies disconnected roughly 60,000 customers last year for falling behind on their energy bills, including roughly one in six households in parts of Milwaukee’s North Side. The commission placed a one-year hold on disconnections at the start of the COVID-19 pandemic, and annual disconnection totals remained below pre-pandemic levels — about 51,000 in 2019 — until 2024.

“Disconnection is always a last resort,” We Energies spokesman Brendan Conway told Wisconsin Watch in an email. “A number of factors in recent years have created unique situations that impact customer bills, including very cold winter weather and very hot summer weather, fluctuating natural gas prices impacted by international events and an increase in federal heating assistance available to people during and after the COVID pandemic that has expired.”

We Energies currently requires that disconnected customers pay at least 80% of their past-due balance to restore their electricity service, with a maximum down payment of $600 for low-income households.

Strand called the $600 cap “atrocious” and far out of reach for low-income households already behind on bills.

Commissioners agreed to lower the minimum payment for all customers to 50% of their arrears and cap the maximum down payment for low-income customers at $100.

How did We Energies, investors and ratepayer advocates respond to the PSC?

We Energies did not publicly object to the commission’s multimillion-dollar cut to its revenue request.

“The Commission’s votes today support key investments for our customers: more Wisconsin-produced energy, continued tree trimming to reduce power outages and undergrounding of power lines to strengthen the grid against severe weather. It also reflects our shared commitment to ensuring that no costs to serve data centers are shifted to other customers,” Conway wrote in a statement after the hearing. “Our typical customer bills are below the national average and in line with customers across the Midwest. That will remain true in the coming years.”

The Citizens Utility Board applauded the commission’s efforts to rein in costs, but Executive Director Tom Content emphasized that regulators could have gone further — especially if state lawmakers gave them a longer leash.

“The savings could be in the hundreds of millions of dollars, but unfortunately not enough to stop an increase from taking effect,” he wrote in a preliminary press release. “After all, the increase sought was nearly half a billion — $449 million — over two years.”

Shares in WEC Energy Group, We Energies’ parent company, hit an all-time high of $120 shortly before Thursday’s hearing. That price fell to $116 by Friday morning.

Strand used the rate case to renew her criticism of Wisconsin’s comparatively hands-off approach to energy planning and legislative Republicans, just two days after Democrats won a trifecta in state government.

“The commission is still tasked with balancing reliability, affordability and environmental responsibility,” she said as the marathon hearing began. The task is challenging, Strand added, because the commission is “hamstrung by an inadequate and outdated regulatory framework” and because “the majority party that has been in power since 2011 has refused to consider beneficial changes.”

The state Senate confirmed Strand to the commission in 2024; her term ends in 2029. Commissioners Nieto and Hawkins are serving without Senate confirmation, enabling Gov.-elect David Crowley to appoint a new majority to the commission next year.

title: NRDC Assessment of BAAJA, the 2026 Permitting & Transmission Bill - CleanTechnica
description:
The product is a bill that combines critically important transmission and grid reforms with significant and concerning changes to federal environmental laws, permitting standards, and judicial remedies.
But transmission is an enabling technology rather than a substitute for policies that directly drive clean energy investment and reduce pollution.
The backdrop, of course, is the Trump administration’s nonstop attacks on clean energy projects, tax incentives for clean energy, and climate standards.
In one fell swoop, this legislation would address these issues, producing the necessary conditions to deploy more clean energy.
The provision’s reach is not limited to energy projects and is not limited to specific agencies or types of permits.
text:
Support CleanTechnica's work through a Substack subscription, on Patreon, or on Stripe. Help us produce all of the high-quality, original content we publish week after week despite the challenges of content-scraping AI, antisocial media, inflation, and other hurdles.

The Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act of 2026 (BAAJA) is the result of years of negotiations on permitting reform. The product is a bill that combines critically important transmission and grid reforms with significant and concerning changes to federal environmental laws, permitting standards, and judicial remedies.

The transmission provisions in the bill would produce substantial and durable benefits, updating an aging power grid by allowing new investments. These reforms, which NRDC has long supported, are an essential component of accelerating the electrification and decarbonization of the power sector and achieving greenhouse gas reduction targets. On their own, these changes are much needed and overdue; they would also help any future clean energy incentives and standards succeed in cutting emissions. But transmission is an enabling technology rather than a substitute for policies that directly drive clean energy investment and reduce pollution.

However, there are a number of concerning provisions that raise substantial issues and reinforce the position of incumbent energy interests. The “project certainty” language is designed to ensure projects cannot be arbitrarily canceled. As drafted, it could benefit fossil fuel, mining, data center, and other industrial projects more than clean energy. It could also limit agencies’ ability to address newly discovered harms, constrain future pollution regulation, and create large taxpayer-funded corporate handouts.

The bill would also weaken key elements of core environmental laws, including the Clean Water Act (CWA), the Endangered Species Act, the National Environmental Policy Act (NEPA), and the National Historic Preservation Act (NHPA). The bill would narrow environmental review across those statutes, diminish state and Tribal authority, constrain public participation, and restrict courts’ ability to stop projects proceeding under unlawful permits. These changes erode fundamental protections for communities.

The backdrop, of course, is the Trump administration’s nonstop attacks on clean energy projects, tax incentives for clean energy, and climate standards. NRDC’s analysis finds in aggregate that the Trump administration’s actions could double carbon emissions from the power sector over the next decade while raising consumers’ electric utility bills by $30 billion per year by 2035. Lawmakers should push for tangible evidence that this has changed before voting on the legislation.

While NRDC is encouraged by the transmission provisions, other elements of the bill are deeply flawed. We will be seeking improvements in the coming weeks and will take a position on the bill before a floor vote.

Below is an assessment of the most positive and most negative elements of the bill. This is not intended to be comprehensive.

Positives

Transmission and grid reform are the bill’s principal strengths

An aging power grid desperately needs updating, and with more extreme weather and surging demand from data centers, getting new electricity connected to the grid quickly is essential to keeping energy costs down and maintaining resilience. In one fell swoop, this legislation would address these issues, producing the necessary conditions to deploy more clean energy.

This legislation would provide a dramatic near-term boost to the nation’s grid by increasing both the amount of power that existing transmission lines can carry and the supply of electricity available to meet growing demand. It establishes procedures that could cut the time to build a major new transmission line to five to six years from 10 years—or sometimes significantly longer—today.

The Midwest’s multi-value projects: How agreeing on who pays can unlock transmission

In 2011, the Midwest grid operator, MISO, approved 17 high-voltage lines costing more than $5 billion and spread the cost across the region based on who benefits. Within about a decade, 16 of the 17 were in service, helping to connect wind power across the Midwest.

Between regions, where no such agreement exists, almost no major lines were approved in the decade after FERC’s 2011 planning rule. The bill tries to bring the Midwest’s approach to lines that cross between regions.

In the short term, it would require utilities to upgrade existing transmission lines and deploy advanced transmission technologies whenever their benefits exceed their costs. This technology can increase the capacity and efficiency of existing transmission lines, reduce congestion, and improve reliability, often at a cost that is 5 to 10 times cheaper than building new transmission. If deployed aggressively in the short term, this could free up more than 100 gigawatts of transmission capacity—enough to power 75 million homes.

Importantly, the bill goes beyond simply requiring utilities to consider these technologies: It directs the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission (FERC) to establish timelines for deployment, makes it easier for utilities to recover their costs, and establishes penalties for utilities that fail to deploy cost-effective technologies.

From PJM’s queue freeze to Southwest Power Pool’s fix

In 2022, PJM, which runs the grid for 13 states and Washington, D.C., stopped taking new requests to connect to the grid while it worked through a backlog of more than 300 gigawatts, 95 percent of it renewables and storage. It didn’t reopen until April 2026, so projects that applied after 2022 are only now starting their studies.

In March 2026, FERC approved a new approach from Southwest Power Pool, which runs the grid across much of the central United States. It plans transmission and new power plants together over 20 years, charges developers a standard up-front fee to connect, and studies projects once a year with a single decision point. The bill would require every region to adopt a process like this within two years and to speed up studies with better data and automation.

The bill makes major interstate power lines easier to build by strengthening federal authority over large interstate transmission lines. Currently, a state can block or indefinitely delay a project that would provide broad regional or national benefits. If a state rejects an eligible project or fails to act within one year, the bill requires FERC to issue a permit for a covered transmission line when a developer seeks federal review and the project satisfies specific criteria. FERC must then spread the costs fairly among all consumers who benefit from the projects.

The bill also requires neighboring grid regions to plan interregional transmission jointly, assess the benefits of potential projects, and establish methods for allocating costs. Despite a FERC order issued in 2011 that was meant to spur these cross-regional power lines, currently, virtually no major lines have been built between regions because there is no durable process for planning them or determining who should pay. The bill addresses this long-standing problem and codifies important elements of FERC’s updated regional planning framework from 2024, known as Order 1920.

The bill will also reduce the long wait times for energy projects to connect to the grid. Approximately 2,000 gigawatts of proposed generation and storage are waiting to connect to the grid, and 85 percent of that capacity is solar, wind, or storage. Projects often wait years for studies and may receive unexpectedly high upgrade costs late in the process. The bill encourages more coordinated planning, provides developers earlier information about costs, and improves data and automation.

Taken together, these transmission and interconnection reforms are a once-in-a-generation opportunity that would produce significant and durable benefits. The reforms would also facilitate the infrastructure needed so that future clean energy incentives and standards could succeed.

Require data centers’ to pay for increased costs driven by their grid demands

The data center provisions could provide protection for existing utility customers and support grid investments by requiring data centers to pay for their impact to the grid. It would direct FERC to develop pricing rules designed to prevent transmission costs created by data centers (generally 20 megawatts or more) from being shifted to other ratepayers and ensure data centers provide financial assurance to avoid costs shifting in the future. FERC would also have to revise transmission pricing policies and require standardized analysis of upgrades and cost-reduction options. These provisions address the transmission portion of the broader effects of rapid data center growth. The bill does not address local air pollution, water consumption, noise, land use, reliance on on-site fossil fuel generation, transparency, or public participation.

Provide a boost to geothermal energy

With geothermal energy poised to be a major player in the clean energy future, the bill provides policy reforms that could increase permitting efficiency and lower some of the barriers to geothermal development. But the geothermal provisions also come with their drawbacks, including the expansion of Section 390’s oil and gas activity categorical exclusion to geothermal development, which allows for significant drilling and production activities to take place on public lands without environmental review.

Negatives

Project certainty provisions could backfire

In an effort to respond to the Trump administration’s relentless attacks on wind and solar projects, this legislation includes “project certainty” language to protect developers from unreasonable attacks. Unfortunately, these provisions could have problematic unintended consequences, including locking in the Trump administration’s preferential treatment of oil, gas, data centers, and mining projects. This part of the legislation could also lead to a slew of industry lawsuits that result in taxpayers paying billions of dollars to private industry.

These “project certainty” provisions would largely prevent federal agencies from canceling, suspending, or changing federal approvals once issued. The provision’s reach is not limited to energy projects and is not limited to specific agencies or types of permits. The legislation sets out a small handful of circumstances in which agencies can modify an issued permit. Notably, while these circumstances include national security or defense concerns, they do not include environmental harm—even if newly discovered, severe, or widespread. Its broad language could even lead to industry arguments and legal claims that operating facilities are protected from subsequently adopted pollution requirements under the Clean Air Act and other statutes. State permits to implement future U.S. Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) standards for power plant carbon emissions, for example, could face legal challenges based on this provision.

And if a project is canceled or amended, a company can go to court to get its permit reinstated—as well as require the government to pay for its litigation expenses and the cost of project delays. The government could also be forced to use taxpayer money to make an additional payment of 25–50 percent of total project costs incurred to the company. For a single large energy project, this could easily amount to hundreds of millions, or even billions, of dollars.

A separate provision would allow energy-project developers to sue agencies for alleged “disparate treatment.” The approach uses a five-year comparison period that could embed the second Trump administration’s energy preferences in the legal baseline, and thus advantage oil, gas, and coal projects. And it prevents agencies acting in good faith from fully defending themselves in court. Successful claims could result in payments equal to 50–100 percent of projected construction costs plus actual damages and legal costs, creating a serious risk that the provision could be gamed and produce large taxpayer-funded payouts.

Environmental reviews and judicial remedies are sharply constrained

The bill makes sweeping changes to our ability to enforce a number of environmental laws. For example, a court that finds violations of the CWA’s “dredge and fill” permit system will be unable to invalidate the permit except in narrow circumstances; a court can never invalidate a permit based on a violation of the NEPA and the NHPA, no matter how severe it finds a legal violation to be. Though a deficient review can be returned to an agency, construction is allowed to continue while the agency corrects its mistakes. The result could be that by the time the agency completes its review, the project may already be largely or entirely built and the damage difficult or impossible to reverse.

Right now, if a court finds that an agency violated NEPA, it can stop the project from moving forward until the agency corrects the environmental review documents. For example, a federal judge put an oil and gas lease in Alaska’s ecologically rich Cook Inlet on hold until the responsible agency corrected its defective environmental review. That reasonable result may not have been possible had this bill been the law.

The bill also excludes activities from NEPA review, expands exemptions for others, narrows the analysis of alternatives, and potentially limits who can bring a case. Collectively, these changes substantially reduce the practical value of NEPA as a means to improve environmental outcomes. Tribes, local organizations, and affected communities may be particularly disadvantaged if they are cut out of the process or cannot stop harmful projects before they cause damage.

Changes to historic preservation law significantly affect Tribal interests

The bill would dramatically curtail the rights and powers of Tribes enshrined in Section 106 of the NHPA, effectively limiting Tribes’ ability to protect their lands and culturally significant places from proposed projects with a federal connection. The bill limits Tribal participation in decisions concerning federally connected projects and what Tribal interests are protected, which, under current law, includes not only artifacts but also sacred places, cultural landscapes, waterways, wildlife, and living ecosystems. Tribal Nations and Indigenous partners have made clear that these changes significantly undermine Tribal sovereignty and the federal government’s nation-to-nation responsibilities.

Examples of NHPA impacts

NHPA, specifically Section 106, has played a critical role in ensuring that permitting processes must integrate Tribal Nation feedback, helping to improve the environmental and cultural resource outcomes for projects, including the Pebble Mine and the Arches and Canyonlands National Parks, due to oil and gas drilling proposals. Proposed changes to Section 106 would place additional areas in further jeopardy—including mining proposals that would impact the Brooks Range and Gates of the Arctic National Park and Preserve, along with drilling proposals in the Chaco region, the Western Arctic, and the Arctic National Wildlife Refuge, respectively.

The Clean Water Act provisions restrict state, Tribal, and federal authority to improve projects and protect water bodies and wetlands

The bill weakens several CWA programs, which will make it easier for activities that pollute or destroy water resources to move forward without adequate safeguards. It limits the ability of states and Tribes to ensure the health of streams, lakes, wetlands, and groundwater when the federal government authorizes activities that impact them. It takes a fast-tracked permitting process meant for activities that have minimal impacts (like boat ramps) and applies it to major projects such as pipelines and highways.

The bill makes significant changes to the Clean Water Act program that gives states and Tribes the ability to demand water quality–based improvements to federal permits. For gas pipelines and transmission projects, reviewing authorities are limited to considering direct discharges, (e.g., just the effects of a concrete structure for a pipeline) rather than broader construction-related effects such as erosion, sediment, contaminated runoff, groundwater pollution, and damage to wetlands and streams, or ongoing impacts from the operation of the project.

For other projects, the bill places a substantially higher burden on states seeking to require protections. Currently, a state can identify a water quality concern, request reasonable changes, and allow a project to proceed with stronger safeguards. A state would now be required to demonstrate harm by clear and convincing evidence (versus reasonable evidence) and show that its proposed condition is the least burdensome means of addressing the water quality concern. In practice, these new hurdles to water quality conditions will be very difficult to overcome, which will likely result in fewer state conditions on permits needed to protect water quality. In addition, the bill would restrict states and Tribes from taking the actions they can today to protect habitat, groundwater (including drinking water supplies), and many small streams and critical wetlands.

How the Clean Water Act change could impact states

If the special provisions for gas pipeline projects had been the law, Pennsylvania likely would not have been able to require the Atlantic Sunrise Pipeline Project to comply with state erosion and sediment laws, and West Virginia likely would not have been able to require controls and compliance monitoring that enabled the state to enforce against the Mountain Valley Pipeline’s violations of runoff requirements.

By shifting and raising the burden of proof, this requirement would jeopardize precautionary state actions, such as a Tennessee decision this spring, when it refused to sign off on an Army Corps permit for a landfill because the project developer had failed to show that pollution from the site would not harm local waters. This kind of state engagement improves projects and does not end them.

The bill also weakens the Clean Water Act’s general permitting program (administered by the U.S. Army Corps of Engineers) for dredging and filling waters. The bill directs the Corps, when creating general permits, to look only at the harm that results from filling in waters. No other water impacts like water pollution or groundwater depletion could be considered. Additionally, right now, most general permits can only be used for impacts of one-half acre or less; this bill would quadruple this threshold, which could allow larger data centers or other major projects to qualify. It also extends the duration of general permits, reducing opportunities for public input on requirements for projects to once a decade. Finally, it requires the Corps to maintain fast-track permits for large “linear” projects that can have major environmental harms, like roadways and pipelines.

The bill weakens other Clean Water Act programs as well. It would curb the EPA’s ability to stop projects that dump dredged or fill material that “have an unacceptable adverse effect on municipal water supplies, shellfish beds and fishery areas (including spawning and breeding areas), wildlife, or recreational areas,” which the agency has invoked rarely, but done so to protect exceptional habitats threatened by highly damaging projects. It would slow the EPA’s development of scientific advice to states about the levels of pollutants that can cause harm to aquatic life or people, and it would delay updates to discharge requirements for industrial polluters and sewage plants; together, these two changes would constrain the ability to control “forever chemicals.”

Endangered species protections are weakened

Language relating to the “best available science” standard could be interpreted to restrict precautionary action when scientific information is uncertain. This is particularly concerning when an imperiled population of a species is difficult or expensive to study and waiting for definitive proof could result in irreversible loss.

The bill also allows states to assume responsibilities currently carried out by the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service. Many states lack the capacity, expertise, or in some cases, the commitment necessary to perform this responsibility effectively, and if a state is not executing its responsibility, there is not a requirement for the federal government to reassume it.

Oil and gas drillers get access to resources below farmers’ and ranchers’ lands

The bill would exempt many wells drilled on private lands that tap into federally owned oil and gas reserves from federal permitting, opening at least 57 million subsurface acres of federal resources to exploitation without federal permits. If passed into law, this provision strips thousands of private landowners across the West of important protections like required notice of industry’s plans to develop on their property, increases the risk that landowners get stuck with orphaned wells and their associated environmental and financial costs, and creates new risks of fraud and abuse as it relates to royalty reporting.

Public lands are handed to the mining industry

The bill allows mining companies to claim an unlimited number of five-acre mill sites on public lands to be used for things like tailing storage—wastewater and rock often containing heavy metals and other dangerous residues—and waste dumps. And it allows mining companies to occupy public lands for any other use relevant to a mining project, regardless of its proximity to the actual mine, meaning roads, pipelines, powerlines, and any other activity formerly requiring a federal permit and environmental review would be allowed so long as the activity is included in the mine’s operation plan.

Policy analysis

The modeling completed to date focuses on greenhouse gas and economic impacts. Available analyses from NRDC and other groups generally project modest to significant greenhouse gas benefits, especially over the long term, but the results vary substantially depending on the provisions modeled, policy baseline, fuel and technology costs, and implementation assumptions.

NRDC’s initial results show modest power sector benefits.

The benefits of additional transmission will generally be greater in a policy environment that drives clean energy deployment. In a baseline with limited support for new clean energy resources, transmission may improve reliability and reduce costs without producing sizable emissions reductions.

The oil-and-gas effects remain uncertain. NRDC has not quantified the bill’s effects on oil-and-gas development. Because the existing baseline already assumes high levels of domestic production growth (oil and gas production have both doubled in the last 20 years), faster permitting may not produce a large increase in emissions compared with business as usual. Nevertheless, the bill could accelerate individual projects, improve their economics, and make approved infrastructure more difficult to regulate or modify later. The risk of locking in that trajectory merits consideration, even if near-term emissions changes appear modest.

Data-center growth creates a particularly important unknown. The grid provisions may indeed enable data centers to finance upgrades and connect to an expanded transmission system. But transmission takes years to plan and construct. In the interim, faster permitting and weaker environmental safeguards could encourage additional on-site or nearby gas generation, particularly in regions with access to existing pipelines or gas fields.

Greenhouse gas emissions are only one measure of the bill’s effects. The modeling does not quantify potential consequences for drinking water, local air pollution, public health, endangered species and wildlife, or other metrics. It also cannot account for the practical importance of judicial remedies in ensuring that agencies and developers comply with environmental law.

Critical changes needed

NRDC is seeking significant improvements to the bill in five areas:

Revise the project certainty provisions: Agencies must retain the ability to address significant and unanticipated environmental or public health harms. The bill must preserve established processes for updating operating permits and applying future pollution standards. Any disparate treatment claim should require credible evidence of intentional targeting, permit review of a complete evidentiary record, use a baseline that does not unduly favor the current administration’s energy choices, and eliminate disproportionate taxpayer funded payments.

Preserve meaningful judicial remedies: Courts must retain the authority to fix unlawful permits and pause construction under the CWA, NEPA, and the NHPA. Legal protections are substantially diminished if courts cannot provide an effective remedy when violations occur.

Restore clean water protections: Congress should remove heightened burdens on states (evidentiary standards); preserve the ability of states and Tribes to address a full range of water quality effects and improve projects; and avoid further weakening of the general permit program.

Retain endangered species protections: The legislation should remove the transfer of important federal consultation responsibilities to states and remove language that could constrain reasonable precautions when scientific information is incomplete.

Respect and uphold Tribal sovereignty: Any changes to the historic preservation law should be developed with Tribal Nations, preserve meaningful consultant, and elevate the unique expertise Tribes hold in identifying and protecting their cultural resources and sacred places.

NRDC will continue to advance technical corrections, including changes needed to address drafting errors and unintended consequences. But technical corrections cannot substitute for changes to some of these structural provisions, for which we will continue to advocate.

text:

Switzer

Clinkenbeard

The Vigo County Area Plan Commission voted Wednesday evening, making a favorable recommendation to the county’s zoning ordinance.

That zoning amendment would allow Battery Energy Storage Systems — or BESS — as a special exception.

The recommendation goes to the Board of Commissioners, said Sydney Shahar, assistant director of the Area Planning Department, which serves both Vigo County and the city of Terre Haute.

The Board of Commissioners take up the matter at 9 a.m. Tuesday at the Vigo County Annex, and it could make a decision on the amendment at that time,

A BESS can be a strategic precursor or a fast-track bridge to a data center.

A BESS can integrate with a data center to provide extended backup power, manage heavy electricity demand spikes and smooth out power fluctuations caused by AI workloads, according to information available online, including AI-generated summaries.

Switzer expects healthy debate at Tuesday’s Commissioners meeting.

“I have heard from numerous members of our community regarding the proposed Battery Energy Storage System (BESS) project, including those who support it and those who have expressed concerns,” he said.

“I respect those differing opinions and believe it’s important that we listen to the public and carefully consider the facts before making decisions that impact our community,” he said.

Switzer added, “I have been transparent about my support for this project. I believe responsible economic development and private investment are important to Vigo County’s future, provided projects meet appropriate safety, zoning, and regulatory requirements.”

Switzer said Area Planning’s BESS exemption doesn’t necessarily mean a data center looms on Vigo County’s horizon.

“There is no direct correlation between a BESS project and a data center,” Switzer said. “Battery energy storage facilities store electricity and help support the electrical grid, while data centers are facilities that consume electricity to operate computing equipment.

“Although both involve energy infrastructure, approving zoning provisions for battery storage does not automatically pave the way for a data center or establish any connection between the two.”

Commissioner Mark Clinkenbeard is a member of Area Plan Commission, but did not attend Wednesday’s meeting.

“I will be looking over the ordinance this weekend and going back and watching the last meeting (video on YouTube),” he said, adding, “We are having our legal counsel look over it.”

Commissioner Mike Morris was contacted a couple of times on Thursday and Friday but had no comment.

In a matter not directly tied to the zoning amendment, the Vigo County Council may be looking at a measure prohibiting it from providing any financial assistance to data centers at its Nov. 16 and 23 meetings.

Councilwoman Nancy Allsup is behind the resolution that initially was to have started its journey before the council this past Wednesday, but the scheduled council meetings were pushed back to the 16th and 23rd. There are, as of yet, no agendas published for those meetings.

The resolution before the council reads in part, “Data center developments may require substantial investments in electrical infrastructure, water and sewer systems, road improvements, emergency services and other public facilities.” It adds, “Discretionary public subsidies for privately operated data centers are not a fiscal priority of Vigo County.”

text:
Air Date: Week of November 6, 2026

The United States Capitol building in Washington, D.C. A new Democratic-majority Congress will convene in early January 2027. (Photo: Noclip, Wikimedia Commons public domain)

Hosts Steve Curwood and Jenni Doering continue our roundtable discussion with Vernon Loeb, Marianne Lavelle, and Dan Gearino of Inside Climate News about voters’ frustration with high fuel prices and the opportunity for a Democratic-led Congress to now focus on clean energy to reduce energy costs. We talk about what voters expect the Democratic party to deliver in the final two years of the Trump presidency and beyond.

Transcript

DOERING: It’s Living on Earth, I’m Jenni Doering

CURWOOD: And I’m Steve Curwood.

We’re here with colleagues from our media partner Inside Climate News, unpacking the blockbuster win for Democrats in the midterm elections and what it could mean for environmental protection during President Trump’s final 2 years in office. So, Marianne, let’s drill down on how energy played with voters, what did we see here?

LAVELLE: Right, some of the polling before the election showed that voters were much more worried about Republican energy policies than they were about Democratic climate policies being costly. And this is after the last two years the Trump administration has been ringing that bell that the Democrats want to give you the costly Green Deal, but voters just were not buying it. They know what they're paying for energy, and they know that that's related to this fossil fuel energy policy of the administration.

CURWOOD: With great profits for the fossil fuel industry through this campaign. I mean, underscored.

LAVELLE: It just so happened that they reported their profits last week, right before the election, and they're like triple what they were last year. And that's not because they're putting out a better product or anything. It's because purely the run-up in global prices.

LOEB: And Trump went on the campaign trail bragging about how great the oil industry profits were, and essentially saying, "I don't really care about people's concerns about pump prices. Isn't it great that all the money the oil industry is raking in?"

LAVELLE: What he said is this is money we're raking in as a country. But that's not how, how consumers experience it. It's really the oil companies that are raking in those profits, and their executives are the ones who have the most shares in those companies and who feel the benefits the most.

DOERING: So I mean, this is fascinating. Like, to what extent do you think Democrats now have the upper hand when it comes to issues like energy affordability, and what do they need to do to deliver on that in this Congress?

LAVELLE: Well, for the last 10 years at least, we've been in this incredibly polarized atmosphere where it's hard to imagine Democrats and Republicans working together on anything. But look at the way people voted, across the board in a bipartisan way, and the people they're sending to Washington know some of the voters were Republicans as well. They're all wanting the same thing, which is action on the out of control costs and the power that industries like the fossil fuel industry, like big tech, have over their lives. And so, I think what you're going to see is the Democrats trying to find some common ground with the Republicans who are now going to be there in the minority, on how they can address these issues that all of their voters said they cared about. I mean, one thing that comes to the top of the list is windfall profits taxes on the oil and gas industry as we were just talking about. What other industry has seen its profits, not its revenue, its profits, triple? And so there's so much that that money could be invested in to transition us away from this vulnerability that we have. The first ideas you're going to see are all going to be about affordability, and of course, the cheapest form of energy are the renewables, and that is the messaging we're going to see around what kind of legislation is going to be tried in the next Congress.

CURWOOD: So, in this tsunami for the Democrats, we've seen this huge switch from control away from the Republicans. But correct me if I'm wrong, but I think the electorate is mostly in the middle, mostly independent, and in many of these elections, the folks who really end up deciding what happens. I don't think there were a lot of defections from the hardcore Republicans this time around. What do the Democrats need to do now in this sector of protecting the environment and dealing with the climate emergency and and energy affordability? What do they need to do to keep that vast middle that, at the end of the day, elected them this time, and if they want to keep getting reelected, will need to show up next time?

LAVELLE: One of the interesting things is the moderate members of the Democratic Party up on the Hill already have gathered in this new Democrat coalition, and have organized, and talking about just these things, putting affordability front and center. And there also has been a lot of effort in the leadership to get the more centrist Democrats working with more left Democrats and seeing where their common ground is, so that the party doesn't have the inter-party fighting that has really made it hard for the Republicans to govern over the last few years. So I think it's a challenge, there's no question, but I think that people are going into this new Congress with a lot of positive vibes, so to speak. At least that's what the sense I'm getting from talking to people. They're not talking about what divides the Democrats, but what they can do together.

CURWOOD: Vernon, talk to me about this.

LOEB: The last time the Democrats did pretty well in the midterms in 2018, they came back to Washington talking about the Green New Deal, and it turned into very quickly a culture war slogan that they got clubbed with over the head for the next two years. Now, they're not talking about the Green New Deal. They're not even talking about climate change. They're talking about data centers and affordability, and those are populist slogans, if you will, that play across both sides of the aisle very effectively. And so they've learned a powerful lesson there, and it's easy now to make the case for solar and wind as cheaper alternatives. With Iran in, in charge of the Strait of Hormuz and gas still sitting at $4.50 a gallon and diesel sitting at $6.30 a gallon, and so the Democrats rhetorically, I think, are in a much smarter, stronger tactical position now than they were in 2018.

CURWOOD: So, looking ahead, you know, the next two years, Mr. Trump is still president of the United States. How does this win stack up against dealing with him in the White House?

LAVELLE: One of the models I've heard some of the Democratic lawmakers talk about is the housing affordability bill that Congress passed that Trump did not want to sign. He actually wanted to put his voter bill in it, and Congress wouldn't do it. But it was a bipartisan bill, and it had just such strong support across the board, and he let it pass without his signature. He let it go into law without his signature. That's kind of the model for what they're looking to do: bills that are just so popular that Trump will either deal with them or will just back away from a fight that just doesn't look good for him or his legacy. But of course, Trump is mercurial, if nothing else, so we'll have to see. One of the energy experts that I talked to today pointed out that a lot of the big environmental legislation of our era, the National Environmental Policy Act, the Clean Air Act, passed with Democratic Congresses and a Republican president, and that divided government sometimes can work if both sides see a way to compromise.

DOERING: Yeah.

CURWOOD: Vernon, you're thinking. I can see.

LOEB: Well, Trump sounded a sort of conciliatory note last night, saying, "Yeah, we'll work with Democrats. We'll figure out a way to do it." How much interest and energy he has left for legislating, he's never had much of a legislative agenda. He's bypassed Congress almost completely. How much energy he has for governing, it remains to be seen. Who knows what we're going to get from Trump in his last two years. A lot of people feel his health is sort of failing. His mental acuity clearly is not what it once was, so I think it's an unknown at this point, and it's also in my mind an unknown how Republicans now will react to him. He kept them in line amazingly well. They were really afraid of crossing him and crossing MAGA, but now he's a lame duck. Everybody's a free agent, and I think you're going to see a lot of Republicans starting to chart a more independent path away from Trump, thinking about their next election in the House two years from now. One of the most interesting things I heard last night was somebody quoting Lindsey Graham from 2015 when Trump came down the golden escalator, and right around that time, Lindsey Graham said, "If we support this man for president, he will destroy us. He will destroy the party, and he will destroy us all." And fast forward a decade, with Lindsey Graham's sister on the ballot, and she loses to a neophyte Democrat pediatrician.

LAVELLE: Because she was handpicked by Trump, and South Carolina voters were very upset at his intervention, and yeah, the irony is unbelievable.

LOEB: Yeah, and if you look at Trump's influence on the Senate races, you can argue that both Democratic seats in Georgia were the result of Trump picks a cycle ago. You can say that Talarico's victory over Paxton was attributable to Trump's support for Paxton. You've got Lindsey Graham's sister, and so Trump clearly gets an assist for the Democrats in about four or five Senate seats.

CURWOOD: Hey Dan, before we go, how can the Democrats keep support of middle America? Take advantage of, of the wins that they've had now to build up something solid there.

GEARINO: Well, to try to kind of unpack that, when's the last time Democrats had a night as good as this? And it wasn't a lot of these wave elections we've seen just in the last couple decades. You have to go way back. You have to go back to post-Watergate. So, who was elected out of the post-Watergate era in Iowa? Tom Harkin was one of those elected. He was one of the Watergate babies as they called them, and you saw this generation of a lot of them were in the Midwest. A lot of them were everywhere. You were winning in conservative areas. Oh wow, a Democrat won there? There were some really politically talented people who may not have won except for the political climate of that very precise moment. But once they got there, they stayed. And I can look at a couple of these people who won in the House and the Senate, and it'd be hard to imagine them losing when they run for reelection in two years or in six years, they're just political talents who happen to be running at the right time. And a key part of that is just listening to your constituents, realizing who you represent, and delivering for them. It is really not that complicated. I think there are names that were part of this election cycle that we are going to have as part of our lives for a very long time because they're good at politics, and that's in Democrat-leaning states, Republican-leaning states, swing states. So yeah, that's, that's kind of how you do it, I think.

CURWOOD: All right, that then brings up the question: dare I ask about 2028?

LOEB: Well, like Dan was just saying, there's a lot of young talent out there in the Democratic field now. You've got Jon Ossoff, who's in his 40s. You've got Turek in Iowa. You've got Josh Shapiro in Pennsylvania. You have Andy Beshear in Kentucky. Got Mark Kelly in Arizona. You've got Gavin Newsom in California. I think all of those guys would fare well against, who-knows-who will be the Republican candidates. But if the MAGA holdovers are still there, I guess it would either be J.D. Vance or Marco Rubio. But I think the Democratic candidates stack up pretty well. And remember, the Senate wins pretty much guarantee the Democrats the Senate through the next presidential election. So you're going to have the presidential election with a Democratic Congress, and you've got Texas in place suddenly that completely changes the whole electoral map that the country has sort of played by for 30 or 40 years. You know, you had that group of swing states that the Democrats had to win. Suddenly, they're not so important anymore if the Democrats win Texas and all those electoral votes. So '28 is going to be, like unbelievably interesting.

CURWOOD: All right, Dan, what do you think?

GEARINO: There's this fascinating inversion of the way this gets talked about, and it's just changed so much in the last year or so. There was a time not long ago when reasonable people would say the Democrats had no bench. You could probably go eight or nine deep with Democrats that would be plausible presidential candidates, and there are a few of them who won yesterday. And then you look at this rupturing of the kind of Trump base; it makes it so that all of a sudden they're the ones that don't have a very deep bench. It's like you've got J.D. Vance and who, you know who would be next Marco Rubio, and then okay, who's fifth or sixth up? And it's just wild, and it just kind of shows things change rapidly, you know. And if you fixate too much on the moment that you're in, you're gonna just go nuts, because things change quick. The piece I'm writing today, I'm trying to fit in this quote from, oh, the former Colorado Governor Bill Ritter, and he had this comment in an interview a couple weeks ago where he was talking about like the swinging screen door, and that the thing is the door hits you in the rear end. You know, basically there are ups and downs in political life, and that reversal can come quick. And I think that that's something on a day when Democrats are just celebrating, they can just see just in recent history how that can turn quick.

CURWOOD: Hey, before we go, of course we are objective journalists. We have views and responses, of course, but one of the dogs in this particular fight is our own profession: the ability to report the news and to function in a democracy with a free press that's enshrined in the Constitution. What does this win by the Democrats mean for press freedom in America, do you think?

LOEB: Well, I think it's important. You know, Trump has shown a willingness to go after the press, to file lawsuits, to intimidate, to throw reporters out of institutions that they have a right to cover, to decide who can come to the Pentagon, who can cover wars, who can go to the White House briefing room, and I think a democratic victory, taking the country back to the norms that we operated under in terms of government and the press for my entire career, which is like going on 50 years now, I think it's an important moment to kind of reestablish those norms, and I think it augurs well for press freedom going forward. The other big thing that, when you talk about press freedom, has really now become ownership of networks. You know, you've got Fox News, you've got CBS now in the hands of a billionaire family. You've got CNN, you know, in the hands of a conglomerate that's more friendly to Trump, and that's something that we really didn't have, you know, a generation ago. That kind of bifurcation, almost, of the mainstream media. So how that's going to play out really remains to be seen. But from my perspective, in terms of picking which reporters can go to the White House briefing room and which ones can't, I, I hope, you know, we're, we're moving to an era where that's not going to happen quite so easily.

DOERING: Well, we want to thank you, Vernon Loeb is Executive Editor of Inside Climate News. Thank you so much for being here.

LOEB: Sure, thanks for having me.

DOERING: And Marianne Lavelle, Washington Bureau Chief at ICN.

LAVELLE: Thanks, glad to be here.

DOERING: And Dan Gearino, clean energy reporter at ICN. Thank you all so much.

GEARINO: Yep, thank you.

LAVELLE: Thank you.

CURWOOD: And thanks to all three of you for coming and keeping the story going. And I'm looking forward to what's coming next.

title: Maine should be rallying behind clean energy permitting reform | Letter
description:
I was disappointed to see Attorney General Aaron Frey sign a letter to Senate leadership (Oct. 21) opposing the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act (BAAJA).
Mainers pay some of the highest electricity rates in the country, driven largely by our dependence on out-of-state fossil fuels, particularly natural gas.
Lowering electricity costs and meeting our climate goals can go hand in hand.
Maine has abundant, low-cost clean energy waiting to come online; transmission and other infrastructure upgrades are needed to deliver it.
New England Clean Energy Connect (NECEC) is now delivering clean Canadian hydropower to New England, displacing fossil fuel generation.

Instead, years of lawsuits and political battles added more than $500 million to its cost — a burden that ultimately falls on ratepayers.

text:
The Chamber of Progress is urging congressional Democrats to introduce legislation in 2027 to require data center operators to cover electricity costs, disclose water consumption, and provide economic benefits to surrounding communities.

In a Nov. 4 memo, the technology policy group outlined its legislative priorities for the next Congress, including three proposed measures designed to address the growing energy and infrastructure demands associated with data center development.

Three proposed bills target electricity, public benefits, and water use

One central recommendation, the Pay Your Own Way Act, would require data center campuses consuming 100 megawatts or more to cover the full incremental cost of supplying them with electricity. The legislation would direct the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission to establish a model electricity tariff for large power users. It would also condition federal grid funding on states adopting equivalent tariff structures.

According to the Chamber of Progress, the proposal would make the Ratepayer Protection Pledge binding on data center operators, aiming to prevent residential customers from absorbing electricity costs associated with large-scale data center demand.

A second proposal, the Public Dollars, Public Benefits Act, would connect expedited federal permitting and access to federal land with requirements that data centers operate without public subsidies. The measure would also establish public registries of financial incentives and direct federal cost-sharing toward shared electric grid infrastructure intended to reduce costs for ratepayers.

The third proposal, the Closed Loop Act, would establish state-level water-use disclosure requirements for large industrial facilities and introduce performance-based water consumption standards. The measure would coordinate water and electricity reviews while providing funding for research and conservation incentives.

Beyond infrastructure and resource requirements, the Chamber of Progress is recommending local hiring commitments, apprenticeship opportunities, and workforce training programs to ensure surrounding communities receive economic benefits from data center construction and operations.

Local opposition adds pressure for greater oversight

The recommendations come amid growing opposition to data center development in communities nationwide.

Sen. Bernie Sanders, I-Vt., who caucuses with Democrats, has also called for restrictions on new facilities, citing local ballot measures voters approved in the Nov. 3 midterm elections.

Data center restrictions appeared on ballots in 40 jurisdictions across 10 states, with voters approving restrictions in virtually every contest, according to preliminary results. A few results remained pending, while Hardwood, N.D., was a notable exception, with voters rejecting restrictions on data center development.

NBC exit polling found that 76% of voters opposed construction of new data centers in their communities. The polling also found that 56% considered data centers a crucial or major factor in their choice of congressional candidates.

“National data center moratorium now,” Sanders wrote in a post on X. “Americans don’t want Big Tech oligarchs wrecking the environment, gutting jobs and threatening humanity’s future.”

Janine Yorio, CEO of Community Digital Technologies, attributed the growing opposition to data centers to the physical visibility of data centers and the disconnect between the communities hosting them and the people benefiting financially from their development.

Data centers, she said, have become the most visible representation of the artificial intelligence industry. However, a moratorium, as Sanders has suggested, would not solve the overarching issue, she explained.

“People are going to expect to be brought along with the AI economy and not left behind by it,” she said.

Practical legislation to address data center concerns could provide that “people that live in data center communities actually own a piece of the data centers themselves. If data centers don’t create jobs, they should still help make local people more prosperous.”

“I do not fundamentally believe that AI will slow down or that data centers will never get built. But the economic framework under which all these things move forward, I believe, is going to change significantly,” she said.

Incoming Democrats outline data center proposals

Data center oversight is also emerging as a priority among incoming Democrats, several of whom have called for greater accountability for the industry’s effects on local communities and energy infrastructure.

Sen.-elect James Talarico, D-Texas, has proposed making data center operators responsible for the costs associated with their facilities. His plan includes ending tax incentives for large technology companies, requiring major energy users to finance infrastructure improvements, and establishing federal standards for new data center projects.

Talarico has also expressed support for closed-loop cooling systems to reduce water consumption and giving local communities greater authority over data center development decisions.

Sen.-elect Adam Hamilton, D-Kan., has similarly called for federal requirements that ensure data centers pay their own electricity costs rather than shifting expenses to residential ratepayers.

Hamilton has also said that companies should earn the support of the communities where they establish operations.

title: COP31 and Climate Action's New Centers of Gravity | Council on Foreign Relations
