text:
Ed.’s Notes: The following article is the final installment in a two-part series covering the 2026 midterm elections. Read Part One here.

Democrats posted strong gains in the 2026 midterm elections, winning control of both the U.S. House and the U.S. Senate.

When the new Congress convenes in January 2027, we will have plenty of new members and staffers to meet.

North Carolina’s results were central to massive change in Washington, DC. From the U.S. Senate to the U.S. House, North Carolina’s voters shaped the national political landscape.

Below is where things stand as of this writing. We conclude with thoughts on what to expect for the rest of 2026 in Congress and what to expect in 2027.

U.S. Senate: Cooper Wins the Open Seat for Democrats

In June 2025, Senator Thom Tillis said he would not run again, and the open seat soon became one of the most closely watched Senate races in the country. Former two-term Governor Roy Cooper, a Democrat, ran against Republican Michael Whatley, a North Carolina native and former chair of the Republican National Committee who had never run for elected office.

According to unofficial returns, Cooper won decisively, 58.72% to 39.09%, flipping the seat and becoming the first Democrat to win a U.S. Senate race in North Carolina since Kay Hagan in 2008. His six-year term begins January 3, 2027. Serving alongside Republican Senator Ted Budd, he gives North Carolina a split delegation. Senator Budd is expected to run for reelection in 2028. Until then, we are waiting to see whether Senator-elect Cooper and Senator Budd can build a bipartisan approach at least on some issues.

U.S. House: New Maps, New Members

When Republicans in the General Assembly redrew the U.S. House districts in 2025, they intended to create districts that favored eleven Republican candidates and three Democratic candidates. It did not work out that way. Before Election Day, Democrats held four of the state’s fourteen House seats; they now lead in ten races. If those leads hold, North Carolina Democrats would control a majority of the state’s Congressional delegation for the first time since 2013.

The Winners

Four of the four incumbent Democratic members were reelected:

District 1: Don Davis defeated Republican Laurie Buckhout in a district redrawn to favor the Republican candidate.

District 2: Deborah Ross won reelection in her safe Democrat district.

District 4: Valerie Foushee won reelection in her safe Democrat district.

District 12: Alma Adams won reelection in her safe Democrat district.

One of the ten incumbent Republican members was reelected without any doubt:

District 8: Mark Harris won reelection in his safe Republican district.

Three other Republican incumbents appear poised to win reelection, but these are so close that a recount could change the result.

District 3: Greg Murphy leads 49.4% to 49.3%.

District 7: David Rouzer leads 49.9% to 49.1%.

District 10: Pat Harrigan leads 49.7% to 48.7%.

The Changes

District 5: Democrat Chuck Hubbard defeated eleven-term Republican Virginia Foxx, but a recount could give the win to Foxx because the margin is only about 100 votes. Foxx is one of the most powerful Republicans in the U.S. House, where she chairs the Rules Committee.

District 6: Democrat Cyril Jefferson defeated one-term Republican Addison McDowell.

District 9: Democrat Richard N. Ojeda II defeated seven-term Republican Representative Richard Hudson. Hudson is among the top leaders in the US House Republican caucus.

District 11: Democrat Jamie Ager flipped the seat held by Republican Chuck Edwards, who withdrew from the election and was replaced by Republican NC House member Jennifer Balkcom.

District 13: Democrat Paul Barringer defeated one-term Republican Brad Knott.

District 14: Democrat Lekesha Womack defeated one-term Republican Tim Moore.

Special note: If the margins in the final November 13 vote tally are less than 1% in any House district, we expect a recount.

Before the Gavels Change Hands: What to Expect in the Lame-Duck Session

The new majorities will not take over until January. In the meantime, the outgoing Congress returns with a long list of must-pass legislation. The lame-duck session begins November 9 and is expected to run until Christmas, with a Thanksgiving break, leaving no more than five legislative weeks to finish this work. The end of a congressional term often gives departing members and outgoing chairs both the freedom and the incentive to close out unfinished business.

Federal Budget

The biggest deadline is December 11, when the short-term spending continuing resolution that has kept the federal government open since October 1 expires. A government shutdown on December 12 is unlikely, but possible. Congress tries to pass 12 annual appropriations bills, but none has become law. The House Appropriations Committee has approved all 12, while the Senate has not taken up any of them. With so little time left, Congress is unlikely to pass the bills individually, so lawmakers will likely choose between combining them into a single omnibus package that sets spending for the year or passing another short-term spending law. Democrats, who take control in January, may prefer the short-term option so they can make the final spending decisions next year.

Agriculture

The Farm Bill, which covers crop programs and the Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program (SNAP), expired on September 30. Before the pre-election recess, the Senate Agriculture Committee reported a 2026 farm bill on a party-line 12–11 vote, and the Senate may take it up during the lame-duck session. A comprehensive farm bill is a realistic year-end goal, but if negotiations stall, another extension is the likely fallback.

Armed Services and National Defense

Congress also needs to pass the annual defense policy bill for fiscal year 2027, known as the National Defense Authorization Act (NDAA). The NDAA sets defense policy and authorizes funding for the military, including construction and other defense projects. The House passed its version in July, but the bill has stalled in the Senate. Even so, Congress has passed an NDAA every year for more than 60 years. Given North Carolina’s large military presence, the bill matters for bases and military communities across the state, and most observers expect it to pass before the end of the year.

FEMA

The National Flood Insurance Program also expires on December 11. If it lapses, the Federal Emergency Management Agency (FEMA) would stop selling and renewing flood insurance policies, and the program’s borrowing authority would drop from $30.425 billion to $1 billion. Congress has extended the program on a short-term basis 36 times since late 2017, and another short extension attached to the spending bill is the most likely outcome.

Healthcare

Several health care programs expire on December 31. These include funding for community health centers and Medicare add-on payments for Medicare-dependent and low-volume hospitals, which many of North Carolina’s rural hospitals rely on. Congress often extends programs like these as part of a government funding package.

What Happens Next?

The 2026 election is a turning point for North Carolina in Washington, DC. The state flipped a Senate seat to Democrats, now has one senator from each party, and will send the most Democrats to the House since 2012, all of which will change how the state’s priorities are advanced in Congress. Still, some races have not been called, recounts may follow, and final results may not be clear for weeks. All results remain unofficial until counties finish their canvass and the State Board of Elections certifies them.

With Democrats leading the committees and setting the agenda in Congress, Democratic members of the state’s delegation stand to gain influence, while Republican members will have to adjust to life in the minority. Alma Adams will become the senior Democrat member of the delegation. If Virginia Foxx loses, David Rouzer will become the senior Republican member of the delegation.

For organizations that engage with Congress, the practical takeaway is to begin building relationships with incoming members and their staff now, while also maintaining contact with incumbents whose races remain unresolved.

Samsung SDI and Alpha Omega Power Sign 1 GWh Supply Agreement for US-Made Energy Storage

Supply deals with AOP totaling 1.5 GWh, with all products to be manufactured at the SPE plant in Indiana

SBB 1.7 features high-nickel NCA prismatic batteries and proven fire safety, supporting AOP projects in the WECC and ERCOT power markets

Samsung SDI expands its North American ESS presence as AOP grows its U.S. storage portfolio

HOUSTON & SEOUL, Korea–(BUSINESS WIRE)–Samsung SDI today announced that its Michigan-based subsidiary, Samsung SDI America (SDIA), has signed a 1 GWh agreement to supply energy storage system (ESS) solutions to Alpha Omega Power (AOP), a U.S. utility-scale battery storage developer and independent power producer. Including an initial contract signed late last year, the two agreements total 1.5 GWh.

AOP plans to deploy the ESS solutions supplied by Samsung SDI for large-scale power projects critical for grid reliability and power demand growth, scheduled to begin construction in the WECC and ERCOT power markets next year.

Under the latest agreement, Samsung SDI will supply its Samsung Battery Box (SBB) 1.7, a fully integrated ESS solution featuring nickel cobalt aluminum (NCA) batteries. All cells and modules will be manufactured at the StarPlus Energy (SPE) plant in Kokomo, Indiana, and delivered by the end of this year.

SBB 1.7 features high-capacity, high-nickel NCA chemistry and delivers 17% higher energy density than its predecessor, SBB 1.5, while maintaining the same 20-foot footprint. The solution also incorporates Samsung SDI’s ESS design expertise, including AI-powered algorithms for early anomaly detection and battery life prediction, and is designed for 25 years of continuous use.

SBB 1.7 has also obtained certifications and met safety standards including NFPA 855, the National Fire Protection Association’s standard for the installation of stationary energy storage systems, and UL 9540, a safety standard for ESS. The solution also incorporates Samsung SDI’s proprietary Enhanced Direct Injection (EDI) technology, which directly injects fire-extinguishing agents into individual battery modules, further enhancing fire safety.

Samsung SDI has secured a series of ESS supply deals with U.S. energy companies this year and continues to discuss potential supply agreements with a number of local customers, with additional orders expected in the near future.

Industry analysts attribute Samsung SDI’s recent contract wins in part to its prismatic battery technology (PrismStack), known for its strong performance and safety.

Samsung SDI is currently the only non-Chinese supplier of prismatic ESS batteries in North America. With strong durability and fire safety compared with pouch-type batteries, its prismatic batteries have helped the company meet the stringent requirements of U.S. energy companies.

Paul Choi, CEO of Alpha Omega Power, said:

American-made ESS from Samsung SDI will play an important role in AOP’s continued growth,

“This second agreement strengthens our domestic supply chain supporting the next generation of energy infrastructure.”

Fabrice Hudry, President ESS, Samsung SDI America (SDIA), said:

Alpha Omega Power is one of the fastest growing independent power producers in the country, and the kind of sophisticated operator we want to partner with to tackle grid reliability challenges,

“With our differentiated technology and local production capabilities, we will continue to expand our business foundation and strengthen our position in the North American ESS market.”

text:
The New Shoreham Town Council met briefly on Monday and at an earlier than usual time so the council chamber could be cleared out and set up as Block Island’s sole polling place for the election to be held the next day.
It took less than half an hour to get through the agenda, which included a public hearing and renewal of mobile food service permits, the signing of a memorandum of understanding with the Block Island Solar Initiative, and the usual agenda items of receiving correspondence, approving minutes of previous meetings, and the appointment of people to boards and commissions.
First Warden Keith Stover started out the meeting with high praise for the Block Island School’s girls varsity volleyball team, which had just had its final game of the season up at the school gym. Although the girls were defeated, Stover said it was a terrific game. “They fought valiantly,” he said.
“If my voice is hoarse...” said Councilor Mark Emmanuelle, admitting he was one of the many people packed into the gymnasium cheering on the team.
Stover also asked Town Clerk Millie Highet how many people had voted early.
Highet said, “We have 400.”
For the record, that’s about 35 percent of the registered voters on Block Island, and on Tuesday morning, the highest turnout so far in the state of Rhode Island for early voting.
There were two items of correspondence received at the meeting. The first was an assent from the Rhode Island Coastal Management Resources Council giving permission for the town to conduct some of the work selected to be done under the Corn Neck Road Resiliency Project. Specifically, the approved work includes dune path restoration along Corn Neck Road, including “dune fencing” and mats, and improvements to the Scotch Beach parking area for drainage and storm-water management. Work done in the parking area is to be done only after September 15 and before May 15 in any given year. (The assent gives a five-year time frame for the work to be done.)
The other correspondence item pertains to Interstate Navigation and a public hearing before the Division of Public Carriers and Utilities on Monday, November 9 at 11a.m. at its offices in Warwick. The hearing is part of the PUC’s approval process for a carrier to take on long-term debt. In this case, Interstate is essentially refinancing existing debt on the
M/V Athena
and adding an additional line of credit with a maximum borrowing level of $500,000.
The council held the first of two required public hearings before the filing of a Community Development Block Grant application in the amount of $1,500,000 on behalf of the Block Island Housing Board. The housing board wishes to use the money to purchase a home on Connecticut Avenue and renovate into four, year-round affordable housing units.
No one came forward with any commentary when Stover asked if anyone wanted to “testify,” except for Chris Warfel, who approached the council with the idea and is a current member of the Housing Board.
Warfel said he wanted to clear up a “misconception” in the community about the project, which was the belief that there was some amount of debt involved. Warfel said there was not.
Emmanuelle said, “It just seems fitting with all Pat Queally did for the community.”
Queally, now deceased, is the owner of the property up for acquisition and has for years rented the home out for workforce housing.
The council set the second public hearing for Monday, November 16.
Mobile Food Establishments come and go and five out of six of them authorized to operate on Block Island were up for permit renewals. The one absent from the list was Payne’s Donuts, which, Highet explained, was simply on another renewal schedule.
There were very few questions asked of the license holders and renewals were approved for Andiamo Zeke, doing business as Aldo’s Bakery (Boat); Block Island Gourmet, LLC doing business as Block Island Gourmet Food Truck; Champlin’s Hotel, Marina and Resort Food Trailer; Alberto Sanchez, Pizza Shack (at Payne’s Dock); and See The Light, LLC, doing business as Southeast Light Delights.
Last year was the first for Sanchez operating the Pizza Shack and he was asked how it went by Stover.
“It was perfect,” said Sanchez. “It was a good asset for that area.”
Jayme Hennessy of the Block Island Solar Initiative was on hand for the discussion and approval of a memorandum of understanding between the town and the Solar Initiative for the installation of two new electric vehicle chargers at Town Hall.
Town Manager Amy Land said the MOU reflected all the things discussed previously with the council when the idea was first floated last spring. Those include some key terms on the signage, and most especially, a phone number people could call if there was a problem.
Stover had been adamant last spring that he did not want people walking into Town Hall to bother staff if there was a problem. “I think everything we talked about is included,” he said of the MOU.
Hennessy said the Solar Initiative had been working with an engineer with Rise Engineering and that had been very helpful. “One advantage of working with the engineer is ideas that we never thought about.”
Hennessy also thanked the council and the people at Town Hall that made the project possible.
Stover said he had recently taken a trip to North Carolina and noticed the build-up of EV infrastructure along the major high- ways.
Hennessy said highways were built up first, and now municipalities. There was grant money available from the federal government, she added, but in order to qualify for it, ADA access must be provided.
Emmanuelle asked about having a charger at the beach.
Hennessy said it was a good idea, but there were concerns about flooding in the parking lot.
The Solar Initiative is also responsible for the installation of the charger at the power company, which has had problems. Hennessy said they were replacing that unit also.
Finally, was the item: Raise items for future agendas.
Land said, “We have a pretty good list we’re working on already,” and the meeting was adjourned.

text:
SAN JUAN – New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani and New York Gov. Kathy Hochul pledged more support for Puerto Rico on Friday as it remains mired in multiple crises, asserting during a trip to the island that the sweeping Democratic win in the U.S. midterm elections will be a boon for the U.S. territory.

“There’s a potential in that we can finally start to deliver for working-class people across this country,” Mamdani said. “What we heard today was the fact that so often what’s described as a natural crisis here in Puerto Rico is in fact a political crisis, one that is the result of political choices.”

Hochul said the election results represent “a whole new day” for Puerto Rico and warned that the federal government will be held responsible.

“What we’ve seen over the last two years is really an abandonment of that commitment," she said. "And we hope to have all those wounds heal, making sure that we continue bringing resources for resiliency, energy projects, building up the grid, as well as healthcare being restored, nutrition programs.”

Mamdani and Hochul are part of a group of New York government officials who are in Puerto Rico for a four-day, annual conference. They met with local nonprofits on Friday as officials announced a $280,000 partnership to help the island confront emergencies.

Puerto Rico struggles to emerge from crises

The partnership between Hispanic Federation and the Federal Home Loan Bank of New York comes as Puerto Rico struggles with chronic power outages and intermittent water shortages while it tries to rebuild from Hurricane Maria and other disasters.

The nonprofit Hispanic Federation said the money would equip 10 community-run resiliency hubs across the island with increased water storage capacity; some also would receive rain-collection systems, kitchen infrastructure and solar power with battery storage.

“We have to start working with the leadership to make sure that the Puerto Rico agenda is not forgotten,” Frankie Miranda, president and CEO of Hispanic Federation, told The Associated Press.

“In Puerto Rico, there are still some huge challenges," he said. “All the public policies have been so harmful to Puerto Rico.”

The announcement comes months after the administration of U.S. President Donald Trump canceled solar projects in Puerto Rico that were supposed to help thousands of low-income families. One project, worth $400 million, would have seen the installation of solar and battery storage systems in low-income homes and those with medical needs.

The U.S. Department of Energy has said the money initially slated for solar projects would instead be used to help maintain Puerto Rico’s crumbling power grid, which was razed by Hurricane Maria in September 2017. The grid, however, was already weakened given a lack of maintenance and investment.

The decisions prompted outrage on the island as federal support for solar projects fades.

Puerto Ricans sue US government

Last week, six Puerto Rico residents sued the U.S. Energy Department and its secretary, Chris Wright, following the scrapping of a $1 billion federally funded program to provide solar power and battery storage to those who most needed it.

“The cost of such systems remains out of reach for the majority of Puerto Ricans,” the lawsuit stated.

Among those suing is 63-year-old Arecibo resident Ileana Ríos, who is diabetic and needs to refrigerate her insulin. Meanwhile, her son has asthma and needs to use a nebulizer, which requires electricity.

The lawsuit noted that Ríos “regularly loses power when the weather is stable and always loses power during storms, sometimes for several weeks at a time.”

The other residents who sued also have serious health conditions and need equipment or medications that rely on electricity.

The lawsuit requests that a judge order the U.S. Energy Department to reinstate the grant program, among other things. The agency did not return a message seeking comment.

The funding loss has been a blow to nonprofits and others who faced months of uncertainty and confusion as they awaited the Trump administration’s decision on whether and how it would continue the program.

“We had a lot of uncertainty. ... At some points it just felt like we were talking to no one," said Sybelle Rodriguez del Valle, director of operations at the energy resilience nonprofit Barrio Eléctrico, which was part of the U.S. Energy Department program.

Barrio Eléctrico provides electric service to more than 500 families and was poised to provide resilient energy for 1,200 families with funds from the federal program. It had only completed about one-third of its projects before the program ended, losing an estimated $16 million to $20 million in funding.

___

Associated Press reporter Gabriela Aoun Angueira contributed to this report.

text:
Keller city leaders have approved a settlement regarding a proposed Westlake data center that includes nearly $1.9 million in payments and new protections for nearby residents, such as noise restrictions and environmental safeguards.

The agreement does not prevent the planned 1.1-million-square-foot project along Highway 377 in neighboring Westlake from moving forward.

The Keller City Council unanimously approved settlement terms with Circle T Owner LP and the town of Westlake. Keller's city manager finalized the agreement on the city's behalf Thursday, the city said.

The Westlake Town Council must still review and approve the settlement at an upcoming meeting.

"Keller's first responsibility has been, and will always be, to protect our residents," Keller Mayor Ross McMullin said in a news release. "Throughout this process, we have fiercely advocated for our residents - especially those living closest to the proposed data center site.

"For that reason, I'm pleased to announce that we have secured the ability to enforce meaningful protections for our residents that span even beyond our own City borders related to Westlake's data center. We will always stand up for Keller and our residents."

The full settlement terms have been made available on the city's website.

The agreement comes after homeowners in Keller's Marshall Ridge neighborhood said they were blindsided by plans for the massive data center just a few hundred feet from their properties.

Concerns about noise, environmental impacts, and the approval process led to lawsuits and a temporary court order blocking Westlake from advancing the project's development agreement. The order was later dissolved.

Residents have also agreed to settle their lawsuit.

"Per legal counsel, we have agreed to terminate our lawsuit regarding the proposed Circle T Data Center in Westlake," the Lakes at Marshall Ridge HOA Board said in an email Thursday night.

"We appreciate the City of Keller and City Council for showing up when we asked. Not only did they listen to the concerns of our community, they took action on our behalf," said Rodney Eiland, Marshall Ridge HOA board member, in the release. "Knowing our city leaders were willing to roll up their sleeves and jump in and fight means a great deal."

"Residents living near the proposed data center site have had understandable concerns about how it could impact our neighborhoods," said Mark Mathews, Lakes of Marshall Ridge HOA member. "We're grateful to Mayor McMullin and the City Council for taking those concerns seriously and working to secure meaningful protections for our community."

The dispute also strained relations between Keller and Westlake, with Westlake voting against renewing its police services contract with Keller. The existing contract runs through October 2028.

What does the settlement include?

Under the agreement, Keller would gain contractual rights to enforce certain noise, screening, and operational requirements at the site, despite its location outside Keller city limits.

According to the city, the settlement includes:

Noise restrictions: Daytime and nighttime noise limits at residential property lines, an independent baseline noise study, and quarterly monitoring for three years after operations begin.

Landscaping: A 10-foot landscaping berm to help screen the facility from nearby neighborhoods. Trees that die or sustain significant damage affecting their screening function must be replaced.

Community funding: A $1.5 million contribution for noise monitoring, environmental mitigation, and other municipal programs and services benefiting Keller residents.

Fire protection: A $300,000 contribution toward Keller Fire Rescue training, equipment, decontamination and other emergency response costs associated with the project.

Generator restrictions: Diesel-powered backup generators must incorporate EPA Tier 4 emissions controls, with generator testing limited to daytime hours.

Grading and drainage: Circle T must provide the project's grading plan, including the proposed berm and associated drainage improvements.

Legal expenses: A $76,000 payment toward Keller's attorney fees and expert consultant costs.

"The city also remains invested in continued statewide discussions and both Gov. Greg Abbott and Governor-elect Gina Hinojosa's directives regarding the demands data centers place on Texas's electric grid and water resources, including the importance of ensuring those facilities bear the costs associated with their operations," Keller city officials said in the news release.

Data centers become a political issue in Texas

The rapid expansion of AI data centers became a political challenge for Republicans ahead of the Nov. 3 midterm elections, amid growing opposition to electricity costs, water consumption, and the impact on nearby communities.

According to Cleanview Research, 75% of data centers under construction in the U.S. and 80% of planned projects are in predominantly Republican states.

Texas leads the nation in data centers under construction. Earlier this year, Abbott directed state agencies to pause the issuance of environmental permits and new grid connections for data center projects.

The issue also became part of the Texas governor's race, in which Democrat Gina Hinojosa defeated Abbott on Tuesday.

President Donald Trump has supported data center development, citing its importance to economic growth and national security. But public opposition has grown, with some Republican leaders, including Abbott, taking steps to restrict new projects.

CBS News Texas will provide updates as more information becomes available.

To the Members of the United States Congress:

On behalf of the undersigned organizations, we urge Congress to pass the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act of 2026, historic comprehensive permitting reform legislation, and send it to the President’s desk as soon as possible. At a time when affordability remains a top concern for American families, there is no greater opportunity to lower costs and improve everyday life than by ensuring needed projects, investments, and other activities can move forward in a timely, predictable, and transparent manner.

Communities across the country are waiting to invest in improvements that will make everyday life better and more affordable. From critical infrastructure and communications networks to natural resource management, water, and all kinds of energy projects, these investments will lower costs, strengthen the economy, create jobs, and improve quality of life in communities across the country. Yet far too often, these improvements are delayed for years by a broken permitting process that has become overly complex, unpredictable, and inefficient.

Permitting reform is ultimately about delivering results. When needed investments are delayed, families and businesses face higher costs, longer wait times, and fewer opportunities. Communities wait longer for congestion relief, the broadband connections needed to support work, education, health care, and entrepreneurship, improved access to clean water, and the energy infrastructure needed to meet growing demand. A more efficient permitting process can help deliver these benefits sooner by reducing unnecessary delays and improving certainty while maintaining strong environmental protections and opportunities for community engagement.

Congress has a historic opportunity to modernize a system that too often delays progress and drives up costs. Americans are ready to see projects built, communities strengthened, and investments translated into real-world benefits. We cannot afford to wait any longer to enact comprehensive permitting reform, which is why we the undersigned organizations urge Congress to pass the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act of 2026 as quickly as possible.

text:
The Washington-based American Biogas Council (ABC) has released new research, which states that the potential to capture energy from food waste is substantial.

Food waste produces biogas when the microorganisms in it break down the organic material, ABC says. Biogas systems capture all the biogas to keep it from going into the air and use it to generate renewable electricity and heat, or it can be processed into renewable natural gas (RNG).

ABC’s research team reports 404 operating facilities across 48 states produce biogas from food waste. About 200 of these facilities operate at farms and wastewater treatment plants and combine food waste with manure or wastewater to capture biogas. According to ABC, another 204 facilities make use of food waste alone, capturing approximately 36 billion cubic feet of biogas annually and representing nearly $3 billion in capital investment.

ABC says its expanded research uncovered projects not previously included in its inventory, showing an increase of 73 percent over last year’s count.

“America is literally throwing away enough renewable energy to power millions of homes,” says ABC Executive Director Patrick Serfass. “The technology to make energy from food waste is already operating, but the potential to turn more of what we routinely discard into a valuable domestic energy resource is enormous.”

Food waste is already producing energy

The facilities identified by ABC handle food waste from food manufacturers, grocery stores, restaurants and other sources. ABC says some capture energy from food and beverage manufacturing, and others process consumer and retail food waste, including food that spoils, is rejected or remains unsold.

Of the 204 food-waste-only facilities, 161 process preconsumer food waste, primarily wastewater from food processing and beverage manufacturing, according to ABC’s research. Another 43 facilities handle retail and consumer food waste, capturing approximately 8.2 billion cubic feet of biogas annually.

ABC says most facilities use biogas to generate electricity and heat. The research states 164 food-waste-only facilities produce power, heat or both, and another 38 upgrade biogas into RNG.

Bigger projects and more investment

ABC says food waste biogas projects are getting larger and attracting more investment. The 42 facilities that have come online since 2020 account for 32 percent of the sector's annual biogas production and 45 percent of its total investment, according to the research. On average, ABC says, these newer projects capture nearly twice as much biogas as earlier projects and cost about three times as much to build.

The momentum continued in 2025, when seven new food waste projects came online, all of which produce RNG. Together, ABC says they added more than twice the biogas capture capacity of any other year since 2020.

ABC estimates that if all 70 million tons of discarded food generated in the United States in 2024 were processed through anaerobic digestion, it could produce approximately 181 billion cubic feet of additional biogas annually—roughly five times the amount currently captured by the country's dedicated food waste biogas facilities.

That additional biogas represents approximately 113 million British thermal units of energy, enough to meet the annual energy needs of approximately 1.5 million U.S. households, ABC says.

text:
This analysis and news roundup come from the Canary Media Weekly newsletter. Sign up to get it every Friday.

Americans aren’t happy about the data center boom, and they made their displeasure pretty clear this Election Day. Voters not only selected a slate of Democratic candidates who campaigned against data centers; they also approved more than 30 ballot measures aimed at reining in the power-hungry facilities.

You could argue that the ​“data center elections” really started a year ago, when Virginians selected Democrat Abigail Spanberger as their next governor. Virginia has more than earned its status as the data center capital of the world, with the latest estimates counting more than 700 facilities around the state, and Spanberger ran on a promise to keep their intense power demand in check.

In the months that followed, it became clear that data center developers were circling in on Great Lakes states and their abundant water resources — and that fighting the facilities was a winning campaign strategy. Take Michigan’s Democratic U.S. Senator-elect Abdul El-Sayed, who made data center regulation a prominent piece of his candidacy, and William Lawrence, a Democrat who won his U.S. House race after showing up at a local council meeting to fight a proposed data center.

Meanwhile in Ohio, Sherrod Brown, a three-term Democratic senator who was ousted in 2024, will return to the chamber. Brown’s campaign painted his Republican opponent as ​“the face of data centers,” even though it cost Brown the support of some union labor allies who’ve backed him for decades but see data centers as creators of construction jobs.

Data centers’ threat is even more palpable in Georgia and Texas, which have more projects in the pipeline than any other state except Virginia. Georgia Sen. Jon Ossoff (D) was easily reelected after criticizing data centers as part of his campaign and investigating their impact on power bills in the Senate. Georgia’s Democratic Gov.-elect Keisha Lance Bottoms has meanwhile pledged a ​“pause” on new data center construction once she takes office in January. And Democrats James Talarico and Gina Hinojosa scored historic wins in Texas for U.S. Senate and governor, respectively, after promising to pursue a slate of data center regulations.

Anti–data center sentiment this election cycle was so strong that even some Republicans promised restrictions — Michigan Senate candidate Mike Rogers called for a one-year moratorium in the state, for example. But some still sided with data centers, like Sen. Darline Graham of South Carolina, who benefited from an industry-funded ad campaign before losing a seat she had been expected to retain.

And when the data center debate showed up in ballot measures across dozens of counties and municipalities, voters gave a resounding response: Rein them in.

More big energy stories

How energy prices showed up on the ballot

Data centers weren’t the only energy issue motivating voters this week. With gasoline prices at their highest level of any Election Day in U.S. history, and falling temperatures getting Americans thinking about heating bills, it’s no wonder that voters were looking for a change.

While President Donald Trump has been promising to curb energy costs since his 2024 campaign, his decisions have driven prices in the opposite direction. Experts say that perhaps his most drastic mistake was starting a war with Iran, spiking oil prices that have yet to return to anything resembling the pre-conflict normal. That impact has been especially obvious in Maine, where half the residents rely on heating oil — and where voters ousted longtime Republican Sen. Susan Collins on Tuesday.

Utility bills were literally on the ballot in nine states this week, as voters selected new members to regulatory boards that oversee utility rate hikes and other energy-related decisions. While most of the states preserved the status quo and elected Republicans, Georgia voters gave Democrats the majority on their Public Service Commission for the first time in 30 years.

What do Democrats’ wins mean for permitting?

As the U.S. Senate prepares for its drastically new makeup come January, it’s also got a major vote to tackle in the next few days. The chamber is planning to vote Nov. 9 on long-awaited energy permitting reform legislation — that is, if newly emboldened Democrats don’t try to reshape the bill.

While the package was crafted by two Democrats and two Republicans, some Congress members on the left have demanded edits to minimize its benefits for fossil fuels and prioritize clean energy development. They’ve renewed that call in the blue wave’s wake, with Rep. Jared Huffman (D-Calif.), who is likely to chair the House Natural Resources Committee in a Democrat-led Congress, saying that voters showed ​“they don’t want this dirty, fossil-fuel-expanding bill.” House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries (D) also called for revisions to the bill to protect tribal sovereignty and blunt impacts to the National Environmental Policy Act.

Bill co-sponsor Sen. Martin Heinrich (D-N.M.) contended that the election results revealed the opposite: Americans are focused on ​“affordability,” he wrote on X, and achieving that requires building more clean energy projects by passing the permitting bill.

CANARY CATCH-UP

More election results: Democrats are poised to take full control of six more state governments, giving them leverage to enact more ambitious clean-energy policies. Voters also approved a handful of clean energy–boosting ballot measures, and rejected some that would prop up fossil fuels and weaken environmental regulations. (Canary Media, Canary Media)

text:
Even before the midterm election results, Roth Capital’s Philip Shen, managing director and senior research analyst, had been hearing that the solar tax credit was still on the minds of many in Washington D.C.

“Our checks suggest that Republicans are open to extending the ITC and 45X. A contact that has insight into the GOP shared that, ‘we are moving into a positive political environment for solar,’” said Shen late this September

If solar was in a positive political environment in late September, then this November’s election creates the environment for tax credit reinstatements

The President has signed an extension before. In December 2020 he signed a two-year solar tax credit extension in 2020 as part of a COVID relief and government spending package.

Since the signing of the One Big Beautiful Bill (OBBB), at least seven federal pieces of legislation have been filed seeking to reinstate some or all of the Inflation Reduction Act’s (IRA) solar-related tax credits. None of these bills has had a committee hearing, and all of them expire when the 119th Congress ends on January 3, 2027, so anything that can be acted on would need to be refiled next year.

S. 2681, Lowering Electric Bills Act

H.R. 5862, American Energy Independence and Affordability Act

H.R. 6900, American Affordability Act of 2025

S. 3722, Lowering Home Energy Costs Act

H.R. 7977, Energy Bills Relief Act

S. 4175

H.R. 8477, American Energy Dominance Act

Each of the bills comes at the law in a slightly different manner, but most seek to simply reinstate the pre-existing language of the IRA. For instance, S. 2681, filed four weeks after the OBBB was signed, strikes the paragraphs that ended the residential credit after 2025 and cut off wind and solar projects placed in service after 2027, and puts the IRA’s emissions-based phaseout back in place. It leaves the rest of the OBBB alone.

H.R. 5862, and H.R. 6900 similarly restore the IRA. Filing S. 3722 revokes the OBBB as well, but only specifically focused on the residential tax credit.

H.R. 7977 goes further than most, getting rid of FEOC, and reinstating grant money, adds in a transmission tax credit, and goes after the administration’s executive orders regarding wind and solar.

It’s as if the OBBBA never existed.

H.R. 8477 – submitted by a Republican – also reinstates the tax credits, but doesn’t re-up electric vehicle tax credits or manufacturing credits.

Sen. Wyden’s S. 4175 reinstates the clean electricity credits, with some nuance. The credits would run until the later of 2032 or six years after any “price or demand increase year,” defined as a year in which the national average retail electricity price rises more than 2% or electricity sales rise. The residential credits would come back for two years after any such year.
